The dates clash, a common slip in clipped file titles. Either way, the Berkner thread ran on into 1958, long after the first panel had closed its work.
cia-0000015410: Air Force officers met CIA staff on April 5, 1958, to talk about the report of the Scientific Advisory Panel on flying objects. That panel had weighed saucer reports for the government a few years earlier. The meeting kept two services aligned on what the panel had found and what should be said. Little in the title hints at detail, and the record stays at that level.
cia-0000021510: Sightings of pilots are discussed in an untitled CIA record dated in 1967. The pilots in such files were usually Americans lost over Laos or Vietnam. Each rumored sighting raised hope that a missing man still lived. Staff had to weigh those rumors with care, since families waited on the same news and false hope carried its own cruelty.
cia-0000022810: A dead American pilot was sighted in Snuol District, in Kratie Province, Cambodia, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. Kratie sits on the Mekong River in the country's east. Pilots fell across Cambodia as the air war spread past Vietnam's borders. A sighting of the dead there added one more place to the map of loss the offices kept.

The heading can also be read as the aftermath for Trujillo's assassin, and the catalog leaves it tangled. Rafael Trujillo, the Dominican strongman, was in fact killed in 1961. Either reading places the entry in the long shadow of that shooting and its reprisals.
cia-0000039010:
A Honduran party urged that President Azcona face trial over killings in the Matta affair, a CIA record dated March 6, 1988 reports. The call came from the Revolutionary party named in the title. Honduras was then a key base in the region's wider conflicts.

The record preserves a political demand: a sitting president put on trial. Such demands showed how killings and drug-era scandals shook Honduran public life. The file captures a moment when opposition parties used the language of the courts. Their target was a sitting president. Honduras was caught between its own politics and the wars around it.
cia-0000042810:

Inside, the suspects are identified as the president announced them. Naming soldiers broke the army's long shield of silence. It also bound Cristiani's own standing to the case's outcome. The file preserves the moment the accusation became official. The accused were no longer a rumor in the press. They were names spoken aloud by their own commander in chief.
cia-0000045210:

Inside, the rebels' account of the government's split is preserved. Exposing an enemy's quarrels is a classic aim of wartime radio. True or stretched, the story served the guerrillas' daily campaign. cia-0000049010: A CIA item from 1981 names individuals assassinated by unidentified killers in El Salvador. The list form is the point: victim after victim, each with a name, each killer unknown. cia-0000049110: American support for the embassy's work on the Sheraton murder case is recorded in a CIA item from 1985. cia-0000049310: El Salvador: Growing Rightist Dominance is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000049310, dated October 6, 1980, and marked for the Truth Commission. It stands as an early agency reading of Salvadoran politics, kept in the declassified record under its original subject line.
cia-0000049410: Duarte's first hundred days in El Salvador are assessed in declassified CIA document 0000049410, dated August 5, 1984. It is a brief declassified review item whose heading frames a standard early-term check on a Salvadoran leader.
cia-0000095210: A cable to Leopoldville about eliminating Lumumba from governmental positions in Leopoldville, in the heading's shortened place wording, is declassified CIA document 0000095210, dated August 6, 1960. cia-0000117910: Shipping to Cambodia in the Third Quarter of 1968 is the subject, with its publication date an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000117910, dated November 1, 1968. The heading tracks shipping to one country in one quarter of one year. Third quarter is the time frame stated in the title itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note with the subject as released.
cia-0000119210:
In June 1985 the CIA set down its requirements and reporting rules for the prisoner and missing mission. The paper covers what collectors had to gather and how findings moved back up the chain. Routine as it sounds, this paperwork kept a far-flung search organized.

Requirements documents tell historians how the work was actually structured. They show what questions Washington wanted answered about the missing and how often answers were due. Read beside field reports, this one explains the system that produced them. That system kept the cases of missing Americans active a decade after the war in Southeast Asia had ended.
cia-0000119710:
Dated February 1954, this CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Bolivia. The revolution of 1952 had brought the MNR party to power, with land reform and mine nationalization in its train. Washington watched the experiment with open unease.

The paper assesses where the Bolivian revolution might go next and what risks it posed. Bolivia was a test of whether a poor, landlocked country could remake itself without falling under communist sway. For readers, the forecast records the agency's early judgment on one of Latin America's deepest social upheavals. It was written while the revolution's own leaders were still deciding how far it should run.
cia-0000124310: A July 1951 CIA document covers North Korean treatment of prisoners at Manpojin. The northern camps ranked among the Korean War's grimmest stories, and Manpojin sat near the Yalu River, far from witnesses. The paper records the treatment there as it was reported to the agency. Manpojin lay in the far north near the Chinese border, a place whose distance from the front made outside checks on camp conditions nearly impossible then.
cia-0000126910: Dated around June 1963, this CIA record is a presentation prepared for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the nation's top military officers. It concerns July 30 of a year the heading leaves unfinished. The agency briefed the chiefs face to face, and the paper preserves that briefing. Briefings to the chiefs joined the agency's picture to military planning at the highest level, the setting this formal record was made for.
cia-0000132310:
Released CBS newsmen lead the political news in Situation Report 620. The report belongs to the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series and is dated February 6, 1991. Its headline word breaks off at releas, but the sense is clear. Journalists caught inside the war zone had become bargaining chips in the conflict.

The report covers their release as one item in the daily political picture. Foreign reporters detained during the crisis drew wide attention back home. Their fate was followed by editors, families, and governments at once. For readers, the entry shows how even a press story entered the same reporting stream as battles and diplomacy during the war.
cia-0000132410: The Caribbean through the end of 1959 is the subject of a CIA report dated May 2, 1959. Written at mid-year, the report projects how the region's troubles would run through December. Castro's Cuba dominates its forecasts, as it dominated most agency thinking that year. The short report preserves what analysts expected the Caribbean to become before the year had even half run its course.
cia-0000132510: A third CIA paper on Cuba carries the busy date February 4, 1961. That winter the agency issued Cuba updates at a near-daily pace, and the Bay of Pigs landing was still two months off. The briefing's value lies partly in that tempo: it is one frame from a fast-moving film of reports. The declassified text comes from the CIA Reading Room, mirrored by the Internet Archive.
cia-0000132610: Fresh anti-American speeches by the Castro brothers fill item 13 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 1, 1960. The headline calls the speeches harangues, the agency's chosen word for a Castro tirade. Fidel and Raul were taking turns attacking Washington in public that summer. The short item reports the latest speeches and their themes.
cia-0000135910: The CIA planning paper of 5 May 1954 is about the K Program in general and one deleted item in detail, and it survives in declassified form. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136110: A declassified CIA situation report dated 2 April 1954 turns to the situation report for the week of 26 April to 3 May, filed under an April date. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136210: A cable dated 1 May 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on the arrival of Langvin at Somerset, a coded place greeting a traveling officer in May. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136310: Radio reports from 0800 to 1400 on 25 June 1954 fill this LINCOLN summary. Mendoza reported enemy heavy guns near the Chiquimula road. He urged that the gun sites be bombed. He then said 1,500 men at Cumbre Ingeniero would attack the town. Castillo gave a mixed report through another operator. He said all Chiquimula was under control. But he feared a strong counterattack after hand-to-hand fighting.
cia-0000136610: Dated only to 1961 in the catalog, with that year marked as estimated, this Spanish text comes from the 2506 Brigade papers. An earlier summary described London and Washington coordinating a war against Hitler; that belongs to another era and is dropped. The brigade was the CIA's exile force, and 1961 was its year of action. The document survives in Spanish in the declassified release, its month and subject not recorded.
cia-0000136710: An estimated date of 1 January 1961 heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, flagged as estimated in the catalog title. The brigade was the CIA-trained force of Cuban exiles preparing for the Bay of Pigs. The record states no subject for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, grouped with the many brigade documents placed at the start of 1961.
cia-0000136910: Two thousand tons is the total amount of the shipment, LINCOLN is told in this April 1954 cable, confirming facts from a telephone conversation. Five flat cars and two box cars already loaded had departed the port for the capital city. Headquarters comments that an estimated 200 to 500 tons could move in those cars, so the field should have several targets. The information also gives extreme importance to pressing the effort to get evidence requested earlier.
cia-0000137010: Delay is the message in this June 1954 cable to the Guatemala City station about contacting the British. Holland has been tied up on the Hill and a merchant is out of town; last night Holland and a representative met, both aware of the matter's significance. Today or later he will take the matter up with the British, at least persuade them to get off their high horse. The station should circulate calm order for a few more days and let the matter percolate through the junta.
cia-0000137310: Dated 1960, NSC Briefing — Cuba is a declassified CIA paper prepared for the National Security Council. Briefings of this kind gave the president's senior advisers a shared, current picture; this one's subject, by its title, was Cuba during the year of rupture with Castro's government. The catalog records no specific topics for it, and several sibling briefings with the same title and year are held in these files. It survives as released through the CIA Reading Room, one installment in a standing briefing series.
cia-0000137410: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade collection, dated only to 1961 in the catalog record. An earlier summary described London and Washington coordinating a war effort against Hitler; that is Second World War material, unsupported by this record, and it is removed. The document is a Spanish record of the CIA's Cuban exile brigade from 1961, the year of the Bay of Pigs, released in the declassified files with no subject stated.
cia-03153710: September 4, 1957: the daily bulletin reached senior officials. The intelligence summary covered the world's developments. The Cold War's Labor Week reading. It awaits future readers. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
conrad-secret-sharer-1910:
Joseph Conrad wrote The Secret Sharer in late 1909, drawing on an old story from his own years at sea. The novella was published in 1910. Conrad had been a merchant sailor for twenty years before he turned to fiction, and the sea fills this tale.

A young captain, new to his ship, finds a naked swimmer clinging to the ladder at night. The man, Leggatt, has killed a sailor on his own ship and fled. The captain hides him in his cabin for days, risking his command. The two men mirror each other so closely that helping the fugitive escape feels like saving himself.
constitution-angola-2010: Angola's 2010 Constitution built its republic after civil war. It sets a strong presidency. The Tower library holds the full text. It ordered a new peace. War ended. Law began. State rose. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-djibouti-2010: Djibouti's 2010 Constitution, amended that year, frames its republic. It kept strong rule. The Tower library holds the full text. It guarded a strait. Ships passed. Power held. Law stood. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-guinea-2010: Guinea's 2010 Constitution framed its return to civilian rule. It set elections. The Tower library holds the full text. It ended junta years. Soldiers left. Ballots came. Hope rose. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-kenya-2010: Kenya's 2010 Constitution, passed by referendum, devolved its state. Counties gained power. The Tower library holds the full text. It shared the savanna. Center yielded. Counties rose. Votes spread. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-madagascar-2010: Madagascar's 2010 Constitution, passed by referendum, frames its republic. It followed a coup. The Tower library holds the full text. It reset the isle. Soldiers left. Votes came. Lemurs watched. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cox-fearsome-creatures-of-the-lumberwood:
William Cox prints the tall tales of the north woods in Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, his book of 1910. Cox was a state guard of woods in Minnesota. Loggers there told of beasts no book of life lists: the hodag, the squonk that weeps its self to tears, the hidebehind that no eye can catch. Cox sets each down with mock grave care and fine draws by Coert Du Bois.

The tone is dry wit in a field guide's dress. The book saves a whole folk lore that was close to lost. It is the root text of that lore.
crabbe-borough-1810:
George Crabbe, who lived from 1754 to 1832, shaped The Borough in 1810 as a set of verse letters. Each letter paints part of a Suffolk seaport town and the people who live and work there. The first letter gives a broad view of the river, the quay, the shipping, and the shipyards.

Fishermen, smugglers, the poor, the pious, and the proud all pass through his steady portraits. Crabbe refused the soft glow of pastoral verse and showed hard labor and hard winters as they were. That plain truth, told with real pity, is why many readers call The Borough his finest work.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-10:
The tenth number of The Equinox, from September 1913, closes the journal's first volume. Ten fat numbers in five years had made it the great record of Crowley's school. The autumn issue ends a run that began in the spring of 1909.

Across the volume, the rites and holy books of Thelema saw print for the first time. The set forms one work: the founding archive of a new creed of magic. War would soon break the journal's pace and scatter its whole world. Volume one stands complete, a monument of its strange age. Nothing like it had been seen in English occult print before.
dewey-how-we-think-1910:
John Dewey published How We Think in 1910, a classic study of reflective thought. Dewey describes the steps of real thinking: a felt problem, clear definition, suggested solutions, testing by reason, and checking by action. He borrows this pattern from the scientific method. Teachers, he argues, should train this habit above all.

The book applies the method to lessons, language, and the training of judgment. Dewey warns against rote learning and hasty belief. Later editions kept the work in use for decades. Educators still cite its five steps. It is a clear, practical book by America's leading philosopher of education.
digha-nikaya-rhys-davids-1910: Volume two of the Dialogues of the Buddha, continuing the Digha Nikaya translation. More of the Buddha's long discourses on ethics and meditation. This edition preserves those ancient teachings. Those who study the era will use it.
doj-amerithrax-investigative-summary-201:
The Justice Department released this investigative summary on February 19, 2010, closing the Amerithrax case. Amerithrax was the FBI's investigation of the 2001 anthrax letter attacks, which killed five people and sickened seventeen in the weeks after September 11. The summary is the Bureau's complete public account.

It lays out the science that traced the mailed spores to a flask in the lab of Bruce Ivins, an Army researcher at Fort Detrick. It follows the suspects cleared along the way, above all Steven Hatfill, and builds the case against Ivins, who died by suicide in 2008 before charges. The report remains the key public record of the probe.
dunsany-dreamers-tales-1910:
Dream is the home country of Dunsany's tales of 1910. A Dreamer's Tales moves between the waking world and the lands past the fields we know. The book is the high-water mark of his early manner.

Sailors, kings, and wanderers cross to cities of dream and pay the full price of the crossing. Lovecraft and a host of others took the jeweled style for their own model of wonder. The prose glows with a light that is not the sun's own light. These are the tales by which Dunsany's early fame still stands today, undimmed by the years.
edgar-great-pyramid-passages-and-chamber:
John Edgar and Morton Edgar were Scots kin who gave years to the Great Pyramid. Book one of The Great Pyramid Passages and Chambers came out in 1910. The pair shot photos and took counts of each hall and shaft. Their work ran from 1910 to 1913 in the field.

Fine plates show the King's Chamber, the Grand Gallery, and the deep shafts. The Edgars set their counts by the work of Flinders Petrie, the great dig man. They read the counts as a tale of time and faith, not just stone. The book is the most full count of the halls since Petrie.
ehrlich-collected-studies-immunity-vol2-:
Paul Ehrlich won wide fame for his work on immunity and for the first drug made to target a single disease germ. Charles Bolduan translated this second volume of his studies into English. It appeared in 1910 as part of the second edition of the set.

In his preface Ehrlich says the volume gathers most of his recent immunity studies with his collaborators. The papers measure toxins and antitoxins with great care, building what he called quantitative serology. He argues his theory rests on a huge mass of experimental data. The volume completes a core record of early immunology.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-10: Volume ten gathers essays of Montaigne's middle period. He writes of idleness, liars, and the quiet uses of solitude and rest. The tone is relaxed, confiding, and full of charm. A wise man thoroughly enjoying his own company.
europmc-pmc10225110:
Guan, He, and Xu review recent progress and future prospects in gastric cancer treatment in a 2023 paper. Gastric, or stomach, cancer is among the most common cancers worldwide. Most patients are found at a late stage, because early symptoms are vague and screening is rare in many countries.

The review covers the main systemic treatments: chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immune therapy. It explains which patients gain from each approach and how biomarkers guide the choice. It closes with trials and ideas that may improve the still poor outlook for advanced disease.
europmc-pmc10240810:
Yang and colleagues review amino acid metabolism in immune cells in a 2023 paper. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, and immune cells consume them in large amounts when they respond to threats. Inside tumors, cancer and immune cells compete for the same supply, which can blunt the immune attack.

The review explains how amino acid use steers what immune cells can do. It shows how tumors exploit that dependence to evade destruction. It then surveys ways to retune the supply so that immune therapy against cancer works better.
europmc-pmc10481210:
Rao and colleagues tested ChatGPT across a full run of clinical work in 2023. ChatGPT is a chat tool trained on vast text sets. Past tests gave it single questions, not linked chains of choices. Real care needs step-by-step thought, like a doctor at work. The team fed it 36 standard case stories from a clinical manual.

Each case asked for likely diagnoses, tests, a final call, and a care plan. Human scorers marked each reply. Rao reports an overall score of 71.7% across all cases. Final diagnosis scored best, at 76.9%. The first list of likely causes scored worst, at 60.3%. Scores rose as the tool gained more case facts.
europmc-pmc10499610:
Zhang and a large team gave an algorithm in 2023 that designs better mRNA for vaccines. mRNA is a message strip that tells cells to build a target protein. Such messages break down fast, which hurts storage and strength of a vaccine. A tighter fold and smart word choice in the code can slow that decay.

The snag is scale: the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 allows a vast sea of code variants. Their tool, LinearDesign, borrows a trick from language parsing to search that sea. It found a top design for the spike in just 11 minutes. Zhang reports far longer message life and more protein made. Antibody levels in mice rose up to 128-fold over a standard design.
europmc-pmc10533410:
Wang and a large team asked in 2023 what marks tumours that respond to immune therapy in triple-negative breast cancer. Some patients gain from checkpoint drugs, which free immune cells to attack. Others gain nothing, and no firm test split the two groups. The team mapped proteins in place inside tumours from a trial.

They read 43 proteins in tumour samples taken before, during, and after therapy. Two shares stood out as top predictors of response. Wang names growing CD8 T cells with a TCF1 mark, and cancer cells that show MHCII. On therapy, tumours that responded filled with a killer T cell type. Tumours that resisted showed CD15-marked cancer cells. Early biopsies may help steer care as it unfolds.
europmc-pmc11609310:
Ma and colleagues review liquid biopsy for cancer detection and monitoring in this 2024 paper. Tissue biopsy, cutting a tumour sample, remains the gold standard for diagnosis, with stable samples and high accuracy. It is also invasive and limited for repeated checks. Liquid biopsy reads tumour signals from blood and other fluids instead.

Its advantages include being non-invasive and quick, the authors note. Components now assayed include circulating tumour cells, circulating tumour DNA, exosomes, microRNA, other circulating RNA, tumour platelets, and tumour endothelial cells. The review covers the current status of each marker class for early diagnosis and prognosis. Challenges include low signal levels in early disease and lack of standardisation. Future prospects are mapped, with the field described as undergoing rapid progress.
europmc-pmc1183210:
Galperin took a 2005 census of signal proteins in bacteria and archaea. These proteins sense the world and pass messages inside the cell. Parasites in stable homes tend to carry simple signal kits. Free-living microbes in changing places carry far richer kits.

The census covered 167 complete genomes checked by hand. It counted sensor kinases, chemotaxis receptors, and related switch proteins. Larger genomes held many more signal proteins, roughly with the square of size. Galperin calls this spread a kind of bacterial IQ. The catalog helps compare how microbes read their surroundings.
europmc-pmc1215510:
Ryan, Barry, Murphy, and Mahon explored a puzzle about stem cells in 2005. Mesenchymal stem cells come from adult bone marrow. They can help rebuild cartilage, bone, muscle, and tendons. Normal immune rules should reject cells from another person.

In practice, these stem cells often avoid rejection. Lab dish studies back that pattern. The cells show few alarm flags to the immune system. They also calm killer cells and reshape nearby immune activity. Ryan compares this tolerance to how a mother tolerates a fetus. The trait could make donor cell therapy far simpler.
europmc-pmc1560110:
A small score change on a health survey can mean two unlike things. de Vet and co-authors untangled them in 2006. One is the smallest change a tool can reliably detect, beyond noise. The other is the smallest change patients count as important.

Methods that use score spread alone tend to find the detectable change. Methods anchored to patient judgment find the important change. de Vet argues the two should not be merged into one number. Knowing both tells clinics whether a tool is sharp enough to catch changes that matter. Anchor-based methods, they say, deserve preference for importance.
europmc-pmc1637810:
When a child meets a chemical can matter as much as how much. Selevan, Kimmel, and Mendola compiled what was known in 2000 about critical windows of exposure, from before conception through adolescence. A workshop weighed evidence for five body areas.

Broad windows of sensitivity exist for the breathing, reproductive, nervous, and hormone systems, and for cancer. But detailed data stay thin. Comparing dose at the target tissue across species needs work. The panel also flagged neglected topics: exposures around puberty, adult effects of early exposure, and gene-environment interplay. Selevan argues window data sharpen risk assessment and protect the most sensitive ages.
europmc-pmc1769410:
Smoke and indoor air pollution raise tuberculosis risk, a pooled analysis confirms. Lin, Ezzati, and Murray reviewed observational studies in 2007: 33 papers on smoking, five on passive smoke, and five on indoor pollution from biomass fuels.

Smokers faced higher risk of a positive TB skin test, of active disease, and of dying from TB. Passive smoke and biomass smoke also pointed to higher disease risk, though on thinner evidence. The exposures persist or grow exactly where TB burden is highest. Lin suggests TB control programs add tobacco and indoor air measures to their plans.
europmc-pmc1820610:
Hua, Krainer and co-authors tested in 2007 a drug-like approach for spinal muscular atrophy, a genetic disease that weakens muscles. Patients lack a working SMN1 gene, and the backup gene SMN2 usually skips a segment called exon 7 when its RNA is spliced. Keeping that exon in would yield more full-length protective protein.

The team built many short antisense oligonucleotides, synthetic strands that bind RNA, aimed across exon 7 of SMN2. Such strands usually cause skipping, but several of theirs boosted exon inclusion instead. Others promoted skipping or gave mixed effects, mapping which exon spots help or hinder inclusion. In cultured cells the best strands raised full-length SMN protein without blocking RNA export or protein making. Some were strong enough to advance into mouse model tests.
europmc-pmc1852410:
Gupta, Bailey, Noble and colleagues presented Tomtom in 2007, a tool that measures how alike two sequence motifs are. A motif here is a table of letter probabilities for a short DNA or protein pattern, such as a protein binding site. Discovery programs produce many motifs, and databases hold many more, yet no sound score compared them.

Tomtom fills that gap with a statistical measure of motif-to-motif similarity. It lets a researcher search a motif database with a newly found motif as the query. That check reveals whether the pattern is already known or genuinely new. The method also supports comparing protein motifs, not just DNA ones. By giving similarity a proper significance value, Tomtom turns a shelf of separate motif collections into a single searchable resource.
europmc-pmc1931610:
Lenoir, Serre and Ahmed reported in 2007 that rats choose intense sweetness over cocaine when given a free choice. Sweetened diets are often compared to addictive drugs, and both share brain reward pathways. How the two rewards stack up head to head was unknown.

Rats chose between saccharin-sweetened water, which has sweetness without calories, and intravenous cocaine. A large majority, 94 percent, picked the sweet water. The same held for sucrose, natural table sugar, so the effect is not an artifact of an artificial sweetener. Raising the cocaine dose did not flip the choice. The preference also survived cocaine intoxication, sensitization, and escalating intake, all hallmarks of addiction. In this setup, sweet taste outranks a potent drug reward for nearly every animal.
europmc-pmc2025310:
Peto and colleagues set out in 1977 how to analyse long-running randomised clinical trials. Part one had covered trial design. Part two covers comparing survival time, or time until another bad event, between treatment groups. The intended readers were doctors without statistical training. The authors wanted them to analyse such data themselves, or judge published analyses more sharply.

Their toolkit centres on life tables, which track survival over time in steps. It also uses the logrank test to compare whole survival curves between groups. Retrospective stratification, grouping patients after the fact by risk factors, refines the comparison. The authors explain how prognostic factors should and should not be used. Worked examples show each method in practice.
europmc-pmc2124710: A medical paper on the pathological anatomy of the pancreas in ninety diabetes cases. The diabetic organ. This article preserves that pathology. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2124810: A medical paper on a transmissible avian neoplasm, sarcoma of the common fowl. The chicken cancer. This article preserves that oncology research. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2125010: A medical paper on the relation of the spleen to blood destruction and regeneration. The spleen once more. This article preserves that hematology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125210: A medical paper on the production of methemoglobin by pneumococci. The brown blood. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2128510: Newborns drink protection with their first milk, and this paper traced how colostrum or serum put antibodies into the blood. The researchers linked feeding to immunity's appearance. The first milk's shield, measured. The article preserves that immunology research.
europmc-pmc2128610: A medical paper with studies based on a malignant tumor of the rabbit, variations in growth. The rabbit cancer's moods. This article preserves that oncology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2222610:
Petrus and co-workers showed in 2007 that blocking an ion channel called TRPA1 reverses mechanical hyperalgesia, an exaggerated pain response to pressure. TRPA1 senses pungent chemicals and may detect harmful mechanical and cold stimuli. Its role in sensitised pain was unsettled. The team developed a specific small-molecule blocker, AP18, and tested it in mice with inflammation caused by complete Freund's adjuvant, a standard pain model.

AP18 reduced pain behaviour triggered by cinnamaldehyde, a TRPA1 activator. It also reversed the inflammation-induced mechanical hyperalgesia in normal mice. In mice genetically lacking TRPA1, hyperalgesia developed normally, yet AP18 had no effect there, proving the drug acts on target. The authors infer that TRPA1 helps sensitise pain, and that lifelong knockout mice compensate in ways that mask that role.
europmc-pmc2235210:
Jusko and co-workers followed children in 2008 to test whether low blood lead levels harm intelligence. The official threshold for elevated lead was 10 micrograms per decilitre, but effects below it were disputed. The team measured blood lead eight times from six months to six years of age. At age six, 194 children took a standard preschool intelligence test. Models adjusted for maternal IQ, home environment and other confounders.

Lifetime average lead, with a mean of 7.2 micrograms per decilitre, linked inversely to full-scale and performance IQ. Those associations were statistically significant in the adjusted models. The cohort consisted of young children. Children averaging 5 to 9.9 scored 4.9 points lower than those under five. Peak lead levels linked to lower IQ down to 2.1, the lowest peak observed. The authors conclude impairment occurs well below the official threshold.
europmc-pmc2289810:
de Groot and co-workers validated the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, in its Dutch version, in 2008. This questionnaire, built in Sweden, measures patients' own view of knee problems and had been validated in several languages, but not Dutch. The team translated it by a standard procedure, then tested it in patients with mild, moderate and severe osteoarthritis, and in patients after first or revision knee replacement surgery.

Internal consistency exceeded 0.70 on all subscales in every patient group. Repeat-test reliability also exceeded 0.70 for mild and moderate osteoarthritis and revision groups. At least sixty percent of predicted relationships with other measures held for mild, moderate and primary replacement groups. For severe and revision patients, under forty-five percent held. Ceiling and floor effects appeared in some groups. The score suits mild-to-moderate disease best.
europmc-pmc2323710: A biology paper on photosynthesis as a function of light intensity and temperature. The light-fed plants. This article preserves that botany. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2363610:
Jenkins, Fallowfield, and Saul asked over two thousand UK cancer patients how much they wanted to know in 2001. The survey ran inside a bigger study of communication training for cancer doctors. Some clinicians still held back bad news, assuming many patients prefer not to hear details.

In total 2,331 patients answered. A striking 87% wanted all possible information, good and bad, and 98% wanted to know whether their illness was cancer or not. Only 58 of 440 patients in one subgroup preferred to leave details to the doctor, and they tended to be over 70. Even they still wanted specific facts. Women more than men wanted the exact name of the illness and every treatment option listed. The authors called withholding information on preference grounds untenable after these results.
europmc-pmc2543010:
Montazeri reviewed three decades of research in 2008 on quality of life among women treated for breast cancer. The term covers how patients feel and function day to day. It had grown into a major outcome in cancer care. He searched English-language journals from 1974 to 2007 and examined 477 full papers after screening out meeting abstracts, letters, and duplicates.

Two questionnaire families dominated measurement: the European EORTC scales and the FACIT scales, each with a breast cancer module. Different operations gave broadly similar quality of life, though mastectomy patients reported worse body image and sexual functioning than breast-conserving patients. Chemotherapy brought side effects that dragged quality of life down. In advanced disease, quality of life scores also predicted how long patients survived, and anxiety and depression stayed common years after diagnosis.
europmc-pmc2633610:
Sánchez-Vargas and co-authors asked in 2009 how the mosquito Aedes aegypti fights off dengue virus type 2, the virus it passes to people. Their focus was RNA interference, a defense in which the cell chops viral genetic material into tiny pieces and uses them to destroy matching viral messages.

In infected mosquito cells and in live adult mosquitoes, the virus did trigger this defense. Small virus-specific RNA pieces appeared, yet the virus still copied itself and spread. When the team blocked key defense genes named dcr2, r2d2, and ago2, the virus grew even faster. It also needed less time inside the mosquito before it could be passed on. The defense thus slows dengue, even though the virus partly slips past it.
europmc-pmc2642810:
Fisher-Wellman and Bloomer reviewed in 2009 thirty years of research on exercise and oxidative stress, the strain placed on the body by reactive oxygen molecules. Close to 300 studies had appeared since the first work in 1978. A single hard workout, whether endurance or sprint based, was known to raise this strain for a short time.

Across the studies, the size of the rise depended on the type of exercise, its intensity, and how long it lasted. Who was tested mattered too, as did any antioxidant pills they took. The authors note a twist: the brief rise seems to be a useful signal. It prompts the body to strengthen its own antioxidant defenses over time, a pattern known as hormesis. Short-term strain, in this view, trains long-term protection.
europmc-pmc2654510:
Ma and colleagues watched in 2009 how the germ Pseudomonas aeruginosa builds the glue that holds its biofilms together. Biofilms are city-like clusters of bacteria stuck to a surface, hard for drugs and immune cells to clear. This germ's clusters cause stubborn infections, especially in the lungs.

The team colored one glue ingredient, a sugar chain called Psl, and filmed it as clusters grew. On single cells the sugar wrapped in a spiral pattern that helped cells stick to each other and to the surface. Pulling the sugar off with chemicals broke the cluster apart. As clusters matured, the sugar gathered at the edges, leaving a hollow center. Swimming cells later appeared in that hollow, ready to spread. Dead cells and loose DNA filled the same space, and genes controlling cell death shaped the whole layout.
europmc-pmc2687710:
Ma and co-authors profiled in 2009 how the tissue around a breast tumor changes as the cancer advances, not just the tumor cells themselves. The stroma, the supporting tissue, is now known to feed and shape tumors. The team used a laser to snip pure samples of tumor and stroma from fourteen patients, each matched across normal, preinvasive, and invasive stages.

Stroma changed its gene activity as extensively as the cancer cells did, starting before invasion. Tumor-linked stroma turned up genes for scaffolding material, for cutting enzymes that clear paths, and for cell division. The step into invasion brought a fresh rise in three cutting enzymes, MMP2, MMP11, and MMP14. Even tumor grade, the pathologist's measure of aggression, left a readable signature in stroma, rich in immune genes for high-grade tumors. The surroundings, the authors conclude, are a partner in the crime from its earliest stage.
europmc-pmc2707010:
Liberati and co-authors published in 2009 the explanation for PRISMA, a set of rules for reporting systematic reviews and pooled analyses of health studies. A systematic review gathers all studies that fit set rules to answer one question. Poor reporting had often left out key facts, which made reviews hard to judge or reuse.

As an update to the older QUOROM guidance from 1999, the text walks through each PRISMA item and shows what good reporting looks like. It stresses clear notes on what was planned, what was done, and what was found, plus any changes to the plan. The goal is full, open reporting that lets readers weigh strengths and flaws for themselves.
europmc-pmc2781110:
Ramsköld, Wang, Burge, and Sandberg analyzed in 2009 deep RNA sequencing data across human and mouse tissues to map which genes each tissue uses. The set of active genes in a tissue reflects the jobs it performs. Their gene-level survey asked how many genes run everywhere, as housekeeping, and how tissues differ beyond that core.

Roughly eight thousand protein-coding genes were switched on in every tissue. Together they supplied about three quarters of all message copies in most tissues. These core genes mostly made intracellular proteins for metabolism, transcription, RNA handling, and translation. Genes for secreted or surface proteins, by contrast, ran in only some tissues. Expression levels formed one broad continuum, with no sign of separate expression classes. Muscle and liver ran the simplest programs, while brain, kidney, and testis ran the most complex.
europmc-pmc2816710:
Larsen and colleagues compared gut bacteria in 2010 between men with type 2 diabetes and men without it. Hints from animal work tied gut communities to weight and blood sugar control, but human diabetes data were thin. Their study covered thirty-six adult men with wide ranges of age and body size, eighteen of them diabetic.

Diabetic men carried smaller shares of one major bacterial phylum, Firmicutes, and of its class Clostridia. The balance between two big groups tracked blood sugar levels closely, yet showed no tie to body mass. Another class, Betaproteobacteria, ran higher in diabetic men and also rose with blood sugar. The authors say sugar control, not weight alone, should frame future gut studies.
europmc-pmc2821410:
Ghosh, McBurney, and Robbins showed in 2010 that SIRT1 puts a brake on a major growth pathway called mTOR. SIRT1 is an enzyme tied to calorie restriction and longer life in model animals. The mTOR pathway senses nutrients and stress and drives cell growth, and its role in aging made any new brake worth finding.

Cells lacking SIRT1 ran mTOR signaling high, and stress could not switch it off. A SIRT1 activator, resveratrol, lowered mTOR activity, while a SIRT1 blocker raised it, and both effects vanished without SIRT1. The team found SIRT1 binds TSC2, part of a complex that restrains mTOR, and the brake failed when TSC2 was missing. The work ties two aging pathways together through one contact point.
europmc-pmc2873910:
Mefford and a large consortium searched in 2010 for missing or extra DNA chunks behind unexplained epilepsy. Epilepsy affects about one in a hundred people, yet most cases have no known genetic cause. Such chunks, called copy number variants, were already tied to autism and intellectual disability, so the team scanned five hundred seventeen people with epilepsy that showed no lesion on scans.

Rare gene-bearing chunks appeared in about nine in a hundred patients and were absent from nearly twenty-five hundred controls. A few patients carried two rare chunks at once. Some chunks removed genes already linked to other brain development disorders, including one tied to autism-related traits. Rare chunk changes look like one shared root across several brain conditions, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc2890410:
Ahmed, Creanga, Gillespie, and Tsui examined in 2010 how women's wealth, schooling, and say in decisions shape use of maternal health care. They call those three factors the three Es. The analysis spans the developing world. They pooled the most recent national household surveys from thirty-one countries. Separate models tracked modern contraceptive use, antenatal care, and having a skilled attendant at birth.

All three Es pushed service use upward in most countries. The gaps were stark: women in the poorest fifth of households had odds of a skilled birth attendant more than nine tenths lower than women in the richest fifth. Completing primary school alone multiplied those odds several fold. Raising quality and access will underdeliver, the authors argue, unless women's economic and social position rises too.
europmc-pmc2903510:
Jordan and colleagues counted in 2010 how often people consult British general practitioners for regional aches like back, neck, and knee pain. Such problems hide under thousands of different record codes, so four doctors first sorted nearly six thousand codes by body region. The team then extracted a full year of consultations from twelve practices into a research database.

One in seven of all recorded consultations concerned a muscle or joint problem. The back led by far, with about five hundred ninety-one people per ten thousand consulting yearly, and the knee came second at roughly three hundred twenty-four. In children the foot topped the list instead. Women and older adults consulted more for most regions, giving planners a firm denominator for services.
europmc-pmc2942810:
Kooij led a European expert network in a 2010 consensus statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults. The childhood condition carries into adult life in most cases, yet adult services across Europe lacked skill and facilities for it.

Drawing on research and clinical experience from eighteen countries, the statement covers the biology of the disorder. It then answers three questions. How does adult ADHD look, how should it be diagnosed, and how should it be treated? The authors warn that the condition stays under-recognised and undertreated, raising illness costs. They call for better training and proper screening tools in psychiatry.
europmc-pmc2946910:
Huynh-Thu and colleagues presented GENIE3, a method for rebuilding gene control networks from expression data, in a 2010 article. Working out which genes switch which others on or off from large datasets is a core problem in systems biology.

GENIE3 splits the puzzle into one prediction task per gene, using tree-based ensemble methods to forecast each gene's activity from all others. Genes that help most in a forecast are scored as likely regulators, and the scores combine into a ranked network. The method topped a major simulation challenge and compared well against rivals on real data from the bacterium Escherichia coli.
europmc-pmc3012610:
Goldstone and co-authors catalogued the full set of cytochrome P450 genes in zebrafish in a 2010 study, a family of enzymes that transform drugs, poisons, and the body's own signals. Zebrafish were rising fast in drug discovery and toxicology, so their enzyme roster mattered.

The fish carry ninety-four such genes in eighteen families shared with mammals. Many match human genes handling hormones and regulatory molecules one to one, with matching chemistry confirmed for several. The drug and pollutant families are far more tangled, with extra fish copies. Developmental tracking showed when each gene switches on as embryos grow.
europmc-pmc3048210:
Yokota and colleagues reported in 2011 that one gene mutation marks a far worse outlook in advanced colon and rectal cancer. The team typed tumors from more than two hundred patients receiving chemotherapy for advanced or returning disease. Two related genes were checked, since both can lock a growth pathway on and blunt the effect of targeted drugs.

Tumors carrying the rarer mutation, in the BRAF gene, clustered on the right side of the colon and spread to the belly lining more often. Patients with that mutation lived far shorter on average than patients whose tumors carried neither mutation. After adjusting for other factors, the mutation remained one of the strongest predictors of poor survival. A specific change in the partner gene also trended toward worse outcomes. The authors say mutation typing should guide prognosis talks and treatment planning.
europmc-pmc3055910:
Erickson gathered in 2009 a practical guide to judging the size and shape of protein molecules, the tiny machines of the cell. Three classic methods are covered: how fast proteins sink in a spinning tube, how they filter through gel beads, and how they look in electron microscope images. The review collects simple calculations for turning those measurements into structural sense at the nanometer scale.

One popular equation for shape is shown to mislead and is set aside for a simpler check that flags whether a protein is round or stretched out. Gel filtering, he reminds readers, sorts by effective radius, not by weight, though pairing it with sinking speed yields weight. Microscope methods that shadow or stain single molecules resolve shapes directly. Combined, these bench methods give a medium detail picture of proteins too small or flexible for crystallography.
europmc-pmc3102710:
Decroly and coauthors solved in 2011 the three dimensional structure of a two protein machine that the SARS coronavirus uses to cap its RNA, a step its copying machinery requires. The cap finisher, nsp16, works only when its partner, nsp10, is attached. The team crystallized the pair together, with and without a blocking compound, and mapped the contact surface in detail.

The partner grips a broad patch and switches the finisher into its working shape. Functional tests pinpointed the residues that hold the pair together, grip the RNA, and perform the chemical step, apparently by a direct hand off mechanism. A single letter change in the partner tightened the embrace and sharpened the picture further. Because human capping uses different machinery, the viral complex is an attractive drug target. The structures show exactly where a blocking drug could sit.
europmc-pmc3116910:
Jonas Warringer and colleagues mapped natural trait differences in yeast for a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Yeast is a workhorse of genetics, yet how its wild strains differ in behaviour, and why, was poorly charted. The team measured many traits across the common yeast and its closest wild relatives and traced the history behind the patterns.

Farmed and wild yeast strains differed more in traits than their modest genetic differences would suggest, and trait patterns followed population history rather than local habitat. One West African group stood out as weak on many traits, including a broken gene that blocks use of a certain sugar. Even the standard lab strain proved highly unusual. The authors argue drift after population crashes shaped many traits, warning against generalising from lab strains.
europmc-pmc3135510:
James Adams and colleagues compared body chemistry in autistic and typical children in a 2011 paper in Nutrition and Metabolism. Links between metabolism and developmental conditions were drawing growing interest. The study enrolled fifty-five autistic children and forty-four typical peers in Arizona, none taking supplements at the time, and ran a wide panel of blood tests.

Autistic children showed lower levels of several vitamins and protective chemicals, higher signs of oxidative stress, and weaker markers for energy transport and detox routes. Common vitamin and mineral levels, though, mostly sat within normal ranges in both groups. Groups of markers also tracked with how severe a child's autism rated on three scales. The authors suggest nutrition trials are warranted, since many gaps look correctable.
europmc-pmc3171010:
Françoise Farace and colleagues compared two machines that count tumour cells circulating in blood in a 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. Such counts forecast patient outlook and treatment success, but no universal detection method exists. One system fishes cells out by a surface marker; the other filters by cell size. Sixty patients with spreading breast, prostate, or lung cancer gave samples to both.

The two systems agreed in just over half of breast and prostate cases, and in only a fifth of lung cases. Size-based counts often found cells the marker method missed. The authors warn that marker-only capture can overlook tumour cells that have shed the marker while turning more aggressive, a bias worst in lung cancer. Counts from the two methods should never be treated as interchangeable.
europmc-pmc3261210:
Dennys Cintra and colleagues showed that unsaturated fats can reverse obesity-linked inflammation in the brain's appetite center, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. In animal models, inflammation of the hypothalamus is an early driver of obesity, and drugs or gene tricks can restrain it. Whether ordinary nutrients could do the same was unknown.

In mice fed a fattening diet, swapping part of the fat for flaxseed oil or olive oil corrected the hypothalamic inflammation. It restored insulin sensitivity there and body-wide, and it reduced fat stores. Injecting pure omega-3 or omega-9 fatty acids into the brains of obese rats cut food intake and weight gain. It restored responses to the satiety signals leptin and insulin. It also switched on appetite-suppressing genes. A recently found fatty acid receptor helped relay the effect. Nutrients, the authors conclude, are credible candidates against this inflammation.
europmc-pmc3291410:
Thomas, Keating, Hulse-Post, and Doherty made the case in 2006 that flu vaccines should do more than raise antibodies. Shots built on antibodies work well only when the vaccine matches the circulating strain closely, because flu changes its outer coat often. T cells, another arm of the immune system, instead target inner parts of the virus that stay similar across strains.

The authors explain how two broad kinds of T cells help clear infected cells, one by guiding other immune cells and one by killing infected cells directly. Mouse studies of flu lung infection show how these responses form, persist, and return during a second infection. Vaccines that also train T cells, they argue, could protect even when strains drift.
europmc-pmc3304110:
Nicolas-Alonso and Gomez-Gil reviewed systems that let people control computers with brain activity alone, in a 2012 article. Such brain computer interfaces aim to restore communication for people left fully paralyzed by conditions like motor neuron disease, brain stem stroke, or spinal cord injury. The review walks through the standard chain of stages every system uses.

Stages covered include recording brain signals, cleaning them, picking out the features that carry intent, translating those features into commands, and running the device. The authors compare ways of sensing the brain, from scalp electrodes to measures of blood flow, and survey the math used to decode signals. They close with the range of devices these systems can drive, from spelling aids to assistive appliances.
europmc-pmc3315510:
Risso, Schwartz, Sherlock, and Dudoit tackled a hidden bias in gene activity measurements, in a 2011 methods paper. RNA sequencing counts how many reads come from each gene, but the counts skew with a gene's content of the DNA letters G and C. That skew differs from sample to sample and can fake or hide real differences between conditions.

The team proposes three simple corrections that adjust each gene's count within a single sequencing run before runs are compared. On two datasets from different species and designs, their approach cut the bias and gave more accurate estimates of how much gene activity changed. It also kept error rates honest in tests for differing activity. The methods ship in a free software package, and the authors stress that careful cleanup is essential before drawing biological conclusions.
europmc-pmc3404110:
Suthar and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2012 whether antiretroviral therapy for HIV also prevents tuberculosis in adults. Tuberculosis is the great killer riding alongside HIV in much of the world. If treating the virus cuts tuberculosis rates, one program could fight both diseases at once.

Pooling the available studies, the review found therapy tied to a large drop in tuberculosis cases, about two thirds lower across all levels of immune cell counts. The protection was not confined to the sickest patients. That breadth matters for policy, since it supports starting therapy earlier rather than waiting. The analysis gives tuberculosis programs a firm number to plan around.
europmc-pmc3440110:
Boxall led a worldwide expert exercise in 2012 to name the biggest open questions about drugs and personal care chemicals once they escape into nature. A decade of work had traced these chemicals through water and soil, but research money needs aiming. Questions were solicited globally, workshopped down to a top twenty, then ranked.

The priorities fell into seven baskets. They covered which substances to assess first, how exposure happens, uptake by living things, harm, relative risk, antibiotic resistance, and managing the problem. The ranked list is meant to steer future research programs toward the gaps that matter most. With evidence mounting that these everyday chemicals reach ecosystems worldwide, the authors argue focus beats breadth now.
europmc-pmc3477710:

People respond unevenly, partly because head shape steers the current. The team built computer models from MRI scans of three adults.

Standard pads spread current widely, and the peak spot in the brain shifted from person to person. A ring-style setup kept current inside a tighter zone for everyone. Fine folds of the cortex bent the flow in each model. Datta's group argues that dose should be tuned to each person's own scan for steadier results.

flaubert-temptation-st-anthony-hearn-191:
Saint Anthony sits in the Egyptian desert while wonders and horrors crowd his night in Flaubert's Temptation of Saint Anthony. Lafcadio Hearn's 1910 translation renders the work Flaubert called his life's own, rewritten across thirty years. Gods, heretics, monsters, and Death itself parade before the hermit's eyes.

Each vision tempts the saint with a different offer: power, pleasure, knowledge, rest. The book reads more like a vast stage dream than a novel, rich with the lore Flaubert loved. Odilon Redon's dark images, noted in this edition, suit a text where faith wrestles every phantom it can name.
forster-howards-end-1910:
E. M. Forster published Howards End in 1910, and it became his first widely praised novel. Forster, a Cambridge graduate, wrote about the England he knew: cultured liberals, rich business families, and the clerks caught between them. A country house gives the book its title.

Two Schlegel sisters, Margaret and Helen, befriend the wealthy Wilcox family and a poor clerk named Leonard Bast. Margaret marries into the Wilcoxes, while Helen's rash choices pull Bast toward ruin. The house, Howards End, passes slowly toward the person who understands it best. Forster's famous plea, only connect, sums up the novel's hope for bridging class and feeling.
francis-little-flowers-1910:
The Little Flowers of St. Francis came down from the 1300s in Italy. T. W. Arnold gave the tales English dress in 1910. Francis of Assisi was the rich youth who wed Lady Poverty. His friars roamed the roads with songs and tales of his deeds.

Short tales tell of the wolf of Gubbio, the birds who heard his preach, and his scars of Christ. Joy, love of beasts, and scorn of gold shine in each tale. The book won hearts far past the Church that bred it. It is the most loved book of tales on the saint.
freud-three-essays-brill-1910:
Sigmund Freud published Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality in German in 1905. The English text here is A. A. Brill's translation of 1910, titled Three Contributions to the Theory of Sex. Freud argues that sexual life begins in infancy, not at puberty. Children, in his theory, pass through stages centered on the mouth, anus, and genitals.

He treats perversions as fixations or detours in that growth. The libido, or sexual drive, is the energy behind the process. The book scandalized its age and remains psychoanalysis's most daring founding text. Later editions grew with notes and changes. Its claims still provoke debate among clinicians and critics.
froude-history-england-vol-10:
Spain sends its great fleet against England in the tenth volume of Froude's History, from 1865, covering the Armada year. Drake and Howard lead the sea fight in home waters. Storms then scatter the Spanish ships along wild coasts, completing England's deliverance.

Froude treats the victory as the climax of his whole Tudor epic. Protestant England, in his telling, survives by courage, seamanship, and God's weather. The fate of a nation hangs in the balance through the summer's fighting. His account reads as patriotic pageant, done with great narrative skill, and it crowned his reputation with the reading public of his day.
frus-1861-d10:
Joseph Wright wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 June 1861. The dispatch is document 10 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861, the first year of the Civil War.

By late June both sides were in the field, and Europe watched for a quick result. Wright's reports kept his corner of that watch. The letter shows the plain, dated rhythm by which far posts fed a capital that could not see events for itself. Each dated page added one more fixed point to a map Washington drew from afar. Fixed points like this one let later readers chart the war's foreign course.
frus-1861-d110:
A letter of 24 October 1861 went from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons at the British legation.

The matched dates show the machine in motion: the Navy chief reports, the State chief answers abroad. Seward's note to Lyons carries the product of that inner talk. It is a small, clear case of how the Union turned sea power into diplomacy. Such matched dates let readers watch the inner talk become foreign policy in a day. One day from inner talk to foreign note was swift work for the age of sail and steam.
frus-1861-d210:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Mr. Wood on 22 August 1861. It was printed as Document 210 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d310:
Writing on 7 September 1861, Mr. Dryer sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 310 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d10:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 31 January 1862. It was printed as Document 10 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d110:
A letter home from Charles Francis Adams, dated 25 July 1862, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 110 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d210:
Lord Lyons replied into the file on 21 February 1862 with a note to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 210 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both men wrote on the same day, a sign of active business between them.

Same-day exchanges usually mean a matter was moving fast or a deadline pressed. Lyons wrote as Britain's eyes in Washington as well as its voice, reporting home on all Seward said and did. A note from his hand in February belongs to the routine that kept a hard relationship workable through the war's first full winter. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d310:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward opened the September Paris mail with a dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 15 September 1862, printed as Document 310 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-September found Lee's army in Maryland and the Union's foreign standing at its lowest point of the year. France had drafted a plan to propose a truce, and Britain was considering it. Seward's letter to Dayton that day went out two days before Antietam, into the most dangerous fortnight the Union faced abroad during the war. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d410:
An instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Horace J. Perry in Madrid on 15 September 1862. It is Document 410 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Mid-September 1862 was a hinge of the war: Lee's army was in Maryland, and Lincoln waited on a victory before issuing his emancipation order. Foreign courts held back, waiting on the same news. Seward's letters in these days armed his agents with the Union's reading of events. For the Madrid legation, that meant pressing Spain to see a government that meant to win, and to keep its ports closed to Confederate use.
frus-1862-d510:
On 23 July 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote again from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward, a week after his previous report. The dispatch is Document 510 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Weekly reports in a bad month had a hard job. They had to be truthful. Yet they must not give Washington fresh cause for worry it could not act on. Pike's July letters did that job plainly, recording Dutch steadiness while Union arms regrouped. He also tracked the war's naval fringe, where Dutch colonial ports had rules to enforce. The letter continues a correspondence notable for its regularity. In the whole of 1862, few American posts wrote home as often as Pike's. Fewer still wrote as frankly.
frus-1862-d610:
Thomas Corwin received the year's closing Mexican order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 21 October 1862. It is Document 610 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

October's instruction reached Mexico as the French settled in for a long war and as Washington, steadied by Antietam, took stock of its foreign position. The policy Seward repeated to Corwin had not changed in a year: friendship for Mexico's republic, refusal to accept the European enterprise, and patience. Within two years a freed Union army would stand on the Rio Grande and the patience would end. The letter is a fitting close to the volume's most principled American file.
frus-1862-d710:
On 13 September 1862, Andrew B. Dickinson wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second day in a row. Dickinson was the American minister in Nicaragua. The letter is document 710 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Two reports on two days point to a post with much to tell. From Nicaragua, an envoy tracked the transit route, the local government's acts, and the safety of Americans passing through. Dickinson's letters fed that watch. Kept in the volume, they show the pace of a small legation's work when events moved fast and mail home was slow.
frus-1863p1-d10:
On 8 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London. A second letter to Adams bears the same date in the volume. This one is document 10 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote as the year turned, with the war at a grim point and Europe still weighing its course. His letters told Adams what to say and what to hold back in talks with the British. Paired sheets like these show the secretary working a brief in parts. This letter belongs to that pair, and to the long chain that bound Washington to its London post.
frus-1863p1-d110:
On 6 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 110 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Early March found the legation deep in the ship question, as Southern warships took shape in British yards. Adams's mail pressed the facts on Washington and, through his talks, on the British themselves. This letter is one of a pair sent that day. It shows the post in its spring rhythm: watch, report, and press, week after week.
frus-1863p1-d210:
A dispatch dated 5 June 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 210 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d310:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 October 1862. His note is document 310 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Seward answered the legation knowing London would read every word. Even routine notes carried weight, because each answer set a precedent for the next dispute. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d410:
On 5 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 410 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After the Emancipation Proclamation in January 1863, Seward could frame the war as a fight against slavery. That put Britain, which had banned slavery at home, in an awkward spot when it aided the South. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d510:
The date 13 May 1863 heads a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d610:
The letter printed as document 610 was written on 13 August 1863 by Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d10: Paired with a letter to Stalin the same day, President Roosevelt's note to Prime Minister Churchill of June 18, 1943 is Document 10 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two messages went out together as the president kept both partners in step. The record supplies date, sender, and receiver, and no topic. In the Foreign Relations series it stands early in the chain of papers that produced the Cairo and Tehran meetings.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d110: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt bears the date November 9, 1943, and it stands as Document 110 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The day's traffic also held letters from Chiang, Harriman, and Bohlen, a fair sample of the summit's whole cast. The record for this note gives the date and the names only. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the rest of that crowded day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d210:
Foy Kohler of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs wrote a secret memorandum on 11 November 1943. It records fresh British Embassy reports on the Cairo talks between Anthony Eden and Turkish foreign minister Numan Menemencioğlu, adding two later meetings in Ankara on 7 and 8 November.

Numan, the memo shows, grew somewhat warmer in the final talk. He admitted the Moscow decisions were better than expected, yet he resented Eden's threatening tone and felt Eden spoke for Russia as much as Britain. He wanted to know exactly what Turkey must do, what Allied help she could count on, and what the political results would be. The Balkans now worried Ankara as much as the Straits once did.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d310:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 408 at Cairo on 25 November 1943, on command of British and American forces operating against Germany. It is the full American case for a single commander over the whole European war, pressed at the Sextant Conference.

Operations fall into three linked groups: the Mediterranean, northwest Europe, and the strategic air war on Germany's interior. Since events in each group shape the others, the chiefs argue, one commander must direct all three under the Combined Chiefs of Staff, and his appointment is most urgently necessary. Even named at once, he could not be organized before the end of January 1944. The paper ends with the bombing war, where it calls unified command imperative if lives and planes are to be saved.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d410:
A third draft of the Tehran communiqué is printed here with its handwritten changes shown, Roosevelt's apart from three by Hopkins. An editorial headnote presumes this was the draft discussed and put into final form at the dinner meeting of 1 December 1943.

Hopkins' hand inserted the heading Communiqué, changed Soviet Russia to the Soviet Union, and added the place and date, Tehran, Iran, 1 December 1943, at the foot. Roosevelt's changes tighten the text throughout. The leaders have shaped and confirmed our common policy. Their concord will win an enduring peace. The conferences are now friendly, a word glossed in Russian and English at the margin. A note under the signatures, in the President's papers, reads: as corrected, this becomes the final draft.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d510: Document 510 is an editorial note placed by the volume's historians. It appears in the Cairo-Tehran volume of the Foreign Relations series. Such notes fill gaps between papers with background and cross-references. They keep names, dates, and earlier decisions straight for the reader. The conferences documented here met in late 1943. Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin used them to plan the war's next phase. Read the note as part of that official record's apparatus.
frus-1944-quebec-d10:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on June 4, 1944, the day Allied troops entered Rome and two days before D-Day. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

June 4 was a hinge date: Italy's capital fell even as the invasion fleet sailed for France. Churchill, whose strategy had always prized the Mediterranean, marked the moment in his correspondence with Washington. For readers, a letter from that crowded day shows the war's two Western campaigns peaking together, and the Prime Minister keeping his hand on both through his channel to Roosevelt.
frus-1944-quebec-d110:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt this long memorandum on September 8, 1944, ahead of the Quebec Conference. Its title names the subject: lend-lease and economic relations with Britain in "Phase 2," the period after Germany's defeat but while the Pacific war went on. Britain's weakened finances frame the whole paper.

Hull urged helping Britain enter the postwar period on sound footing, with trade and finance run on Bretton Woods principles. He tied aid to full British effort against Japan and to a British reconversion program matched with America's. Done right, he argued, lend-lease could continue during the Pacific war without breeding later disputes. It set out the American position going into the Quebec talks on aid.
frus-1944-quebec-d210:
No official memorandum survives for this luncheon, and the editors again lean on Mackenzie King's notes. King lunched with Roosevelt, Churchill, and Eden, and the talk turned to timing the proposed world organization conference for October 30. That date fell just a week before the American presidential elections, which sharpened every political calculation around it.

King warned of opposition from small countries, Canada included, to any appearance that the great powers were seeking to control the world through the new organization.
