Churchill described the disagreement with Stalin over the council's powers, especially a Soviet veto in disputes where the Soviet Union was itself a party. Eden's diary adds that Churchill explained why Eden could not accept Roosevelt's Hyde Park invitation.
frus-1945-50-intel-d10:
Tamm sent Hoover another inside memorandum on 17 September 1945. The FBI's leadership was tracking the intelligence reorganization plans day by day that month. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Staff papers like Tamm's kept Hoover briefed on moves by the White House, the Budget Bureau, and the military services. Each report sharpened the bureau's sense of where the new central agency might cut into FBI ground. For readers, the value is in the accumulation: the volume prints the bureau's watch in near-real time. This memorandum is one tick of that clock, three days before the president dissolved the OSS and redrew the map.
frus-1945-50-intel-d110:
Souers wrote to Hoover of the FBI on 19 April 1946. The new director of central intelligence addressing the FBI's chief opened the most delicate channel in the volume. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The CIG and the FBI divided the world between them in theory. Foreign work went to the group. Home work and Latin America stayed contested, by wartime claim. Every letter between their chiefs walked that border. Readers can read Souers's approach to Hoover as diplomacy between sovereigns, which, in bureau terms, it was. The exchange that follows in the volume, letters and counter-letters through 1946, decided how America's two secret empires would share a hemisphere.
frus-1945-50-intel-d210:
Dated 14 March 1947, this memorandum runs from George M. Elsey to the President’s Special Counsel (Clifford). The State Department prints it as document 210 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d310:
On 1 June 1949, the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner) sent a memorandum to Members of His Staff. It stands as document 310 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA was settling into its shape, while the Dulles Report's advice worked its way through office after office.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d410:
Fisher Howe, deputy special assistant for research and intelligence at the State Department, wrote to Sheppard on 9 January 1950. Sheppard served as a special assistant to the Secretary. The memo is document 410 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The note moves from the intelligence bureau to the Secretary's inner office in one step. Such short links mattered, since the bureau's reports did no good if they sat unread. Readers can see how State Department analysts kept a path open to the top of their own house. Sheppard's desk was a gate through which many such notes had to pass to reach the Secretary.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d10: General John Deane, who headed the American military mission in Moscow, reported to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 17 October 1944. His message is document 10 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta. Deane dealt daily with Soviet officers, so his reports gave Washington a soldier's view of cooperation with an ally whose help the war effort still required.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d110:
Acting Secretary Stettinius sent the President a German control agreement on 25 November 1944 and asked for a quick answer. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, forwards a photostatic copy of the deal reached in the European Advisory Commission. The commission's minutes of 14 November, when the agreement was signed, came with it.

The agreement sets up the Allied control machinery for Germany during the surrender period. Stettinius stresses that it grew from close consultation with the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the War and Navy Departments. Approval from the President would let Ambassador Winant tell the commission that the United States accepts. Copies were also going to the Secretaries of War and the Navy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d210:
France asked outright for a seat at the Big Three conference, and Stettinius sent the request to the President on 18 January 1945. His covering note, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, transmits Ambassador Caffery's telegram with the French text in full. The note is dated from Paris on 16 January.

The Provisional Government says it learned from public reports of the planned meeting of the three allied powers. That meeting will fix the terms of their cooperation in the war. Paris then sets out its standing. The fighting in the West runs on French soil or hard by her frontiers. France is straining to the full extent of her present strength. The claim to be heard, the enclosure argues in effect, follows from where the war is being fought.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d310:
Supplying friendly forces in freed Europe is the subject of a United States Chiefs of Staff memorandum written at Malta on February 1, 1945. It deals with gear for Allied and liberated forces, with Greece at the front of the queue. A new Greek army was to take over guard duty inside Greece, and its needs had been spelled out in a theater message.

Most items, the memo notes, could come from British stocks in the Mediterranean or on the way there. But every issue made for this purpose would need replacement later. The paper shows supply, not strategy, filling much of the chiefs' working day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d410:
Matthews sent Stettinius a suggested reparations paper on February 9, 1945, with this covering note. The draft, meant for Molotov and Eden, rested on the Russian proposal of basic principles. Its first two sections followed the Soviet text almost word for word. Eden had suggested added words in the first paragraph.

Matthews also advised a question for Molotov: at what prices — that is, prices of what year — would the total of reparations be fixed? The attached draft itself has not been found, the editors note. A handwritten tag credits "Doc" Matthews as author. The cover note shows how technical points hid inside the grand reparations fight.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d510:
Matters on Poland have reached a dead end, Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on April 7, 1945 — and laid the blame on the Western ambassadors. In his view, Harriman and Clark Kerr, the American and British members of the Moscow Commission, had departed from the principles of the Crimea Conference. They had introduced new elements the conference never provided.

At Crimea, Stalin argued, all three leaders had treated the functioning Polish Provisional Government as the kernel of the new government of national unity. It was subject to reconstruction, not replacement. The ambassadors, he charged, now read the bargain differently. The letter, given in translation, is the alliance's Polish quarrel stated by its strongest party.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d10:
Churchill decided to risk a snub in this short telegram to Truman of May 15, 1945. Your number 39 has just arrived, he writes. I agree with what you say. I will take a chance of getting a snub from Stalin by sending him a telegram urging a friendly tripartite meeting.

The editors note the risk was real. In March, Churchill had ended a message to Stalin hoping their difficulties would be swept away if only they could meet. Stalin's reply had ignored the sentence entirely. This three-line wire thus records a deliberate gamble: the Prime Minister would ask plainly, and take the answer he got.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d110:
Edwin Pauley, the American representative on the Allied reparations commission, cabled President Truman from Moscow on June 29, 1945. The top secret telegram is document 110 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Pauley was working in Moscow with his Soviet and British counterparts on how much Germany should pay for the war.

Pauley says he is bending every effort to have a proposed reparations plan ready to lay before the three heads of government at their meeting. Soviet negotiator Maisky and Britain's Monckton expect to attend, and Pauley hopes to be there too, as Truman had discussed with him before he left the United States. He asks that the Army be told to arrange places for himself, Dr. Lubin, and four others.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d210:
Secretary Byrnes answered Justice Jackson from aboard the cruiser Augusta on July 12, 1945. The brief telegram is document 210 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Jackson had reported from London that the war crimes trial talks were slow and technical, and that he dreaded the Big Three debating the subject.

Byrnes appreciates the report and agrees with Jackson: the subject is too technical for detailed discussion by the Big Three. But if he finds discussion unavoidable, he writes, he will try to let Jackson know in time for a consultation with the President and himself. The reply kept the war crimes charter where Jackson wanted it, in the hands of the lawyers in London, while the leaders dealt with it only in broad terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d310:
Barnes took up the Soviet plan for Bulgaria's Control Commission on July 12, 1945, and set it against an older promise. He quoted Ambassador Winant's letter of October 22, 1944, to the Soviet side. That letter said the commission would work under instructions from all three allied governments.

Against that standard, Barnes measured the new Soviet talk of mere consultation. Consultation, he argued, was not joint control. The cable asks Washington to see the gap between the armistice promise and Soviet practice in Sofia. It reached the Department days before the Potsdam conference opened, capping a month of warnings from Sofia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d410:
A sudden Soviet shift is reported in Winant's cable from London of July 10, 1945. He thanks the Department for its prompt action of July 8, which was meant to ease the French zone agreement to completion. Yet after a long discussion the night before, the European Advisory Commission still could not complete the agreement.

Gousev, the Soviet representative, now said he did not know whether his government would approve postponing the fixing of France's Berlin area. Moscow might wish the French area described within the agreement itself, and he must consult his government. Winant assumed the shift came on instructions from Moscow, since Gousev had known the proposal since June 29.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d510:
Poland's frontiers frame an extract from the briefing book paper on suggested American policy toward Poland, dated June 29, 1945. The Crimea Conference, it recalls, settled Poland's eastern frontier by adopting a slightly modified Curzon Line as the Polish-Soviet boundary. It also recognized that Poland should receive substantial additions of territory in the north and west.

The new Polish government was to be consulted on their extent, but final delimitation of the Polish-German frontiers was to await the peace conference. Meanwhile, the paper notes, the Lublin government had taken over almost at once all the territory of pre-1939 Poland, as the German population withdrew. With Soviet consent and help, it then took over German lands in the east as well.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d610:
A short extract from a British Chiefs of Staff memo of June 30, 1945, forms document 610 in the Potsdam papers. It is part of the joint debate over basic objectives, strategy, and policies for the war. The full text of the British memo is printed earlier in the volume as document 600.

The extract's weight sits in one quoted passage from the U.S. paper under review. Among the added tasks to aid the grand strategy is this one. The Allies should encourage Russian entry into the war against Japan. They should also give Russia such aid to her war-making power as is needed and practical in that link. The British note that they agree in full with the U.S. memo, subject to their earlier remarks. None of those remarks touched this passage on Russia.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1010: Admiral Ernest King, chief of naval operations, sent this short telegram from Babelsberg on July 26, 1945. It follows from Anglo-American talks at the conference on captured German small craft. King directs that an officer be chosen, in consultation with Commodore Moran, to sit on the Capcraft Commission. That body selects captured craft, including tugs. The chosen officer must be fit to pick tugs suited to American purposes. He is to report to the commander of naval forces in Europe for temporary duty on the commission.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1110:
Writing from Washington on 18 July 1945, the Acting Secretary of State addressed this message to Will Clayton. Clayton was an assistant secretary who handled the money side of foreign policy. The message went out on the second day of the Potsdam Conference.

With the president and the secretary of state in Germany, the home office still had to keep policy in step with the team abroad. Clayton was the man Washington turned to on trade, loans, and the cost of the peace. A note to him at this moment shows the capital checking with its own expert. It is one link in the chain that tied the summit to the home front.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1210: On 29 July 1945 the Acting Secretary of State in Washington wrote to the Secretary of State at Potsdam. It is a home-office message between the department's two leading men, sent in the summit's final days. Joseph Grew held the acting post while James Byrnes led the team in Germany. Word between them kept the department's two halves in step.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1310:
Stimson wrote to Harrison on 23 July 1945. The war secretary's replies kept the Interim Committee's work aligned with the summit's course. By that date the American leaders were settling how the new weapon would enter the war's endgame.

A note on this channel carried the atomic file's direction from the man who owned it. Stimson's hand guided both the committee in Washington and the brief at Potsdam. This message is his guidance at the second week's start. It belongs to the small set of papers through which the bomb's use was shaped, far from any public eye.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1410:
Caffery sent a fifth cable to Secretary Byrnes on 6 August 1945, part of the densest single-day run in the volume's French papers. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Five cables in a day from one post is close to a paper siege. Caffery knew Washington's habits and pressed his case while the Potsdam results were still fresh and open to shaping. Each cable in the run takes its own file or point, so readers should not expect repeats. Together they show an ambassador using the cable room as an instrument, and they give the French section of the volume its driving rhythm.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710:
Lieutenant Rigdon's log of the President's trip to the Berlin Conference opens on July 6, 1945. Extracts form document 710 in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The log runs day by day to August 7, 1945.

The first entry follows the party out of Washington that night. Truman left the White House by motor car at 9:40 p.m. with a small staff group. At Union Station the special train waited on Team Track No. 2. Secretary Byrnes came aboard at 10:15 p.m., while Admiral Leahy and others had boarded earlier. At 11 p.m. the train rolled for Newport News, Virginia. There the heavy cruiser Augusta waited to carry the President across the Atlantic. The next morning's entry notes the same pier had served President Roosevelt's Crimea trip that year.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-10:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the first plenary session, July 17, 1945, run parallel to the Thompson minutes. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen, a U.S. adviser, took his own record as Stalin proposed Truman for the chair.

Cohen has Truman stress the urgency of preparing for the European settlements. The first concrete proposal was the draft for a Council of Foreign Ministers. Churchill suggested it be referred to the foreign secretaries. Stalin agreed to that procedure, but voiced his doubt over China in a council for the European peace. Truman then stated the U.S. policy toward Germany in his own words. The Control Council, he thought, should start to function at once under the agreement already made. His draft of principles for that council was laid before the meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-110:
Another set of Thompson minutes records Potsdam talks on July 25, 1945. The conference often ran several meetings in a day, and note-takers split the load. Thompson's sets, printed in the second Potsdam volume, form a near-daily spine for the American record. This set covers a further session from a crowded day.

Readers meet the session's flow: topics in order, speakers in turn, points left hanging. Minutes like these let later readers test claims about who agreed to what. They also catch the strain of the schedule itself. By late July the talks had run a week with the largest questions still unsettled.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d810:
Barnes reported from Bulgaria on July 23, 1945, in document 810. The representative in Sofia wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His post stood inside a control commission where the Soviet voice ruled. The report entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Barnes's mid-conference report carries the pressure of his position. He reported facts his hosts would rather have hidden. Readers gain a clear sense of Bulgaria's slide from the Western orbit. The document shows reporting as a form of resistance: to write the truth home was to keep a claim alive. His letters remain a key source on the Balkans' turning.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d910: American staff drafted this short memorandum on July 22, 1945, as one response to the Soviet definition of war booty. It quotes the Soviet text in full. Under that definition, the paper says, little or nothing will remain to take as reparations from the American zone. The United States therefore accepts the definition. For the present, it will run its zone without regard to reparations as such. The editors note the paper was an alternative to the next document in the volume.
frus-1952-1954-iran-vol-10:
Volume ten of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1952 to 1954 covers Iran from 1951 to 1954. The Office of the Historian publishes the series from declassified records. The volume's center is the 1953 coup that remade Iran and shadowed its relations with the West for decades.

The documents trace the oil nationalization crisis under Premier Mohammad Mossadeq, and Britain's campaign to win Washington over. The joint operation, called TPAJAX by the CIA, overthrew Mossadeq in August 1953 and restored the Shah's power. Cables show the planning, the paid crowds, and the quick consolidation after. The volume is the official paper trail of the coup.
frus-1961-1963-cuba-vol-10:
This tenth volume of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1961 to 1963 covers Cuba from January 1961 to September 1962. The Office of the Historian publishes the series from declassified files. The Kennedy years in Cuba policy begin here, at their most violent.

The documents cover the Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961 and its bitter aftermath. Covert operations against Castro, run under Operation Mongoose, fill many pages. The embargo hardens, exile raids multiply, and intelligence watches Soviet shipping ever closer. The volume stops just before the missile crisis, which its sequel takes up. It is the fullest official record of the secret war on Castro.
frus-1977-80v29-d110: A 1977-1980 FRUS letter from President Carter on Panama. The canal treaties. This document preserves that letter. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
gao-gaoreports-b-293073-10: Creative Information Technology refused to quit — March 2005, round ten, docket B-293073.10 — and GAO's ruling answers the latest challenge. Ten protests, ten full hearings; this one was number ten. Persistence earned the same careful review. The review was careful. The tenth was judged.
gao-gaoreports-b-296510: Evergreen Fire & Security took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297136-10: TPL doubled its June 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer each, and the record stays clean.
gao-gaoreports-b-297210: WorldWide Language Resources tripled its November 2005 protest — three case numbers, one language-services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Triple filings get one careful answer. Three dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298110: Bristol Group took its June 2006 contract fight to GAO — the Union Station venture — and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Landmark deals get the same full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-308010: Borrowing airplanes on a handshake drew GAO's fiscal eye in 2007 — could the farm agency share aircraft this way? The ruling reads the money law against the deal. The call decides whether the wings were legally borrowed or just hopefully borrowed.
gao-gaoreports-b-310210: A 2007 GAO ruling settling a tech-contract fight from Strategic e-Business Solutions, Inc. The firm said the agency ran an unfair race for the work; the ruling tests that claim and calls the winner. For tech firms hunting federal deals, rulings like this draw the foul lines of the bidding game.
gao-gaoreports-b-311310: This 2008 GAO ruling is about agency Tender Official at Rhonda Podojil. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-316010: This 2008 GAO ruling is about incorporation by Reference at 2008. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-316510: This 2008 GAO ruling is about prohibition in the 2008 Consolidated Appropriations Act at Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1010: Treasury cut overseas attaches in 2005, and GAO's report says the department reduced the number of financial envoys. The findings take the measure. The report shows the money diplomats were thinned. The reduction had to be understood. The money diplomats were thinned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-210: Diabetes coverage got a GAO checkup in 2005, and the report covers health plan coverage of services and supplies. The review reads the benefits. The patients deserved the insulin and the strips. The coverage was examined. The patients deserved the insulin and the strips.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-410: Park permits were leaving money on the table in 2005, and GAO's report says charging the allowed fees could raise revenue. The park service got a clear nudge: take what the rules already permit. The gates were open, the fees were not. The money was there for the taking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-710: Identity theft outreach was underway in 2005, and GAO's report says some efforts to promote awareness of new consumer rights had begun. The findings give the partial credit. The report warns that the victims deserved knowing their rights. The efforts had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-10: The EEOC's restructuring needed a more thorough approach in 2005, and GAO's report says actions had been taken, though efforts could benefit. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the civil rights agency deserved good management. The efforts had to be thorough.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1010: Grieving war families needed better help in 2006, and GAO's report says the war department needed firm rules for aiding them. The findings demand the structure. The report warns that the kin of the fallen deserved the best care. The aid had to be excellent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-110: Weapon program managers needed better support in 2006, and GAO's report says better backing was required to improve outcomes. The findings prescribe the support. The report warns that the arsenal's builders needed good bosses. The support had to be better. The arsenal's builders needed good bosses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-210: Counting migrant remittances gave different answers in 2006, and GAO's report says different estimation methods produced different results. The findings compare the math. The report warns that the money sent home deserved honest counting. The methods had to be weighed. The money sent home deserved honest counting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-310: The IRS's systems overhaul needed finishing in 2006, and GAO's report says the agency had to complete efforts to develop guiding policies. The findings demand the follow-through. The report warns that the tax machine's modernization needed rules. The efforts had to be completed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-710: Medicare drug plan phone lines were fast but sloppy in 2006, and GAO's report says call center responses were prompt but not consistently accurate. The findings test the answers. The report warns that the seniors calling for help deserved truth. The accuracy had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-810: The TVA was tackling its debt in 2006, and GAO's report says the authority planned to reduce borrowing while meeting power demand. The findings do the math. The report warns that the lights had to stay on while the debt went down. The plan had to balance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1010: Yucca Mountain's nuclear-waste dream hung on paperwork in 2007 — GAO's report says the Energy Department's quality program had improved, but the license bid's fate was murky. The findings probe whether the desert dump could survive regulatory muster. Decades of waste, one shaky plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1110: A tax credit paid in paychecks was flopping in 2007 — GAO's report says the advance earned-income credit saw thin use and tiny dollars. The findings show a good idea dying in the details: workers did not claim it, and cheats gamed it. The report asks whether the advance was worth the trouble.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-310: The high-risk list got its 2007 update, and GAO's report refreshes the roster of the government's most troubled programs. The findings name the repeat offenders. The report reads as the watchdog's most-wanted poster for waste. The list was long, and the excuses were short.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-110: The full 2007 GAO report on the terror watch lists: who keeps them, who checks them, and where the holes are. GAO found boss-level watch too loose, screens too leaky, and good uses too few. The report backs the fix list with hard proof — the case file behind the push to run the nation's suspect lists like they matter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-610: GAO published its findings on September 11: HHS Needs to Develop a Plan That Incorporates Lessons from the Responder Health Programs in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
garland-other-main-travelled-1910:
Other Main-Travelled Roads came from Harper as a sunset edition, with rights dates of 1892, 1899, and 1910. Garland opens with verses on prairie folks, starting with the pioneers. They rise, he writes, to mastery of wind and snow, and go like soldiers into strife.

Nearly twenty years after his first farm tales, Garland returns to the same ground here. The farms look familiar, and the struggles have not vanished. Time has passed, though, and the tone grows riper and more thoughtful. With the first volume, the book forms a full portrait of rural life in the Middle West at the century's turn.
goldman-anarchism-other-essays-1910:
Emma Goldman published Anarchism and Other Essays in 1910 in New York. Goldman, a Russian-born lecturer and publisher of Mother Earth magazine, was then the best known anarchist in America. The essays gather her talks on the subjects that filled her halls.

Goldman defined anarchism as freedom from government and from the dead weight of church and property. Other essays treat patriotism as a threat to peace, marriage as an economic bargain, and the traffic in women as a product of poverty. She wrote in a direct, urgent voice for working readers. The book stands as the American anarchist manifesto of its era and the clearest short statement of her thought.
hagenbeck-beasts-and-men-1910:
Carl Hagenbeck, the great animal dealer of Hamburg, told his life in Beasts and Men in 1910. His men traded beasts from every wild corner of the earth. In its pages sits the first Western print of a giant dinosaur said to live in the Congo.

Hagenbeck reports what his agents heard of a huge beast in the swamps and rivers of the far interior. He sets the tale down with care, as a dealer's note on stock not yet caught. The story grew into the hunt for Mokele-mbembe, the Congo's famed living dinosaur. Expeditions still sail on the strength of Hagenbeck's few pages.
hegel-phenomenology-baillie-1910:
G. W. F. Hegel published The Phenomenology of Spirit in 1807, the founding text of his philosophy. The English text here is J. B. Baillie's translation of 1910. Hegel traces how consciousness grows, stage by stage, toward full self-knowledge. Sense, perception, understanding, and self-awareness each fail in instructive ways.

The famous master and slave passage shows selves forming through struggle and work. Later parts move through culture, religion, and history toward absolute knowing. Hegel's dialectic, in which ideas grow through conflict, shaped Marx and many others. The book is dense and demanding. It remains a summit of German idealism and modern thought.
hicks-stoic-and-epicurean-1910:
R. D. Hicks wrote Stoic and Epicurean in 1910 as a clear English guide to the two great schools that led Greek thought after Aristotle. Both schools taught in Athens, drew loyal bands of pupils, and shaped Roman life for centuries. Hicks treats each school on its own terms and in plain terms.

He walks through their views on nature, logic, and knowledge, then gives most space to their rival ways of life. The Stoics taught calm in the face of fate. The school of Epicurus taught quiet pleasure and freedom from fear. Hicks wrote for the general reader, and his survey long served as the first book students were handed on these schools.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume ten carries on Carlyle's thunderous biography of Old Fritz: the Prussian army, that perfect instrument, and the king who played it. Drill, discipline, and the miracle of survival against empires fill the narrative. Carlyle at full power, for readers who can take it strong.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-10:
Hedda Gabler burns a manuscript, manipulates her circle, and courts ruin out of boredom and pride. The Master Builder follows Halvard Solness, an aging architect who climbs his own tower toward doom. Archer's tenth volume, from 1908, pairs Ibsen's two most fascinating self-destroyers.

Hedda remains the role great actresses measure themselves against, brilliant and trapped at once. Solness fears the young, clings to his fame, and hears a younger woman knocking at the door. Ibsen's psychology cuts deepest in these late plays. Fear of decline and hunger for freedom drive both plots. The volume shows a master in his sixties outwriting everyone younger.
james-moral-equivalent-war-1910:
The Moral Equivalent of War began as an address and was published in 1910; it is James's most famous short piece. A pacifist who honored soldiers, he asked how a society could keep the virtues war breeds, discipline, loyalty, and sacrifice, without the killing.

His answer is a conscription of youth into peaceful service: an army enlisted against nature, sent to mines, roads, and fisheries to earn civic honor by labor. The proposal influenced later service programs like the Civilian Conservation Corps. James admits the scheme's difficulty and presses it anyway. The essay remains the classic statement of his moral imagination.
jargon-file-2-9-10:
Eric Raymond edited version 2.9.10 of the Jargon File, the hacker's dictionary. Programmers at early labs built the file over years of shared use. It records the slang, jokes, and lore of their culture.

Entries define terms from real work and pure play alike. Foo, bar, and countless coinages get their due. Short essays explain hacker manners, humor, and pride in craft. The file is part glossary and part folk record. It reads like geek poetry in places. Anyone curious how early coders talked, joked, and saw themselves will find no better primary source.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-10:
Brébeuf's long study of the Huron people crowns Volume 10, from 1897. Thwaites devotes the book to the Huron mission in the year 1636. No writer of the age left a fuller account of Iroquoian life in print.

Towns, councils, feasts, dreams, and beliefs unfold in Brébeuf's calm prose. He explains kinship, healing rites, and the great feast of the dead. His respect for Huron thought sets the text apart from its time. Scholars still call it study of a culture before that field had a name. It was written in a bark mission house, by firelight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyon-leoni-myer:
Myer Lyon, known on stage as Leoni, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 as both opera singer and cantor. He began as a chorister at London's Great Synagogue, alongside his nephew John Braham. His voice was said to surpass his nephew's in sweetness. He first sang at Covent Garden in 1775, in Artaxerxes. He died at Kingston, Jamaica, about 1800.

The article traces his double career across the Atlantic world. He helped manage an English opera house in Dublin and sang at the Royalty Theatre. He ended as cantor of the synagogue in Kingston, the first trained cantor in the English colonies. He composed music for theater and synagogue alike. His name survives in the hymn tune Leoni, taken from his singing of the closing hymn Yigdal. A Wesleyan minister set it to The God of Abraham Praise, and it spread through English hymnals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-majority-10310:
Majority is treated in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia under two meanings in Jewish law. The first is a legal principle: doing the greater part of an act can count as doing the whole. Cutting most of the throat passages in slaughter, for example, makes an animal fit for food. A child mostly born is counted as born.

The article sets the principle's limits and its second sense. Majority beats the rival principles of presumption and proximity. It never applies in money cases, and witness numbers do not settle testimony. A hundred witnesses can be undone by two. The second meaning is the age of maturity. The Bible sets no single age, though army service and the half-shekel began at twenty. The rabbis tied adulthood to puberty, about thirteen for girls and fourteen for boys. The entry is a compact guide to a rule that runs through ritual and civil law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-margulies-samue:
Samuel Hirsch Margulies, a rabbi of Florence, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Brzezan, Galicia, on October 9, 1858, he descended from Rabbi Ephraim Zalman Margolioth. He was educated at the theological seminary at Breslau. His career then moved steadily west and south.

The article lists his pulpits in order. From 1885 to 1887 he served Congregation Newe Shalom in Hamburg. Weilburg in Hesse-Nassau followed until 1890. Since 1890 he had been chief rabbi of Florence. In 1899 he also became principal of the Italian rabbinical college, later moved to Florence. His writings include a study of Saadja's Arabic translation of the Psalms, printed at Breslau in 1884. Two Passover sermons and a work called Poet and Patriot followed. By 1904 he was editing the Rivista Israelitica. The entry shows a Galician scholar heading Italian Jewry's rabbinate and school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maybaum-siegmun:
Siegmund Maybaum, a rabbi in Berlin and a leader of Germany's rabbis, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman. Born at Miskolcz, in Hungary, on April 29, 1844, he studied at the yeshivot of Eisenstadt and Pressburg, at Breslau's university and Jewish seminary, and took his doctorate at Halle in 1869. Pulpits at Alsó-Kubin and at Saaz led in 1881 to Berlin, where he also taught at the Lehranstalt, the college for Jewish scholarship.

Maybaum founded the rabbinical society of Germany and, as its president, called the first congress of German rabbis at Berlin in 1884. The entry calls him one of the most eloquent rabbis in the country and notes the professor's title granted in 1903. His books trace his pulpit scholarship, from studies of anthropomorphism in the Targum to histories of the priesthood, prophecy, and the Jewish sermon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melville-lewis-:
Lewis Melville was the pen name of Lewis S. Benjamin. Benjamin was an English man of letters born in 1874. Joseph Jacobs and I. L. Bril enter him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His whole short list of books circles one novelist. It holds a "Life of Thackeray" in 1899. It holds "Thackeray's Stray Papers" in 1902. It holds an introduction to Thackeray's works too. That piece was issued in 1903 and 1904.

His one trip away from that devotion was "In the World of Mimes," also of 1902. He also wrote for the "Fortnightly Review," "The Bookman," "Temple Bar," and other English periodicals. The notice is among the briefest in the volume. It rests on one source, the Literary Year-Book for 1904. It catches him at the start of a career spent editing and championing Thackeray.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-d:
Meshullam ben David was a German tosafist of the twelfth or early thirteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 notices him through the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn. He was the son of David ben Kalonymus of Münzenburg. His father was himself a tosafist and liturgical poet. Meshullam's scholarly world is mapped by his correspondents. They were R. Baruch, Simhah of Speyer, and Isaac Or Zarua. His name and opinions appear in their responsa. They appear in the "Mordekai" too.

The notice ends with a caution typical of these entries. In the "Mordekai" on Hullin, a Meshullam is cited. Gross, in his "Gallia Judaica," thinks that Meshullam is another man. He thinks it is Meshullam of Melun. The trail of a glossator who wrote no surviving book runs through other men's footnotes. The encyclopedia leaves the identification honestly unsettled.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modon-simson-ha:
Simson ha-Kohen Modon, a Mantuan poet born on August 1, 1679, was his congregation's polished face to power, as Isidore Singer and S. J. Levinson tell it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. An accomplished linguist, he was sent to Vienna to do homage to Emperor Charles VI and came home with the emperor's goodwill. Rabbi David Finzi then steered him to poetry.

His collection Ḳol Musar appeared at Mantua in 1725, with some of Finzi's own poems inside, and Venice printed his Keter Torah and an elegy for his teacher Judah Brill. The tour de force was Shigyon Shimshon, three hundred lines each beginning with the same letter. He also compiled an alphabetical rabbinical encyclopedia, Sefer Zikronot — which, like the poem, never left manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordo-lazare-11:
Lazare Mordo, born in 1744, was physician and honorary rabbi of Corfu. That combination tells its own story, as a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco shows in 1906. He studied at Venice and Padua. In 1814 he was appointed chief physician of the island. He was esteemed by government and populace alike for learning and philanthropy.

When he died in 1823, the Corfiote poet Delviniotti composed an elegy in his honor. Mordo left numerous works in manuscript. The one that reached print was his Nozioni Miscellanee Interno a Corcira of 1809. It was dedicated to the Senate's president. It preserves the names of the physicians who had served Corfu before him, several of them Jews. Civic memory was kept by the island's doctor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-judah-lob:
Moses Judah Löb ben Samuel was a Russian rabbi and author born at Turetz in the government of Minsk. Herman Rosenthal and N. T. London wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He married into the family of Rabbi David Tebele of Minsk. When David died, Moses succeeded him and held the Minsk rabbinate for thirty years.

With his brother-in-law Saul Hayyim he prepared the Bet Dawid for the press. His own treatises, Mille di-Berakot and Mille di-Nezikin, treat the laws of blessings and the recovery of damages. Some responsa of his remain in manuscript. He died at Minsk in 1889, and his son Jacob followed him as rabbi there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muller-david-he:
David Heinrich Müller was an Austrian Orientalist born at Buczacz in Galicia on July 6, 1846. Isidore Singer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Trained at Vienna, Leipsic, Strasburg, and Berlin, he became professor of Oriental languages at Vienna in 1885. He also taught Hebrew and religious philosophy at the Vienna Jewish seminary.

Müller's long list of works centers on South Arabia: its castles, its inscriptions, and its old language. He edited the versions of Eldad ha-Dani and wrote on Ezekiel and on the meter of the Prophets. His 1903 book compared the laws of Hammurabi with the legislation of Moses. In 1897 he led a learned expedition to South Arabia and Socotra.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-tribe-:
The Tribe of Naphtali numbered fifty-three thousand four hundred men at Sinai, the Jewish Encyclopedia article records. Written by the editorial committee and J. F. McLaughlin, it follows the tribe's land and wars. In the march Naphtali camped with Dan and Asher as the rear guard. Its lot in Canaan was among the fairest, running from the Jordan lakes northward.

Josephus calls that country the very ambition of nature, an earthly paradise. From Naphtali came Barak, who led ten thousand men against Sisera at Deborah's call. The tribe also rallied to Gideon and sent David a great host at Hebron. Assyria deported its people early, yet Isaiah foresaw the same region seeing the dawn of deliverance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-necho-and-11410:
Necho ruled Egypt from 610 to 594 B.C. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and George A. Barton for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was son of Psammetich I, of the twenty-sixth dynasty. Herodotus credits him with a bold canal project. He tried to join the Nile to the Red Sea.

Phoenician sailors for Necho circled Africa in three years. In 608 he marched into Asia for spoil. King Josiah tried to stop him at Megiddo and died. Necho chained Jehoahaz and set Jehoiakim in his place. Judah paid him a heavy tribute in silver and gold. Four years later Nebuchadnezzar crushed him at Carchemish. He fled home and never regained Asia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-newport-11510:
Newport was Rhode Island's capital and a colonial trading giant. Joseph Jacobs, L. Hühner, and Max J. Kohler wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Roger Williams founded it on broad religious toleration. Fifteen Jewish families arrived from Holland in 1658. Their congregation took the name Jeshuat Israel.

Portuguese Jews after 1740 made Newport rich and busy. Jacob Rodrigues-Rivera brought sperm-oil making to America. Aaron Lopez became New England's great merchant prince. He owned thirty vessels when the Revolution began. The town's synagogue, finished in 1763, still stands today. Its cemetery was bought in 1677 by two merchants. The Revolution ruined Newport's trade and scattered its Jews. In 1790 the congregation addressed President Washington in friendship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novoaleksandrov: Novoaleksandrovsk is a Russian city in the Kovno government. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The census of 1897 counted 6,370 people there. No fewer than 4,277 of them are Jews. Artisans number 445 among the Jewish residents. Sixty pupils study in the Talmud Torah. Thirty small ḥadarim teach 240 more children. A private Jewish school opened in 1897. Two charities aid the sick and the poor. One synagogue and five prayer houses serve the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onias-from-hebr:
Onias was the name of high priests of the Second Temple. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The order here rests on the works of Josephus. Those works are not sound on all points, the piece warns. Josephus lacked good sources for this span of time.

Onias the First was son of Jaddua, by that account. Some link him to Areus, a king of Sparta. That link may rest on a forged set of letters. Onias the Second was son of Simon the Just. He was a boy when his father died young. His uncles held the high priest's post till he grew. Josephus calls him a man of greed and small wit. He would not pay the tax due to Egypt's king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottinger-jacob-: Jacob Joseph Öttinger was a German rabbi at Berlin. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Glogau in the year 1780. He died at Berlin on November 7, 1860. He read with Hirsch Samose and learned the rabbis' books well. In 1820 he was called to Berlin as a help rabbi. Five years on he was made the town's acting rabbi. His firm stand on Reform is stressed in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pentapolis-i-e-:
Pentapolis is a Greek word for a group of five cities. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Bible world knew three such groups. Each group lay in a different land. The name works like Decapolis, a group of ten.

The first group is the cities of the plain. Sodom and Gomorrah head that famous list. The second group is the five Philistine cities on the coast. Gaza and Gath belong to that group. The third group stood in Cyrenaica, in north Africa. Jews carried their war of 70 there as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-sir-be:
Sir Benjamin Samuel Phillips was lord mayor of London. He was born there in 1811 and died there in 1889. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He began as a tailor's son in the family firm.

Phillips built Faudel, Phillips and Sons with his brother-in-law. He served the Board of Deputies for thirty years. He fought long to lift the legal bars on Jews. London made him alderman, then sheriff, then lord mayor in 1865. He raised a vast cholera fund in that term. Queen Victoria knighted him for his service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plock-plotzk-12:
Plock was a government of Russian Poland, on the Vistula. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1897 it held 50,473 Jews among 553,094 souls. No Pale government held fewer Jews in all. Its towns each get their own short notice.

The capital, also called Plock, held 10,000 Jews. They formed over a third of the whole city. Synagogues, a Talmud Torah, and a hospital served them. Hasidic feeling kept the rabbinate changing hands. Seventeen years in the chair counted as very long. Mlawa and Przasnysz held thousands of Jews each.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posquieres-or-o:
Posquières, also called Vauvert, is a town in the Gard in France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews are known to have lived there since the twelfth century. Benjamin of Tudela came to the town about 1165. He found a community of forty members there.

At the head of the town stood Abraham ben David. His school drew students from lands far away. He gave them a warm welcome in his own home. In 1172 he spent a short time in prison. His foe had him seized on a charge. The entry follows the town through those years of fame and strain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psalms-midrash-:
Midrash Tehillim is an old Jewish tale-note on the Psalms. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It has been known since the eleventh century. Nathan of Rome cites it in his word book. Isaac ibn Ghayyat cites it in his law book as well.

Rashi cites the work on many Bible verses. It is called Agadat Tehillim in some of those places. From the twelfth century men called it Shoher Tob too. That name caused mix-ups with a like work on Proverbs. The article sorts out the names, the age, and the prints. It shows how the tales gloss the psalms verse by verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovitz-josh:
Joshua ben Elijah Rabinovitz was a Russian rabbi of the Minsk land. Isidore Singer and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Shat near Kaidan in 1818. He died at Nesvizh in 1887. His father, known as Elijah Ragoler, taught him Talmud. That home schooling made him a rabbi in his teens.

At eighteen Rabinovitz wed the daughter of a rich man of Kletzk. He then led the yeshivah of that town. In 1847 he became its rabbi as well. Twenty years on, Nesvizh called him to its rabbinate. He served that town for the rest of his life. The entry keeps the bare bones of a rabbi's career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rebekah-12610:
Rebekah was the wife of Isaac and daughter of Bethuel. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, and the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Genesis tells how Abraham's servant found her at a well. She drew water for him and his camels.

The article follows her life after that meeting. She stayed childless for nineteen years, then bore twins. Those twins were Jacob and Esau. At Gerar she and Isaac claimed to be siblings. Later she helped Jacob win the blessing meant for Esau. She urged Jacob to flee to her brother Laban. A rabbinical part debates her age at marriage. The entry joins a Bible story to later debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reuss-eduard-wi:
Eduard Wilhelm Reuss was a Protestant theologian born on July 18, 1804. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Strasburg. He died there on April 15, 1891.

The article says he studied Oriental languages at Halle and Paris. Gesenius and Silvestre de Sacy were his teachers. In 1834 he became a professor in his native city. He claimed his first lectures set out a bold thesis. The Priestly Code was the latest layer of the Pentateuch. Graf and Wellhausen later won fame for that same view. Reuss translated the whole Bible into French. That work filled sixteen volumes from 1874 to 1888. He also wrote a history of the Old Testament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romanelli-samue:
Samuel Aaron Romanelli was a Neo-Hebrew poet born on September 19, 1757. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Mantua. He died at Casale Monferrato on October 17, 1814.

The article calls him gifted but unsteady in habits. He traveled early, spending four years in Morocco. His popular book describes those experiences in Barbary. He later lived in Berlin, Vienna, London, and Lille. He supported himself by teaching and occasional poems. Weddings and patriotic feasts commissioned much of that verse. His scoffing at religion made him many enemies. He lived in great poverty for most of his life. He translated plays and the prayer book between languages. The entry paints talent without stability or ease.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothschild-davi:
David Rothschild was a German rabbi and author born at Hamm, Westphalia, on November 16, 1816. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He began as a preacher in his native town of Hamm.

In 1850 Rothschild was called as rabbi to Aachen, and in 1862 to Alzey. He stood with the Reform movement in German Judaism. His first book, from 1847, examines the oath of the Jews theologically. He published the Psalms with reflections and prayer, plus an Aachen prayer book. A late work, from 1877, defends the philosophy of Spinoza.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jaco:
Samuel ben Jacob ibn Jam' was rabbi of a North African community in the twelfth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He stood on intimate terms with Abraham ibn Ezra.

Ibn Ezra dedicated his Hai ben Mekiz to Samuel in friendship. He also praised Samuel's three sons, Judah, Moses, and Jacob, in the dedication. Samuel wrote a supplement to Nathan ben Jehiel's great dictionary, the Aruk. Extracts of it were printed from a Parma manuscript centuries later. Two Arabic works, on slaughtering law and on ethics, are credited to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schottlander-ju:
Frederick T. Haneman joined Isidore Singer to write this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Julius Schottländer. He was a German merchant. Schottländer was born at Münsterberg, in Silesia, on March 22, 1835. He set up there as a wool and grain merchant. In 1859 he moved his business to Breslau. From 1864 to 1869 he leased the Mittel mill from that city.

Schottländer supplied armies in two wars. He contracted for the sixth Prussian corps in 1866. He served the third German army in 1870 and 1871. Later he worked in milling, mining, cement, bricks, and sugar. He also dealt in real estate. In 1890 he retired to a large farm in Silesia. He gave largely to charities in Breslau and Münsterberg. He also spent much to beautify his home town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semalion-13410:
Semalion is a puzzling name found in a passage about the death of Moses. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Ancient commentators disagreed over whether the name meant a man or an angel. Modern scholars link it to a Greek word meaning giving a sign.

Rashi took Semalion for a scholar, while others made him an angel. Later sources name an angel Semalion who rules a month and a season of the sun. The entry also notes a Greek use as a title of Zeus. Short as it is, the piece shows how one unclear word drew centuries of debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shaving-13510:
Shaving covers the Bible's rules and customs about cutting hair and beards. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the topic. Mosaic law bars shaving the corners of head and beard. Priests get a special warning not to break that ban.

Ezekiel tells priests neither to shave bare nor let locks grow long. They should only poll, or clip, their heads neatly. The Talmud describes a costly layered cut worn by nobles. High priests had it done each Friday, and kings each day. Common folk shaved close, keeping only ear-locks and beard ends. The entry shows how hair marked rank, cost, and holiness in ancient Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-nethan:
Simeon ben Nethaneel was a tanna of the first generation, pupil of Johanan ben Zakkai. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He married into the family of Gamaliel the First. His own family was a noble priestly line.

His teacher praised Simeon for piety and fear of sin. Simeon taught that man's best habit is foresight. One should weigh the outcome of each deed carefully, he said. The worst practice to shun is failing to pay debts. No legal rulings by Simeon have been preserved at all. One sentence on prayer shows his deep piety clearly. Never neglect the Shema and daily prayer, he urged. Beg mercy in prayer, and let conscience accuse you of nothing. The entry keeps a moral teacher's voice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-smol-von-derenb:
Smol von Derenburch, or Samuel of Derenburg, was a court banker. Isidore Singer and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He served the archbishops of Magdeburg in the fourteenth century. He died after October 5, 1382. Two brothers, Marquard and Ephraim, helped him in his deals.

Records show Smol acting for the archbishop in many matters. In 1365 he sat on a commission over a salt mine dispute. In 1366 his name stood on the archbishop's bond. Archbishop Peter gave Smol and his children special privileges in 1372. Pope Gregory XI rebuked that favor in a letter from Avignon. Smol had set up a synagogue in a former chapel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinberg-samue:
Samuel Steinberg was a Hungarian historian born at Güssing on December 16, 1857. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at Gratz, where he earned his doctorate in 1882. In 1895 he became a lecturer at the University of Vienna.

In 1901 Steinberg was appointed professor of history at the German University of Prague. He wrote essays for historical journals on many topics. His work focused most on the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. In 1897 he published a book of German diplomatic reports. The short entry gives readers his career path and main field of study. It shows how Jewish scholars held posts at major universities of the time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-summons-14110:
A summons is a court order that calls a defendant to appear. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. A court messenger carried the writ for the rabbis. Ignoring it counted as contempt of court. Village servers had to try at least three times.

Court sat on Mondays, Thursdays, and the Monday between. If the messenger missed the man, his wife could take the notice. A neighbor could receive it as well. A defendant who skipped three court days faced contempt. He then had thirty days to apologize. Failure meant excommunication by the court. The entry quotes a sample contempt order in full. Readers see how rabbinic courts enforced their authority in practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tallit-14210:
The tallit is the fringed prayer shawl of Jewish worship. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Men wear it over their clothes at prayer. Custom once limited it to married men. Modern practice adds boys after their bar mitzvah.

A tallit spreads out flat like a sheet. Weavers make it of wool or silk in white. Black or blue stripes mark its ends. Fringes called zizit hang from its four corners. Numbers commands those fringes in the Mosaic law. The pious prefer coarse wool from the Holy Land. Such a shawl is nicknamed the Turkish tallit. Russian wool runs finer and almost pure white. American silk mills at Paterson now supply most silk ones. The entry details a garment's cloth, bands, and making.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-of-solom:
Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem, the first Temple, is the subject here. George A. Barton wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It follows the accounts in Kings and Chronicles. Solomon built for seven years, starting in his reign's fourth year.

David had bought the site and stored materials for the building. Hiram of Tyre sent skilled workmen and timber from Lebanon. The stone house stood sixty cubits long and was overlaid with gold. Its innermost room, the Holy of Holies, held two huge cherubim. Their wings met in the center and touched both walls. The article walks through the porch, side chambers, and courts in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-titles-of-hebre:
Hebrew books are known by their titles, not their authors' names, this article notes. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Students cite Pene Yehoshua without knowing who wrote it. Bibliographers therefore list Hebrew books by title first.

Tradition credits the Great Assembly under Ezra with Bible titles. Torah, Prophets, and Writings named the three great parts. The five books of Moses later took their opening words as names. Bereshit, Shemot, and the rest came from first key words. Talmud sections took titles from their contents instead. Geonic works followed the same habit. Saadia's Book of Creeds and Opinions is one example.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-frederik-:
Frederik Jacob Trier was a Danish physician of high standing in Copenhagen. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born there in 1831, he died there in 1898. He took his medical degree in 1860. His essay on duodenal ulcer won early notice.

From 1861 he edited a leading medical weekly for thirteen years. He also co-edited a Nordic medical archive journal. His university named him professor in 1881. From 1874 he served as resident physician at the Communal Hospital. He presided over the medical section of an 1884 congress. That congress drew physicians from many countries to Copenhagen. He also helped revise the Danish pharmacopoeia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ury-adolphe-sim:
Adolphe Ury was an Alsatian rabbi who rose to lead Strasburg's community. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Niederbronn in 1849, he studied at Strasburg's lyceum. Paris's rabbinical seminary gave him doctor and chief rabbi degrees. His thesis treated arts and trades of ancient Jews.

He became rabbi of Lauterburg in 1875 at twenty-six. Brumath called him to its rabbinate ten years later. In 1886 he began teaching Bible and history at Strasburg. That school closed for lack of funds in 1890. Lorraine then chose him chief rabbi, seated at Metz. In 1899 he became chief rabbi of Strasburg and Lower Alsace. He still held that post in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wechselmann-ign:
Ignaz Wechselmann was a Hungarian architect and philanthropist. He was born at Nikolai, in Prussian Silesia, in 1828. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Budapest on January 17, 1903. He studied at Berlin and then at Vienna. There he assisted the architect Ludwig Förster.

In 1856 Wechselmann moved to Budapest for Förster. He supervised the building of the great synagogue there. Most grand buildings raised in Budapest before 1890 were his designs. They include palaces, mills, churches, and the Burg Bazar. Failing eyesight ended his career in 1890. His will gave millions to blind institutes and teachers. Half the aid went to Jews, half to Christians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiernik-peter-1:
Peter Wiernik was a Russo American journalist. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Wilna in March 1865. His father, a preacher, taught him Talmud at home. Otherwise he was self taught. In 1885 he emigrated to the United States.

Wiernik settled first in Chicago. He began as a typesetter on the Jewish Courier. Within five years he rose to its editor. In 1898 he moved to New York. He has worked on Yiddish papers there since. He now serves on the Morgen Journal staff. He also contributes to the Jewish Encyclopedia itself. His History of the Jews appeared in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-woolf-edward-15:
Edward Woolf (1803-1882) was a musician and novelist who worked in London and New York. Cyrus Adler and Abram S. Isaacs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in London, he led bands in that city first. In 1839 he crossed the sea to New York.

In New York he led bands and taught music. He sang as choir chief in a synagogue as well. He wrote tales for The Jewish Messenger in its early years. Three of his novels are named in the entry. His five sons all won note in their own fields. One taught art in New York for forty years. One wrote plays and songs for the stage. One drew street scenes that made him famed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zweifel-lazar-e:
Lazar Zweifel was a Russian writer who defended Hasidism and made peace between Jewish factions. Herman Rosenthal and Judah David Eisenstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Moghilef on April 15, 1815, he died at Gluchof on February 18, 1888. From 1853 he lectured at the rabbinical seminary of Jitomir, until it closed in 1874.

Zweifel built his books from excerpts of rabbinical works, which fill most of his pages. His best-known work, Shalom al-Yisrael, defends Hasidism in four volumes. It traces Hasidic ideas to Maimonides, Bahya, and Luzzatto, and to Luria's Cabala. He also defended the Karaites, spoke kindly of Reform, and wrote poetry in Hebrew and Yiddish.
jonson-alchemist-1610:
Ben Jonson, Shakespeare's great rival and friend, wrote The Alchemist for the King's Men in 1610. Jonson set the comedy in a London emptied by plague. A master has fled the city, leaving his house to a scheming servant.

The servant Face joins the fake alchemist Subtle and the prostitute Dol Common to run a confidence shop. Gullible visitors pay for lucky charms, magic metals, and astrological advice, each greedier than the last. Jonson's plot spins faster and faster until the master returns at the worst moment. The play is a brilliant machine of greed, disguise, and comic justice, still a favorite on stage.
journal-of-discourses-vol-10:
Plural marriage meets open defense in Volume Ten, published in 1863. Young argues the doctrine from the Tabernacle pulpit without flinching. The nation, deep in civil war, is dared to object if it will.

Sermons ground plural marriage in scripture and in claimed revelation. Speakers frame the practice as a test of faith and obedience. The prophet stands at his most defiant in these bold discourses. Outsiders read such pages to grasp what made Utah so distinct. The volume remains key for anyone studying the doctrine's public face in Utah. Its frankness sets it apart from later, more guarded treatments.
lehmann-mysticism-heathendom-1910:
Edvard Lehmann was a Danish scholar of religion whose Mysticism in Heathendom and Christendom appeared in English in 1910. The book is a comparative study of mystical experience across faiths, East and West. Lehmann writes with a historian's caution about wild claims.

He surveys ecstasy in Greek cults, Sufi Islam, Hindu devotion, and Christian monastic life, noting shared patterns and real differences. His calm method treats mystics as witnesses to be weighed, not as saints or frauds by default. The book helped comparative religion find a sober voice on its most heated topic. Readers meet a guide who respects each faith's own account of itself.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-10:
Part Ten reaches Chapter 46, on enchantments and enchanters. Twain arrives too late for New Orleans's great annual Mardi-Gras. He recalls seeing the Mystic Crew of Comus twenty-four years earlier. Knights and nobles wore Paris-made gorgeousness for one night only.

Giants, dwarfs, and grotesques followed in the torchlit procession. Modern spectacle, he hears, far exceeds that memory in splendor. A secret Rex leads followers whose identities stay hidden. The mystery, Twain judges, serves romance rather than police fears. Gentlemen of position fill Rex's following, proud of belonging. Romance, not police, explains their hidden personalities, Twain says.
love-s-labour-s-lost-pg1510:
Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost opens in the King of Navarre's park. King Ferdinand and his lords Berowne, Longaville, and Dumaine plan a life of study. They swear to fast, to sleep little, and to see no women. The Princess of France then arrives on her father's business.

Her ladies Rosaline, Maria, and Katharine match the lords wit for wit. Don Armado, a fantastic Spaniard, and Costard the clown add foolery. The schoolmaster Holofernes piles learned nonsense on every scene. Love letters go astray, and disguises fool no one for long. At the end, Marcadé brings news that turns comedy grave.
manning-fourth-dimension-simply-explaine:
Henry Parker Manning put this book out in 1910 from the pages of Scientific American. The press had run a prize bout for the best plain tale of the fourth dimension. Manning took the post of editor for the set. The book holds the best of the prize texts.

Clear tales show cubes, shadows, and flat worlds used to hint at higher space. Each writer finds a fresh way to make the hard thought plain. The bout brought the fourth dimension to a mass crowd in the States. The book stands as a key source on how the idea went wide.
mark-twain-a-biography-volume-iii-part-2:
Volume three, part two of Paine's biography closes the life, 1907 to 1910. A chapter on honors from Oxford opens this final part. Old Clemens travels to Bermuda with his friend Twichell once more. They seek their landlady of thirty years before, and find her daughter instead.

The island is as fresh and full of bloom as ever, he finds. Such gentle scenes fill the last years at Stormfield. Twain jokes, rages, and charms his way toward the end. He died in 1910, with Halley's comet that had attended his birth. Paine's farewell is tender, full, and authoritative. No life of Twain has ever replaced this one.
mark-twain-s-letters-complete-1853-1910:
Mark Twain's Letters, complete for 1853 to 1910, fill six volumes here. Albert Bigelow Paine arranged them with comment throughout. His foreword claims a man's letters reveal him most truly. Not literary letters, but those written under the press of circumstances.

Twain, he says, was a man of few restraints and no affectations. In letters as in talk, he spoke what was in his mind. The collection is not a full life story, but its supplement. Pilot, miner, husband, father, and bankrupt all write in turn. Rage, jokes, grief, and business fill the thousands of pages. Together they form the essential self-portrait of Mark Twain.
mark-twain-s-letters-volume-6-1907-1910:
Volume six of Mark Twain's Letters, 1907 to 1910, is the last. It opens with letters of 1907 and an Oxford degree. The new home at Redding, his Stormfield, rises in these pages. A February letter thanks J. Howard Moore for The Universal Kinship.

Moore had praised Twain's concern for the general welfare of mankind. Twain answers that the book speaks his own long-cherished opinions. Age, loss, and honors crowd the final correspondence. His daughter Jean's death darkens the last Christmas. The letters end only months before his own death in 1910. They form a moving farewell in his own voice.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-10: Tenth in the series, etext 3560 holds volume ten by Bourrienne. A year, 1809, is printed in the head note with its title. Widger produced the file, last changed in November 2001 by its own note. Yet the sample preserves nothing beyond that head matter and license. No readable memoir passage appears anywhere in it. The honest record for this entry is therefore short: author, volume, and file history alone.
my-novel-volume-10:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's tenth book argues the world stays much the same. He quotes Charron on wisdom's uneven spread among men. No one thinks his own share of judgment too small, Charron notes. The tale, Lytton says, proves that dry remark.

Riccabocca builds his rules of life on Machiavelli's great book. Randal Leslie turns knowledge into a tool for outwitting honest folk. Dick Avenel fights his way up with blows and kicks. Baron Levy stands for gold itself, cold and magnetic. The volume weighs old vices in new dress, and finds human nature stubbornly unchanged.
nasa-tm-19660023504-range-safety-data-fo:
G W Solmon and E L Leonard, of the Range Safety Section at Marshall, issued this data report on June 17, 1965, for the Saturn SA-10 flight. Range safety protects people and property if a launch goes wrong. Its data define where debris could fall and when a flight must be ended. The section sat inside Marshall's Flight Mechanics Branch, in the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory.

Reliability analysis of upper stages forms part of the supporting work, per the catalog note. Two upper stages, S-IV-8 and S-IV-10, are named there. Safety data had to be ready before SA-10 could be cleared to fly. Reports like this one are the written base on which a launch day go decision rested.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-10:
Chrysostom's homilies on the Gospel of Matthew fill volume ten of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, from 1886. There are ninety of them, preached at Antioch around 390. Philip Schaff's set gives them in full English dress.

Sermon by sermon, Chrysostom walks through Matthew's gospel, explaining the text and then turning it on his hearers. Rich dress, theater-going, swearing, and neglect of the poor all take their hits. His style is direct, vivid, and full of pictures from daily life. The Matthew homilies are the largest surviving body of preaching from the early church. They still set a standard for verse-by-verse preaching.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-10:
Ambrose of Milan's selected works and letters fill volume ten of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Ambrose, a Roman governor made bishop by popular cry, became the model of a bishop who could face down emperors. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

His treatise on the duties of clergy reworks Cicero for the church. Other works treat the sacraments, virginity, and the Holy Spirit, and his hymns taught the West to sing its faith. The letters show him rebuking Emperor Theodosius after a massacre and forcing public penance. Augustine, who heard him preach and took baptism from him, stands in his debt. The volume is the Latin church finding its voice.
nietzsche-genealogy-morals-samuel-1910:
Friedrich Nietzsche published The Genealogy of Morals in 1887, three linked essays on where morals come from. The English text here is Horace B. Samuel's translation of 1910. Nietzsche traces good and evil to a revolt of the weak against the strong. Slave morality, born of resentment, redefined weakness as virtue.

The second essay traces guilt and bad conscience to old debts and punishment. The third asks what ascetic ideals mean for priests, scholars, and artists. Nietzsche's method of genealogy shaped later ethics and cultural critique. The prose is fierce and clear. Few books question morality with such force.
nostradamus-les-propheties-french-1710:
Michel de Nostredame, called Nostradamus, wrote his famed verse forecasts in 16th century France. The text here is a French printing of 1710, in the tongue his first readers knew. The work is known in short as the Centuries, for its sets of one hundred verses.

Each verse is a quatrain, a four line rhyme full of dark hints and strange names. Kings, wars, and plagues fill the lines, though the sense is left for readers to guess. The book made its author the most famed seer of the West, and debate on it never ends.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume ten completes Penzer's Ocean of Story, the ten-volume edition of Tawney's Kathasaritsagara begun in 1924. Somadeva's frame closes as Naravahanadatta wins his fated place among the Vidyadharas. The ocean of story, gathered in eleventh-century Kashmir from centuries of Indian tale, comes to rest at last.

Penzer's final apparatus rounds out a comparative index of motifs unmatched in its day. Tawney's translation, honored here in full, had waited forty years for such an edition. Scholars of folklore treat the set as a working library in itself. General readers finish with the sense of having sailed a whole literature. No English story collection of the age attempts this scale and completes it.
openalex-w1969593010:
Lutz Roewer and a large international team studied Native American genes. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in the year 2013. In Europe and Asia, genes track language and geography. Such matching evidence was lacking for South America. The team tested Y-chromosome variation across the continent.

They compared genetic patterns with languages and with place. The title reports a continent-wide decoupling of the three. Genes did not follow language or geography as expected. That split sets South America apart from other continents. The result reshaped views of the continent's peopling. It warns against simple stories of migration and settlement.
openalex-w1978700210:
Daniel Bausch and Lara Schwarz wrote this outbreak analysis. It appeared in the year 2014 in the catalog record. Ebola virus disease had returned, this time in Guinea. Over 350 cases were counted at their writing. The case fatality ratio stood near seven in ten.

The culprit was the Zaire ebolavirus species, they report. It is the most lethal Ebola virus known. Fatality ratios can reach nine in ten cases. The title frames the outbreak as ecology meeting economy. Poverty, forests, and weak health systems shape spread. The piece urges response that fits local conditions.
openalex-w1987104810:
Moisés Selman, Annie Pardo, and Naftali Kaminski wrote this review. Their paper is dated 2008 in the catalog record. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis scars the lungs without known cause. Embryonic signals guide lung growth before birth in humans. Those signals also govern cell change and tissue talk.

The authors discuss evidence that such programs restart wrongly. Switched-on developmental pathways may drive the scarring process. Epithelial cells and their neighbors miscommunicate in the disease. That framing suggests new drug targets in those pathways. It also explains why the disease resists simple repair. The review shaped later thinking on lung fibrosis.
openalex-w2007400810:
Juan Santos, Luis Coloma, Kyle Summers and colleagues traced the origins of Amazon frogs. Their paper appeared in PLoS Biology in 2009. The Amazon holds a huge share of world amphibian diversity. The team asked where that diversity came from. They focused on poison frogs and their relatives.

They rebuilt the frog family history with gene data. They also dated key splits and mapped ancestral ranges. Their results rejected an Amazon origin for the group. The Andes were the main source of lineages entering Amazonia. Many Amazon lineages arrived in the late Miocene. Diversity rose after repeated arrivals and local spread.
