plaw-111-269-2010: Public Law 111-269 is the Indian Veterans Housing Opportunity Act of 2010. It changes one term in the Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act of 1996. Under that act, disability pay from the Department of Veterans Affairs no longer counts as income for a family. The rule covers pay for service-linked disabilities of a family member, and survivor pay of the same kind. The act was approved on October 12, 2010.
plaw-111-270-2010: Public Law 111-270 of 2010 extends the time given to build a visitor center at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. The power rests with the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund, Inc., under a 1980 law. The act rules that references in title 40 of the code to a seven-year span for such projects count, for this one, as a span ending November 17, 2014. The act was approved on October 12, 2010.
plaw-111-271-2010:
Public Law 111-271 carries the long title Redundancy Elimination and Enhanced Performance for Preparedness Grants Act. It amends the Homeland Security Act of 2002. Its targets are the reporting duties tied to homeland security preparedness grants.

The act orders the FEMA chief to report to Congress within 90 days on redundant reporting demands placed on state, local, and tribal grant holders. The report must list each item of data the agency asks for in running the grants. The act's stated second aim is to build real performance measures for those grant programs. Covered grants include those under sections 2003 and 2004 of the Homeland Security Act.
plaw-111-272-2010:
Public Law 111-272 is the Law Enforcement Officers Safety Act Improvements Act of 2010. It amends title 18 of the United States Code. The subject is the right of law officers to carry concealed weapons across state lines.

The act makes clear that Amtrak Police officers, Federal Reserve officers, and federal executive branch officers count as qualified law officers under the section. It defines firearm to include ammo that federal law does not ban, while leaving out machine guns and silencers. It also ties the loss of the right to discipline that could end in suspension or loss of police powers.
plaw-111-273-2010:
The Secure and Responsible Drug Disposal Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-273. It amends the Controlled Substances Act to allow take-back disposal of controlled substances in set cases. Congress aimed at the misuse of prescription drugs left in home cabinets.

The findings call nonmedical use of prescription drugs a growing problem, above all among teens. They cite a Justice Department report that overdose deaths from prescription opioids rose 114 percent from 2001 to 2005. One report cited found a third of new abusers in 2006 were aged 12 to 17. Congress tied the problem to prescription drugs kept at home, where teens can reach them.
plaw-111-274-2010:
The Plain Writing Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-274. It requires that federal documents issued to the public be written clearly. Its stated purpose is clear government communication that the public can understand and use.

The act defines a covered document as one needed to get a federal benefit or service, or to file taxes, or one that explains such a benefit or a duty. Plain writing is defined as writing that is clear, concise, and well organized. The act then sets duties for agencies to prepare for and meet these standards.
plaw-111-275-2010:
The Veterans' Benefits Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-275. It amends title 38 of the United States Code and the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. Its aim is to improve the laws run by the Veterans Affairs chief.

Title I covers jobs, small business, and schooling, with items on work-study aid, training for veterans' employment staff, and an energy jobs program for veterans. It also names a Pat Tillman Veterans' Scholarship Initiative. Title II turns to housing and homelessness, starting with new funding for the Homeless Veterans Reintegration Program. The act was approved on October 13, 2010.
plaw-111-276-2010: Public Law 111-276, approved October 13, 2010, names a post office building in San Jose, California. The Postal Service site at 4285 Payne Avenue is now the Anthony J. Cortese Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in April 2010 and the Senate that fall.
plaw-111-277-2010: Public Law 111-277, approved October 13, 2010, names a post office building in Brighton, Michigan. The Postal Service site at 100 Orndorf Drive is now the Joyce Rogers Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in July 2010 and the Senate in late September.
plaw-111-278-2010: In Public Law 111-278, approved October 13, 2010, Congress named a post office building in Cleveland, Ohio. The Postal Service site at 13301 Smith Road is now the David John Donafee Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in July 2010 and the Senate in late September.
plaw-111-279-2010: Public Law 111-279, approved October 13, 2010, names a post office building in Los Angeles, California. The Postal Service site at 3894 Crenshaw Boulevard is now the Tom Bradley Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in July 2010 and the Senate in late September.
plaw-111-280-2010: Public Law 111-280 is the WIPA and PABSS Extension Act of 2010. In two one-line changes to the Social Security Act, it extends two programs by one year. The Work Incentives Planning and Assistance program and the Protection and Advocacy for Beneficiaries of Social Security program both run through 2011 instead of 2010. The act also adds a yearly report duty for groups funded under the first program, covering the benefits advice they gave.
plaw-111-281-2010:
The Coast Guard Authorization Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-281. It authorizes appropriations for the Coast Guard for fiscal year 2011. Title I also sets the approved levels of military strength and training for the service.

Title II holds a long list of Coast Guard matters. The contents name civilian Coast Guard judges, pay back of medical travel costs, and Coast Guard entry into the Armed Forces Retirement Home system. Other items cover grants to world maritime groups, a report on sexual assaults in the Coast Guard, and the home port of Coast Guard vessels in Guam.
plaw-111-282-2010:
Public Law 111-282 is the United States Secret Service Uniformed Division Modernization Act of 2010. Its sole purpose is a move of legal text from one code to another. Pay and hours rules for current members of the Uniformed Division sat in the District of Columbia code.

The act moves those rights into the United States Code, as a new chapter 102 in title 5. The chapter's contents list terms and rules for basic pay, starting pay rates, and service step adjustments. They also cover technician posts, promotions, demotions, and clothing allowances. It was approved on October 15, 2010.
plaw-111-283-2010:
The Pre-Election Presidential Transition Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-283. It amends the Presidential Transition Act of 1963. Before this act, federal transition help for a winning candidate began only after the general election.

The act lets the head of the General Services Administration offer set transition services and facilities to major party candidates before the voting. The notice must come within days after the last nominating convention and must spell out what is on offer. A candidate who accepts gets the help from that point until election day. The act was approved on October 15, 2010.
plaw-111-284-2010:
Public Law 111-284 is the Mount Stevens and Ted Stevens Icefield Designation Act of 2010. It names a mountain and an icefield in Alaska for Ted Stevens, who served in the Senate from 1968 to 2009. The findings call him Alaskan of the Century, as named by the Alaska Legislature in 2000.

The findings trace his life from wartime service as a transport pilot with the Flying Tigers, where he won two Distinguished Flying Crosses. They recall his work as a United States Attorney and as a top lawyer at the Interior Department. There he helped win the law that made Alaska the 49th state in 1959.
plaw-111-285-2010: Public Law 111-285 of 2010 extends a spending deadline for disaster aid grants. The funds are extra Social Services Block Grant money given to the Department of Health and Human Services after disasters in 2008. Under this act, the money stays open for spending through September 30, 2011. The money flows through the Administration for Children and Families. Congress also tagged the act as an emergency measure under the budget rules in force at the time.
plaw-111-286-2010:
Public Law 111-286 is titled The Physician Payment and Therapy Relief Act of 2010. Its first part amends the Social Security Act rule set by an earlier 2010 act on Medicare doctor pay. That rule had set a payment update for June through November 2010.

The act stretches that update through December 31, 2010, one month more. Its second part softens a payment cut for therapy services paid under the same fee schedule. For services from January 1, 2011, the cut for multiple therapy services in one visit is 20 percent instead of the 25 percent set in a late 2010 agency rule.
plaw-111-287-2010:
Public Law 111-287 is the International Adoption Simplification Act of 2010. Congress passed it in late 2010. It restores two carve-outs for children adopted from abroad by United States citizens under the Hague pact on cross-border adoption. One carve-out concerns proof of shots, and the other concerns the age limit for siblings.

The act amends the Immigration and Nationality Act so the shot-proof carve-out reaches the Hague adoption class. It then rewrites the sibling rule for a child under 16 filed as an immediate relative. The child must be adopted in a Hague state, or be coming from one to be adopted here. Among its terms, officials must be sure that proper care will be given to the child once admitted.
plaw-111-288-2010: Public Law 111-288, approved November 30, 2010, names a post office building in Lynbrook, New York. The Postal Service site at 100 Broadway is now the Navy Corpsman Jeffrey L. Wiener Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the Senate in July 2010 and the House in November.
plaw-111-289-2010: Public Law 111-289 is a joint resolution of the 111th Congress that sets one date. It appoints the day for the first session of the 112th Congress to begin. That session is to open at noon on Wednesday, January 5, 2011. The resolution was approved on November 30, 2010, after passing the Senate and then the House in mid-November.
plaw-111-290-2010: Public Law 111-290 is a joint resolution making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2011. It does so with a single date change to the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011, Public Law 111-242. In place of that act's earlier cutoff date, it inserts December 18, 2010. The change kept the federal government funded for two more weeks. The resolution was approved on December 4, 2010.
plaw-111-291-2010:
Public Law 111-291's enacted short title is the Claims Resolution Act of 2010. It is a settlement law passed by the 111th Congress in December 2010. Its titles settle long-running claims against the federal government.

Title I settles the Individual Indian Money Account court case. Title II funds the final settlement of claims from the Black Farmers discrimination court case. Title III, the White Mountain Apache Tribe Water Rights Quantification Act, approves a water rights deal for that tribe. Its parts cover the tribe's water rights, waivers of claims, and a rural water system.
plaw-111-292-2010:
The Telework Enhancement Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-292. It orders the head of each executive agency to set up a policy under which staff may telework. Telework means doing one's job from an approved site other than the normal office.

The act adds a new chapter 65 on telework to title 5 of the United States Code. The chapter sets terms for agency telework duties, staff training and oversight, and policy support. It creates a Telework Managing Officer post in each agency. It also requires reports on how the programs are working.
plaw-111-293-2010:
Public Law 111-293 of 2010 is called the Help HAITI Act, short for Help Haitian Adoptees Immediately to Integrate Act. It helps orphans from Haiti who were paroled into the United States after the earthquake of January 12, 2010. The parole policy had been announced on January 18, 2010.

The act lets the Homeland Security chief adjust such an orphan's status to lawful permanent resident. The child must be in the United States, be admissible as an immigrant, and apply within three years. No more than 1,400 children may gain status this way. The act was approved on December 9, 2010.
plaw-111-294-2010:
The Animal Crush Video Prohibition Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-294. It amends title 18 of the United States Code to ban interstate commerce in animal crush videos. Such videos show animals being crushed or otherwise killed for a sexual fetish.

Congress found that every state and the District of Columbia already ban extreme cruelty to animals, such as crushing, burning, drowning, or impaling. It reasoned that many crush videos are obscene and so fall outside free speech protection. It also found that grave cruelty is part and parcel of making and selling these videos.
plaw-111-295-2010:
Public Law 111-295 is the Copyright Cleanup, Clarification, and Corrections Act of 2010. As its name says, it tidies the copyright laws rather than remaking them. Most of its changes are made to title 17 of the United States Code.

One part eases Copyright Office procedures, so a sworn certification for recording a document may be sent in electronic form. Another part repeals an expired section, section 601, and fixes the heading of chapter 6. That chapter now reads Importation and Exportation, matching its place in the code's contents. The act was approved on December 9, 2010.
plaw-111-296-2010:
The Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-296. It reauthorizes the federal child nutrition programs. Title I of the act is called A Path to End Childhood Hunger.

That title's first part reforms the National School Lunch Program, with easier direct sign-up, foster children counted as eligible, and grants to grow school breakfast programs. Other parts cover the Summer Food Service Program and meals in child and adult care. They also cover the food program for women, infants, and children, known as WIC. It was approved on December 13, 2010.
plaw-111-297-2010: Public Law 111-297, approved December 14, 2010, names a federal building in Pensacola, Florida. The building at 100 North Palafox Street is now the Winston E. Arnow Federal Building. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name. The bill passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 1 of that year.
plaw-111-298-2010: Public Law 111-298, approved December 14, 2010, names a federal building and courthouse in Rapid City, South Dakota. The building at 515 9th Street is now the Andrew W. Bogue Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name. The bill passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 1 of that year.
plaw-111-299-2010: Public Law 111-299, approved December 14, 2010, names a Government Printing Office building in Pueblo, Colorado. The building at 31451 East United Avenue is the Frank Evans Government Printing Office Building. The name holds for the span in which the building is occupied by the Government Printing Office. During that span, any mention of the building in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name.
plaw-111-300-2010: Public Law 111-300, approved December 14, 2010, names a post office building in Fall River, Massachusetts. The Postal Service site at 2 Government Center is now the Sergeant Robert Barrett Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in November 2010 and the Senate on December 2.
plaw-111-301-2010: Public Law 111-301, approved December 14, 2010, names a federal building in Baltimore, Maryland. The building at 6401 Security Boulevard, long known as the Social Security Administration Operations Building, is now the Robert M. Ball Federal Building. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name. The bill passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 1.
plaw-111-302-2010:
The Coin Modernization, Oversight, and Continuity Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-302. It gives the Treasury chief power to research new materials for the nation's coins. It also raises congressional oversight of coin production and keeps some collector items going.

The act lets the chief test metallic materials inside or outside the Treasury and seek input from labs and coin metal suppliers. In that work the chief must weigh the effect on current suppliers. The chief must also weigh how new coins would work in daily use, in vending machines, and in coin handling gear.
plaw-111-303-2010:
The American Eagle Palladium Bullion Coin Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-303. It authorizes a new bullion coin made of palladium, a precious metal. Congress meant it to give buyers a cheaper way to invest in precious metals.

The coin is a 25-dollar piece weighing one troy ounce of .9995 fine palladium, in a size the Treasury chief sets. Minting waits for a marketing study sent to the chief and to Congress. The chief must buy palladium mined in the United States first, where that is feasible, and may turn to other sources when it is not.
plaw-111-304-2010: Napa, California's post office building on 2nd Street now carries the name of Tom Kongsgaard. Public Law 111-304 made the change, with approval on December 14, 2010. The building stands at 1351 2nd Street. Its full name under the act is the Tom Kongsgaard Post Office Building. When a federal law, map, regulation, or record mentions the building, that name is the one it must use. The House passed H.R. 6237 in November 2010, and the Senate passed it on December 2.
plaw-111-305-2010: Public Law 111-305 renamed a post office building in Eureka, California, for Sam Sacco. Approved December 14, 2010, the act covers the Postal Service building at 337 West Clark Street. It is now the Sam Sacco Post Office Building. That name controls in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records. The measure, H.R. 6387, passed the House in November 2010 and cleared the Senate on December 2.
plaw-111-306-2010:
Public Law 111-306 of 2010 requires the accreditation of English language training programs. It amends the Immigration and Nationality Act, the law that sets who may enter the United States. The change touches the student visa class used for language study.

After the change, such a student must attend an accredited language training program. Accredited means approved by an accrediting body that the Education chief recognizes. The rule starts 180 days after the act. A three-year grace span lets certified programs that are still seeking accreditation keep taking such students. The act was approved on December 14, 2010.
plaw-111-307-2010: Public Law 111-307 is the Asian Carp Prevention and Control Act of 2010. With one added clause, it places the bighead carp on the federal list of injurious species in title 18 of the code. The clause names the species by its Latin name, Hypophthalmichthys nobilis. Species on that list may not be imported into the United States or shipped between states. The act was approved on December 14, 2010.
plaw-111-308-2010:
The Federal Buildings Personnel Training Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-308. It provides for the training of the people who run federal buildings. The work falls to the head of the General Services Administration.

Within 18 months, that head must name the core skills such staff need, after asking trade groups and training providers and taking public comment. The skills cover building operations and upkeep, energy management, water saving, and safety, including electrical safety. For each skill, the agency must name a course, certificate, degree, or license that proves it. Staff must then show each skill within one year.
plaw-111-309-2010:
The Medicare and Medicaid Extenders Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-309. It extends a set of expiring rules in the Medicare and Medicaid programs. Title I of the act is a list of those extensions.

The list covers a doctor payment update, hospital wage reclassifications, and a floor on geographic pay adjustments. It extends an exceptions process for therapy caps and add-on payments for ambulance services and mental health care. It also extends the Qualifying Individual program, Transitional Medical Assistance, and special diabetes programs. Title II then holds a few added fixes, such as a repeal of a delay in a payment system.
plaw-111-310-2010: Public Law 111-310, approved December 15, 2010, names a post office in Washington, D.C. The Postal Service site at 2 Massachusetts Avenue, NE, is now the Dorothy I. Height Post Office. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 2.
plaw-111-311-2010:
Public Law 111-311 is the Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation Act, called the CALM Act for short. It orders rules on the volume of audio on television commercials. The rulemaking falls to the Federal Communications Commission.

Within one year, the Commission must adopt a rule that makes a named industry practice on audio loudness for digital television binding. The rule reaches broadcast stations, cable operators, and other multichannel video providers, but only as to the ads they transmit. It takes effect one year after adoption. A provider in financial hardship may win a one-year waiver, with one renewal.
plaw-111-312-2010:
The Tax Relief, Unemployment Insurance Reauthorization, and Job Creation Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-312. Its printed purpose line speaks of airport funds, copied in error from an earlier bill, but its contents are tax law. The act amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

Title I extends, for a time, the tax relief first passed in 2001 and 2003, and again in 2009. Title II extends relief from the alternative minimum tax, with a higher exemption amount. It also extends AMT relief for nonrefundable personal credits. It became law on December 17, 2010. Each extension is labeled temporary in the contents.
plaw-111-313-2010:
The Truth in Fur Labeling Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-313. It amends the Fur Products Labeling Act to improve how fur goods are labeled. The core change ends a labeling exemption for goods with only a small amount of fur.

With the exemption struck, such goods must be labeled like other fur products, starting 90 days after the act. The act adds a narrow new exemption for face-to-face sales by the person who trapped or hunted the animal, at a home or craft fair. It also orders the Federal Trade Commission to review its Fur Products Name Guide within 90 days.
plaw-111-314-2010:
Public Law 111-314 of 2010 enacts a new title of the United States Code. Title 51, called National and Commercial Space Programs, gathers existing laws on national and commercial space programs into one place. It is a codification act, not a new space policy.

The act states that its aim is to match the understood intent of Congress in the original laws. In restating them, it removes ambiguities, contradictions, and other flaws. Its later parts make matching changes to other laws, set transitional and savings terms, and repeal the old texts now restated in title 51.
plaw-111-315-2010:
Public Law 111-315 of 2010 amends the Water Resources Development Act of 2000. It extends and reshapes a program under which outside public bodies may pay to speed up Army permit reviews. The permits concern projects or activities for a public purpose under Army jurisdiction.

The Army chief may take and spend such funds, after public notice, to hasten the review of that body's permit. The act adds guards to keep decisions impartial in fact and in process. Reviews paid for this way must be checked by the district or division commander and must use the same steps as any other permit review.
plaw-111-316-2010: Public Law 111-316 of 2010 improves office operations for the Architect of the Capitol. The Architect runs the Capitol grounds and buildings. Section 1 lets the Architect set basic pay for up to 32 staff posts. The top rate is the highest Senior Executive Service rate for the area. Section 2 frees leftover funds from fiscal years 2007 through 2010. Those funds were given for Capitol Police buildings and grounds. They may now be used to acquire real property for the Capitol Police, by purchase, lease, or transfer.
plaw-111-317-2010: Public Law 111-317 is a joint resolution making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2011. Like the joint resolution passed days before it, it works by changing one date in the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011. That date becomes December 21, 2010. The change bought three more days of federal funding while Congress finished its work. The resolution was approved on December 18, 2010.
plaw-111-318-2010:
The Social Security Number Protection Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-318. Its aim is to limit access to Social Security account numbers. It amends the Social Security Act in two ways.

First, no federal, state, or local agency may print a person's Social Security number, or any part of it, on a check the agency issues for payment. That ban starts with checks issued three years after the act. Second, no such agency may employ prisoners, or hire them by contract, in any job that would let them reach other people's Social Security numbers.
plaw-111-319-2010:
The Red Flag Program Clarification Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-319. It amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act as to the identity theft guidelines that apply to creditors. Those guidelines are the red flag rules on spotting identity theft.

The act narrows the term creditor for this part of the law. It covers creditors who use consumer reports, send data to credit bureaus, or advance funds to a person. It leaves out a creditor who advances funds only for costs tied to a service that creditor itself provides. An agency may still pull in other creditors by rule where accounts face a real risk of identity theft.
plaw-111-320-2010:
The CAPTA Reauthorization Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-320. It reauthorizes the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act. It also renews three more laws. Two are the Family Violence Prevention and Services Act and the Abandoned Infants Assistance Act of 1988. The third is the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment and Adoption Reform Act of 1978.

Title I updates the findings in the child abuse act with fiscal year 2008 data. About 772,000 children were found by states to be victims of abuse and neglect that year. Close to a third of child deaths from maltreatment were blamed on neglect alone. The act was approved on December 20, 2010.
plaw-111-321-2010:
Public Law 111-321 is the Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010. Its printed purpose line speaks of small business programs, a leftover from the bill's earlier form, but the text repeals the ban on open service by gay troops. That ban sat in section 654 of title 10 of the code.

Section 2 rests on a full review of repeal ordered by the Defense chief on March 2, 2010. The review weighs effects on readiness, unit cohesion, recruiting, and family readiness. It also weighs training, rules on conduct, facilities, and benefits, and any needed changes to military justice law.
plaw-111-322-2010:
The Continuing Appropriations and Surface Transportation Extensions Act, 2011 is Public Law 111-322. Its printed purpose line speaks of military construction spending, a leftover from the bill vehicle. Its first title in fact extends the continuing funding law for 2011.

Title I moves the end date in the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011 to March 4, 2011. It also adds a new section 147 that defines who counts as an employee and who counts as a senior executive. Those terms set the reach of a federal pay provision that follows in the act. It was approved on December 22, 2010.
plaw-111-323-2010:
The Hoh Indian Tribe Safe Homelands Act is Public Law 111-323. It takes land into trust for the Hoh Indian Tribe, whose homeland lies by the Hoh River. A map dated May 14, 2009, shows the parcels at issue.

One parcel is about 37 acres of federal land run by the National Park Service, south of the Hoh River. From the date of the act, all United States rights in that land are held in trust for the tribe, with no further step needed. The act also deals with about 434 acres of land the tribe already owns.
plaw-111-324-2010:
Public Law 111-324 of 2010 reauthorizes and enhances Johanna's Law. That law backs a national campaign to raise public awareness of gynecologic cancers. It amends section 317P of the Public Health Service Act.

The act adds 18 million dollars for the campaign for fiscal years 2012 through 2014. It also orders the Health chief to consult nonprofit gynecologic cancer groups when running the campaign. Those groups must work both to conquer such cancers and to reach out to state and local bodies. Their advice guides best practices for sharing cancer facts with varied groups of people.
plaw-111-325-2010:
The Regulated Investment Company Modernization Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-325. It amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to update rules for regulated investment companies. Such companies are the legal form behind most mutual funds.

Title I covers how these companies carry capital losses from year to year. Title II adds saving rules for firms that fail the gross income and asset tests. Title III turns to dividends and payouts, covering dividend labels, earnings and profits, and the pass-through of tax-free interest dividends and foreign tax credits in a fund of funds.
plaw-111-326-2010: Public Law 111-326, approved December 22, 2010, names an airport traffic control tower in Spokane, Washington. The tower at Spokane International Airport, and any successor tower at that site, is the Ray Daves Airport Traffic Control Tower. Any mention of the tower in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name. The bill passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 9 of that year.
plaw-111-327-2010:
The Bankruptcy Technical Corrections Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-327. It makes technical corrections to title 11 of the United States Code, the bankruptcy code. Most fixes relate to changes made by Public Law 109-8, the big bankruptcy reform of 2005.

The corrections are small and precise: a phrase added twice to a definition of a debtor's home, a widened term for patient records, and fixed cross-references. One swap changes a cite from section 362(n) to 362(o). Another strikes a stray section number from a list. None of the fixes states a new policy.
plaw-111-328-2010:
The Kingman and Heritage Islands Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-328. It amends the National Children's Island Act of 1995. The subject is two islands in the Anacostia River held by the District of Columbia.

The act widens the uses the District may make of Kingman and Heritage Islands. Use for recreation, environmental, or school purposes is no breach of the 1995 act, so long as it fits two plans. Those are the Anacostia Waterfront Framework Plan of November 2003 and the District's Comprehensive Plan. The plans named were both drawn up for the District's growth and its riverfront.
plaw-111-329-2010: Public Law 111-329 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2010, Part IV, the fourth such stopgap that year. It moves the end date for the fuel and ticket taxes that fund the Airport and Airway Trust Fund from December 31, 2010, to March 31, 2011. The trust fund may keep spending through April 1, 2011. The act also extends the airport improvement program, with effect from January 1, 2011.
plaw-111-330-2010: Public Law 111-330 of 2010 makes only technical corrections to the Coast Guard Authorization Act of 2010, Public Law 111-281. The fixes take effect as if made when that act passed. One inserts missing opening quotation marks in a quoted passage. Another fixes a misspelling, changing stewrdship to stewardship. Others swap single words, such as part for section, and renumber quoted sections. No fix changes the sense of the 2010 act.
plaw-111-331-2010:
The Truth in Caller ID Act of 2009 is Public Law 111-331, enacted in December 2010. It amends the Communications Act of 1934 to bar the faking of caller identification data. The practice is often called spoofing.

The act makes it unlawful to cause a caller ID service to send false or misleading data with intent to defraud, cause harm, or gain something of value wrongly. The ban reaches both phone services and internet voice services. It does not bar a caller from blocking their own number. The act also orders the Federal Communications Commission to write rules within six months.
plaw-111-332-2010:
Public Law 111-332 bears the short title National Foundation on Fitness, Sports, and Nutrition Establishment Act. It sets up a foundation to back the work of the President's Council on Fitness, Sports and Nutrition. The foundation is a charitable nonprofit corporation, not a federal agency.

Working with the Council's office, the foundation lists programs and events where joint private and public effort would help. It promotes private gifts of money and property for those activities. It may not accept any federal funds. Section 3 of the act sets up its board of directors.
plaw-111-333-2010: Public Law 111-333 is the Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site Designation Act. It gives a Massachusetts historic site a longer name. The Longfellow National Historic Site in Cambridge is now the Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site. Any mention of the old name in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the new name. The act was approved on December 22, 2010.
plaw-111-334-2010: Public Law 111-334 of 2010 amends the Act of August 9, 1955, the law on leases of Indian trust land. It adds five tribal landholdings to the list of lands that may be leased for up to 99 years. The additions are trust land of the Coquille Indian Tribe and of the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians. They also cover the Confederated Tribes of the Coos, Lower Umpqua, and Siuslaw, the Klamath Tribes, and the Burns Paiute Tribe. The act was approved December 22, 2010.
plaw-111-335-2010:
Public Law 111-335 is the Longline Catcher Processor Subsector Single Fishery Cooperative Act. It concerns fishing vessels that catch and process fish in the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands. The Commerce chief may approve one fishery cooperative for that subsector.

Approval requires a request from members holding at least 80 percent of the subsector's licenses. No member may take more than 20 percent of the Pacific cod open to the subsector, apart from quota held for community development groups. The subsector must file its cooperative contract with the chief by November 1 each year.
plaw-111-336-2010: Public Law 111-336 of 2010 makes a small change to the Act of August 9, 1955, on leases of Indian trust land. In one clause it adds land held in trust for the Kalispel Tribe of Indians and the Puyallup Tribe of Indians. In a second clause it adds the Puyallup Tribe, the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community, and the Kalispel Tribe. The act was approved on December 22, 2010.
plaw-111-337-2010:
The Early Hearing Detection and Intervention Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-337. It amends the Public Health Service Act on the early finding and treatment of hearing loss in young children. The section it rewrites is section 399M of that act.

The act widens the program from infants to newborns and infants and adds diagnosis to its screening and treatment aims. States must build systems for hearing screening, prompt follow-up testing, and fit medical, hearing, and school help for children found with hearing loss. The act stresses family-to-family support in the first months after a child is identified.
plaw-111-338-2010: Public Law 111-338 is the Formerly Owned Resources for Veterans to Express Thanks for Service Act of 2010, or FOR VETS Act. It amends title 40 of the code on gifts of federal surplus goods. The change adds one class of groups that may receive such goods through state agencies. The new class is a group whose members are substantially veterans and whose spokespeople are recognized by the Veterans Affairs chief. The act was approved on December 22, 2010.
plaw-111-339-2010:
Public Law 111-339 of 2010 requires reports on the management of Arlington National Cemetery. It was passed after errors in gravesite records at the cemetery came to light. Two reports are due within one year of the act.

The Army chief must account for the gravesites, stating whether each is rightly identified, labeled, and occupied, and must give a plan and timetable to fix any faults found. The Comptroller General must report on how contracts at the cemetery are managed and overseen. That review covers contracts to automate burial operations and the computer systems used for them.
plaw-111-340-2010:
The Museum and Library Services Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-340. It amends and extends the Museum and Library Services Act, the law behind the federal agency that funds museums and libraries. Title I holds general terms.

Those terms cover definitions, the duties of the agency's Director, staff, and the board, plus awards, research, and hearings. Title II turns to library services and technology, with funding, state plans, and grants. It also covers the Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian Program, which trains librarians. The act was approved on December 22, 2010. Grants flow to the states under set state plans.
plaw-111-341-2010: Public Law 111-341 is the Criminal History Background Checks Pilot Extension Act of 2010. It extends the Child Safety Pilot Program set up by the PROTECT Act. The program lets youth-serving groups run criminal history checks on volunteers and staff. The act does so by striking the words 92-month in that law and inserting 104-month. The act was approved on December 22, 2010.
plaw-111-342-2010:
The Preserving Foreign Criminal Assets for Forfeiture Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-342. It amends title 28 of the United States Code. Its target is the proceeds and tools of foreign crime held inside the United States.

The act rewrites the part of that title on restraining orders. To keep property open to seizure under foreign law, the government may ask a court for such an order at any time, before or after a foreign nation starts its forfeiture case. The order must follow the due process guards set for like orders in title 18.
plaw-111-343-2010: Public Law 111-343 of 2010 orders the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to fully insure Interest on Lawyers Trust Accounts. Such an account is a trust account set up by a lawyer or law firm for a client, known by the short name IOLTA. The act works by widening a term in the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, as added by the Dodd-Frank Act. The widened term counts such a trust account as a noninterest-bearing transaction account. The change took effect on December 31, 2010.
plaw-111-344-2010:
The Omnibus Trade Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-344. It extends trade adjustment assistance and certain trade preference programs. It also amends the Harmonized Tariff Schedule to change some duty rates for a limited time.

Title I extends trade adjustment assistance, the aid program for workers hurt by foreign trade. A second part of that title improves health coverage for those workers. It makes the health credit cheaper, extends COBRA benefits for some aid recipients and pension plan retirees, and adds coverage through voluntary employee groups. It was approved on December 29, 2010.
plaw-111-345-2010:
The Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act is Public Law 111-345 of 2010. It guards consumers against hard-sell tactics on the internet. Congress passed it after a Senate committee probe into online sales tricks.

The findings say hundreds of trusted online shops shared buyer billing data, even card numbers, with outside sellers in return for payments. That sharing was called data pass. The outside sellers then used misleading tactics to bill millions of buyers for membership clubs they did not want. Congress found this had shaken trust in online commerce and harmed the economy.
plaw-111-346-2010: Public Law 111-346 is the Helping Heroes Keep Their Homes Act of 2010. It extends added mortgage guards for service members that were due to expire. The guards sit in the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, as strengthened by a 2008 housing law. With two date swaps, the end of the enhanced guards moves from December 31, 2010, to December 31, 2012. A linked start date moves from January 1, 2011, to January 1, 2013. The act was approved on December 29, 2010.
plaw-2010: Hotaru Nakama Ferschke is the beneficiary of Private Law 111-2, approved on December 22, 2010 (S. 1774). The act makes her eligible for an immigrant visa or for adjustment of status to lawful permanent resident, setting aside the caps in the Immigration and Nationality Act. Entry before the filing deadline counts as lawful entry for her adjustment. She had two years to file with fees, and the Secretary of State then reduces her birth country's visa pool by one.
plos-pbio-0020110:
Vincenzo Costanzo, Tanya Paull, and Max Gottesman examined a DNA damage alarm protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mre11 gathers with partner proteins where DNA breaks. The team found that Mre11 can also line up short, straight DNA pieces and build signaling groups on them.

Those groups switch on the cell's damage response, the system that pauses growth and starts repair. Showing that Mre11 can assemble them on simple DNA helps explain how the alarm starts so fast. Faults in this system cause human disorders with high cancer risk. A clear view of the first steps gives researchers firm ground for studying those diseases.
plos-pone-0000010:
Pierre Smeesters, Anne Vergison, Dioclécio Campos, and co-authors compared the same germ in two very different places in 2006. Group A Streptococcus is the bacterium behind strep throat and, at its worst, rheumatic fever. Its strains vary by region. The team charted that variation in Belgium and in Brazil.

Their epidemiologic landscape compares which strep types circulate in each country and how common each one is. The differences matter for vaccine design, because a vaccine aimed at European strains may miss Brazilian ones. The study is a reminder that a germ's map is local, and prevention plans must be drawn country by country.
plos-pone-0000110:
K. P. Arunkumar and Javaregowda Nagaraju surveyed insect and worm DNA in PLOS ONE in 2006. A palindrome in DNA reads the same forward and backward. The control region of the mitochondrial genome, which manages how that genome is copied, turned out to hold unusually long palindromes in insects and nematodes.

Long palindromes can fold the DNA into hairpin shapes, which may help or hinder copying. Finding them concentrated in the control region hints they do a job there rather than sitting as clutter. The survey spans many species, so the pattern is broad. It gives genome readers a feature to check when they sequence new mitochondrial genomes, and a clue about how those genomes run.
plos-pone-0000210:
José Fayos and Carolina Fayos published this applied computing paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It uses Kohonen neural networks, a type of self-organizing map, to mine wind data. Data mining here means sorting large wind records into patterns that forecasters and engineers can use.

Wind patterns drive weather forecasts, wind farm output, and building safety. A neural network that groups wind behavior into clear types can make those records easier to read. The paper shows the approach at work, an early example of machine learning applied to routine meteorological data.
plos-pone-0000310:
Isaias Glezer, Ariel Chernomoretz, Samuel David, and colleagues published this neuroimmunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inflammation in the nervous system can save neurons or kill them. The authors identify genes involved in the balance between neuronal survival and death during inflammation.

Which way inflammation tips decides outcomes in stroke, injury, and diseases like multiple sclerosis. A gene list for that balance gives researchers defined targets to push toward survival. The work maps the molecular side of a long-observed clinical puzzle. The pattern also offers a way to test drugs meant to protect neurons during brain inflammation.
plos-pone-0000410:
David Bressler, Nicole Spotswood, and David Whitney reported a surprising brain signal in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In fMRI scans, most active brain areas show a stronger blood signal, but some show a negative one, a dip called the negative BOLD response. It was often treated as noise or as mere shutdown. The team tested what the dip in the visual cortex actually carries.

The authors found that the negative response holds precise, stimulus-specific information about what the person was seeing. That makes the dip a signal worth reading rather than discarding. Brain imaging studies that use it could extract more detail about how the visual system represents the world.
plos-pone-0000510:
Maxence Vieux-Rochas and colleagues used vitamin A's active form to probe how vertebrate jaws arose, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Retinoic acid can cause craniofacial malformations when its levels are wrong during development. The team studied the molecular dynamics of those malformations, drawing implications for the origin of gnathostome jaws, the hinged jaws of most vertebrates.

Jaws were a revolution in animal evolution, and their origin from gill arches is a classic problem. A chemical that predictably reshapes the face exposes the gene circuits that pattern it. Linking those circuits to the jaw's first appearance connects a birth-defect mechanism to one of evolution's biggest inventions.
plos-pone-0000610:
Enikö Sonkoly and colleagues asked whether tiny RNA regulators help drive a common skin disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that fine-tune gene activity. The paper was titled MicroRNAs: Novel Regulators Involved in the Pathogenesis of Psoriasis? It examined their role in psoriasis. In that disease, skin cells multiply too fast and inflammation persists.

If microRNAs are mis-set in psoriatic skin, they could explain changes across many genes at once, a pattern single-gene studies struggled to unify. The question mark in the title was honest for 2007. MicroRNA research was young. The paper was among the early tests of its reach into skin disease.
plos-pone-0000710:
Eleanor M. Weston, Adrian E. Friday and Pietro Liò measured faces for evidence that mate choice shaped human evolution. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study considers sex differences in facial structure in the context of development. At puberty, the height of the upper face, between lip and brow, develops differently in males and females. Those differences, they show, are not explicable by simple size or growth accounts alone.

Biometric evidence of that kind supports sexual selection as the shaping force. Faces carry signals used in judging mates, so selection could sculpt them directly. If so, the hominin face records social and mating pressures, not just diet, climate, and ancestry.
plos-pone-0000810:
Lucia Regales, Marissa N. Balak, Yixuan Gong and colleagues built mice whose lung tumors carry a drug-resistance mutation, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The EGFR T790M mutation confers acquired resistance to kinase inhibitors in human lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR mutations. It is occasionally detected before treatment, and may also confer genetic susceptibility to lung cancer. Studying its role in tumor formation needed a living model.

The team developed mice with lung tumors expressing the T790M mutant. Such models let researchers watch resistance arise, and test next-generation inhibitors against it in a whole animal. Lung cancer drugs often fail exactly at this mutation, so a faithful model is strategic ground for drug development.
plos-pone-0000910:
Nicola Viebig, Emily Levin, Sebastien Dechavanne and colleagues disabled a malaria gene and watched what changed, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Malaria in pregnancy is a major cause of illness and death for mothers and newborns. Much of the harm comes from infected red blood cells sticking in the placenta in huge numbers.

The sticking depends on a parasite gene called var2csa. The team disrupted that gene and report that the placental adhesion trait was impaired. A result like this matters for vaccine hopes: a protein needed for sticking is a natural target. It also confirms, by removal, what var2csa actually does.
plos-pone-0001010:
Tara Young, Michael Tsai, Bin Tian and colleagues showed that ordinary gene messages can free a stalled transcription engine, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A factor called P-TEFb is a key regulator that lets gene reading run at full length. It first drew wide notice as a factor HIV needs to copy itself.

P-TEFb is often held back by a small RNA called 7SK. The team report that cellular messenger RNA can activate transcription elongation by displacing that 7SK RNA. In other words, the products of gene reading help release the brake on further reading. The finding adds a feedback loop to a central control in gene expression.
plos-pone-0001110:
Cedric Laguri, Rabia Sadir, Patricia Rueda and colleagues characterized a new variant of a cell guiding signal, in PLOS ONE in 2007. CXCL12 is a chemokine that steers cell migration and tissue homing for many cell types. It works through its receptor CXCR4 and through heparan sulfate, a sugar chain on cell surfaces.

An alternative splicing route produces a gamma isoform with an extra piece. The team show that piece is an unstructured, positively charged domain that regulates the signal's activity and its binding to both partners. A tail that changes grip changes where cells are sent. Migration signals guide development, immunity and cancer spread alike.
plos-pone-0001210:
Histones are the spool proteins DNA wraps around, and chemical marks on them help control gene activity. Kangling Zhang and colleagues catalogued those marks in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Studies in mammals and yeast had found some marks conserved at the same positions and others unique.

The authors report distinctive core histone post-translational modification patterns in Arabidopsis. Post-translational modifications are chemical tags added after a protein is built. A plant-specific map of these tags supports work on gene regulation in crops and in the field's favorite model plant.
plos-pone-0001310:
Therapeutic antibodies are often built as chimeras: mouse variable regions, which grab the target, joined to human constant regions, which the body tolerates. Marcela Torres and colleagues asked whether the constant regions are truly interchangeable, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They exchanged murine and human immunoglobulin constant chains and measured the consequences.

The authors report effects on the kinetics and thermodynamics of antigen binding, and on chimeric antibody autoreactivity. In other words, the supposedly passive half of the antibody changes how the working half behaves. Antibody engineers need to know that the scaffold is not neutral.
plos-pone-0001410:
Aurore Schneider, Jonathan Garlick, and Christophe Egles wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gel that may speed wound healing. Skin wounds that fail to heal cause lasting harm and high care costs. The team used tiny self building protein fibers as a scaffold for repair. They combined this nano scale tool with skin care methods.

In their tests, the fiber scaffold sped the closing of the wound surface. New skin grew over the wound at a faster rate. A scaffold that the body takes well could help chronic wounds that now resist care. The work is an early step toward dressings built at the level of molecules.
plos-pone-0001510:
Ashverya Laxmi and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on light and a plant hormone carrier. Light steers many steps of plant growth. Root growth is shaped by light sensed in the shoot, with the hormone auxin as the courier. The team asked how light moves a key auxin carrier inside root cells of Arabidopsis.

They show light is vital for where the carrier, called PIN2, sits in the cell. That seat sets the flow of auxin through the root. A light to carrier link helps explain how shoots and roots grow in step. It also matters for crops grown under changed light.
plos-pone-0001610:
Melanie Sekeres and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on gaps in trial registers. Since 2004, top journals have asked that all trials be logged in a public register at the start. World and journal bodies set what each log should hold. The team checked how well logs report who leads each trial on the science side.

They found leadership facts are oft left poor or blank in the logs. That gap hides who is in charge and who to hold to account. Registers can only build trust if their fields are filled with care. The study gives register keepers a clear fix list.
plos-pone-0001710:
Jing Huang, Qini Gan, Limin Han, and their co-authors studied a lifespan-linked protein in aging human cells for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Sir2, a protein that uses NAD to remove chemical tags from other proteins, modulates lifespan in yeast, worms, and flies. Its mammal counterpart is SIRT1, which also helps cells survive stress.

The team asked whether extra SIRT1 can fight ordinary cellular senescence, the state where old cells stop dividing. They report that SIRT1 overexpression antagonizes senescence, with the ERK and S6k1 pathways switched on. The full text gives the fibroblast tests and the pathway data. The work adds molecular detail to the long-running question of whether sirtuin-boosting drugs could slow cell aging.
plos-pone-0001810:
Chia-Chyi Liu, Shiang-Chi Lee, Michael Butler, and their co-authors compared vaccine production cells for dengue virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Dengue has four serotypes, DEN-1 to DEN-4, and a vaccine must grow all of them stably. The team investigated replication kinetics of the four serotypes in Vero cells and MRC-5 cells grown on Cytodex 1 microcarriers. One virus, DEN-4, was recovered from an infectious cDNA clone.

They report high genetic stability of dengue virus propagated in MRC-5 cells compared with Vero cells. The full text gives the growth curves and mutation counts. A production cell line that keeps the virus unchanged is valuable, since drift during manufacture can weaken or alter a vaccine.
plos-pone-0001910:
Annalisa Grimaldi and co-authors used treated mats to draw stem cells out of tissue in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Stem cells take their cues to become a given cell type from signals around them. Though research is intense, how this shaping works at the base level is still not fully clear.

The team placed mats soaked with growth factors into living tissue, then gathered the cells that moved in. The trapped cells showed a range of traits, giving the lab many cell types to study from one pull. A simple way to harvest stem cells where they live could aid both basic study and future repair work.
plos-pone-0002010:
Zhong-jin Yang and co-authors tested an artificial oxygen carrier's effect on brain blood flow in rats, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The carrier, Oxycyte, is a perfluorocarbon emulsion that carries oxygen far better, volume for volume, than blood. The brain guards its own blood flow tightly to meet its need for fuel.

The team thinned the rats' blood to a set volume with the emulsion and measured regional flow in the brain. If a blood substitute starves or floods the brain, it is not safe, however well it carries oxygen. Flow data of this kind are a needed safety check before human use.
plos-pone-0002110:
Agata Kolodziejczyk and co-authors catalogued signal chemicals in the first relay of the fly's visual system, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The lamina is the most peripheral synaptic region of the fruit fly's visual system, and its wiring has been comprehensively described. It is used as a model for how synapses develop and adapt, yet its neurotransmitters were less fully mapped.

The team charted components of signaling by glutamate, GABA, and acetylcholine, three main nerve messengers, in lamina cells. A chemical parts list completes the wiring diagram: form plus chemistry is what a circuit model needs to predict behavior.
plos-pone-0002210:
Nicole Cameron and co-authors studied how a rat mother's care shapes her daughters' later reproductive life, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In humans, early family life predicts the age of puberty, teen sexual activity, and the age of first pregnancy. Like patterns appear in other species, where mothers pass effects to offspring without changing DNA.

The team examined how varied maternal care in rats programs sexual behavior and the hormone system that runs reproduction, the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Their work shows early care can set lifelong patterns in the brain and body. Findings like these frame how early life gets under the skin.
plos-pone-0002310:
Ayelet Di Segni, Keren Farin, and Ronit Pinkas-Kramarski reported a new binding partner for a family of cancer receptors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The ErbB receptor family sits on cell surfaces and drives growth signals. These receptors are major contributors to malignant change and are overproduced in many human cancers.

The authors identify nucleolin, a protein best known from the nucleus, as a new interacting partner of ErbB receptors. A partner can change how a receptor signals, how long it stays active, and how drugs reach it. Each new connection in the ErbB web offers another point where cancer signaling might be interrupted.
plos-pone-0002410:
A research team led by Zhang reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Jingxian Zhang, Balasubramanyam Addepalli, Kil-Young Yun, and others. Its subject is a Polyadenylation Factor Subunit Implicated in Regulating Oxidative Signaling in Arabidopsis thaliana. Plants respond to many unfavorable environmental conditions via signaling mediated by altered levels of various reactive oxygen species (ROS).

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002510:
Work from Edwards and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Albert O. Edwards, Sung J. Lee, Brooke L. Fridley, and others. Its subject is density of Common Complex Ocular Traits in the Aging Eye: Analysis of Secondary Traits in Genome-Wide Association Studies. Genetic association studies are identifying genetic risks for common complex ocular traits such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

The subjects used for discovery of these loci have been largely from clinic-based, case-control studies. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002610:
In 2008, Hiroi and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Makoto Hiroi, Teiichi Tanimura, Frédéric Marion-Poll, and others. Its subject is hedonic Taste in Drosophila Revealed by Olfactory Receptors Expressed in Taste Neurons. Taste and olfaction are each tuned to a unique set of chemicals in the outside world.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002710:
Catriona M. Harris led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was evaluating the influence of epidemiological parameters and host ecology on the spread of phocine distemper virus through populations of harbour seals. The catalog record names Catriona M. Harris first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Outbreaks of phocine distemper virus (PDV) in Europe during 1988 and 2002 were responsible for the death of around 23,000 and 30,000 harbour seals. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002810:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Mariana Gil and colleagues addresses does an insect's unconditioned response to sucrose reveal expectations of reward?. Authorship is credited in the record to Mariana Gil and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. We asked whether and how a sequence of a honeybee's experience with different reward magnitudes changes its subsequent unconditioned proboscis extension response (PER) to. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002910:
James Doroghazi and Daniel Buckley examined how soil bacterial communities are spread out in 2008. Ecologists describe such patterns with a species abundance distribution, which shows how many kinds are common and how many are rare. For microbes, the shape of that pattern had been hard to pin down.

Using a fingerprinting method called GC-TRFLP, the PLOS ONE study found evidence that soil bacterial communities follow a lognormal pattern. In that pattern, most kinds sit at middling counts with a long tail of rare ones. The result helps soil ecologists compare communities on a shared footing.
plos-pone-0003010:
Adam Coleman, Xiuli Yang, Manish Kumar and co-authors tested a Lyme disease protein long thought to aid immune evasion in 2008. Borrelia burgdorferi cycles between Ixodes ticks and mammal hosts. It makes at least five surface proteins that acquire complement regulators, thought to help it resist host defense.

One of them, CRASP-2, does not contribute to complement resistance or host infectivity, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, a clean negative result prunes the list of true evasion factors. Vaccine and drug efforts against Lyme disease can focus on proteins that actually matter. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003110:
Andreas Martin Lisewski applied information theory to protein folding errors in 2008. Transmission of genomic information from coding sequence to protein structure during synthesis is subject to random errors. Shannon's noisy channel theorem, from communication theory, sets limits on reliable transmission despite noise.

Random amino acid mutations and protein misfolding lead to a Shannon limit in sequence-structure communication, the title claims. Published in PLOS ONE, the framing treats the cell as a channel with a capacity limit. That view may explain why error rates in translation sit where they do. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003210:
Szymon M. Kiełbasa and Martin Vingron study self-regulating genes across vertebrates in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Feedback loops are the simplest building blocks of transcriptional regulatory networks, so their behaviour over evolution is of prime interest. The authors address whether the number of autoregulatory feedback loops is enriched in higher organisms. They begin by analysing such loops in available data.

The title reports that transcriptional autoregulatory loops are highly conserved in vertebrate evolution. Readers see a basic circuit kept across long spans of time, which suggests it does essential work. Conservation maps like this help separate core control design from lineage-specific extras.
plos-pone-0003310:
Lidia De Filippis, Daniela Ferrari, Laura Rota Nodari and colleagues immortalize human neural stem cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Human neural stem cells represent an essential source of renewable brain cells for both experimental studies and cell replacement therapies. Their relatively slow rate of proliferation and physiological senescence in culture make their use cumbersome under some experimental conditions.

The team use the c-Myc mutant T58A to immortalize the cells. Readers get a method to expand brain stem cells without the usual slowdown. A stable supply is needed before cell therapy or drug screening with human neurons can scale up.
plos-pone-0003410:
Walter R. J. Taylor and colleagues tested a flu drug delivery route in this 2008 study. The drug oseltamivir is the standard oral treatment for severe H5N1 bird flu. Very sick patients often cannot swallow pills safely. Doctors can give the drug through a nasal feeding tube instead.

The team measured drug levels in the blood of adult patients in Vietnam. Levels after tube dosing reached the range judged adequate for treatment. No injected form of the drug existed at the time. The result backs tube dosing when severe flu patients cannot swallow.
plos-pone-0003510:
Martin Löwer and co-authors catalogued secreted enzymes of the ulcer bacterium in this 2008 paper. Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach and causes lasting inflammation. Its exported proteases may drive that damage and even cancer risk. Proteases are enzymes that chew through proteins.

The team screened the bacterial proteome for proteins likely to be exported. Several candidate proteases emerged from that sequence screen. One, called HtrA, showed real proteolytic activity in tests. The inventory names suspects behind a very common chronic infection. This germ infects about half the world, though most carriers never feel it.
plos-pone-0003610:
Murali Krishna Ghatkesar and co-authors measured molecular binding with tiny beams in this 2008 paper. When two molecules bind, two physical changes occur. Their masses combine into one larger mass. The structure of at least one partner also changes, causing mechanical stress.

Their nanomechanics method reads those changes on a small cantilever. Bending beams thus report binding without labels or dyes. The approach characterizes molecular interactions more completely than mass alone. Such label-free tools serve drug screening and basic biology. Binding strength decides whether a drug works at all in the body.
plos-pone-0003710:
Jens M. Nygren and David Bryder published this blood study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Lifelong blood production rests on rare stem cells in the bone marrow. These hematopoietic stem cells were long viewed as mostly idle next to their fast-dividing offspring. Older tools could not count their divisions inside the body.

The authors built a new assay that traces a cell's division history in vivo. It showed that stem cells which divide faster lose their self-renewal power sooner. The trade-off helps explain how the blood system balances renewal across a lifetime.
plos-pone-0003810:
Marie Thibonnier, Jean-Michel Thiberge, and Hilde De Reuse published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Bacteria rescue ribosomes stuck on broken messages through a quality control system called trans-translation. It needs a small RNA, SsrA, and a partner protein, SmpB, to free the ribosome and tag the faulty protein.

In Helicobacter pylori, the ulcer bacterium, the team found this rescue system is essential for life. The protein tagging step is also required for resisting stress and for taking up DNA. Such an essential step is a potential weak point for new antibiotics.
plos-pone-0003910:
Charlotte Lahoute, Athanassia Sotiropoulos, Marilyne Favier, and co-authors studied muscle aging in mice in 2008. Aging muscle loses mass and gains fat and scar tissue, a decline called sarcopenia. Many genes shift with age in muscle, yet the drivers stay unclear. One candidate is serum response factor, a gene switch called SRF.

The team studied skeletal muscle that lacks SRF. Such muscle showed signs of aging ahead of schedule. The result names SRF as one guard against early muscle decline. It offers a lead for research on keeping strength later in life. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004010:
Roosa Leimu and Markus Fischer pooled studies of local adaptation in plants in a 2008 meta-analysis. Local adaptation means populations thrive best in their home conditions. The idea matters for evolution, conservation, and climate change work. How general it is in plants had not been systematically judged.

Their PLOS ONE article combines results from many plant studies. They also ask which species, population, and habitat traits shape adaptation. A pooled view shows where home advantage is strong or weak. That guides seed transfer and planting choices under climate change. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004110:
Jeremy R. Haag, Olga Pontes, and Craig S. Pikaard studied two plant-specific polymerases in 2009. Plants have five nuclear RNA polymerases, more than other eukaryotes. Polymerases IV and V are found only in plants. They drive small-RNA-guided DNA methylation, which silences genes.

Their PLOS ONE article tests the metal-binding sites of Pol IV and Pol V. Both metal A and metal B sites proved required for silencing. Without them, siRNA-dependent methylation failed. The result confirms these polymerases work as true enzymes in the pathway. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004210:
Han-Jun Jin, Chris Tyler-Smith, and Wook Kim published this population genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Koreans are generally classed as a northeast Asian group based on geography. Yet Y-chromosome studies had shown that the Korean population carries lineages from both southern and northern East Asia.

To untangle that history, the team analysed mitochondrial DNA, inherited from mothers, alongside Y-chromosomal markers inherited from fathers. Comparing the two sides of ancestry sharpens the picture of how Korea was peopled. The study weighs how much of the population came from each direction.
plos-pone-0004310:
Sarah Louie and colleagues published this signalling study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Wnt signals guide cell fate, proliferation, polarity, and movement as vertebrate embryos grow, acting through beta-catenin-dependent and independent pathways. Wnt signals are among the oldest in animal life. Dishevelled is a scaffold protein required for this signalling, gathering other proteins around it.

The team studied Hipk1, a protein that associates with Dishevelled. They report that Hipk1 tunes the beta-catenin signalling pathway. A modulator attached to the central scaffold can tune one of the embryo's most important signals up or down. Tuning it changes how cells read Wnt messages.
plos-pone-0004410:
Two opioid receptors push impulsivity in opposite directions. Mary Olmstead, Abdel-Mouttalib Ouagazzal, and Brigitte Kieffer report that split in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. Impulsivity is a primary feature of many psychiatric disorders, including ADHD and drug addiction.

Impulsivity covers failing to delay rewards and failing to withhold a motor response. Using a signaled nose poke task, the authors show mu and delta receptors regulate motor impulsivity oppositely. That contrast could guide drugs that tune one receptor but not the other. It refines models of addiction and self-control. Motor impulsivity is the urge to act, distinct from choosing delayed rewards.
plos-pone-0004510:
Two typhoid-causing Salmonella types arrived at the same deadly trick by different roads, show Wei-Qiao Liu, Ye Feng, Yan Wang, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. More than fourteen hundred Salmonella types cause gut illness that usually passes on its own. A few, including Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi C, cause typhoid, a whole-body infection that can kill.

It was not known whether the typhoid agents came from one common ancestor or evolved separately. Comparing their genes, the team found paratyphi C diverged from a gut relative, Salmonella choleraesuis. Its disease style converged with typhi's. In plain terms, nature invented typhoid more than once. That matters for vaccines, which may need to cover separate lineages.
plos-pone-0004610:
Thyroid hormone switches genes in the developing cerebellum, and Hongyan Dong, Carole Yauk, Andrea Rowan-Carroll, and co-authors mapped where it binds, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Thyroid hormone is critical to normal brain development, but the mechanisms operating in this process are poorly understood. Without enough of it, a child's brain development suffers lasting harm.

The team used a method called ChIP-on-chip, which fishes out DNA regions bound by a protein and identifies them on a chip. They sampled the cerebellum of mice fifteen days after birth and captured regions bound by the thyroid receptor beta. The resulting list of binding sites and target genes shows, concretely, which genes the hormone throws its switches on during a key window of brain growth.
plos-pone-0004710:
Chehani Alles and colleagues compared gene activity in breast cancers that lack the estrogen sensor, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Such cancers tend to have worse outlook, higher grade, and distinct traits under the microscope. Within them, one subgroup stands out for its own gene pattern and course.

The team merged many studies and ran gene set tests split by sensor status. They found raised activity of two growth drivers in the basal subgroup. Clear driver maps can help split breast cancer into truer types. That split guides which drugs to test for each type. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004810:
Stefan Koestler and colleagues measured F- and G-actin concentrations in lamellipodia of moving cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells protrude by polymerizing monomeric G actin into polymeric F actin at the tip of the lamellipodium. Filaments depolymerize toward the rear in a treadmilling process, supplementing the G actin pool for new rounds of polymerization at the advancing front edge.

Direct concentration measurements test that classic model. Values show how much building material is available locally. Quantitative data constrain models of cell crawling. Crawling underlies wound healing, immunity, and cancer spread. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004910:
Simon Reinke and colleagues studied influence of recovery and training phases on soccer players body composition and immunity, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Professional soccer players endure lengthy seasons with high physical stress maintained throughout. The recuperation period before next pre season is generally considered short but sufficient. The team tracked peripheral vascular function and immune system markers across recovery and retraining in elite athletes.

Recovery restores most markers but not all equally. Short off seasons may accumulate fatigue across careers. Monitoring guides individualized load management. Elite sport science informs occupational health. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0005010:
When a cell dies by apoptosis, its DNA is chopped into pieces. The first cuts were thought to land randomly. Miriam Di Filippo and Giorgio Bernardi showed otherwise in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used an entirely new approach on chicken liver cells. Their focus was early apoptotic DNA fragmentation.

The early cuts strike only a few specific regions. Those regions are open chromatin, where DNA is loosely packed. The precision suggests a programmed first strike. Random shredding comes later, if at all. The finding rewrites the opening chapter of cell death. It raises new questions about how the cutting machinery chooses its first targets.
plos-pone-0005110:
Dried bloodstains hold DNA that forensic scientists prize. Ancient DNA researchers prize it too. A worry was that aging hemoglobin damages that DNA. April Marrone and Jack Ballantyne tested the worry in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hemoglobin is the iron-carrying protein of red blood cells. In the dry state, it changes over time.

Those changes did not increase oxidative DNA damage. Dried blood keeps its DNA safer than feared. The finding reassures anyone reading genes from old stains. Crime labs can trust aged samples a bit more. Ancient DNA work gains the same reassurance. The study turns a plausible fear into a tested non-issue.
plos-pone-0005210:
Macrophages are immune cells that swallow invading bacteria, a process called phagocytosis. Staphylococcus aureus can survive that swallowing, turning the macrophage into a refuge. Koziel and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that the swallowing also changes the macrophage itself.

After taking in the bacteria, macrophages raised their levels of anti-death factors that keep the cell alive. A living host cell shelters the bacteria inside it. That bargain helps explain why staph infections can persist, and it points to the host cell's survival program as a treatment target. If the host cell stays alive, the germs inside it stay safe too, so drugs that break that truce could clear infections that now come back.
plos-pone-0005310:
For a synapse to release its message, vesicles must dock at the membrane in a precise molecular embrace. Camoletto and colleagues studied one docking partnership in PLOS ONE in 2009, between the proteins syntaxin1 and Munc18. A lipid called sphingosine turned out to regulate it.

Mice lacking an enzyme that breaks down sphingolipids model a disorder with mental retardation, making them useful for this question. The work shows lipids are not passive packing in synapses. They actively tune docking, which links lipid balance to healthy brain signaling. Fat and sugar signals share the stage at the synapse, so a fault in fat balance could dull the mind in ways that pure protein views would miss at first glance.
plos-pone-0005410:
Antibodies against two malaria parasite surface proteins, MSP3 and MSP6, help a protective mechanism that stops parasite growth. Both proteins share a small signature section at one end. Singh and colleagues extended that story to a whole gene family in PLOS ONE in 2009.

A conserved multi-gene family in Plasmodium falciparum induces cross-reactive antibodies. Cross-reactive means the antibodies hit several family members, not just one variant. Broad coverage is precious in malaria, where the parasite often escapes by varying its surface. Parts of this parasite stay the same while the rest of its coat shifts,.
