The team developed their protocol, called OPTIS, from a comparative review of teaching principles and refined it through expert rounds.

Piloting used both video-recorded lessons and live observation. Two independent observers reached almost perfect agreement with each other, and each stayed consistent over time, as measured by a chance-corrected agreement statistic suited to the data. Expert review supported the tool's foundations and its power to predict what it aims to capture. The authors present OPTIS as a psychometrically sound lens for researchers and school developers studying teaching quality across subjects.
plos-pone-0356910:
Xiaoxia Jia and colleagues model how city firms might cooperate to cut waste when the costs of doing so can be shared. Cities need industry to shrink its waste stream, but each firm weighs its own costs and gains. The study first maps material flows and life cycle impacts. That finds the nodes where cuts matter most. Then it runs a game model in software. Firms linked in a network copy or abandon cooperative moves over time.

Moderate penalties and positive spillovers between neighbors encouraged cooperation most reliably. Cost sharing and fair benefit splits also helped, but only within sensible ranges, and effects shifted with network size. Jia and colleagues advise cities to tune incentives to the local business network rather than copy one national recipe.
plos-pone-0357010:
María Carmen Martínez-González leads a team of eight testing whether needling a deep calf muscle changes how the foot bears weight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The tibialis posterior, buried behind the shin, steers the arch when walking, and hidden trigger points in it may distort foot loading. Eighty-two adults with such trigger points were assigned to real deep dry needling or a simulated version, with foot pressure measured on a walking platform before treatment and at three points afterward.

Right after needling, pressure under the heel rose in the treated group. A day later, average pressure rose while contact areas shifted, including less forefoot contact. By seventy-two hours, every difference from baseline had vanished. The authors conclude a single session rearranges foot loading only briefly, which matters for clinicians deciding whether the technique can support longer term gait correction plans.
plos-pone-0357110:
Sarah Al-Rihaymee leads a systematic review of whether a little-studied mouth bacterium belongs on the list of gum disease suspects. Known gum pathogens do not fully explain why disease severity varies so much between people. The review gathered observational studies in healthy adults that compared the bacterium's presence in people with gum disease against people with healthy gums, in spit or in plaque below the gumline.

Across eight studies from three continents, the bacterium turned up more often, and in larger shares, in disease than in health, with enrichment clearest in advanced stages. The authors rate the certainty as low, since most studies were snapshots rather than follow-ups. Al-Rihaymee and colleagues call for stronger designs before the bacterium earns a firm causal label.
plos-pone-0357310:
Weirui Zhang and three colleagues studied what Chinese school textbooks teach about the nature of science, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They read senior secondary geography textbooks in light of sustainable development, a theme the books are meant to carry. Textbooks shape whether students see science as fixed facts or as inquiry.

Zhang's team identified gaps between what the books claim about science and how they present it. They also pointed to reforms that would show science as argument and testing, not just lists to memorize. In a country teaching millions of students, textbook wording matters at huge scale. Better books can shape how a generation judges evidence on climate and resources.
plos-pone-0357410:
Rena Hidaka and fellow researchers pilot a monthly program in Tokyo that teaches children about mouths, chewing, and food at community cafeterias. These cafeterias serve local families, and the team added a chewy meal plus a short talk on teeth and balanced eating. About fifty children and thirty parents joined six sessions, answering surveys before and after the program.

Children looked inside their own mouths more often and used fluoride more after the program. Fewer children said they ignored balanced eating, and parents reported serving more meat, dairy, and root vegetables at home. Because there was no comparison group, Hidaka and colleagues treat the gains as promising early signs and call for a fuller trial to confirm them.
plos-pone-0357910:
Atefeh Allahbakhshian and three colleagues traced how uncertainty affects heart patients' lives, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. People with coronary artery disease live with gnawing doubt about their future. The team ran a pathway analysis linking quality of life in these patients to their coping strategies, perceived stress, and illness uncertainty.

Allahbakhshian's pathways reveal where support could break the chain from uncertainty to poor quality of life. If coping strategies carry much of the effect, teaching better coping becomes a concrete intervention. Cardiac care often stops at the artery; this work insists the mind's burden is part of the disease. Nurses and counselors gain a map of which link to strengthen first for each patient.
plos-pone-0359210: Aujla and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on gene copy changes in a national Canadian data bank. HostSeq holds genetic data from people across Canada. The team charted the full spectrum of copy number variation, places where chunks of DNA are missing or repeated. Such a spectrum gives doctors a baseline: which changes are common and harmless, and which stand out in disease.
plos-pone-0359310:
Jie Wang and co-authors set out a protocol in 2026 for comparing three sets of criteria used to classify antiphospholipid syndrome. This autoimmune condition makes blood more likely to clot and complicates pregnancies, and classifying it consistently is essential for research. The planned study is a systematic review with network meta-analysis, a method for comparing several options across many studies at once.

The criteria under comparison are the Sapporo criteria, their revised version, and the newer 2023 criteria from two major rheumatology bodies. The protocol fixes the questions and methods in advance, so the eventual results can be judged against a public plan. Which set performs best shapes who counts as a patient in every future trial of this disease.
plos-pone-0359810:
Kulthoom Qureish and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about dengue fever in Kenya. It tests vector competence, whether mosquitoes can pick up and pass on dengue-2 virus. The mosquitoes are Aedes aegypti sampled at selected sites in Lamu County, split into groups resistant or susceptible to the insecticide permethrin.

Comparing the two groups matters because spraying programs assume resistance only affects survival, not virus spread. If resistant mosquitoes also differ in how well they carry dengue, control plans need rethinking. Malaria and dengue control teams in coastal Kenya are the readers who must weigh insecticide choices against disease transmission.
pmc-13194210:
Masaki Iino, writing alone in 2026, proposes a concept called Integrative Intelligence, a way of describing how people judge well when time, roles, and body signals must be held together at once. It is not a new ability or stage, Iino argues, but a mode already hidden in ordinary judgment that shows under the right conditions.

The study uses self-ethnography, the author studying his own experience, drawing on mountaineering logs, body data, dialogues with an AI, and later reflections. Four linked lenses are developed, including an inner conference of viewpoints and AI as a reflective surface. Three mountain cases show the same constraint pattern producing distinct modes of judgment, supporting the claim that the mode is context-sensitive.
pmc-13194910:
Bijaya Kumar Muni leads a 2026 signal processing paper on estimating the direction of arriving signals, a task used in radar, sonar, and wireless networks. The classic MUSIC algorithm locates signal sources precisely but falters in chaotic, noisy, or highly correlated conditions. The authors set out to harden it.

Their method adds a robust cost function, Tukey Biweight, which down-weights wild data points, and models chaotic signal behavior with a Chebyshev-based generator. Monte Carlo simulations, repeated random trials, compared four variants. The combined chaotic and robust version consistently gave the best accuracy and resolution, especially at low signal-to-noise ratios and high signal correlation. The authors propose it for practical wireless and radar systems.
pmc-13197110:
Hiwot Abebe Haileslassie and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study of a pulse food toolkit for preschool children. Pulses are dry beans, peas, and lentils. Early tastes shape later eating, so the toolkit aimed to make pulses familiar in childcare centers.

The program ran three months in two centers in Saskatoon, with fifty children and eight staff. It mixed weekly lessons, new recipes, a food guide for cooks, and parent newsletters. Children got slightly better at naming chickpeas, beans, and peas, though gains were not firm proof. Children still ate more of the usual dishes than the pulse dishes. Staff views and food content checks round out the pilot's lessons.
pmc-13198510:
Jefté Peper-Nascimento and colleagues studied stress and sepsis effects on rat brain growth factors in a 2026 paper. Sepsis is a life-threatening body-wide response to infection. Long mild stress can reshape brain chemistry, so the team asked whether the two combine to lower nerve support proteins.

Rats went through a sepsis procedure, then thirty days of mild stress drills. Blood and two brain areas were tested for five support proteins and two stress hormones. Stress raised both hormones, while sepsis alone did not. Stress lowered four support proteins in both brain areas, with or without sepsis. Sepsis alone also lowered several, with strength by protein and region. No combined boost appeared.
pmc-13199410:
Christina Sauter and colleagues studied hidden neck spread in nose and sinus cancers across centers in a 2026 review. These cancers are rare, and no standard rule guides neck surgery when scans look clear. Doctors must choose between preventive neck dissection, removing neck nodes, and watchful scanning.

The study pooled 438 patients treated from 2012 to 2022. Hidden spread appeared in eight percent of patients whose necks looked clear on scans. One fourth got preventive neck surgery. Squamous cell type was the sole early risk flag for hidden spread. Patients with hidden spread had far worse five-year disease-free survival. Given the low spread rate, the authors question routine preventive surgery and urge case-by-case calls.
pmc-13200610: Yefei Zhang and colleagues are authors of a 2013 article retracted by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, as recorded in a 2026 notice. The article claimed a small RNA molecule blocked cell death in vessel lining cells exposed to oxidized cholesterol. An inquiry found image editing and duplication shared with another paper submitted at the same time by a different group. The board lost trust in the findings and retracted the work. The authors were informed and gave no comment.
pmc-13201610:
Worries about fertility after cancer can weigh heavily on survivors, and a 2026 study headed by Shaimaa Mohamed Amin examines how a partner's support fits into that burden. The research article tests whether partner support carries part of the link between reproductive health concerns and psychological distress.

The cross-sectional study surveyed 202 married female cancer survivors, aged twenty to forty-nine, attending oncology departments at Tanta University Hospital in Egypt. Greater reproductive concerns came with greater distress, while stronger partner support came with less of both. Statistical mediation analysis supported a partial indirect effect through partner support, leading the authors to recommend couple-focused counselling in survivorship care.
pmc-13202010:
Removing excess fluid is delicate when septic shock has weakened the heart, and a 2026 study protocol by Jing-Chao Luo sets out to test a hormone treatment for that phase. The protocol describes a single-center trial of recombinant human brain natriuretic peptide in adults recovering from septic shock with cardiac dysfunction and volume overload.

Thirty patients will receive a bolus followed by an infusion lasting up to seventy-two hours, with monitoring already in place. The main measure is the within-patient change in a venous return pressure gradient shortly after treatment begins. Secondary measures cover heart function, tissue perfusion, and congestion, with blood pressure instability as the key safety endpoint.
pmc-13202710:
Negative skin tests do not always rule out drug allergy, and a 2026 case report by Nur Betül Baştuğ İnan shows that gap for the antibiotic teicoplanin. The article presents a patient whose skin prick and intradermal tests for teicoplanin were negative, yet who reacted during a supervised drug challenge.

The 66-year-old woman had been referred with suspected drug allergy after treatment that included teicoplanin a week earlier. During provocation testing she developed an immediate skin reaction despite the reassuring earlier test results. The authors note that reports of IgE-mediated teicoplanin allergy are rising, and they argue this case tempers claims that skin testing reliably predicts such reactions.
pmc-13213710:
Priya Arya and colleagues present in 2026 two newborns with Williams syndrome whose vocal cords were paralysed, an unusual pairing. The syndrome, caused by a small chromosome deletion, already demands care from many specialties, and airway feeding problems add heavy complexity.

One early-term infant had both vocal folds paralysed and went home with a tracheostomy plus a feeding tube. The second had one-sided paralysis and likewise needed a feeding tube and feeding therapy. The authors link the problem to deletion of the elastin gene region, which weakens connective tissue. Their account documents each infant's hospital course and treatment, offering guidance for teams facing similar fragile newborns.
pmc-13216110:
Michael Y Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 case series on outcomes after laser treatment for symptomatic retinal breaks, tears in the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. Laser sealing is the standard defence against retinal detachment.

The series covered 600 eyes from 572 patients. Detachment followed in 43 eyes, and extra laser treatment was needed in 66 eyes, most often for the original break. Multiple breaks, a replaced lens, and bleeding inside the eye raised the detachment risk, while multiple breaks also predicted retreatment. Results were similar whether residents or senior doctors performed the first treatment. The authors recommend regular follow-up after the initial laser session.
pmc-13216710:
Koutarou Matsumoto and co-authors present a 2026 validation study from a Japanese emergency department, testing whether general-purpose AI chatbots can predict poor recovery after bleeding inside the brain. Fast prognosis shapes early decisions, and specialists are not always at hand.

Using admission data and CT images, GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 scored discrimination close to a purpose-built machine learning model, with areas under the curve around 0.84 to 0.85. Their predictions were highly reproducible across runs. Calibration, however, lagged: the chatbots systematically underestimated risk, and their overall accuracy measures trailed the specialist model. Feeding model outputs into the prompts helped modestly. The authors position the chatbots as explanation aids beside, not instead of, dedicated prognostic models.
pmc-13217210:
Ünal and colleagues test whether a chemical pathway in the blood tracks brain inflammation in children with ADHD. Attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder affects school, social, and family life, yet its biology stays partly unclear. The team measured kynurenine pathway products, which are made when the body processes tryptophan, in children never yet treated with ADHD drugs.

Blood came from 51 such children and 36 healthy peers of similar age and sex. Comparing the products and their ratios let the team probe links between immune activity and the disorder. If certain patterns hold up, they could point to inflammation's role in ADHD and, one day, to blood markers that support diagnosis.
pmc-13217710:
Karin Cato and co-authors present a 2026 mixed-methods study of how routine needle procedures, vaccinations and blood tests, are softened for babies in Swedish child health care. The work is framed by Kolcaba's Comfort Theory, sorting findings into relief, ease, and transcendence.

Sixteen professionals, forty parents, and twenty-seven infants up to five months old took part. Practice that eased the experience included preparing parents with honest information about pain and relief options, and supporting them during the procedure. It also included keeping the setting calm and using comfort measures such as breastfeeding or sweet solutions. Safety handling of the infant and a sense of well-being afterwards also mattered. The authors distil the findings into practical steps clinics can adopt without drugs or new equipment.
pmc-13217910:
Yibo Chen and colleagues published a 2026 review on the host factors that shape Chikungunya virus infection. The virus spreads through mosquito bites and causes fever, rash, and joint pain that can linger for months or years. No approved antiviral drug targets it directly, so attention has turned to the human proteins the virus depends on.

The review maps how host factors control each stage of the viral life cycle, from cell entry and genome copying to assembly and release. It also weighs how these factors differ across cell types and drive inflammation and chronic joint disease. The authors judge which host targets look most druggable and survey drug candidates aimed at viral proteins and host dependencies alike. Because host-directed drugs sidestep the resistance that rapid viral mutation creates, the review frames them as a promising route toward treatment.
pmc-13219110:
Tejas Subramanian and Sravisht Iyer reply to a letter criticizing their study of frailty and outcomes after minimally invasive spine surgery in 2026 correspondence. Their work linked a high score on the five-item modified frailty index to worse outcomes and lower return to activities after one- or two-level fusion surgery. The letter writers raised concerns, and this response answers them point by point.

The authors accept several limits, including the small number of frail patients and bias in which patients received follow-up CT scans, and agree prospective studies are needed. They note the link between frailty and outcomes grew stronger across frailty levels, a dose-response pattern supporting the finding. Suggestions to model the index continuously, use time-to-event methods, and test removing one index item are welcomed as extensions. Confounders such as bone density and opioid dose matter but were not the study's target.
pmc-13220810:
Jin Yang and colleagues review risk prediction models for blood clots in multiple myeloma in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, and the verdict is unflattering. Myeloma patients clot at high rates, and models that flag the riskiest patients could target prevention, but clinicians had no account of whether the scores work. Four databases were searched to March 2026.

Fourteen studies covered seven assessment tools between them. Across the studies, 7.9 percent of myeloma patients developed venous thromboembolism. Pooled accuracy for the tools ranged from poor to modest, with areas under the curve between 0.57 and 0.68, and two related scores, IMPEDE VTE and its successor, performed least badly. Almost no study checked whether predicted risks matched observed ones, every study carried a high risk of bias on appraisal, and all models were published as formulas nobody has road-tested. The authors recommend updating and externally validating the tools rather than minting new ones.
pmc-13222010:
Yaqin Xiong and Zhihui Li write a 2026 letter questioning how a study of sitting time and urinary leakage framed its mediation results. The original work used cross-sectional data, where exposure, mediator, and outcome are measured at one time point. Xiong and Li argue such a design cannot support the strong mechanistic reading the paper's language encourages.

Body mass, diet inflammation scores, and a blood ratio served first as adjustment variables, then as mediators, which blurs what each estimate means. No causal diagram or sensitivity checks were reported. Baseline patterns also cut against a simple inflammation story. The letter urges authors to present such pathways as associations consistent with a mechanism, not proof of one.
pmc-13222410:
Yihang Xu and co-authors evaluate a cell-surface protein called SDC2 as a marker in gastric cancer, in a 2026 multi-center cohort study. Survival analyses were combined with pan-cancer comparisons, tissue staining, and single-cell data to test how SDC2 expression relates to patient outcomes and tumor behavior.

High SDC2 expression tracked with shorter survival, confirming it as an independent risk factor in their models. Tumors with more SDC2 showed more varied microenvironments, lower mutation burden, and weaker predicted response to immunotherapy. Similar expression patterns appeared across several other cancers. The authors propose SDC2 both as an early detection aid and as a possible treatment target worth developing.
pmc-13222610:
Mahmut Onur Kulturoglu, Lutfi Dogan, and Mehmet Ali Gulcelik compare complication rates across oncoplastic breast surgery techniques used after drug therapy, in a 2026 records study. Five hundred fifty-six patients who had level II oncoplastic surgery following neoadjuvant treatment between 2019 and 2025 were grouped by technique, from racquet and vertical patterns to batwing and letter-shaped mammoplasties.

Racquet and vertical patterns removed larger tissue volumes than the others. Those two groups also suffered clearly more overall and major problems, including wound opening, infection, and fluid collections. Standard severity grades and a combined index ran higher there too. The choice after drug therapy, the data suggest, carries real consequences for recovery.
pmc-13223710:
Yang Song and co-authors use microwaves to bond soy protein with fenugreek gum, aiming for a better food ingredient, in a 2026 study. Soy protein isolate loses solubility near its isoelectric point, limiting drinks and emulsions. Three minutes of microwave treatment at high power drove the grafting reaction between protein and gum.

Solubility in that problem range nearly doubled after treatment. Emulsifying activity roughly tripled, stability rose more than sevenfold, and antioxidant capacity climbed sharply too. Structural measures showed the protein unfolded and bound the gum covalently. Five minutes of treatment overshot, clumping the protein and erasing gains. A short microwave window, the work shows, can upgrade plant protein fast.
pmc-13225010:
Yisheng You and co-authors report a 2026 randomised trial comparing two ultrasound-guided nerve blocks for recovery after keyhole chest surgery. One block targets muscles along the back, the other the space beside the spine, and a third group received standard multi-drug pain relief only. In total, 129 patients were assigned across the three arms.

Recovery quality scores a day after surgery were significantly higher in both block groups than in controls. Block patients also reported less pain at rest and while coughing during the first hours, needed less opioid during surgery, and pressed their pain pumps less often. Nausea, vomiting, and dizziness were less common too, and the back-muscle block matched the established spinal-space technique.
pmc-13227810:
Madita Mühlhaus and a German research network measure a 2026 sepsis signal inside patients' blood cells: activation of toll-like receptor 4, the sensor that detects bacterial toxins and fires inflammation. Drugs blocking this receptor helped animals but failed in human trials, raising the question of whether the receptor is even active in most patients. Blood samples from one hundred sepsis patients were tested on day one and day four with a sensitive proximity assay.

Overall activation was strikingly low, usually under one signal per cell. A minority subgroup, though, showed clearly raised activation, and those patients died at significantly higher rates within thirty days at both time points. The link held after adjusting for severity, age, infection site, and sex, defining a high-risk subtype.
pmc-13233010:
Isabella Zai and Adrian Zai published a 2026 cohort study asking whether common skin conditions raise the risk of later anxiety in young adults. Conditions such as acne, psoriasis, and dermatitis affect many people aged 18 to 22 and can cause lasting distress. Using the TriNetX electronic health record network, the pair matched young adults with a skin diagnosis against similar peers without one, excluding anyone with earlier anxiety.

The skin condition group developed anxiety more often at one, three, and five years, and the gap between groups widened over time. Time-to-event analysis showed a modest but steady rise in risk, with hazard ratios between 1.12 and 1.14. The authors argue that skin care for young adults should include attention to mental health.
pmc-13234010:
Duorui Wang and colleagues published a 2026 robotics study on a gecko-inspired adhesive that can grip almost any surface. Robot hands struggle with objects that are fragile, heavy, or oddly shaped when they rely on squeezing. The team's adhesive stacks three layers: tiny mushroom-tipped structures that adjust their stiffness to microscopic roughness, a rigid film, and soft pillars that bend to match large contours.

The whole structure grows in one manufacturing step under an electric field. It held ten times more strongly than conventional designs across varied surfaces. Mounted on a multi-fingered robot hand, it lifted delicate, heavy, rough, and irregular objects, even under twisting loads. The authors present the pad as a route to gentler, more versatile robotic grasping.
pmc-13234710:
Aysha Imtiaz and co-authors investigated in 2026 whether sound waves plus friendly bacteria can improve the health value of Chinese yam. Chinese yam is a tuber long used as food and traditional medicine in East Asia. It carries compounds linked to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immune effects. Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria can free more of those compounds from the tuber matrix.

Combining multi-frequency ultrasound with mixed bacterial cultures forms the processing idea under study. Ultrasound helps break plant tissue so bacteria and enzymes can reach trapped compounds. The work sets out to measure bioactive content, antioxidant activity, and structural changes after treatment. Earlier conventional fermentation left part of the yam's chemistry underused, including many secondary compounds. The authors frame the combined method as a way to raise the functional quality of yam products.
pmc-13236810:
Sharma and colleagues build a sensor for a cancer drug from layered sheets of a material called MXene. MXene sensors suit bedside testing, but the sheets oxidise easily and often need added chemicals to work. The team trapped a dye, methylene blue, between the layers as a built-in signal source, removing the need for loose reagents.

Their screen-printed platform detects erdafitinib, a drug used against bladder and other cancers. A built-in signal trapped in the layers should stay steadier than chemicals floating free in a sample. If it holds up in real fluids, such strips could check drug levels quickly in clinics that lack full laboratories.
pmc-13237410: Rice panicle research is the subject of a correction by Wu and colleagues. The study compared hybrid rice with its parent lines, profiling how gene messages are trimmed during early grain development. The correction concerns the methods wording for collecting tissue and extracting high-quality RNA, and the corrected and original versions are set out side by side. Exact extraction steps decide whether other labs can repeat the sequencing work, so the journal records the fix in full.
pmc-13239110:
Alex W Bajcz and colleagues introduced P.I. Charter in 2026, a web application that gathers point-intercept aquatic plant survey data from across Minnesota. Dozens of agencies and groups survey lake plants for their own purposes, leaving valuable records scattered and hard to combine. The app, built in R Shiny, accepts submissions, cleans and merges them automatically, and returns recognition and visualizations as incentives to contribute.

Since launch it has drawn thousands of visitors and hundreds of submissions, with repeat contributors filing surveys in minutes. Four case studies show the pooled database planning new surveys, watching for cryptic invasions, linking plant occurrence to environment, and tracing lake plant change over time. The authors share the experience as a model, while warning that accessible design in Shiny takes real effort.
pmc-13239510:
The Nigerian Surgical Research Collaborative measures surgical site infections after abdominal operations across fifty-three Nigerian hospitals. Infection after surgery is a heavy burden in poorer countries, where it lengthens stays families can ill afford. Reliable, current numbers have been scarce in Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, which has held back efforts to cut that burden.

Their prospective study is a snapshot audit: infections counted as care happened, alongside the factors that raised or lowered risk. Hospital-by-hospital data at this scale can show whether the drivers are antibiotics, theatre practice, or patient condition. That tells surgical teams where the next naira spent on safety will do the most good.
pmc-13239710:
Satoshi Kurita and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of harms from exercise programmes for frail older adults. Exercise clearly helps this group, yet falls, injuries, and other unwanted events during trials have never been gathered together in one analysis.

The review will search four databases for randomised trials involving people aged sixty or older whose frailty was measured with a validated method. Independent teams will screen studies, extract event data, and judge bias risk with a standard Cochrane tool. Pooled risk ratios will compare event rates between exercise and control groups, with extra analyses by programme length, frequency, and setting.
pmc-13239910:
Georgina V Hume and co-authors read shark bite scars on dolphins to measure predation risk along southeast Queensland in a 2026 study. Attacks by large sharks are rarely witnessed, yet healed scars on photographed animals offer a record of how often dolphins are targeted and where.

Fresh wounds pointed mainly to tiger sharks and white sharks, with bites clustered near the tail stalk. Half of the Australian humpback dolphins photographed carried scars, a higher share than either bottlenose species. Sheltered waters held more scarred animals than open coasts. Statistical models confirmed humpback dolphins, especially adults in sheltered habitat, face the greatest attack risk.
pmc-13241410:
Gajdošová's team in Olomouc built a gold cone sensor that detects a mood drug and serotonin side by side. Raman light scattering reads molecular fingerprints from the cone arrays. The cones pack gaps under twenty nanometers, creating dense, uniform hot spots. The build is large-scale, cheap, and kept simple on purpose.

Sertraline showed down to 88 nanograms per milliliter, the lowest Raman figure yet. That sits a hundredfold below levels in patient blood. Serotonin showed at 27 nanograms per milliliter, beneath levels seen even in low mood. Both were read side by side in fake spinal fluid, untreated.
pmc-13241610:
Salifu and a Ghana-UK team describe a community-led effort to build death literacy around palliative care in Ghana. Death literacy means the knowledge and confidence to face dying, death, and loss. In Ghana, open talk about death is often discouraged, and palliative care is scarce. The COMPASS-Ghana project used a participatory theory-of-change approach.

Activities included a thirty-seven-person stakeholder session, a planning workshop, and a focus group with nursing and midwifery students. Three themes emerged: shared language about death, care rooted in existing community forms, and collective agency. Participants shifted toward treating death as a shared community concern. The authors argue such locally grounded work fits public-health palliative care.
pmc-13242010:
Jingjing Wen and Hui Ye report a 2026 study of stem cell vesicles for diabetic wound healing. Fat-derived stem cells release tiny parcels called exosomes that can help wounds, but the active ingredient was unknown. The team focused on a sugar-burning enzyme named ALDOA.

In high-sugar cell cultures that mimic diabetes, the vesicles sped cell movement and raised energy output from sugar breakdown. Wounds in diabetic mice also healed faster with treatment. The enzyme was scarce in sugar-stressed cells, and vesicle treatment pushed its level above normal. Removing the enzyme from vesicles erased the benefit, while adding extra enzyme copied it. The authors identify enzyme delivery through exosomes as a route to better diabetic wound care.
pmc-13242810:
Michal Klimek and co-authors publish a 2026 comparison of online tools used to plan astigmatism-correcting lens implants in cataract surgery. Different tools can recommend different lens powers and angles from the same eye measurements. The study compared one manufacturer calculator against several society-hosted engines.

Records covered well over a hundred operated eyes, with the same measurements fed into every calculator. Relevant disagreement between the main pair appeared in about three fifths of eyes, mostly as stronger lens steps from the manufacturer tool. Disagreement clustered in eyes with one astigmatism orientation and a stronger back corneal curve. Other engines disagreed even more often. The authors advise consulting several tools for the high-risk pattern, while noting orientation groups where choice hardly matters.
pmc-13243010:
Yimin He and co-authors publish a 2026 clinical study comparing two add-on physical treatments for rosacea alongside oral doxycycline. One group used a device called the Shumin treatment instrument, while the other used red light therapy. Both groups treated twice weekly for twelve weeks, and skin microscopy tracked objective change.

The device group reached a higher overall effectiveness rate than the red light group. Life quality scores improved more in the device group, and affected hair follicle counts also did better. Mite counts fell in both groups without a clear between-group difference. Relapse after treatment was notably less common in the device group. The authors judge the device pairing safe and more effective in this preliminary comparison.
pmc-13243110:
Chao Zhang, Yunfeng Ni, and Dong Han carried out this 2026 hospital study of older patients who had both chronic bronchitis, a long-term lung condition, and a heart attack. They asked whether a simple blood-based score of immune activity and inflammation could predict who would die in hospital.

The study covered 252 patients, of whom 48 died. Those who died had higher inflammation markers at admission. The score, called SII, predicted deaths well on its own, and it did even better combined with two other blood measures. The authors suggest this cheap score could help doctors spot high-risk patients early.
pmc-13244510:
Gabriela Cejas-Añón and colleagues profiled the enzyme cocktail secreted by the fungus that feeds leaf-cutting ants. Their study appeared in Mycobiology in 2026. Leucoagaricus gongylophorus farms inside ant nests, digesting leaves the ants cannot eat themselves. The team grew it on four foods: glucose, a cellulose derivative, xylan, and pectin, then measured growth, enzyme output, and the full set of secreted proteins over time.

Glucose fed the most growth, while pectin, the food the fungus liked least, provoked its richest enzyme response. Pectin cultures topped the charts for three enzyme classes and secreted the most varied protein set. Proteomics found 290 proteins in all, about two-thirds of them secreted, with ninety-three shared across every diet. The shared core stayed stable while amounts flexed with the menu. For industry, the message is that diet tunes this digestion kit, which could be borrowed for breaking down plant waste.
pmc-13246810:
Germain and co-authors charted day-night rhythms of stress-hormone by-products in women with very low body weight, in this 2026 Endocrine study. They compared four small groups: women with acute anorexia nervosa, women recovering from anorexia, women who are constitutionally thin without an eating disorder, and healthy controls. Blood was sampled twelve times across twenty-four hours in hospital under standard meals and activity.

All three low-weight groups ran higher average levels of the measured compounds than controls, and several markers peaked around midday in a clear daily rhythm. Levels rose as body mass and a growth marker fell. The authors suggest the midday elevation reflects metabolic stress, with possibly different mechanisms behind the same pattern in anorexia and natural thinness.
pmc-13247010:
Li, Geng, and Zhou mapped two decades of flexible electronics research in this 2026 Discover Nano bibliometric study. Instead of reviewing devices, they analyzed the literature itself, using VOSviewer and CiteSpace software on publications from 2006 to 2025 to chart who publishes, where, on what topics, and how the field's themes connect to neighboring domains.

Publication grew steadily and then accelerated. China and the United States dominate output, with South Korea and Japan also significant; the most productive author was Wei Huang, while John A. Rogers carried the strongest collaboration links. Frequent keywords included graphene, films, and nanoparticles. The authors name four future directions, among them multimodal integrated sensors and machine learning enhanced sensors for health monitoring, as strategic guidance for newcomers.
pmc-13247310:
Johansen, Ziegler, Agyemang, and co-authors revisit a slippery gene variant and colon cancer risk in this 2026 letter in Cancer Communications. The variant, called TGFBR1*6A, shortens a run of alanines in a growth-control receptor. Standard gene-scanning chips miss it because its DNA stretch is chemically awkward to copy, and earlier risk studies were small and ignored genetic ancestry, leaving the evidence murky.

The team engineered mice carrying the human variant and crossed them with a polyp-prone strain: variant carriers grew about half as many intestinal polyps. They then extended the work to a large family-based human case-control study adjusted for ancestry. Their combined evidence recasts the variant as a modifier of colorectal cancer development rather than a simple risk factor, and argues for studying variants that routine scans overlook.
pmc-13248110:
Tsujimoto and colleagues ran a small pilot study, published in 2026, on hormone testing after pituitary surgery. Adults who remove a nonfunctioning pituitary tumor often develop growth hormone deficiency. Confirming that diagnosis needs a stimulation test that burdens patients and staff, so the team looked for a simpler early signal in routine blood work.

Among thirty-five patients, those who proved deficient had lower levels of two thyroid hormones, FT3 and FT4, after surgery. A third hormone, TSH, did not differ between groups. The authors suggest the two thyroid values could help doctors decide which patients truly need the fuller stimulation test.
pmc-13248510:
Ran and co-authors refined risk prediction after thyroid cancer surgery, in a 2026 Annals of Medicine study. Doctors judge relapse risk with the American Thyroid Association system, then give radioactive iodine. The team asked whether a blood marker measured after surgery, stimulated thyroglobulin, could sharpen forecasts of who responds excellently to that treatment.

They analyzed more than eleven hundred patients treated at one Chinese hospital. Adding the marker, its ratio to another hormone, and antibody levels lifted prediction accuracy a great deal over stage and risk class alone. The fuller model also sorted patients into more useful follow-up groups. The authors propose it as a companion to the standard risk system.
pmc-13249110:
Rémi Deleuse and co-authors present images of a giant false aneurysm of the heart's main chamber in a 2026 case. Their patient was a 53-year-old man with a past lymphoma treated by strong chemotherapy and stem cell transplant. A year earlier he had chest pain that was read as heart lining inflammation.

Scans at the new center showed a huge pouch off the side wall of the left ventricle, partly filled with clot. The pouch measured over six centimeters and held about 700 milliliters. It marked a contained rupture after a missed heart attack. Surgeons repaired it with a prosthetic patch. The case warns how quietly such damage can grow.
pmc-13250110:
Ahmed and colleagues publish a correction to their Scientific Reports study of heat shock factor-1 in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. The original 2026 paper reported that this factor eases stress inside the cell's protein-folding compartment. This notice fixes display problems in the paper's first figure and its accompanying legend.

The corrected figure shows genes switched on by the factor during heat stress, plus reporter images tracking a stress response signal in normal and silenced worms. Labels attached to the supplementary information files were also wrong and have been fixed. The authors state that the original article has been corrected, so readers should rely on this updated figure and legend.
pmc-13252710:
Alva Lütt and a large team measure craving with body signals in virtual reality in this 2026 study. Craving predicts relapse in alcohol dependence, and therapy deliberately exposes patients to drinking cues in safe settings so they can practise resisting.

Sixty-one patients entered virtual bar and living room scenes plus a neutral scene, while sensors tracked skin response, heart rate, pupil size, and breathing. The alcohol scenes raised self-rated craving clearly and sped skin responses, breathing, and pupil widening. The team matched body reactions against felt craving to learn which signals track it best. Such measures could sharpen virtual exposure therapy design.
pmc-13253810:
A. Mavillonio and co-authors review neurodegenerative spliceosomopathies in a 2026 mini-review. These are disorders caused by faults in the spliceosome, the machine that edits genetic messages before they are read as proteins. Although every cell carries the machine, its failure hits certain tissues hardest, especially the retina and the nervous system.

The review covers spinal muscular atrophy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and retinitis pigmentosa as the leading examples. It explains how defects in building the machine's small nuclear particles, assembling the complex, or maintaining editing accuracy lead neurons and light-sensing cells to degenerate. Some mechanisms are shared across the diseases while others are specific to each. Why particular tissues bear the brunt remains an unresolved puzzle the authors highlight. They also survey emerging treatments that aim at the splicing process itself. The piece frames splicing correction as one of the more promising shared strategies across this family of diseases.
pmc-13254210:
Xiaoping Tang and a large team map cell talk in liver disease in a 2026 study. Mallory-Denk bodies are protein clumps seen in chronic liver disease and fibrosis, or scarring. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing, the team found a distinct group of liver cells tied to these clumps.

Signals between cell types ran through the HGF/MET axis, a growth signal pathway. That path raised a protein called UbD and a swelling signal, forming a self-feeding loop that built clumps and scar tissue. Mice lacking UbD formed fewer clumps and scars, and human biopsies showed the same raised signals, marking a drug target.
pmc-13254510:
Zhengkang Fan and colleagues build a system that predicts whether a kidney tumor is malignant by reading both the chart and the radiology report in a 2026 retrospective study. Many kidney masses turn out benign, so better preoperative prediction could spare patients unneeded surgery. The catch is that telling tumor details hide in free-text CT reports, which structured records leave untapped.

The cohort came from University of Florida Health records spanning 2011 to 2024, restricted to adults with a documented kidney mass and at least one preoperative CT report. The pipeline combined standard record variables, from diagnoses and medicines to vital signs and labs, with language-derived features. A locally run large language model pulled kidney-specific findings and abnormality traits out of each report, checked against hand annotations. The team compared single-source baselines against early, middle, and late fusion strategies for combining the streams.
pmc-13255010:
Lea Haverbeck Simon and a large team test a care workflow for breast cancer in a 2026 pilot trial. The CORE program folds exercise and rehabilitation into care from diagnosis through 24 weeks. Seventy-two women with stage I to III breast cancer and planned surgery were assigned, two to one, to CORE or standard care.

Fifty-nine women had usable data, most with stage I disease. Physical function change did not differ clearly between groups at 24 weeks. Exercise engagement leaned better in the CORE group by survey and by motion tracker, with a modest effect size. The authors call for a larger, powered trial.
pmc-13255210:
Zhao and co-authors review how clinicians manage the long-term complications that follow chronic spinal cord injury. Years after injury, patients face problems across motor, breathing, cardiovascular, gut, and bladder systems, which drive repeated hospital stays and heavy costs. No cure exists, so care combines rehabilitation, drugs, neuromodulation, and surgery.

The review finds current practice still mostly reactive, treating symptoms as they arise, with limits in durability, access, and patient engagement. The authors call for a shift toward proactive, patient-centered care built on multidisciplinary teams and individualized plans. They expect neural regeneration and precision medicine to move management from easing symptoms toward restoring function.
pmc-13255910:
Gábor Lorászkó and co-authors present a 2026 case report of glaucoma in a four-year-old female Siberian tiger kept at a zoo. The tiger had behaved fearfully, aggressively, and disoriented since arriving months earlier, as if she could not see. Examination under general anesthesia confirmed the suspicion.

Pressure inside both eyes was markedly elevated, and the back of each eye showed lesions of advanced glaucoma. Her pupils no longer reacted to light, apart from drug effects from the anesthetic. The team also documented seizure episodes, one type during anesthesia recovery and brief stereotyped bouts seen since her arrival, without proving a link to the eye disease. Surgery was not feasible at the site. Weighing welfare, staff returned her to her familiar enclosure, where she could move safely despite blindness.
pmc-13256510:
Rong Zhou and colleagues report a 2026 food-science study treating low-glycemic rice starch with heat and limited moisture to slow its digestion further. Ordinary rice starch digests fast and spikes blood sugar, so a physical, chemical-free treatment is attractive. Starch was treated for ten minutes at one hundred, one hundred ten, or one hundred twenty degrees.

Treatment shrank swelling and leaching, lowered long-range crystal order while tightening short-range order, and cut average molecule size. Mild treatment strengthened gels, while hotter treatment softened them. Digestion slowed meaningfully: rapidly digestible starch fell, resistant starch more than doubled, and the hottest sample's estimated glycemic index landed in the low range. The authors offer the results as groundwork for low-GI rice products built by physical processing alone.
pmc-13257110:
Ireneusz Walaszek leads a 2026 study of inflammatory signals and hand function in carpal tunnel syndrome. The condition causes pain and limits daily tasks for many workers. Fifty-five surgical patients rated their disability while tissue samples were tested for six mediators.

Two signals pointed in opposite directions. Higher VEGF, a vessel-growth factor, accompanied a lower chance of severe disability scores. Higher TNF-alpha, a classic inflammatory signal, accompanied greater risk of severe disability. The other four mediators showed no clear link. Because sampling happened once, cause and effect cannot be separated. Hand surgeons and researchers gain candidate markers worth tracking over time. Prospective studies could show whether these signals predict recovery after surgery or merely reflect current damage.
pmc-13257210:
Valeria Zuccalà leads a 2026 pathology study of the invasive front in colorectal cancer. The tumor edge is where cancer cells meet stroma, immune cells, and new vessels. Fifty-two surgically removed, non-metastatic tumors were scored for budding and four front markers.

Small detached clusters, called tumor buds, were graded by international criteria. Stromal, vessel, macrophage, and mast cell measures were combined into a simple zero-to-four score. High grade, vessel invasion, node spread, and heavy budding each tracked a higher combined score. The pattern suggests that several remodeling processes advance together at the edge. Pathologists get a hypothesis worth testing in larger groups with outcome data. The authors are explicit that clinical use must wait for that validation.
pmc-13258010:
Heleen Neeltje Willemijn Duighuisen and colleagues present a 2026 qualitative study of why leprosy diagnosis is often delayed in Colombia. Leprosy, also called Hansen's disease, can be cured with multi-drug therapy, but late diagnosis can leave lasting disability. The team ran twenty-four in-depth interviews with people affected by leprosy in Cesar and Valle del Cauca, two regions where the disease still occurs. They mapped each person's path toward diagnosis and treatment.

Delays came from three levels: personal, community, and health system. Reasons included limited leprosy training among health workers, poorly organized leprosy care, cost and access barriers, low public awareness, and stigma against patients. The authors call for dedicated leprosy care centers, active case finding, and awareness work for health workers and communities to cut stigma and speed diagnosis.
pmc-13258310:
Mustafa Ay and Rabia Sari ask whether inflammation ratios at intensive care discharge still predict death after sepsis in a 2026 cohort study. Four hundred sixty-one patients treated between 2013 and 2015 were followed for deaths at twenty-eight days, six months, and two years. Four blood ratios and severity scores were tested for prognostic power.

Septic shock patients died far more often at every horizon than sepsis patients without shock. Raised discharge ratios for neutrophils and for C-reactive protein relative to albumin separated survivors from non-survivors in raw comparisons. Full modeling judged whether each ratio added independent signal beyond severity scores. Discharge planners gain a caution: inflammation at the door out still carries meaning, yet shock history dominates. Ratios may help flag who needs closest post-discharge watching.
pmc-13258410:
Marilina García-Aranda and a Spanish research network followed colorectal cancer patients for a full decade after surgery. Eight hundred thirty-eight people treated in Basque Country public hospitals joined the prospective study, starting in twenty ten. Their 2026 report separates deaths caused by cancer from deaths with other roots.

Four in ten patients died within ten years, and about two-thirds of those deaths came from the cancer itself. Advanced stage drove cancer deaths, while general frailty and other illnesses shaped the rest. Folding both risks into one model sharpened the picture of who stays vulnerable. The authors say such models can tailor follow-up for survivors.
pmc-13259110:
Cristina Fornacelli and coauthors judge a spectral camera for color checks of purple old books in a 2026 study. The camera was set next to a trusted color tool on proof tiles and on real books in place. Purple dyed pages are frail and can not travel to labs.

In the lab the camera matched the tool well, though a steady bias showed. On site truth fell, due to mixed stuff and tight capture space. Rank of colors stayed true, which helps checks across time. Maps of color showed dye spread and harm marks in clear form. Care staff gain a no touch survey tool, with frank limits on exact color claims.
pmc-13259210:
Majid Aalizadeh and coauthors use many light waves plus machine learning for color based sensing in a 2026 study. Plain color tests read strength at one picked wave and throw the rest of the spectrum away. Food dye mixes in water served as the test case.

A pick routine chose twelve waves with the most signal from full spectra. A plain line model on those waves cut guess error a huge amount next to the one wave way. Cross checks kept the pick honest and stopped false fit. No gear change was called for to gain the gain. Test kits for health, farm, and plant use could take this path next.
pmc-13261010:
Meijie Shang and colleagues wrote a 2026 methodological letter responding to a trial of an anti-inflammatory diet, alone or combined with acupuncture, for depression in type 2 diabetes. They praise the topic's clinical value and the trial's framework for testing acupuncture. Then they raise four design concerns they say future research should refine, starting with the lack of a sham acupuncture control group, which leaves placebo and attention effects unexcluded.

Their second concern is timing. A significant drop in glycated hemoglobin after only eight weeks seems early, since that marker reflects about 120 days of blood sugar. Fasting glucose also showed no matching difference. Third, the mix of diabetes drugs across groups was not adequately controlled, which could confound weight and metabolic outcomes. Fourth, without a pure acupuncture group, the data show an additive effect, not the claimed synergistic interaction.
pmc-13261310:
Yiyi Wang and colleagues described in 2026 a new species of non-biting midge from China, named Kaluginia wangi. The genus had never been recorded in China before. Their description rests on three adult males, detailed drawings, and family trees built from five molecular markers.

Gene evidence placed the new species in a strongly supported branch beside its known relative, Kaluginia lebetiformis. Body features separate the two, including the count of antenna segments and the structure of the male genitalia. The team's deeper lesson concerns preparation: the same specimen mounted on slides under different conditions showed different shapes. Such artifacts can bend taxonomic conclusions for insects with fine structures. The authors urge meticulous slide work and cross-checking between body evidence and molecules.
pmc-13262410:
Catharina Voss and colleagues examine moment-to-moment mood patterns in young people in a 2026 journal article from Germany. They compare teens and young adults with no suicidal behavior, those with suicidal thoughts only, and those who had moved to plans or attempts. Phone prompts captured low mood, anxiety, stress, irritability, hopelessness, and loss of pleasure in daily life.

The community sample held 1,180 people aged 14 to 21, with phone data for 1,072 over four days, eight times a day. Mood networks at a single moment looked much alike across groups. Over time, though, mood states were more tightly linked in the action group. Links between irritability, loss of pleasure, stress, and hopelessness differed by group in added tests.
pmc-13262710:
Josh M Morganti and Adam D Bachstetter comment on new research into why brain injury hits older adults harder, in a 2026 journal article. Traumatic brain injury kills and disables older people at the highest rates. The study discussed used single-cell gene reading, chemical profiling, and tissue checks in mice, with checks in human injury tissue.

Aged brains leaned on an inflammatory microglial state, a state of the brain's immune cells, driven by a sensor called NLRP3. Young brains favored a different, more protective cell state. Blocking NLRP3 or its driver in mice improved survival, and a repurposed drug also helped. The commentators say age now maps onto specific cell targets that drugs can reach.
pmc-13263010:
Clare Tsz Kiu Yu and co-authors pilot a virtual reality mindfulness program for anxious teens in Hong Kong in a 2026 journal article. Mindfulness training can ease anxiety, but teens often lose interest in standard formats. Their version used a CAVE room, an enclosed space with nature scenes projected on three walls, over an eight-week group course.

All 42 enrolled teens, with a mean age near 15, finished the study, and most attended at least eight of ten sessions. No one dropped out and no harms were reported. Survey scores for anxiety and stress did not change significantly. Body measures of stress control, based on heart rhythm variation, did improve. Teens in group interviews reported better calm, focus, and sleep.
pmc-13264010:
Hero Ibrahim Hassan and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on dental care use by older adults who get home care in south-eastern Norway. Many in this group can use public dental care for free. The team mapped how often they went, and what helped or held them back.

Of 116 people, with a mean age of 83, about two thirds said they saw a dentist each year, while about one in four went only for urgent problems. Most could get free public care, yet only 66 knew that, and just over half used the right. Knowing the right, having more teeth, and using private dentists each linked to more visits.
pmc-13264110:
Ravi Desai and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare pregnancy-related cancer found in the bowel. Gestational choriocarcinoma usually starts in the uterus after a pregnancy event, yet this case appeared in the cecum, part of the large intestine, and had already spread. Its bleeding and hormone pattern mimicked a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, a dangerous look-alike that can mislead emergency teams.

The report stresses considering this cancer when pregnancy hormone levels stay high and no pregnancy is found in the uterus. Surgery is usually avoided, but it may be required to stop bleeding or remove resistant disease. Fast chemotherapy, surgery when needed and close coordination are presented as critical to lower harm in a young patient group.
pmc-13264310:
Serela S Ramklass reflects on health care leadership during COVID-19 in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, in a 2026 study based on group talks. Managers and senior staff from therapy, nursing and medicine at seven public hospitals joined focus groups about leading through volatile and unclear crisis conditions. Their accounts were read through a leadership change framework to trace how people adapted when systems strained, staff suffered and staff groups pulled apart under competing urgent demands.

Five themes emerged, including low readiness rooted in training gaps, weak staff support feeding burnout, and allied health voices being left out of decisions. Other themes traced a shift from rigid routines toward frontline innovation and their own leadership growth. The findings feed advice for crisis leadership training that includes mental health support and genuine cross-team inclusion in planning.
pmc-13264410:
Wen Chao Xu and colleagues build a light-activated nanocomposite gel for atopic dermatitis in a 2026 study. Eczema of this type disrupts life quality, and current drugs carry side effects or weak effect. Their gel loads bee venom peptide melittin onto iron and gold shell particles inside a temperature-sensitive base. The design aims to combine immune calming, antioxidant action, antibacterial effect and skin repair in one topical preparation tested on skin cells and animal lesions.

Particles formed evenly, captured much of the peptide load and produced a porous, body-friendly gel. Under near-infrared light, treated skin cells lowered a key allergy signal and reactive oxygen levels. Bacterial growth and biofilm formation were suppressed in tests. Multi-action topical platforms could reduce reliance on steroids for flares.
pmc-13264610:
Yara A Sultan, Ahmed Sameh, and Samah A Gamel present a 2026 framework for running offshore wind farms without harming birds. Turbines can strike migrating birds, and older safeguards like radar or alarms often react late or cry wolf. Their system pairs a deep learning bird spotter with the farm's control system.

The spotter was trained on more than 90,000 images covering 525 bird species. It sorted birds with accuracy above 99 percent in tests, beating four standard methods. In simulation, it answered in under 30 milliseconds and the control system acted within 40. The model sorts birds by species and judges how close they are, so turbines can respond by risk zone. The authors warn that real sea trials are still needed.
pmc-13264910:
Amanda T Goodwin and colleagues present the INDEX study protocol, published in 2026, on hospital admissions for scarred lung disease. Fibrotic interstitial lung disease can flare suddenly, and such flares carry high death rates. Most prior research covers only one subtype, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Many admitted patients who fall outside flare criteria remain unstudied.

Case notes from admissions during one year will be reviewed across several centres. Staff will record symptoms, tests, treatments, and survival. The main outcome is survival without transplant at ninety days. The results should describe real-world care and highlight factors linked to outcomes for future trials.
pmc-13265010:
Thanh Dinh Le and colleagues published a 2026 study of blood sugar targets in older adults with type 2 diabetes in Vietnam. Targets are tailored to each elder's health, and whether men and women miss them for different reasons was unclear. The team surveyed outpatients aged 60 and over in late 2025.

Of 537 patients, 25.5 percent missed their personal target, with near-equal rates in men, 24.8 percent, and women, 26.4 percent. Overall, missing linked to taking many drugs, limits in daily tasks like shopping and cooking, and having diabetes for at least five years. In men, long diabetes duration was the main factor. In women, dependent income, many drugs, and task limits each mattered. The authors suggest geriatric checks and sex-aware care in clinics, while calling the findings hypothesis-generating.
pmc-13265210:
Juncheng Bai and colleagues study a plant flavonoid called astragalin in lung adenocarcinoma, in a 2026 combined data and laboratory study. This lung cancer often escapes controlled cell death. A combined death programme called PANoptosis offers a possible target. Network methods predicted astragalin targets and death-related genes.

Overlap analyses produced fifty-nine candidate genes. Machine learning prioritised a four-gene signature tied to the cell cycle. All four genes were raised in tumours and linked to poor outlook. Docking tests predicted strong binding by astragalin. Treating lung cancer cells lowered those genes and triggered death-related changes.
pmc-13265410:
Kenta Yamauchi, Masato Koike, and Hiroyuki Hioki present a fast staining method for thick mouse brain slices, in a 2026 protocol. Three-dimensional staining shows molecular organisation inside intact tissue. Slow antibody penetration and weak signals limit such work. Tiny engineered antibodies fused to an enzyme were combined with signal amplification.

The protocol covers tissue preparation, antibody binding, and amplified fluorescent detection. Targets became visible through slices one millimetre thick within three days. Signal strength rose several-fold over standard fluorescence methods. Cell bodies and fine processes of nerve and support cells could be seen. The method should speed structural studies of brain tissue.
pmc-13265710:
Sheng Zhong and colleagues review body clocks as hidden drivers of muscle and bone disorders, published in 2026. Daily rhythms are set by a master clock in the brain and local tissue clocks. Light, food, and activity can sync or disrupt them. Shift work and irregular meals commonly cause disruption.

The review covers clock roles in bone, cartilage, tendon, and muscle physiology. Disruption contributes to disorders through several pathways. Treatments that reset clocks or time medicines to rhythms are discussed. The authors argue that understanding these rhythms offers prevention and treatment opportunities for common musculoskeletal conditions.
pmc-13266410:
Sofía Toribio Castelló and a large team share 2026 gene results from the SintraRev trial in blood cancer care. The trial tested early use of the drug lenalidomide in people with a marrow disorder marked by a missing piece of chromosome 5. These patients were anemic but did not yet need blood transfusions.

Gene testing covered 51 patients, followed for a median of about 61 months. The most common gene changes were in SF3B1 and TP53. In the drug group, the main cell clones shrank in many patients, while clones stayed stable or grew in all placebo patients after two years. Early treatment did not push clones toward acute leukemia.
pmc-13266610:
Jing Zhou and the team present a partly self-run protocol for producing screening antibodies in hamster ovary cells (2026). Discovery work needs dozens of purified antibodies in ten-milligram amounts. Old custom making is slow and costly. A high-producing engineered cell line anchors the workflow.

The products are captured straight inside the culture using magnetic protein beads. A partly self-run cleaning system then processes them. Skipping spinning, filtering, and column loading saves time and money. Dozens of constructs per week were made as routine at screening quality. The approach also transfers to other common making cell lines.
pmc-13267410:
Kathryn Goetzke and Veronica O'Brien wrote a 2026 review arguing that hope should be a tool for the world's development goals. The United Nations goals cover poverty, health, schooling, and the environment. A 2023 report found weak progress on over half the targets, with about 30 percent stalled or going backward.

The authors warn that repeated failure breeds hopelessness, which is linked to anxiety and depression. Hope, they note, is a skill that can be taught, not just a feeling. Teaching hope has shown gains in health, schooling, and work in past research. They call for spreading hope programs worldwide so people keep acting on the goals. This is a narrative review, drawing together selected past work rather than testing a new program.
pmc-13267510:
Latifa Greche, Nicolas Virlet, and Malcolm J Hawkesford present a 2026 method for measuring wheat heads in 3D. The wheat head, or spike, holds the grains, and its shape affects yield. Hand measuring is slow and error-prone, which blocks large breeding studies. The team built a scanning pipeline that rebuilds each spike as a sharp 3D cloud of points.

Software lines the scans up and extracts length, volume, and cross-section shapes on its own. New measures capture zones of failed spikelets and the branching of spike parts. The 3D traits matched classic measures such as spike and seed weight. The method separated 12 wheat types into clear shape groups, from long to compact. The authors offer it as a fast, harmless tool for breeders.
pmc-13267810:
MeiXiu Huang and colleagues report a 2026 study of lasting high-risk HPV infection and the body's defenses. HPV is a common virus; its high-risk types can drive cervical cancer when infection persists. The team studied 165 patients at one Chinese hospital from 2021 to 2022: 49 whose infection persisted and 116 whose infection cleared.

The persistent group showed a more disturbed vaginal environment, with worse cleanliness grades, higher bacterial imbalance scores, and more enzyme signs of imbalance. Their shares of two T cell types, CD4 and CD8, were lower than in the cleared group. One type, CD8 killer T cells, stood out as an independent factor tied to persistence. The authors suggest checking both vaginal balance and CD8 levels to spot high-risk patients.
pmc-13268110:
Asteria H Kimambo and colleagues present a 2026 interview study on improving tissue sampling at a national hospital in Tanzania. Fine-needle aspiration uses a thin needle to draw cells from a lump; it is cheap and often the main diagnostic route in poorer countries. Ultrasound guidance and instant on-site checking of samples make it far more accurate, but both are hard to set up.

The team interviewed 23 stakeholders, from pathologists and surgeons to lab scientists and administrators. Barriers included missing training in cell diagnosis, the need for new equipment and supplies, and no way to bill patients for the procedure. Helpful factors included overseas training partnerships and eager leadership. Suggestions included systematic training, a clear referral path, a named champion, stronger lab systems, and workable payment rules.
pmc-13268410:
Clara Sanches Bueno and colleagues present a 2026 analysis of over 1.1 million varicose vein surgeries in Brazil's public system. Varicose veins are common and mostly affect women, but sex differences in surgery were little studied in poorer countries. The team examined every public-sector operation from 2007 to 2024, comparing age, travel, and death rates by sex.

Women accounted for about 81 percent of operations. Men had surgery slightly older, at a median of 49 against 47, and traveled between cities a bit more often. Deaths were rare for both sexes but clearly higher in men. The authors argue biology alone cannot explain the gaps: care-seeking habits and structural unfairness also shape who gets surgery and when. They call for interview-based research on the reasons.
pmc-13268710:
Yuki Kondo and Ippei Suzuki present a 2026 study validating an automatic video system that tracks posture in Parkinson's disease. Bent and leaning postures affect about a fifth of patients, but clinics measure them from single photos, missing change over time. Their system combines pose-estimation software with image segmentation to read trunk angles every second. Fourteen patients with posture problems stood for two minutes while tablets filmed them.

Against hand-measured angles from 140 video frames, the system matched excellently for forward bending at the waist and chest after an optional first-frame calibration. Sideways lean matched well. Continuous tracking caught posture slowly worsening during the stand, something photo checks cannot show. The authors say the tool can sharpen both clinical assessment and research on posture in Parkinson's.
pmc-13268810:
Maureen S Bonness reported a 14-year field study in 2026 on cypress knees in a swamp in southwestern Florida. Cypress knees are woody parts of tree roots that stick up out of the ground. Bonness asked when these knees grow, and what role flood water plays.

Thirty knees were measured each month from 2012 to 2025. Most growth came from June through September, and only when water stood above the ground. Growth slowed each October and was rare from November through March. Wet summers with longer floods brought more growth, while dry summers brought almost none. Average growth was 0.39 centimeters a year, with one knee reaching 3.6 centimeters in a single season.
pmc-13269410:
Hadil Mohamed Aboelenin and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on an early marker of kidney damage in children with type 1 diabetes. The standard urine test often shows damage only after it is well established. A protein called FABP1, released when kidney tube cells are hurt, may signal damage sooner.

Ninety children were compared: 30 with kidney disease, 30 with diabetes but no kidney disease, and 30 healthy controls. Blood FABP1 was higher in the kidney disease group than in both other groups. It rose alongside the standard urine measure and blood fats. A cut point above 189 separated the groups, catching 63 percent of cases with 73 percent exactness. The authors propose it as an added test.
pmc-13269510:
Dinara Yerlanova and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 surveying health workers on infection risks in pregnant women with inflammatory rheumatic diseases. These diseases and their treatments raise infection risk during pregnancy. An online survey with 30 questions reached specialists in many fields.

A total of 201 workers from 36 countries replied, and 72.1 percent were rheumatologists, joint and immune specialists. Lupus, vasculitis, and rheumatoid arthritis were rated the highest-risk diseases. Screening was most often advised for hepatitis B, urine infections, and hepatitis C. Uncontrolled disease and high-dose steroid use topped the risk factors. Too few specialists and missing team care were the biggest barriers named.
pmc-13269810:
Myong-Wuk Chon and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on social support among student survivors of the Sewol ferry disaster, which killed 304 of 476 passengers in 2014. Sixty-six student survivors were assessed twice a year from 2016 to 2021. Surveys measured support, traumatic stress, and complicated grief.

Support paths split into four groups, from low starting support to the highest. One group started moderate and rose over time. Compared with the highest support group, that rising group had a higher risk of strong traumatic stress symptoms. Both the low group and the rising group faced higher risk of probable complicated grief. The authors say students with low or shifting support need closest watching.
pmc-13270210:
Anna Nikula and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on children's behavior four weeks after sedation for painful procedures in emergency care. Parents of 128 children who had received nose-spray sedation or laughing gas were interviewed by phone. A standard questionnaire measured behavior changes since the procedure.

Changes were reported in only 13 children, or 10.2 percent: eight negative and five positive. Children with negative changes were younger, with a median age of 5.7 years against 9.4 years for unchanged children. They and their parents were less willing to use the same method again. Parent satisfaction was also lower in that group. Pain scores during the procedure showed no link with later negative changes.
pmc-13270710:
Anna Hörberg is lead author of a 2026 document analysis of how new staff are brought into the Swedish ambulance service. New ambulance workers must handle varied, unpredictable cases from day one, often with low confidence and strain, yet their schooling covers only part of the skills the job needs.

The authors studied induction programme materials from 23 ambulance organisations covering all 21 Swedish health regions. They grouped the training content into six areas, from driving and navigation to safe care settings and organisational knowledge, plus a seventh group on teaching methods. They conclude induction needs stronger evidence and teaching design, covering people skills, ethics, and belonging as well as clinical skills.
pmc-13270810:
Jenny Lander led a 2026 case-control study of slow, unsteady walking in older adults and its links to enlarged brain fluid spaces. Such walking problems and enlarged spaces are both common in old age, and the study asked whether standard imaging signs for a treatable condition called INPH truly match the walking problem.

From 6,467 people aged 65 to 84 who were screened, doctors identified 81 with the typical higher-level gait disorder and 192 matched controls. The disorder's prevalence was 5.8 percent. Those affected were older, scored worse on thinking tests, and showed larger fluid spaces and other imaging features more often than controls.
pmc-13270910:
Linda Åkeflo is lead author of a 2026 qualitative interview study titled Chipped but not broken. It covers life more than five years after radiotherapy for meningioma. Meningioma is the most common brain tumour in adults. These tumours are usually benign, but treatment can leave lasting headache, tiredness, and thinking problems.

Twenty people took part in online interviews, 17 treated with proton beam therapy and three with standard radiotherapy, most over six years earlier. Two themes emerged: adjusted life circumstances and reduced autonomy. Some described lasting symptoms that reshaped daily life, yet also built new routines and accepted new limits. Others felt more dependent on family.
pmc-13271510:
Xiaoyu Meng is lead author of a 2026 journal article presenting PianoGym, a simulator for two-handed piano rhythm training. Training must keep the hands in precise time while respecting limits on player fatigue. Feedback normally arrives only after an exercise ends, so the training problem is framed as decision-making with delayed, partial information.

The authors add a two-layer safety system: a slow layer tracking long-term fatigue budgets and a fast guard screening each next exercise against current fatigue estimates. Their planning controller, PianoMPC, reached mastery in about 24 to 28 steps across three learner profiles, with feasible rates of 0.90 to 0.95, beating simpler bandit and value-based agents under the same guard.
pmc-13271910:
Chenyang Li and colleagues investigate in 2026 whether a standard severity score relates to sepsis among intensive care patients with bowel disease who died. Sepsis drives much of the death toll in this group, yet early warning remains hard. The score studied sums how far body measures stray from normal on ICU arrival.

From a large critical care database, the team selected 190 adults with inflammatory bowel disease who died during their stay, 55 of them with sepsis. Higher scores tracked with sepsis even after adjustment, and the top quarter of scores carried nearly five times the odds. The authors treat the result as a lead for study, not proof.
pmc-13272210:
Martie van Tongeren is lead author of a 2026 occupational health study of heat stress among sugarcane workers in Thailand, who labour in very hot, humid conditions. The study measured environmental heat across full shifts and counted workers' heat-related symptoms, including severe symptoms linked to heat stroke.

Among 295 workers in Nakhon Sawan Province, recruited in cooler and hotter months of 2023, average adjusted full-shift heat exposure was high, with over forty percent exposed at the top range measured.
