Dustin C. Brown and colleagues synthesise and study paired ruthenium carbonyl complexes in a 2026 article. Such phosphine-supported pairs can catalyse small-molecule changes, from alkene shifts to hydrogenation. Fluorinated acetate bridges give the metal centres a fresh electronic setting that may tune that activity.

One trifluoroacetate-bridged compound was made by two routes and its structure was solved. Measured and computed traits are set beside three kin compounds that vary the bridge and phosphine parts. Past work links the twist angle between phosphines to alkene shift activity, though one study found no such link and pointed to electron donation instead. The new data add a fluorinated case to that debate.
pmc-13331710:
Georgios Mavrogenis and colleagues present a 2026 technique report on removing a stubborn recurrent growth from the duodenum of a 70-year-old woman. The 1.5 cm adenoma had regrown after several earlier removal attempts and sat in heavy scar tissue, which makes cutting in the thin duodenal wall risky.

Their combined method filled the bowel with salt water, used clip-and-band traction to hold the tissue taut, and applied a hook-and-drag cutting motion in the scarred areas. Working under general anesthesia with surgical backup, they removed the growth in one piece, closed the site with clips, and the patient recovered without problems. The authors suggest the mix of methods can make such fibrotic duodenal cases safer to treat.
pmc-13332710:
Yu Kuei Lin and co-authors surveyed United States adults with type 1 diabetes in 2026 on how low blood sugar still affects daily life despite modern monitoring and pump technology. Nearly everyone using continuous glucose monitors or hybrid closed-loop pumps still feels the drag of hypoglycaemia.

The analysis covered 796 adults recruited through the T1D Exchange, 23 percent using monitors alone and 77 percent using closed-loop systems, who completed a 12-domain impact questionnaire. Overall, 96 percent reported at least one life domain harmed, and 31 percent reported harm in 10 or more domains, led by sleep, leisure, emotional well-being, spontaneity, and exercise. Closed-loop users surprisingly reported worse impacts than monitor-only users in leisure, fitness, spontaneity, sex life, and work. The authors urge routine clinical attention to low-sugar burden and more work on why technology alone does not lift it.
pmc-13333410:
Elena Uyy and a team profiled the blood of diabetic foot patients in a 2026 study, looking for a pattern of damage signals rather than stray markers. Diabetic foot syndrome mixes poor circulation, chronic inflammation, and wounds that will not heal, yet its molecular footprint was ill defined.

The team used high-resolution protein measurement on plasma from diabetic patients with and without the foot syndrome, including degrees of limb ischemia. They found a set of acute-phase and stress proteins shifted together. The set includes serum amyloid A1 and A2, amyloid P component, and S100A8. It also includes defensin alpha 1B, fibrinogen chains, a heat shock protein, thymosin beta 4, fibronectin, and tenascins. In diabetic mice with ischemic wounds, blocking the danger sensor TLR4 changed several of the proteins, lowering some amyloid-linked ones. The authors frame the signature as evidence that damage-associated signals drive inflammation in this complication.
pmc-13333510:
Guangbi Fu and colleagues report a counterintuitive link in a 2026 cross-sectional study: among type 2 diabetes patients, higher vitamin B12 levels went with more diabetic retinopathy, not less. B12 shortfalls are common in diabetes and earlier work tied deficiency to eye damage, so the direction of the finding cuts against habit.

The analysis reused data on 413 adults with type 2 diabetes seen in Guangdong between December 2017 and November 2018, with eye disease graded by ophthalmologists. After adjustment for confounders, each 100-unit rise in B12 carried 49 percent higher odds of retinopathy. Patients in the top third of B12 levels, at or above 398, showed higher odds than the bottom third, at an odds ratio of 11.83. Curve modelling confirmed a straight-line relationship, and no subgroup, by sex, age, or kidney function, changed the pattern. The authors stress a snapshot cannot prove B12 causes eye disease, only that the association runs the unexpected way.
pmc-13333710:
ShangJun Li, Avijit Deb Nath, and Md. Hadi Al-amin authored a 2026 computational study of how cooperation evolves in repeated games between self-interested agents. They focus on memory-two strategies, which respond to the last two rounds of play between both sides.

Their framework joins a Q-learning multi-agent engine with Moran, Wright-Fisher, and replicator selection rules, tested across eight simulation experiments. Under standard Prisoner's Dilemma payoffs, play settled at a high cooperation rate near 0.814 on average. Memory-two strategies made up 61.0 percent of the settled population and always took over when invading a fully defecting population. Cooperation survived moderate noise but collapsed past a clear threshold. The results map where long-memory reciprocity can hold in artificial and human systems.
pmc-13333810:
Jing Luo and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol testing Tiao Shen Li Yan acupuncture for swallowing problems after stroke. Acupuncture often improves swallowing in this group, yet nobody has mapped how it reorganizes brain networks.

The randomized, single-blind, sham-controlled trial will enroll 46 patients with post-stroke dysphagia, split evenly between real and sham acupuncture given 30 minutes a day, five days a week, for six weeks. Resting-state functional MRI and diffusion imaging will track connectivity changes, while swallowing assessments, a videofluoroscopy-based measure, cognition testing, and a quality-of-life questionnaire capture clinical change. Twenty healthy volunteers provide reference scans. As a protocol, the article reports the design and planned outcomes rather than results.
pmc-13334410:
Manuel Jesús Enciso-Ripoll and co-authors mapped Spain's public dental workforce in a 2026 cross-sectional analysis. Spain has one of Europe's densest dentist supplies, yet public coverage is thin and uneven across regions.

Data came from transparency requests to all 17 autonomous communities plus Ceuta and Melilla, registration records, and health ministry sources. In 2024-2025 Spain counted 42,860 active dentists, about 84.68 per 100,000 people, but only 1,685 salaried public dentists, leaving an average load near 31,590 residents per public dentist. The public share ranged from 2.0 percent in Madrid to 7.6 percent in Castilla-La Mancha. Another 6,810 accredited private providers joined public programs in mixed-model regions. The numbers frame a planning problem about equity, not raw supply.
pmc-13335810:
Shan-Shan Rao and co-authors identified a gut bacterial protein that protects bone in a 2026 study of the gut-skeleton axis. Signals from gut microbes reach distant organs, but the actual messenger molecules were unknown.

The protein, Amuc_1473, rides in vesicles shed by the commensal bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila. It directly encourages bone formation and restrains bone-eating cells by binding two regulators, NELF-E and RPL26, that govern transcription pausing and protein production. Levels of the protein fell in bone and blood across many bone-loss settings, from aging and estrogen loss to smoking, chronic stress, alcohol, and high-fat diet. Intermittent fasting restored the bacterium, the protein, and bone quality in these models, tying a popular diet pattern to a concrete microbial mechanism.
pmc-13336510:
Yixin Zhu and co-authors built a deep learning system that proposes new near-infrared fluorescent dyes in a 2026 study. Near-infrared imaging sees deep into tissue with little background glow, but finding good fluorophores by hand is slow, expensive labor.

Their system runs two modules: a predictive one, sharpened by transfer learning to cope with scarce data, estimates optical properties, while a generative module drafts candidates that chemists can actually synthesize. Three suggested molecules, NTDT-TPA, NPA-BTD, and DPP-TPA, were made and tested to validate the pipeline. NTDT-TPA was packed into nanoparticles and performed in cells and living animals as a fluorescence imaging agent. Knowledge transfer between tasks let the small dataset punch above its weight.
pmc-13336910:
Jiawen Chen leads a large 2026 team wrapping boron carriers in macrophage skin to treat glioblastoma. This brain tumor resists cures because the blood-brain barrier blocks drugs and the tumor stifles immunity. Boron neutron capture therapy kills tumor cells selectively, but standard boron agents reach the brain too weakly.

The membrane coat crosses the barrier, homes to tumors, and dodges immune clearance using the macrophage's own tricks. In mouse gliomas it delivered 53.15 µg per gram of boron-10 to tumors, a level 3.09-fold above uncoated particles in the study comparison. Neutron shots extended survival by 50 days and woke up immunity in the reported model. Adding anti-PD-1 therapy cleared tumors fully in half the mice.
pmc-13337110:
Xiangyu Xu and co-authors reveal how dividing cells share their endoplasmic reticulum fairly in a 2026 study. This membrane network, sheets near the nucleus and tubes at the edges, must split evenly between daughter cells. At division entry the pattern reverses: tubes gather around the centrosomes while sheets move outward.

A division kinase tags the tube-shaping protein RTN4, which then partners with Rab11 and rides dynein motors toward the centrosomes. That gathering tubes the nearby network and guarantees symmetric inheritance, which in turn helps other organelles split evenly and division proceed faithfully. Fair organelle sharing turns out to be actively engineered, not left to chance.
pmc-13337410:
Fatih Mehmet Uğurlu and colleagues survey earthquake trauma among athletes in Turkey in a 2026 study. The sample held 359 athletes living in 11 provinces hit by the Kahramanmaraş earthquakes of February 6, 2023, reached by snowball sampling. A standard scale measured post-earthquake trauma levels alongside personal details.

Average trauma scored 65.84 on the scale used, above the midpoint and classed as above-average by the authors. Women reported more symptoms than men. Athletes who lost relatives or lost a home also scored markedly higher than those who did not. The authors conclude that athletic life alone does not buffer disaster trauma, and that bereavement and housing loss deserve targeted mental health support after quakes.
pmc-13337510:
Marthe Sophie Kilian leads a 2026 team measuring late kidney damage after radiation that grazes the kidneys. Precise ablative radiotherapy for kidney tumors controls cancer well, but long-term renal safety data are thin. The retrospective cohort screened 731 trunk radiotherapy patients and kept 232 whose kidneys received meaningful incidental dose, tracking kidney function over time.

Worsening kidney disease appeared in 46.98% of patients during a median follow-up of 170 days in the cohort analysis. Higher mean and maximum kidney doses independently predicted decline, with a steady dose-response and risk cut-offs near 18.7 Gy and 19.0 Gy in the exploratory analysis. Female sex also raised risk. Severe toxicity stayed rare, supporting careful, kidney-sparing treatment planning.
pmc-13337710:
Jeong-Hoo Lee and colleagues test two yogurt-related bacteria as possible oral probiotics in a 2026 study. Streptococcus mutans and Streptococcus sobrinus help drive tooth decay by building plaque biofilms. Blocking settlement, rather than killing bacteria outright, is the strategy explored here.

Strains DM287 and DM294 of Streptococcus thermophilus came from yogurt and from the tongue coating of healthy adults. Both cut plaque mass by about three quarters in a wire model assay reported by the authors. They also lowered pathogen biofilm and reduced sticking under test conditions. Growth tests suggested the effect was not mainly from killing, supporting a gentler route to decay prevention.
pmc-13339010:
Yidian Wang and Piero Macchi simulate missing-link defects in a metal-organic framework in a 2026 study. Ultra-low dielectric materials are vital for smaller electronics, and the framework HKUST-1 is a candidate. Removing some links might lower its dielectric response further.

A polarizable force field was tuned against the clean material, then applied to flawed versions. Defects cut dielectric susceptibility by up to about 30 percent in the reported simulations, reaching a constant near 1.5 as modeled. Response fell in a straight line as defects rose, driven by lower polarizability. Even few defects sped dielectric relaxation, suggesting deliberate flaws as a design tool.

The review weighs peer-reviewed studies, earlier reviews, and guidelines to judge whether the technology genuinely shortens the road to surgery or merely promises to.
pmc-13401810:
Chuchu Zhao and co-authors describe a 2026 case of granulomatous mastitis, a chronic inflammatory breast condition that mimicked infection for months. Their patient was a 24-year-old woman with right breast pain and a growing mass that lasted four months.

She was treated first as a breast abscess, through several antibiotic courses and surgical drainage. Steroid shots into the lesion brought no improvement, while new areas were hit too. A scan suggested an inflammatory lesion, tests stayed negative, and a core biopsy finally showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation, proving granulomatous mastitis. As things worsened despite all that, methotrexate, a drug that damps the immune system, was started, and at about seven weeks she felt broadly better. The authors stress early biopsy when a seeming abscess will not behave like one, and the hard call of when to switch from antibiotics to immune treatment.
pmc-13402010:
Ayodeji S Erubu and co-authors audited whether patients starting mental health medicines at a hospital in South-West Nigeria got the basic checks guidelines call for. Records covered first-contact patients seen from January 2024 through December 2025, judged against NICE and Royal College of Psychiatrists standards. Of 345 patients reviewed, 262 received at least one psychotropic medicine and entered the audit.

Simple bedside checks did well, with weight, vital signs, and movement screening recorded for every patient. Blood and heart tests lagged badly: kidney tests reached only about a quarter of patients, heart tracings about one in nine, and no one had prolactin checked. Inpatients scored far higher than outpatients. The authors call for local protocols, better access to tests, and repeat audits to close the gap.
pmc-13402310:
Konstantinos Kapelios and colleagues present bMINTY, a local web app that keeps the results of high-throughput sequencing studies tidy, searchable, and reusable. Gene studies produce huge result sets, and key facts often scatter across papers, supplements, and repositories, which blocks reuse. Most labs reuse ready gene expression tables rather than rerunning raw data, yet no single portable tool tied those tables to their study details.

bMINTY stores details for studies, assays, and result files, including workflow versions, genome annotation versions, and single-cell identities for cell-level work. Query results export as RO-Crate packages, machine-readable bundles that can ride along as publication supplements next to public analysis code. Kapelios and the team built the tool around FAIR goals: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable data. The pitch is less new science than better housekeeping for science already done.
pmc-13402610:
Haoyin Zhong and co-authors give chemists a way to time the single steps of the oxygen evolution reaction, the slow half of water splitting that bottlenecks many energy devices. Catalyst design has leaned on bulk traits matched to overall activity, leaving the speed of each elementary step hidden. Their open-circuit voltage-pulse method pauses electron flow to the circuit while hydroxide keeps feeding electrons, isolating the step that forms the OOH intermediate.

Paired with a pulse method timing the OH deprotonation step, the framework shows dopants split the work: iron speeds OOH formation, while manganese speeds deprotonation instead. A nickel iron manganese catalyst built on that split improved both steps at once and performed better overall. The authors offer the step-timing approach as a practical ruler for finding strong electrocatalysts faster and with less guesswork.
pmc-13403010:
Tamas Toth and co-authors report a 600 gram girl born at about 25 weeks whose gut disease tore a hole in her stomach at 24 days old. Neonatal gastric perforation is a rare surgical emergency of premature, extremely low birth weight infants, with high mortality. She had developed necrotizing enterocolitis in her third week, then worsened with a swollen belly and free air inside.

Emergency surgery found a single hole in the back wall of the stomach ringed by dead tissue, exactly where the feeding tube tip sat. Surgeons trimmed the dead edge minimally and closed the hole in two layers. She survived a long intensive care course scarred by repeated sepsis, liver bile stasis, chronic lung disease, and a later adhesive blockage needing a second operation. The authors argue the necrotic margins favor ischemic injury from severe gut disease over tube trauma.
pmc-13404010:
Satoshi Yoneda and co-authors described in 2026 how a focused burn treatment stopped bleeding from neck-of-womb growths in three pregnant women. Such growths in pregnancy raise the risk of late miscarriage and early birth. All three cases looked like pregnancy-type growths on exam and ultrasound.

Doctors seared only the growth surface to stop the bleeding, alongside oral gut-support therapy. Bleeding stopped at once in all three women. The growths then shrank step by step until none could be seen. Each woman went on to deliver at full term. The gentle option deserves wider study, the team says.
pmc-13405610:
Steffany Martins Moreira and colleagues study first foods beyond milk for babies in the western Brazilian Amazon, in a 2026 analysis. Data come from the MINA-Brazil birth cohort in Cruzeiro do Sul, Acre, with 774 children seen at one year and 854 at two years. Diet was captured by a day-long recall at each visit.

Quality indicators follow World Health Organization advice: food variety, meat or egg eating, ultra-processed food and days with no fruit or vegetables. Meat or egg eating reached 79 percent at age one and 89.9 percent at age two in the reported figures. Ultra-processed food was also common, a mixed picture. Social and health factors are modelled in layers from distant to close causes.
pmc-13406310:
Amina McDiarmid argues in a 2026 essay that Alzheimer's drug discovery must look beyond antibody treatments. Approved anti-amyloid immunotherapies clear brain plaques, yet how much real thinking and daily function they save stays disputed. Three named drugs anchor the discussion: aducanumab, lecanemab and donanemab.

Treatment slows decline by roughly twenty to thirty percent in some patient groups, the essay notes, but absolute gains remain modest. Benefit concentrates in early disease with low tau burden. Swelling and bleeding in the brain occur often enough to matter for safety and cost. McDiarmid warns that statistically clear trial results may not translate into meaningful real-world benefit.
pmc-13406810:
Mihaela Zaharie led a 2026 study of preterm babies who developed bloodstream infections caused by Gram-negative bacteria in a specialist newborn unit. The team looked back at cases from 2022 and 2023, covering both infections appearing soon after birth and those starting later.

Later-starting infections were more common, and Klebsiella pneumoniae was the organism found most often. Resistant bacteria were linked to about half the cases, and roughly one baby in four died in hospital. Among survivors checked at 18 to 24 months, about 38 percent showed developmental problems, mostly in language and thinking skills. Being born earlier stood out as the clearest predictor of both death and later impairment, pointing to early treatment and planned follow-up.
pmc-13408710:
Steffen Herff and colleagues listen in 2026 to the forearm muscles of twenty-two drummers to learn what years of practice do to the electrical chatter of individual motor units. Surface sensors recorded two wrist muscles while drummers of widely varying experience played a steady one-handed pattern at five speeds. The team extracted the shape of each muscle spike and modelled how it changed with lifetime practice hours.

Experienced players kept steadier timing and struck more evenly between hands, as expected. Their muscle spikes also fired more often, lasted less time, and carried fewer peaks, a signature the authors read as more efficient muscle use rather than simply stronger contraction. The pattern depended on which muscle, which arm, and how fast the tempo ran. The results offer rare physiological evidence that long training refines the motor units themselves.
pmc-13410410:
Hafiza Aasia Malik and colleagues review in 2026 how bacterial membranes are being reshaped into cancer vaccine platforms. A bacterium's outer skin naturally alarms the immune system, which makes it a strong carrier. Engineers can also fix tumor markers onto that skin so the body learns both targets at once.

Forms covered include tiny shed vesicles, emptied bacterial shells, membrane pieces, and blends fused with tumor membranes. Tests in mice with melanoma, lung, breast, and brain tumors showed hotter immune attack inside tumors and help alongside other therapies. New tools, from gene editing to computer-guided antigen choice, speed design. Safety fixes such as softening toxic lipid parts remain central before human use.
pmc-13410610:
Zhouyang Gao and co-workers study in 2026 why some laying hens eat more than their body and eggs seem to need. The gap between actual feed use and expected use, called residual feed intake, reflects inborn metabolic differences. Breeding for a low gap could cut feed costs, yet late laying life was little studied.

Hens matched for weight and egg count were split into low-gap and high-gap groups. Low-gap hens used protein and dry matter better and showed stronger antioxidant defenses. Their gut walls also looked steadier, with firmer seal proteins and calmer immune signals. Chemical profiling of blood and droppings pointed to amino acid, fat, and energy pathways as the main ground of difference.
pmc-13410710:
Nicky Ahadi, Jeeyeon Kim, Daniel Whibley, and Maxwell Barnish weigh in 2026 the evidence that music-based therapy aids recovery in multiple sclerosis. Music methods range from walking to a beat to imagining movement while listening. Small studies have hinted at gains, yet the overall picture was scattered.

Six databases were searched, and 23 studies with 955 participants met the rules for inclusion. Motor function was the outcome checked most often, then quality of life. Beat-cued walking and music-guided movement imagery showed the most steady gains, covering speed, distance, stride, and symmetry of gait. Results for other outcomes stayed murky. Differences in methods and small samples cap how firm any claim can be.
pmc-13410810:
Jiazheng Lin and co-workers build in 2026 a personal genome for a liver cancer patient and use it to hunt tumor changes that standard references miss. Universal reference genomes hide patient-specific variation in repetitive or complex DNA stretches. Their approach assembled both copies of the patient's genome almost completely.

Long-read and chromosome-contact sequencing built paired assemblies from tumor and healthy tissue of the same person. Using the healthy assembly as the reference sharpened read alignment and cut ambiguous matches. Extra small and structural changes surfaced, including some in the hard-to-read centromere regions. Gene activity read by parental copy flagged candidate drivers, and lab tests backed two regulatory suspects for follow-up.
pmc-13412010:
Michael P Dorsch and colleagues report the ManageHF randomized trial in 2026, testing phone-app prompts that coach heart failure patients at home. About 900,000 older Americans are hospitalized for heart failure each year, and missed symptoms or salty diets often send patients back. The app sent just-in-time messages on spotting worsening symptoms and cutting dietary sodium, arranged in a two-by-two design with an active control group.

Recruitment faltered during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the trial stopped early with 62 patients enrolled and 43 finishing twelve weeks. Participants averaged 55 years of age, and most had a weakened heart pump. Too few patients finished for firm conclusions, so the authors stress better recruitment plans for future app trials.
pmc-13412410:
Lai, Liu, Lei, and Chen test, in 2026, whether adding the targeted drug lenvatinib to the dual immunotherapy nivolumab plus ipilimumab fixes that regimen's weak early tumor control in unresectable liver cancer. That flaw cost lives in the first year of the pivotal trial. Their retrospective Taipei series covered 104 patients, 82 on the doublet alone and 22 on the triple combination, with weighting methods to balance the groups.

The triple therapy controlled disease far more often, an 81.8 percent disease control rate against 39.0 percent for the doublet in the analyzed cohort, while responses lasted a similar 21.4 versus 21.8 months once achieved. Median progression-free survival stretched from 3.2 months to 10.2 months with lenvatinib added, and the adjusted hazard ratio of 0.44 confirmed the benefit, though overall survival did not significantly improve. High blood pressure, proteinuria, and mouth sores came more often with the triple regimen, while liver function scores stayed stable.
pmc-13412510:
Cem Terece, Simge Tezel Yozgat, and Volkan Karataşlı compare two stitch materials for cervical cerclage in a 2026 pilot study. Cerclage, a stitch that holds a weak cervix closed during pregnancy, is usually placed with braided polyester, and makers' versions differ in construction. Records covered 22 women who had McDonald cerclage at one centre during 2024 and 2025, split evenly between Mersilene and Uniester sutures.

Delivery timing, maternal complications, and newborn outcomes showed no significant differences between the material groups. Median delivery arrived near 35 weeks in both arms of the study. Operating time ran about three minutes shorter with Uniester, a gap short of statistical significance. Carrying twins emerged as the only independent predictor of early birth in their models.
pmc-13413910:
Bo Zhang, Ronggang Wang, and Feng Wang review in 2026 the state of forward osmosis, a way to clean water by pulling it through a film with a strong draw fluid. No pump pressure is used, so the method saves power and fouls less than reverse osmosis. Drawbacks stay real, though. Flow runs lower, few films are sold, and the draw fluid costs money and power to refresh. Their survey covers film types, draw fluid groups, fouling kinds, and live uses.

Applications span sea water desalting, power from mixed waters, and waste water reuse. Fouling comes in mineral, organic, lump, and germ forms, but lands more gently than in pumped systems. The authors see the field move toward pulling value from water, such as lithium from hot spring brine.
pmc-13415610:
Bruna Paviani and co-authors profile the chemistry of grape pomace, the skins and seeds left after winemaking, from four California varieties in 2026. White wine pomaces from Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc held more leftover sugar and wider sugar chain diversity than red pomaces from Pinot Noir and Merlot. Advanced mass spectrometry identified thirty-nine oligosaccharides, built mainly from six carbon and five carbon sugars.

Two flavanol compounds, catechin and its mirror form epicatechin, made up to half of measured phenolics in Chardonnay pomace and about 45 percent in Pinot Noir. Glucose and fructose dominated the sugar building blocks. The molecular map supports turning this winery residue into valuable ingredients.
pmc-13416810:
Ri-Xin Jiang and co-authors revise the ground beetle genus Broscosoma in China, in a 2026 taxonomic paper. The genus holds 62 known species across western Europe and east Asia, with China especially rich at 45 recorded forms. Their work describes seven species that are new to science, each from a different part of the country.

New species come from Guangdong, Sichuan, Guizhou, Zhejiang, Fujian, Hubei with Chongqing, and Chongqing alone. Drawings show body form and key traits for each one. A full checklist and a distribution map for species outside two major upland regions are included. The authors expect more diversity to emerge from wider work in south China.
pmc-13417710: A 2026 correction notice fixes significance marks in a figure of a study on transdiagnostic cognitive behavioural therapy and long term quality of life across anxiety and depression. The notice is a correction only, stating that one arrow value in the psychological quality of life model wrongly carried significance stars, while another value was missing stars it should have shown. A corrected figure replaces the original, and no results or conclusions are changed.
pmc-13418610:
Devkota and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a toddler whose Wilms tumor, the most common kidney cancer of childhood, first showed up as a blocked bowel. The boy was two and a half years old, with a week of belly pain, swelling, and vomiting. Scans showed a large tumor on the right kidney pressing where the small bowel begins.

Surgeons operated, removing the right kidney and adding a bypass from the stomach to the small bowel. Lab study confirmed stage III disease with favorable cell features. The child healed well and went on to drug treatment and radiation. Most Wilms tumors appear as a painless belly lump, so a blocked bowel as the first sign is rare. Doctors should keep this tumor in mind when a young child has an unexplained bowel block.
pmc-13419410:
Pamela S. Lee and colleagues gather infection prevention experts to test popular myths that keep single-use plastics flowing through hospitals. United States hospitals produce millions of tons of waste each year, much of it plastic from infection control work. Habits held for safety can drive heavy plastic use even when proof behind them is thin.

Eight experts from fields spanning infectious disease, prevention, quality, and sustainability built the list of myths together. A wider survey then asked infection specialists how they judged the same common practices. Each myth was weighed against current published evidence. Naming myths plainly gives hospitals cover to drop wasteful routines that add cost and emissions without making patients safer.
pmc-13420310:
Żurowska and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare eye case in a 76-year-old man treated for sleep apnoea with a CPAP machine. CPAP means a mask that blows air steadily to keep airways open at night. He came to an eye cancer clinic with suspected tumour, plus floaters, flashes, and tunnel-like vision in his left eye. Scans instead showed a large choroidal detachment, meaning fluid had lifted the eye's middle layer.

Eye pressure rose and sight worsened over the first weeks despite steroid and pupil-dilating drops. Doctors added pressure-lowering drops, and over sixteen weeks the detachment slowly settled. No tumour was found at any point. They advise eye teams to consider breathing therapy history when a detachment has no clear cause. The case also shows that careful watching and drops can succeed without surgery.
pmc-13420710:
Beyza Tağraf and colleagues run a randomized trial pairing a plant-rich ketogenic diet with intermittent fasting in early-to-mid Alzheimer's disease. Eating patterns that shift the brain toward ketone fuel may steady failing energy use in this disease. Cognition and brain structure were measured at the start and again at six months.

By a reliable-change yardstick, 93 percent of the diet group held stable, and 7 percent improved. Among controls, 70 percent held stable, and just over 3 percent improved in the same analysis. Group change scores differed firmly in statistical terms. Response tracked each person's metabolic type and brain integrity at entry. The authors present diet-plus-fasting as a candidate support, not a cure, and call for wider trials.
pmc-13421310:
Abhinav Ayyadevara and ten colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about a drug target in Ph-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. This high-risk subtype relapses often. Three-year survival sits near 65 percent. They focus on BRG1, a motor protein of the SWI/SNF chromatin complex that early B cells need.

In solid tumours, losing a related gene makes cancers depend on BRG1's partner protein, yet blood cancers show the reverse pattern: they depend on BRG1 itself. The team's experiments found this leukaemia subtype selectively sensitive to BRG1 blockade. They present that sensitivity as a therapeutic vulnerability worth exploiting, since options after relapse remain poor.
pmc-13421610:
Angeliki Margoni, Kostas A Papavassiliou and Athanasios G Papavassiliou argue, in a 2026 paper, that care for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease should watch for kidney cancer as well as kidney failure. The disease affects roughly one person in a thousand. It is the leading inherited cause of end-stage kidney failure. Observational data also link it to about double the usual risk of renal cell carcinoma.

The authors caution that the risk estimate rests on mixed datasets, and that intensive scanning of cystic kidneys may simply find more cancers. They sketch the biological steps that could carry a cystic kidney toward cancer and propose risk modelling with a multistep, precision surveillance programme. Their aim is proportionate vigilance rather than alarm.
pmc-13422010:
Anders Thorsted and co-authors model how depemokimab, an ultra-long-acting antibody drug, moves through the body and lowers blood eosinophils in asthma and chronic sinus disease with nasal polyps. The drug targets interleukin-5 and is designed for twice-yearly dosing. Their 2026 analysis pools data from three early-phase and four phase III trials.

The pharmacokinetic analysis included 961 participants and the combined analysis 1,324 participants. The model predicted a half-life of 47 days with negligible build-up between doses. A single 100 milligram dose cut blood eosinophil counts to under a quarter of baseline, and levels stayed suppressed across the 26-week dosing interval, with a small rise at the end. No patient factors required dose adjustment. The authors conclude the modelling supports twice-yearly 100 milligram dosing.
pmc-13422810:
Megumi Hazumi leads a thirteen-author team following a Japanese community cohort for nineteen years, in a 2026 study, to test whether an irregular daily rhythm predicts earlier death. Social rhythm — the regularity of sleep, meals and activity — had been suspected of mattering, yet long-term evidence on specific causes of death was scarce.

Nearly one hundred thousand adults aged forty-five to seventy-four rated their rhythm at entry. Those calling it irregular died at consistently higher rates at every checkpoint, with a nineteen-year risk about a tenth higher in relative terms. Death by illness and accidental death both rose; suicide risk was elevated only at some horizons. National death records supplied the outcomes. The authors argue rhythm regularity belongs in preventive health thinking.
pmc-13423310:
Yacoby-Halevi and colleagues mined the United States FDA adverse event database from 2010 to 2024. They checked the safety of ticagrelor in adults aged 75 and older. Ticagrelor is a potent blood-thinning drug used after heart attacks. Its reported side effects were compared against clopidogrel, an older alternative. The comparison ran separately in younger and older patients.

The analysis covered 6,476 ticagrelor-related reports. Of those, 1,681, or 26 percent, involved older adults taking the drug. In that older group, ticagrelor showed no excess reporting of breathlessness, brain bleeding, complete heart block, or gout. That held against younger users. Acute kidney injury was the sole event reported more often in older adults. Its reporting odds ratio was 2.3, against 0.6 in younger patients. Gastrointestinal bleeding and several other bleeding events were reported less often in both age groups.
pmc-13424110:
Zhouen Peng and six colleagues test whether the support plate inside a basketball shoe, carbon fibre, nylon, or none, changes leg loading and muscle work during game movements. Twenty recreational male college players performed jumps, 45-degree cuts, and lateral shuffles in one standard shoe fitted three ways, while force plates and muscle sensors recorded the action.

Across tasks, outside forces and joint moments at the toe, ankle, and knee stayed broadly similar whatever the plate. Muscle activity differed only in narrow spots, most clearly in the thigh muscles during cutting, and joint co-contraction ratios held steady. The authors conclude plate material tunes feel and support without materially raising external loads, a useful boundary for shoe designers.
pmc-13424210:
Noora Said and three co-authors revisit, with post-pandemic calm, what is actually known about COVID-19 and diabetes. Early in the pandemic, diabetes stood out as a top predictor of severe illness and death. Later reports of diabetes appearing after infection raised a new possibility. Influence might run in both directions.

Their review weighs proposed mechanisms, from viral effects in the pancreas to changes in insulin-sensitive tissues. It also audits the big pooled analyses on new type 1 and type 2 diabetes after infection. Strengths and weaknesses of the underlying studies get explicit treatment. The authors separate findings that survived scrutiny from those born of the rush, giving clinicians a steadier map of the two-way link.
pmc-13424310:
Yeseul Kim leads a nineteen-author effort to find diagnoses for children with developmental delay or intellectual disability whose standard exome sequencing came back empty. Two newer technologies were applied to 87 such children: optical genome mapping, which photographs whole chromosomes for large rearrangements, and complete long-read sequencing, which reads long DNA stretches directly.

Six children gained a pathogenic or likely pathogenic answer, four large structural changes and two single-letter changes. The mapping method added diagnoses in 4.71% of cases and the long reads in 6.98%, each catching changes the other missed. Disputed cases were checked with further sequencing, and one deep intron variant was proven harmful in a lab assay. The authors propose a stepwise diagnostic route.
pmc-13424810:
Kurniawan and colleagues present a 2026 case of a baby girl with suspected Cornelia de Lange syndrome. The condition shapes growth, the face, and the limbs before birth. A twenty-eight-year-old mother was referred during pregnancy because her baby measured small. Ultrasound showed shortened forearm bones in both arms, slow growth, and excess fluid around the baby.

An elective caesarean at thirty-seven weeks delivered a girl weighing 1,446 grams. She showed the syndrome's facial signs, including thick eyebrows, a short nose with a sunken bridge, and a long, smooth groove above the lip, alongside the arm malformations. The authors review how such limb findings on prenatal ultrasound can point to the syndrome early. They stress that its severity varies widely, so prognosis depends on which organs and symptoms a given child has.
pmc-13424910:
Kawata and colleagues examined in 2026 whether a blood protein called transthyretin, measured before surgery, predicts recurrence after curative removal of stage I to III colorectal cancer. Transthyretin reflects both nutrition and inflammation and falls quickly when health declines. The team studied 536 patients treated at one hospital from 2014 to 2024, using sex-specific cutoff values for low levels.

Patients with low transthyretin had clearly worse recurrence-free survival than those with high levels. Low levels more than doubled the risk of recurrence after other factors were counted. The signal was not equal across ages, though. It was strongest in younger patients and faded steadily in older ones, and levels ran lower in women and dropped with age. The authors say the test helps most when read with the patient's age and sex in mind.
pmc-13426210:
Dianzhi Feng and colleagues evaluated planting performance of sandy soil solidified with biopolymer and plant fiber in a 2026 environmental study. Yellow River silt mixed with 1.5 percent xanthan gum and 0.6 percent jute fiber formed the growing medium, tested at three compaction levels with oat as the indicator plant. High biopolymer content can hinder growth, so the team proposed a layered structure of residual soil, solidified soil, a seed layer, and raw soil cover.

That structure produced germination above 85 percent, with moderate compaction growing best, soil temperature between 23 and 28 degrees, and moisture holding between 10 and 20 percent across depths. The design counters surface hardening while improving water and heat movement.
pmc-13426410:
Galí and colleagues showed in 2026 that winter convection in the Labrador and Irminger Seas injects fresh surface carbon deep into the ocean, a route missing from most carbon budgets. How much carbon the deep ocean receives matters for climate accounting. Drifting robot profilers in those seas caught repeated green pigment signals a kilometer down during strong mixing winters from 2014 to 2017, evidence that surface plankton were being carried down whole.

The deep particles looked like fresh plankton material, distinct from the usual sinking crumbs. Models tied the deep supply to how much water convection stirred. In strong years, mixing delivered roughly a third to nearly half of the combined carbon supply to the deep layer, rivaling sinking itself.
pmc-13427110:
Junge and co-authors describe the first nickel complexes holding tin and lead analogues of alkynes. Alkynes are the carbon triple-bond units found all through catalysis. Their heavy versions are extremely rare for the heavier elements of group 14. Direct mixing of the tin or lead dimers with a nickel starting material failed. So the team found another route.

Instead, they generated the heavy dimers inside nickel's coordination sphere. They used a reductive group elimination, with hydrogen release from tin hydride precursors bound to the metal. Structural measurements combined with computations showed the products are best described as sigma-complexes. In those, the metal binds the single bond between the two heavy atoms side-on. The authors call this a new bonding mode in organometallic chemistry. It expands how chemists can think about activating heavy-element bonds at transition metal centers for future catalysis.
pmc-13427810:
Jinbo Luo and co-authors search, in a 2026 study, for body-clock genes that matter in fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. Daily rhythm genes help run the liver, and their disruption may feed fat buildup and inflammation. The team combined two public datasets of liver samples with a list of 248 rhythm-related genes. Statistical filtering and network analysis narrowed the field to genes that shifted together with disease.

Machine learning settled on three key genes, named SOCS2, FBXO27, and HMMR. A scoring chart built from them separated patients from controls in both datasets. Immune cell checks tied two of the genes to mast cell activity, a clue about inflammation in the liver. Drug prediction pointed to compounds that might act on these genes. The work stays computational, yet it hands wet-lab teams a short, testable list.
pmc-13428210:
Mehran Mottahedi and co-authors report, in a 2026 case, emergency heart surgery during pregnancy in a teenager with Marfan syndrome. Marfan weakens the aorta, and pregnancy adds strain that can tear or balloon it. Their patient was 19, pregnant for the first time, and 15 weeks along when palpitations led to scans. Imaging showed a giant bulge of the aortic root and upper aorta, a leaking valve, and a weakened heart pump.

After counseling on risks to mother and baby, the team replaced the root and valve in a Bentall operation without ending the pregnancy. Heavy bleeding forced a delayed closing of the chest, plus transfusion support. Scans afterward showed the new valve working and the baby still alive. She went home on day 11, a rare outcome the authors credit to close teamwork.
pmc-13428310:
Lívia Maria Martins Aragão and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, trials of light therapy for a chronic mouth condition called oral lichen planus. The disease causes sore, sometimes ulcered patches inside the mouth and has no cure. Standard steroid treatment helps but brings side effects with long use. Photobiomodulation uses low-level light to calm tissue without drugs. The team searched seven databases through March 2025 and kept 15 clinical trials.

Combined results showed light therapy eased pain slightly more than standard drug care. Disease severity and anxiety scores did not differ clearly between approaches. Light therapy did bring higher rates of complete healing of the mouth lining and fewer returns of lesions in the erosive form. No side effects were reported for the light treatment. Stronger trials are still wanted before firm guidance follows.
pmc-13428710:
Jessica L. Fernandes and co-authors explore, in a 2026 study, how anxiety disorders pair with body chemistry during the pandemic years. More than 300 million people live with an anxiety disorder, and oxidative stress may play a part. Oxidative stress means harm from reactive molecules outruns the body's defenses. The team compared 116 adults with an anxiety diagnosis against 234 adults without one, recruited in Brazil between September 2020 and July 2021.

Standard scales scored anxiety, low mood, stress, daily rhythms, thinking, and day-to-day function. The anxiety group fared worse on all of them, with more stress and more broken daily rhythms. Blood tests showed lower total antioxidant capacity in the anxiety group at first pass. Once the team corrected for the many tests run, that blood gap no longer held up. The authors keep oxidation as a thread worth more study, while the mood and rhythm findings stand on firmer ground.
pmc-13429110:
Qiu, Wu, and Liu reviewed in 2026 urinary tract infections among hospital patients with gynaecological cancers at a hospital in Meizhou, China. Such infections can halt cancer treatment, stretch stays, and raise costs. The team pulled records for 659 patients treated in 2024, covering tumor type, treatment, and infection details, and screened the data for risk factors with layered statistics.

Qiu found cervical cancer was the largest group, followed by womb lining and ovarian cancers. Just over half the patients had a ureter stent placed, and nearly three in ten kept a urine catheter for a week or more. The infection rate was about six in a hundred patients. Three factors raised risk on their own: a catheter kept a week or longer, which roughly quadrupled the odds, obesity, and having fewer than two deliveries. The authors use the findings to target prevention at catheter care and high-risk patients.
pmc-13431010:
Mukoma and colleagues reported in 2026 on the views of biokineticists, specialists in exercise therapy, about early detection of long-term diseases in rural South Africa. Diseases such as diabetes and heart disease hit rural areas hard because care is far away and diagnosis comes late. The team interviewed ten registered biokineticists, chosen on purpose, about screening, referrals, teamwork, and barriers in the health system.

Mukoma found four linked themes: weak professional recognition, screening work already under way, community-based prevention, and structural barriers. The specialists did run checks, exercise programs, and health talks, but referrals were fragmented and few people knew their role. Cost and distance also blocked rural access. Weak links to primary care and the national insurance plan broke the chain of care. The authors call these specialists an underused resource and urge policy fixes.
pmc-13432910:
Dante DeAscanis and co-authors argued in 2026 that the gate complex in the cell core does more than pass traffic. It works as a sorting hub for the most risky DNA wounds. Where a wound sits in the core shapes how safe its repair runs. Wounds in repeat-heavy, packed, or frayed-end zones carry the gravest risk of bad swaps.

Three jobs recur across life forms. Pore zones can hold risky wounds apart from poor repair ground. Pore ties can also steer which repair path a wound takes. Loose pore parts may roam to wounds and steady the local state while blocking harmful RNA-tinged scraps. The authors sort firm proof from hints based on place or gene nudges, and they flag open puzzles on pore mix and safe versus rogue repair.
pmc-13434010:
F Tessari and N Hogan tested in 2026 what caps the force a person can push, pitting wrist stiffness against arm pose in a rig built for the task. People steer touch with ease despite slow muscles and long nerve lags. Most touch work needs force, and force may hinge on how stiff the push path can hold.

Sound adults pushed at full will on a swivel rig that let the team dial wrist torque room up or down. Two arm poses faced off as well. Force fell hard as wrist room shrank. Arm pose moved force by a hair at most. The authors read stiffness, not pose, as the wall that caps human push.
pmc-13434110:
Oriol Busquets and co-authors built a stem cell bank in 2026 of sixty-five lines. The lines share one root stock, yet each carries a picked Parkinson's fault. The bank gives the field clean, matched disease models. The brain disease kills mid-brain reward cells in slow steps. Gene-cut human stem cells offer a sharp lab for its roots.

Full gene reads showed gaps between lines stay tiny, most born of drift in dish life, not cut slips. Twin clones per fault tame that drift. The bank ships free to labs, with best-practice notes for like banks.
pmc-13435910:
Burton and colleagues wrote a 2026 opinion piece on antibody drugs for severe breathing diseases. New national guidance backs one antibody drug as add-on care for COPD. That stance differs from the rules for the same drug in asthma care. Many patients carry both asthma and COPD, so the split creates confusion.

The authors run a large severe asthma service and share their audit data. They ask which clinic should own patients whose diseases overlap like this. Fair access to the drug is at stake in that decision, they argue. What counts as treatment success may also need a fresh, personal definition. They question whether the drug should stay second-line in asthma care. Patients carrying both diseases often fare worse than those with either alone.
pmc-13436110:
Plank and co-authors test whether twenty minutes of talk can help tell two easily mixed-up diagnoses apart in this 2026 proof-of-concept study. Adults seeking an autism workup often wait years, and borderline personality disorder produces overlapping social difficulties, yet no tool splits them apart. The team recorded paired talks and let machine learning read the interaction itself.

From 120 conversation partners they pulled more than 800 features on speech patterns, facial expressions during speech, movement amount, and how well partners synced. Models built on each feature family alone all beat chance. They could tell autism talks from borderline ones. Stacking the models pushed balanced accuracy to nearly 82 percent using only microphones and webcams in the setup described. The authors stress clinical testing still lies ahead, but the scale is the point: no special equipment or lengthy testing.
pmc-13436810:
Fanqi Zeng comments on new standards proposed for sociology in 2026. Three standards win praise: join theory with data, practice open science, and keep a careful line between study and politics. Zeng argues the frame still centers on Europe and North America.

Two shifts demand a wider frame, the comment holds. Knowledge making clusters in the Global North, while artificial intelligence reshapes methods everywhere. Reciprocal work with Global South partners answers both shifts at once, Zeng proposes. Shared projects can absorb AI disruption and fill data gaps together. Standards grow stronger, not weaker, when the map widens.
pmc-13437210:
Dong Kyun Kim and Joon-Yong Jung warn medical researchers that a language model's hidden thinking budget can quietly shape study results. Their 2026 piece explains test-time compute: the extra processing a model spends reasoning before it answers. Newer reasoning models may sample many answers, search through paths, check their own work, or fix early drafts, and sellers now let users set how much effort the model spends.

That setting acts like an unreported lab condition, the authors argue. Two studies testing the same model at different effort levels may reach different scores and draw rival claims about skill. Reasoning models have matched or beaten doctors on some diagnostic tasks, which raises the stakes for clean methods in medicine. Its core plea is that medical studies name and fix this budget, so results can be repeated, compared fairly, and trusted when tools move toward patient care.
pmc-13438210:
Barry Brook, John Alroy, and Jessica Jones look back on four years of Cambridge Prisms: Extinction, a journal they helped launch to give extinction research a home. The field stretches from deep fossil time to today's losses crossing into policy and the humanities. Their 2026 editorial marks the journal's first impact factor and takes stock of the early years.

Review papers drew the map first, pulling conservation biology, paleontology, modeling, policy, and social science into one conversation. The journal now sits in the top rank of its fields by citation measures, which the editors cite as proof the idea was sound. A new format, Extinction Accounts, will dissect single extinctions one by one. The editors restate a boundary: broad, yes, but extinction itself must stay central, or the journal becomes a general biodiversity outlet. Their tone is that of founders handing a young venue its second, harder assignment.
pmc-13440710:
van Loon and Kaufman tested the Dutch Meaningful Roles program, which gives primary school children purposeful classroom roles to feed autonomy, competence, and relatedness and thereby build a kinder classroom climate. The cluster randomized study covered 2,337 students and 225 teachers across 42 schools, with 20 schools delivering the program and 22 serving as controls.

Across the full sample the program produced no significant effects on the student outcomes measured at mid-year or year's end. Teachers in program schools did report stronger attitudes toward stimulating prosocial behavior and autonomy in their pupils over the year. Only in the subgroup where implementation fidelity was ideal, some 202 to 253 students, did small benefits appear, mainly at mid-year in the analysis. Those students showed better need fulfillment, classroom climate, school safety and well-being, and less antisocial behavior, making fidelity the decisive factor.
pmc-13442810:
Jing-Jing Du and colleagues design one small compound that blocks two cancer shields at once in a 2026 study. Computer fits, binding tests, and cell assays screened and checked the lead compound, named CP-1.

In a reporter cell system that reads T-cell switch-on, CP-1 restored function at a mid dose of 0.9 micromolar strength. Docking maps show the compound sits tight in both target pockets. The authors offer CP-1 as a lead for drugs that free immunity on two fronts.
pmc-13444210:
Fu and colleagues chart how disability from back pain unfolds over five years in older adults who seek primary care in the Netherlands. Their 2026 study uses the BACE-Dutch cohort of 669 adults aged 55 and over, with disability scored on a standard questionnaire at set points from six weeks to five years. A grouping method sorts patients into paths, and the team checks which starting traits predict each path.

Four paths emerged. Two groups, together about two thirds of patients, improved, most of the gain coming in the first six months. One group stayed at moderate disability, and the smallest group, about one in nine, stayed highly disabled. Starting traits tied to worse paths included older age, higher body weight, stronger pain, leg pain that radiates, past back pain, depressive symptoms, and gloomy beliefs about recovery. Clinicians could use those flags early, the authors suggest.
pmc-13445210:
Markus Schwerzmann and colleagues gather expert agreement on when doctors should start serious illness talks with adults who were born with heart defects, published in 2026. A second panel of patients and advocates judged the agreed cues apt. The list gives care teams a common starting point for timely talks.
pmc-13445410:
Xuezhen Chen and colleagues survey undergraduates on how often they learn with digital tools in AI-rich settings, and whether they feel their studies move faster for it, in a 2026 study. The authors treat felt speed, named perceived academic acceleration, as an outcome apart from grades. Confidence in one's own skill forms the proposed middle step.

Replies from four hundred twenty students fed a chain of statistical checks. More frequent tool use went with stronger confidence, and stronger confidence went with a greater sense of speed. Drive to learn may set the edge of the link, though that test fell short of firm proof. The authors stress the results show links, not cause, since all measures came from one point in time.
pmc-13447310:
Li Bai, Shuai Luo and Qiang Wang compare treatments for pneumonia with sudden kidney injury in a 2026 records review. Both organs failing at once leaves clinicians with few proven options. Continuous blood filtering, which slowly cleans the blood, formed the base treatment, while an added anti-inflammatory drug called ulinastatin was tested for extra benefit.

One hundred patients treated between 2019 and 2024 were split by the regimen their doctors had chosen. Both groups improved on inflammation, kidney, lung and urine measures after treatment. The combined group ended with lower inflammation markers and lower waste levels in blood, plus stronger breathing measures and higher response rates overall. Since doctors chose the regimens rather than chance, the authors present the added drug as promising rather than proven.
pmc-13448410:
Echeverria-Ortegon and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract MMDA-08, a systematic review and meta-analysis on stereotactic radiosurgery added to dual immunotherapy in melanoma brain metastases. The question was whether adding precisely targeted radiation to nivolumab and ipilimumab improves outcomes when melanoma has spread to the brain.

Pooling time-to-event results from studies found in three databases, the combined treatment was associated with better local control at treated sites. The hazard estimate pointed to roughly thirty percent lower progression risk, though the confidence interval was wide and crossed no-effect. Overall survival showed essentially no improvement, and control of new distant brain lesions was inconsistent across studies. The authors acknowledge most included studies were retrospective, with mixed treatment timing and likely selection bias. Their conclusion is measured: radiosurgery helps control treated lesions within a multidisciplinary strategy, without a demonstrated survival benefit.
pmc-13448510:
Guo and colleagues test whether nurse led, guideline driven coordination improves clot busting care for acute ischemic stroke, where a clot blocks blood to the brain. Their 2026 study enrolls 231 patients who got the nurse coordinated pathway and compares them with 231 matched patients drawn from past records. Advanced stroke nurses ran the steps from imaging to treatment, and the team scored early recovery on a standard stroke scale at 24 hours.

Early major improvement came for about 57 percent of the coordinated group against 42 percent of controls, a clear edge. Functional independence also ran higher, near 78 percent against about 69 percent in controls, and quality of life scores were better through 90 days. Each step ran faster: imaging, vessel puncture, and drug delivery all took less time. Bleeding in the brain was less common under coordination, while deaths did not differ.
pmc-13449410:
Dhaliwal and colleagues pooled in 2026 trials of the Forgotten Joint Score, a patient questionnaire used after total knee replacement. Unlike older scores, it asks how far patients can forget their artificial joint in daily life, a quality tied to satisfaction. The team searched three databases for randomised trials that reported this score alongside standard measures, covering different alignment methods, implants, and robot help.

The new score showed no ceiling effect, the bunching at the top that blinds older scales, while its rivals did. It also detected real post-surgery gains where two standard scores could not. No subgroup of technique or implant stood apart, though newer work hints at an edge for one alignment style. The authors back wider use of the score in knee studies.
pmc-13449810:
Nesreen Shahrour and colleagues report in 2026 two teenagers with elkonyxis. This uncommon nail defect is a punched-out depression eating into the plate from its root. A review of the scattered literature accompanies the cases. The nail's growth matrix is delicate, and both chemotherapy drugs and the acne drug isotretinoin are known to disturb its keratin production. Few reports, though, describe this exact defect in adolescents on medication.

The first patient was a seventeen-year-old girl on isotretinoin at a cumulative dose of 77 milligrams per kilogram. After acrylic nails were removed she developed painful changes, including granuloma-like tissue at one thumbnail fold and elkonyxis of the other thumb. The second case arose during infliximab treatment alongside a paradoxical psoriasis-like eruption the drug itself provoked. The authors argue clinicians should recognize medication-linked matrix injury early, since stopping or adjusting the culprit drug protects nails still forming.
pmc-13449910:
Lyu and Zhou reported in 2026 a case of dedifferentiated liposarcoma, an aggressive fat-tissue cancer, growing behind the abdomen of a 66-year-old woman. Her left abdominal mass was found by chance. Contrast scans showed several neighbouring soft-tissue lumps in the retroperitoneum, the space behind the gut lining. Some held only traces of fat and showed odd ring-shaped and nodular calcium deposits.

Lyu describes the tumors' slow-in, slow-out brightening pattern on scans, a clue the authors stress for spotting this cancer type. After surgery, marker tests found both MDM2 and CDK4 proteins in the tissue, confirming the diagnosis at the molecular level. Nine months later, scans showed the cancer had returned locally, and she began further treatment. The authors urge doctors to weigh this diagnosis for fatty abdominal masses with little fat and strange calcification, and to confirm it with gene-linked testing.
pmc-13450610:
Dan Li and co-authors describe in 2026 a gel coat for tooth implants that uses sound waves to fight germs and grow bone in sore gums. Implants often fail in people with gum disease, since germ films block early bone grip and swelling weakens the hold over time. The gel joins two flat sheet materials that make an electric field when ultrasound hits them.

Early on, that field kills germs so bone can grip the implant. Later, the gel calms immune cells by way of a signal path named JAK-STAT, which shifts the tissue toward repair. New nerves and blood vessels then guide fresh bone growth, a route the authors offer for raising implant success in gum disease.
pmc-13450710:
Yogesh Dwivedi, Kevin Prall, and Richard Shelton review in 2026 the role of tiny RNA pieces in post-traumatic stress disorder. The illness lasts for years in some people after trauma, while others recover, and the reasons are still murky. The tiny pieces, microRNAs, tune how strongly many genes are used at once.

Shifts in these pieces can change stress hormone responses, fear memory, and swelling signals in the brain. The review draws on blood and tissue work in people plus animal studies of fear and stress. The authors see the pieces as a shared thread across species and a possible base for future tests and care, while proof is still young.
pmc-13452210:
Chen, Keeler, and Wu wrote a 2026 commentary on why some liver cancers shrug off immune therapy. Drugs that free the immune system help only a small share of liver cancer patients. Many tumors keep immune cells locked out of the tumor area. The authors focus on a study that pins part of this lockout on one protein.

The study under review found that SMYD2, a gene-tuning protein, runs high in such tumors. Blocking SMYD2 with two test drugs slowed tumor growth in lab and animal work. The blockade also reshaped the tumor surroundings so immune cells could enter. Tumors with an overactive Wnt signal, a growth pathway, benefited most clearly. Pairing SMYD2 blockers with immune drugs is the next step proposed.
pmc-13452410:
Min Ho Ju and eight co-authors study blood transfusion in adults kept alive by a heart and lung support machine called VA ECMO. Their 2026 paper asks how much red cell blood a patient gets early on, and at what blood level the first unit is given. The work draws on a shared registry from six large hospitals in South Korea.

The registry held 2,020 adults who started the support between 2018 and 2025, and the main group kept 1,708 people still on support after one day. Among those who got blood, the team tracked the blood level just before the first unit and the pattern of later units. The study links those early patterns to death in hospital, a question with no settled answer for this machine. Its design treats timing and dose as the key signals, not transfusion alone.
pmc-13453010:
Kumar and colleagues study how planarians, small flatworms with strong powers of regrowth, fight bacteria with an old family of immune proteins. pmc-13453310:
Xingyi Li and co-authors present SpatialModal, a computational framework that combines gene expression and tissue images in spatial transcriptomics, a technique mapping gene activity in place. Existing methods struggle to integrate the two data types. Their 2026 paper uses graph learning with a two-level contrastive strategy, which trains the model by matching related representations and separating unrelated ones.

It revealed brain architecture in both species, separated distinct regions of the breast cancer microenvironment, delineated Alzheimer's disease patterns, and traced developmental trajectories in the embryonic heart. Performance stayed strong even on datasets without images, which the authors say broadens its use across platforms. Code and data are publicly archived, and the authors present the tool as a robust way to decode spatial heterogeneity in complex tissues.
pmc-13453510:
Goo, Taratula, and Taratula describe a way to steer medicine-carrying nanoparticles to lung tumors in this 2026 report. The team instead swapped one ingredient, replacing normal cholesterol with a charged version called DC-cholesterol.

pmc-13453610:

Writing, he argues, mirrors a scientist's judgment and professional identity, not just technique.

Writing first in one's own language, he argues, deepens thought and builds clear logic, while AI can help later with translation. pmc-13454110:

In that span 27,510 deaths were recorded, including 9,192 from cardiovascular causes. Exercisers died at lower rates across the board. The gaps ran 12 to 16 percent for all causes and 16 to 20 percent for early death, with heart death 10 to 15 percent lower. The shield held even with hypertension, diabetes, obesity, or smoking in the picture. The safest corner paired no risk factor with exercise. The authors back exercise as a broadly usable lever in high burden populations.
pmc-13454610:

When dITP docked, the filament reshaped step by step into a new form. In that form, the SIR2 partner woke with NADase activity, an enzyme action that drains a key cell molecule. pmc-13454810:

pmc-13454910:
Qian Song and five colleagues build, in a 2026 study, machine learning models that predict leg vein clots in older patients with hip fractures. Clots struck 66 of 400 patients during their stay. Diabetes appeared in about a third of the group and more than doubled clot odds. Seven learning methods competed, and a random forest model won with strong accuracy scores. Importance analysis ranked diabetes measures, age, albumin, a clot marker, and immobility at admission among the top signals. The authors offer the model for targeting preventive blood-thinning care at admission.
pmc-13455110:
Lova Wilske and four colleagues untangle, in a 2026 optics study, why metal nanoparticles inside nanofluidic channels can look bright, dark, or invisible under a microscope. The authors predict uses in sensing volumes too small for ordinary optics to resolve, where such contrast control becomes a measurement tool.
pmc-13456910:

pmc-13457210: Implanting brain-recording motes one by one with hair-thin carbon fiber electrodes — fast and minimally invasive. Joseph G. Letner, Jordan L. W. Lam, and others develop the method. pmc-13457310: energy-making patterns body signals for Kawasaki disease — identified by gene data research. Tingting Hu, Shaoyong Lin, and others identify them. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is Kawasaki gene data research. It spots energy-making patterns-related promise body signals and predicts their promise regulatory correlations very with care today.
pmc-13459010:
Patrick K. Mukadi leads a large Congo-based team that measured prior mpox exposure in 2026 among people at higher risk in Kinshasa and Goma. Their blood survey enrolled 1,823 participants between April and June 2024, including sex workers, men who have sex with men, and other at-risk residents. Overall, just under three percent of participants reacted to the test, with the highest share among the broader at-risk group rather than sex workers. Age was the strongest predictor in their model, with older participants more often reactive. The findings suggest quiet exposure in Congolese cities before sustained city outbreaks, a pattern that matters for watching mpox return.
pmc-13459210:

The defensive compounds instead rose and fell, peaking at the middle and final stages sampled. pmc-13459410:

pmc-13461310:
Cai and colleagues profiled in 2026 stress and burnout among schoolteachers in urbanising China, where both problems run high. Past work often treated teachers as one group, missing hidden subgroups. In the high group, emotional exhaustion was the hub instead. The webs were tightly linked overall, which suggests stress and burnout feed each other dynamically. pmc-13461410:

The gap ran from about four-tenths to half a standard unit, a large effect in education terms. It appeared in both younger children and teenagers, and grew steadily with the level of distress. pmc-13461610:

Minority migrants reported stronger psychological settling than Han migrants, and the gap held across several subgroups and under a second outcome measure. Moving with family, larger households, and active social networks each carried part of that advantage. The authors urge policy to treat ethnic communities as resources, not burdens. pmc-13461710:
Gautam and co-authors decoded a 2026 comparison of drought responses in two horsegram types, a hardy legume grown in dry regions. It also rushed into seed production early, a drought escape strategy that yielded well despite later wilting. pmc-13461810:
Wang and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica, a rare childhood bone disorder, in the knee of a nine-year-old boy. pmc-13461910:
Matsuda tested a 2026 rat study of gentle early exercise after a focal stroke, asking whether it protects the calf muscle that holds the body against gravity. From the next day, exercising rats ran twenty minutes daily on a treadmill at low intensity for up to twenty-eight days. Matsuda found better beam walking and neurological scores by day twenty-eight in the exercise group.
