pmc-13462210:
Yurong Wu and Rui Xu review, in a 2026 article, how gut microbe chemicals from a family of amino acids may drive heart and blood vessel disease. Standard risk factors predict heart disease only partly. The chemicals come from three related amino acids in protein foods: phenylalanine, tryptophan, and tyrosine. Microbes convert them into products that can help or harm vessels. Tags on tyrosine also play a part.

One product makes platelets overactive and injures heart muscle, raising the risk of heart events. The tryptophan route splits: one branch promotes artery clogging and kidney-linked vessel harm; a sister product protects vessels. Tyrosine tags draw immune cells to vessel walls and disable protective enzymes. High levels of one tag predict bad heart events. Combining several markers may sharpen prediction beyond standard models, though proof across populations is still needed. Blocking the gut routes shows promise.
pmc-13462810:
Min-Jae Kim and co-authors wrapped antiviral RNA in shell derived nanoparticles to make a sprayable crop vaccine that survives on leaves. Sprayed double stranded RNA can silence a plant virus through RNA interference, but naked RNA degrades and enters leaves poorly. In their 2026 study, RNA matching the coat protein of turnip crinkle virus was made in bacteria and complexed with chitosan tripolyphosphate particles. They were sprayed on Arabidopsis plants, with imaging and sequencing tracking delivery and protection.

Full complexing occurred at a one to one particle to RNA ratio, and the particles shielded the RNA from degrading enzymes and heat in the stability tests. Treated leaves showed stronger RNA uptake signals and more virus targeting small RNAs than naked RNA controls, evidence the cargo was processed inside plant cells. Most importantly, sprayed plants carried significantly less viral RNA systemically at seven and fourteen days.
pmc-13463510:
Ma and colleagues described in 2026 a new species of crocodile newt from the Xuefeng Mountains of southwestern Hunan, China. Specimens from the Huangyan area had long been filed under a known species, Tylototriton wenxianensis. Gene trees and body measurements together showed the mountain population is distinct, adding to a genus that has grown fast this century.

The authors name the animal Tylototriton sheni and give a full account of its looks, measurements, and the traits that set it apart from close kin. The genus now counts more than 50 species across Asia, with about half in China. These salamanders favor cool, moist highlands and are sensitive to habitat change, so each newly separated species matters for protection plans.
pmc-13463710:
Song and colleagues pooled in 2026 the evidence linking a simple blood index to atrial fibrillation, the common irregular heartbeat. The triglyceride-glucose index combines two routine blood values and stands in for insulin resistance, a state where the body responds poorly to insulin, which is thought to drive this heart rhythm problem. The team searched five databases to September 2025 and pooled observational studies with a random-effects model.

Song included 19 studies with over twenty-five thousand people in total. Patients with the fibrillation had clearly higher index values than those without, including in new-onset and post-surgery subgroups. Each one-unit rise in the index came with more than double the overall risk of the condition. Results varied a lot between studies, though sensitivity checks held up. The authors present the cheap index as a useful risk flag, not a diagnosis on its own.
pmc-13464010:
Djeneba Dabitao leads a large team in Mali that links sex hormones to tuberculosis outcomes. Men fall ill with active lung tuberculosis more often than women, and biology may drive part of that gap. The team followed patients with active disease, people with latent infection, and healthy peers of like ages.

Before treatment, men with active disease carried lower testosterone than the other male groups. Levels climbed back to healthy ranges by month two of treatment. Testosterone strongly foretold cure, while estradiol, the main female hormone, shifted little with disease. Hormone levels also tracked with immune signal levels in blood. The shifts hint that the disease itself bends hormone balance in men.
pmc-13465010: Fuguang Zhao and eleven co-authors publish a correction to their 2025 study of artesunate in drug-resistant bladder cancer cells. The notice is a correction only. It reorders the first two authors to reflect their contributions and rewrites the statement of who did each task. It also adds a data note saying the raw data come from the first author's doctoral thesis, held at the university library in Mainz. The authors state the fix is administrative and leaves the science untouched.
pmc-13465610:
Yuanjie Cao and colleagues describe a real-world program, published in 2026, using templates printed in three dimensions for each patient to guide brachytherapy in advanced cervical cancer. Shaped from scans taken before treatment, each template steers catheters along planned paths into hard-to-reach tumor areas. The program treated 120 patients in a row at their center.

Curved channels with flexible plastic catheters handled spots that straight needles could not reach well. Target coverage met guideline aims while doses to bladder, rectum, and bowel stayed acceptable, and placement proved quick with few severe side effects during follow-up. The authors offer the workflow as a workable route for bulky or uneven tumors that standard applicators fit poorly.
pmc-13466310:
Furong Wang and colleagues model how steel fibers change the way cemented mining backfill breaks, in a 2026 simulation and testing study. Backfill made from coal waste fills mined voids, and its failure behavior matters for safety underground. Their computer model used the real size spread of waste rock and sand particles rather than uniform grains, with fibers scattered at random.

Compression tests and microscope images backed the model, which captured stress bunching inside coarse lumps and fibers bridging across cracks. A fiber share just under one percent worked best, lifting peak strength by about a quarter and leftover strength by about two fifths. Failure shifted from brittle snapping toward a slower, squeezing mode.
pmc-13466410:
Giovanni Ventura and Mariachiara Bianco introduce a special issue on two lab methods used in medicine, writing in 2026. Paired together, mass spectrometry and chromatography can reveal a molecule's makeup and measure its exact amount inside messy body material. Eight papers make up the set.

The editors read the papers along two lines. The methods serve as tools for measuring things that answer real clinic questions, and as engines for grasping disease itself. Topics include marker hunting, how the body handles drugs, and care fitted to the person. Sharpness and reach are the selling points, since body fluids mix thousands of compounds that weaker methods cannot pull apart.
pmc-13466710:
Michele Golino and a large team review two look-alike heart emergencies that strike mainly women: a torn inner wall in a heart artery and a stress-stunned heart chamber, in a 2026 article. Both can follow emotional or physical stress and share roots in adrenaline surges, fragile vessels, and hormone effects. Because their signs overlap, one is often mistaken for the other.

Newer evidence suggests the two conditions appear together more often than once thought. The authors propose a stepwise diagnostic path combining risk sorting, artery imaging, inside-the-artery pictures, and heart MRI. Care advice then branches by which condition, or which mix, the work-up finds.
pmc-13466810:
Dingpei Han and colleagues report the first use of a 5G-linked remote robotic scope to mark lung nodules before surgery, in a 2026 case report. A fifty-three-year-old man with no symptoms carried two hazy nodules in his right lung, one in the upper lobe and a smaller one below. Both needed removal, and precise marking beforehand guides the surgeon to tissue that fingers cannot feel.

Working from a remote console, the surgeon steered the robot to each spot and injected a glowing dye, with network delay holding steady at roughly twenty-odd milliseconds. Keyhole surgery then removed wedges of lung around the marked sites, guided by the glow. The case targets the gap between expert centers and distant hospitals.
pmc-13467510:
Lei Tian, Kaixin Shi, and Siyi Pan report a 2026 rat study on whether breathing bergamot essential oil can ease long-lasting fatigue from heavy exercise. The citrus oil is known for calming inflammation and oxidative stress, a form of cell damage from reactive molecules. Rats were put through a progressive exercise program and exposed daily to the oil or its main components, then tested for endurance and muscle condition.

Oil inhalation improved swimming endurance and steadied fatigue-related body measures. In the muscle itself, two inflammatory signals fell, a damage marker dropped, and a protective enzyme grew more active. The treatment also shifted markers tied to muscle repair. The authors read the pattern as the scent acting on muscle inflammation, oxidative stress, and regeneration pathways at once, rather than simply masking tiredness.
pmc-13469910:
Yukai Zhao and co-authors refine in 2026 a signal method for spotting early bearing faults in slow turning machinery. Slow shafts hide their fault signatures under heavy noise, and the standard spectral technique misses weak periodic clues. Their upgrade adds a filtering stage that locks onto the repeating rate at which a bearing fault strikes, stripping away unrelated interference.

A second stage then boosts the faint periodic energy that marks a developing fault. Tests used simulated signals at several noise levels plus real bearings with inner and outer race damage turning at sixty revolutions per minute. The combined method pulled out the full set of fault frequencies and their harmonics where conventional approaches failed. The authors aim the tool at offshore wind turbines, where surprise shutdowns are costly.
pmc-13470710:
Chang Liu and Baoshan Jia examine in 2026 how warm airflow ages coal and raises its risk of catching fire on its own. Deep mines run hot, and leftover coal sits for weeks in moving warm air. The team exposed lignite samples for thirty days to air flowing at set rates. The air was held at either a mild or a hot pretreatment temperature. The samples then went into lab instruments that track weight and heat flow.

Eight marker temperatures and the energy needed to start oxidation were computed by two standard methods. Hot pretreatment lowered the early marker temperatures across the board, making ignition easier. Temperature mattered more than airflow speed. Surprisingly, mild heat with slow airflow produced the strongest activation, dropping the energy barrier the most. The authors warn that coal left in warm, poorly ventilated spots may be the most dangerous.
pmc-13470810:
Souza and colleagues developed a 2026 method to measure cadmium, a toxic metal that builds up in the body, inside Brazilian makeup products. Eyeshadows and blushes can carry cadmium from manufacturing, and children face special risk. Their method uses magnetic nanoparticles to pull cadmium out before a flame based instrument measures it.

The validated method was applied to twenty-nine shop bought products, including thirteen made for children, by Souza. Cadmium appeared in sixteen products, just over half, reaching levels the team reports as high in the worst case. Standard risk models put non-cancer risk within acceptable limits for these exposures. Cancer risk estimates, however, exceeded acceptable limits in every cadmium positive product, and children's products modelled about three times higher risk than adult ones.
pmc-13472910:
Aidan R Cole and thirty-six colleagues published this 2026 study showing how the secretions of chemotherapy-aged ovarian cancer cells help tumour cells break away and spread. Cisplatin pushes these cancer cells into senescence, a halted state. In that state they pump out a cocktail called the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Using cell culture and mouse models, the team dissected which ingredients of that cocktail loosen attachment. They traced the metabolic wiring behind the effect.

Fructose turned out to be a key ingredient. Secreted by senescent cells, it increased cancer cell detachment. A high-fructose diet increased tumour dissemination in mice. The mechanism ran through mitochondrial complex I and a metabolic axis that lowered cholesterol in the cell membrane, weakening adhesion. Because ovarian cancer's high recurrence rate may partly reflect this spread effect, the authors flag the secretome as a target. They also flag dietary fructose.
pmc-13473410:
Yang and colleagues present a 2026 case report and literature review of a triple strategy against a rare, aggressive blood cancer, blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm. The patient, a 55-year-old man with relapsed disease in his nervous system, had no matched donor for the standard donor transplant. After chemotherapy he reached a full metabolic response, though trace disease remained in his marrow.

He then received high-dose conditioning and his own stem cells back, followed by CAR T cells engineered against CD123, a marker on the cancer, and maintenance with the drug venetoclax. The course included a severe immune reaction, which was managed. Stacking three consolidations aims at durability without a donor. One pioneering case cannot set a standard, but it maps a route for patients who relapse with no donor available.
pmc-13474510:
Resül Çolak and Murat İnanç Cengiz study quality of life and dental fear across gum disease stages in 2026. Just under one thousand clinic patients took part in Türkiye between late 2018 and late 2019. Groups ranged from healthy gums to mild and severe gum disease. All filled in two short surveys, one on daily life impact and one on fear of dental hygiene care.

Life impact scores climbed step by step as gum disease grew worse. Most survey sections differed across groups, with the severe group worst off. Clinical measures such as pocket depth and tooth loss were also logged for each person. The links suggest gum care plans should address fear and daily burden, not teeth alone.
pmc-13474610:
Mohamed El Fiky and colleagues compare two replacement valve types in Egypt in 2026 using past studies plus a surgeon survey. Mechanical valves last long but need lifelong blood thinners, while tissue valves wear out sooner. Forty-one local studies were reviewed, and 128 heart surgeons shared real practice views. Local results were set against global patterns to shape advice.

Unlike global data, repeat surgery rates in Egypt ran lower with tissue valves than with mechanical ones. Bleeding ran higher with mechanical valves both locally and worldwide, while survival and stroke looked alike. Age and ability to take thinners drove most choices. The authors urge case-by-case picks rather than a fixed rule.
pmc-13474710:
Maddy Power and Madeleine Baxter explore how poverty shapes the mental toll of food insecurity in the United Kingdom in 2026. Sixty-two people on low incomes were interviewed three times over two years. Talks covered food access, aid use, mental health, and unfair treatment. The authors looked closely at how income source, parenting, and ethnicity changed the experience.

Struggling to afford food deepened the stress of life on a low income and fed anxiety and low mood. People on benefits described sharper food stress than those with wages. Parents felt shame at failing to feed children well, which pulled families away from others. Food holds deep cultural weight, which can raise the hurt when it runs short.
pmc-13474810:
Pezoa-Soto and colleagues launched GRNContext in 2026, a web platform that shows gene regulatory networks as they actually run in specific cancers. Existing databases map every possible link between transcription factors, the proteins that switch genes, and their targets, but they do not say which links are active in a given tissue. The team layered gene activity data from a large cancer atlas onto a human reference network covering 33 cancer types.

Machine learning and statistical checks were merged into one consensus score that ranks and filters the most plausible regulators for each gene in each cancer. Users can browse, compare, and download these cancer-specific networks in any major browser. The authors offer the platform, free online, as a working resource for forming hypotheses and guiding translational research on how gene control goes wrong in tumors.
pmc-13476210:
Kai-jie Liu and co-authors weigh a deep sequencing test in 2026 for lung infections in older adults. Records covered 522 patients aged fifty-five to sixty-nine at one Shenzhen hospital. A subset of 168 got both sequencing of lung wash fluid and standard culture. Detection rates and costs were compared between paths.

Sequencing found far more germs than culture, with overall detection near ninety percent versus twenty-seven percent. True pathogen detection also ran more than three times higher. The sequencing path saved money per patient on net, with larger savings where a pathogen was found. Timing mattered, as late testing tended to erode the gain.
pmc-13477010:
Harrison R Herrera and co-authors define why patients need redo aortic valve surgery in 2026 after a first mechanical valve. Records held 379 straight cases at one large center from 2000 to 2023. Infection led the reasons at about a quarter, followed by tissue overgrowth blocking the valve. Median wait to redo sat near ten years.

Infection cases arrived sicker, ran longer in surgery, and died in hospital far more often. Past the first year, survival leveled across reason groups. Age, diabetes, dialysis, prior heart attack, and urgent timing predicted death, not the redo reason itself. Counseling can stress timing and health state over cause.
pmc-13478210:
Cho and colleagues fed mice a Western diet in 2026 to model fatty liver disease, then tested whether a probiotic bacterium could soften the damage. The strain, Bacillus subtilis pb2441, was compared against dapagliflozin, a diabetes drug known to help fatty livers. Western feeding fattens the liver, inflames it, and scars it, and the team read the liver's gene activity to see how each treatment answered.

Both treatments partly reversed the liver fat seen under the microscope, and both lowered liver triglycerides, the stored fat measured chemically, though only the drug group's drop reached significance. Gene patterns moved the same way in both groups, with fat-building genes turned down and fat-burning genes restored toward normal in the treated mice. The probiotic's effects ran consistently weaker than the drug's, so the authors present it as a partial, drug-like influence worth further study.
pmc-13478510:
Li and colleagues present a faster correction method in 2026 for electrical imaging tools lowered into oil-drilled wells, where oil-based mud blocks the usual current paths. The mud layer between the tool's electrodes and the rock distorts every reading, so it must be stripped out mathematically. Their method simulates the tool in open- and short-circuit states, models three impedance layers, and solves directly for the mud's share of the signal.

An iterative step then adjusts rock resistivity, permittivity, and tool standoff until the readings at several frequencies agree with each other consistently. Tests on computer-built rock models showed the method separating mud interference across the full measurement range the tool covers. A real field well application confirmed the workflow, producing quantitative maps of rock resistivity and related traits that the authors say support sharper images of fractures and bedding underground.
pmc-13478810:
Alan Blum, Yuhui Yao, and Jeremiah Mock wrote a 2026 commentary questioning claims that e-cigarettes caused New Zealand's recent faster drop in daily smoking. Another research group had credited the decline to government-endorsed vaping for quitting, framing it as a harm reduction success. The commentators argue that this reading overstates what the data support.

Smoking decline in New Zealand, they note, built over six decades through clean air laws, advertising limits, tax rises, plain packaging, and shifting public norms, long before vaping spread. Māori communities still carry a heavy smoking burden that demands careful claims. E-cigarettes avoid combustion, yet nicotine harms the heart and vessels, and long-term effects on lungs and mouth remain unsettled. The authors warn against exporting the New Zealand story as proof of benefit beyond its context.
pmc-13479410:
Mohammedsefa Arusi Dari and coauthors published a 2026 case report of stones in both nasal passages, a condition called bilateral rhinolithiasis. Rhinoliths are calcified masses that grow around material lodged in the nose, usually on one side only. Fewer than ten two-sided cases appear in the medical literature, and the condition is easily mistaken for chronic sinus disease.

Their patient, a 55-year-old Ethiopian man, endured ten years of blocked nose on both sides, foul discharge, nosebleeds, facial heaviness, and headache, with only brief relief from sinusitis treatment. Camera examination and computed tomography showed large stony masses reaching toward the throat, about three by four centimeters each, without bone damage. Endoscopic surgery under general anesthesia removed them whole. Symptoms resolved at once, tissue analysis confirmed mineralized rhinoliths, and no regrowth appeared at six months.
pmc-13479710:
Yanpeng Li and colleagues published a 2026 blood proteomics study of aging inside chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a leading cause of death where age is the dominant risk factor. Seventy plasma samples, half from patients and half from healthy controls, were split into younger and older subgroups around ages fifty and seventy. A mass spectrometry method measured hundreds of proteins at once.

The instrument detected 534 proteins, and 413 passed quality filtering for analysis. Statistical workflows flagged proteins differing by disease and age together, then tested whether their levels tracked lung function scores. Diagnostic curves judged how well the aging-related proteins separated patients from controls. The authors seek blood markers that explain why lungs deteriorate faster in some patients as they age.
pmc-13479810:
Hongyi Zhao and coauthors published a 2026 cohort study of triple therapy for liver cancer too advanced for surgery. The mix joins chemo delivered into the liver artery, the drug lenvatinib, and immune checkpoint blockers aimed at PD-1. Records covered 209 patients treated from 2016 to 2022, split between dual therapy without immunotherapy and the triple combination.

Math weighting evened the groups on starting gaps before results were compared. Midpoint survival ran about 16.5 months with triple therapy against about 13.4 months with dual therapy in the adjusted look. Tumor shrinkage, treatment dose, and noted side effects were also set side by side. Backward-looking designs leave room for hidden bias, so the authors call the work a first look while reporting a survival hint worth testing in a forward trial.
pmc-13480110:
Karaçelik wrote in 2026 on a grave case in which a heart hole fix try hurt the child it meant to help. The child, a girl of 18 months, had a hole between the heart's lower rooms. A tube fix was tried and then called off. In two hours she had a vast stroke and a bleed under the brain's shell. Tube fix of such holes swaps for open surgery, and strokes in child tube work are rare but can wreck a life.

The case team lays the blame first on thin blood in the run: the one clot check sat below the floor that child guides set. Sleep like rest in such work can hide the first nerve signs. A dye used for X-ray sight may have stung the young brain too. The hub has since raised its first blood thin dose and checks clots each half hour.
pmc-13480210:
Mohammadreza Rahimian and Mohammad Aghazadeh-Soltan-Ahmadi offer a 2026 genome study of the bacterium behind fire blight, a fierce disease of apple and pear trees. The team compared 317 bacterial strains and 227 viruses that infect bacteria, called phages, hunting for shared attack genes and signs of an arms race between host and virus.

Many attack genes in the blight bacterium matched genes in germs that strike plants, people, and animals, which points to gene swapping across species. Some bacterial proteins that cut cell walls closely matched phage proteins, hinting they began as phage tools. Defence systems in the bacteria lined up with phage counter-defence genes in clear, non-random patterns. The map may guide phage-based sprays against fire blight, though lab proof for the predicted links still lies ahead.
pmc-13480310:
Popsuj and colleagues report in 2026 a set of tested gene-editing guides for the sea squirt Ciona robusta. The larva of this simple marine animal runs its nervous system on just over 200 neurons and sensory cells. Researchers use Ciona to study how brains develop, but many key neural genes lacked proven CRISPR guides, the short RNA strands that steer the cutting enzyme to one spot. The team designed and validated 25 guides against eight conserved genes.

Every guide produced insertions or deletions at its target site when checked by DNA sequencing of the edited region in the embryos tested. Most genes yielded at least one guide editing more than 30 percent of sampled copies, though the gene Dmbx topped out at 25 percent efficiency in the trials. Comparing results with two prediction algorithms, the authors recommend using both scores together, since the newer one tracked real editing rates somewhat better than the older.
pmc-13482010:
Aragon and a hospital team in the United States reported in 2026 on one man's early rehab with virtual reality after a severe brain injury. The patient, in his mid thirties, had left intensive care with the sight faults that often follow head trauma. He took six short bedside sessions in a calm scene called Beach Stroll, worn through a headset that tracked his eye aim. Each round ran at most six minutes, with blood pressure, pulse, pain, and anxiety checked before and after.

The man called the rounds soothing and the best part of his stay. His pain and anxiety scores fell or held steady across the set, and his pulse and blood pressure stayed calm. The team judged brief VR eye rehab workable and welcome even at this raw stage of care. They stress the need for trials with more patients to test real gains in sight.
pmc-13482610:
Jichao Ma and co-authors present a 2026 model that predicts how resting brain regions fire together from the wiring between them. Older diffusion models miss negative links, where one region quiets as another wakes. Their field model lets excitatory and inhibitory cells interact across regions, then a Fourier-based deep network reads both slow and fast signal parts to sharpen the forecast.

Tests used a large public connectome set with ninety regions, split into one hundred training and one hundred held-out people. Forecast maps tracked real maps with a mean match far above the older diffusion model. Negative links appeared in the forecasts, as they do in real data. Steadier scores across people add trust. Better structure-to-function maps may guide surgery planning and sharpen theories of thought and mental illness.
pmc-13483610:
Sining Li and co-authors create a plant-based charcoal designed to pull two common water pollutants out of solution. Published in 2026, the work starts from cotton stalks and adds nitrogen during heating with melamine to reshape pore structure and surface chemistry. Three recipes with different ingredient ratios were compared for capturing tetracycline, an antibiotic, and methylene blue, a dye.

The middle recipe performed best, combining tiny pores with nitrogen-rich surface groups and reaching very high uptake for both pollutants in laboratory tests. Capture followed patterns consistent with a single surface layer and time-dependent binding involving several interaction types at once. After four reuse cycles the material kept over nine tenths of its capacity. The design offers a route to turn farm waste into a reusable water cleaner.
pmc-13483710:
Leah E Allen leads a 2026 study of two food supplements paired with diet and exercise in adults with excess weight. All take part in a strict diet and a weekly exercise plan for 56 days. Each day they take a dummy pill, a muscle-linked compound called L-BAIBA, or that compound plus grains of paradise, a ginger kin thought to raise body heat. Groups are matched by sex and lean mass, and no one knows who gets what.

Tests at the start and at two, four, and eight weeks track rest burn rate and body shape. Hunger, mood, and blood risk marks are checked too. Food intake is logged in three-day records all through the study. Since all groups share the diet and exercise load, gaps between groups can be tied to the pills.
pmc-13483910:
Hao Zhang embeds copper-halide crystals inside clear glass to build an ultraviolet sensor that reaches wavelengths ordinary detectors miss. Published in 2026, the composite uses gadolinium ions as a bridge between the glass host and embedded Cs3Cu2I5 nanocrystals, letting energy cascade down and convert deep ultraviolet light into visible light. Transfer efficiency approaches completeness.

Response spans 180 to 350 nanometers, reaching into the vacuum ultraviolet range below 200 nanometers that single-material detectors cannot cover. Because the glass stays clear to visible light and can be made large, it pairs with silicon sensors and camera chips for imaging. Resolution reached 34.7 line pairs per millimeter, well beyond conventional ultraviolet arrays. Security warning and environmental monitoring systems that need cheap wide-range ultraviolet eyes are the target uses.
pmc-13486110:
Gabriel D Rodrigues and a large team review radon spa care for joint and spine diseases. The care uses low-dose radon gas in baths and caves, a long habit in central Europe and parts of Asia. Proof of gain stays in dispute. This 2026 review weighs how the care might work, what trials show, and what it may do to heart health. Risks and rules are weighed too.

Lab work hints that radon tunes how cells handle stress and immune signals. Pain-linked chem levels shift as well. Clinic reports tell of less pain and better movement in three diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and osteoarthritis. Gains in life quality are also told. Mixed methods and side treatments like heat blur the true source of gain. The heart angle gets a close look as a path for fresh trials.
pmc-13486710:
Petrović and colleagues boosted a small RNA molecule inside glioblastoma cells to test whether it can strengthen standard treatment for this brutal brain cancer. Median survival stays under fifteen months despite surgery, radiation, and the drug temozolomide. Their 2026 study raised levels of the molecule, miR-219, in tumor cells grown flat and as three-dimensional spheres, then combined it with radiation and the standard drug.

Extra miR-219 dialed down two target genes linked to tumor growth, REST and AKAP13, in the treated cells. Treated cells lost malignant behaviors, growing and invading less than untreated controls in the assays reported. Spheres of tumor cells also died more readily when miR-219 joined radiation or drug treatment. Petrović frames miR-219 replacement as a candidate add-on therapy, while stressing that all evidence so far comes from laboratory cultures.
pmc-13486910:
Jack McGarrigle and colleagues expose a fast-growing gambling sector that operates outside United Kingdom gambling law. Published in 2026, the analysis covers online prize draws and competitions selling entries for cash, cars, and houses, sometimes with multimillion-pound pools. An estimated 7.4 million consumers spent about 1.3 billion pounds last year across more than 400 operators.

Lottery law requires payment, prizes, and pure chance together, and operators escape that definition through a token skill question or a free postal entry route. Only 6 percent of entries use the free route, and that route can cost more than paying, raising doubts about the legal requirement that free entry be no less convenient. Nearly all operators incorporated after 2015. A regulatory loophole with mass-market scale is documented in plain terms.
pmc-13487310:
Li and colleagues reviewed how China keeps enough expert malaria microscopists trained after eliminating the disease, when real cases grow rare and skills rust. Microscope diagnosis remains a backbone of surveillance, and certified experts anchor the national reference laboratory network. Their 2026 review covers six rounds of World Health Organization competence courses run in China from 2017 to 2024, plus a national course modeled on them from 2019 onward.

Certified microscopists from the international courses formed the core workforce staffing quality assurance across the country. The national course spread assessment to provincial levels with a revised schedule and scoring system detailed in the paper. Competency grades from top to basic tracked who could certify others' work. Li argues this layered training pipeline is how elimination gains survive the quiet years when malaria barely appears.
pmc-13487910:
Helen Louise Malherbe and colleagues estimate the burden of rare diseases in South Africa in a 2026 analysis built from Orphanet, a global rare disease database. They pooled published figures on how common each disease is, set against national population data for 2024. Cases from cancer, infection, or poisoning were left out, along with disorders lacking usable data on how common they are.

Nearly 3,730 disorders were counted, covering just over half of the listed Orphanet entries. The team figures about 4.8 percent of South Africans live with one of these conditions, roughly three million people in total. Most disorders begin in childhood, and many cause lasting disability. The authors urge stronger newborn screening, earlier diagnosis, and fairer access to costly treatments.
pmc-13488210:
Sarah Hachmer and F. Jeffrey Dilworth review how gene enhancers help muscle stem cells read their surroundings during repair in a 2026 article. Enhancers are DNA switches that turn genes on from a distance, guided by proteins that open or close the DNA packaging. Muscle stem cells must move from rest to growth to mature muscle, taking cues from inflammation, matrix, nearby cells, metabolism, and physical forces around them.

Recent work shows enhancer maps and three-dimensional DNA folding shift a great deal during regeneration. Aging and muscular dystrophy distort those maps, leading to wrong gene responses and weak repair. The authors argue that fixing enhancer control could open new treatments, since these switches sit where many niche signals converge.
pmc-13490610:
Gabbrielli and team ran over two thousand simulated experiments to answer a small question with big consequences for published charts. With few replicates, should error bars pool data or use each treatment's own spread? Applied science papers routinely face analysis-of-variance designs with three to six replicates per group. Their 2026 Monte Carlo study compared pooled against individual standard deviations under varying sameness of variance, and graded two statistical tests as guides for choosing.

Pooled estimates proved more accurate when groups shared variance, especially with four or fewer replicates per group in the simulations. Individual estimates won once variance differences grew moderate and replication reached five or more. Levene's test guided the choice better than the rival Fmax test overall, particularly with at least six replicates. Gabbrielli turns the results into a decision rule researchers can apply before drawing a single error bar.
pmc-13491710:
Wai-Yin Cheng and five co-authors review in 2026 how daily body clocks govern the conversation among gut, brain, and immune system, and what happens when those clocks slip. Circadian rhythms, roughly twenty-four-hour cycles driven by light and dark, shape sleep, metabolism, and immunity. The reviewers trace how disrupted rhythms alter gut microbes and immune signaling in ways that may feed brain inflammation and degeneration.

Sleep disturbance often appears before memory symptoms in dementia, and poor sleep lets amyloid-beta, a protein linked to Alzheimer's disease, build up. Shift work that scrambles internal timing has likewise been tied to higher risk of cognitive problems. The authors propose that restoring healthy daily rhythms, and the microbial rhythms that follow them, could become a strategy to slow neurodegenerative disease.
pmc-13491810:
Atefeh Shamsi and Robabe Khalili map in 2026 what is known about psychosocial help for children living through armed conflict. Searching five databases produced 7,729 records, of which fifty sources met the criteria. The reviewers kept solid effectiveness trials apart from feasibility and guidance material. Seventeen sources counted as effectiveness studies, the rest as context or practice evidence.

Help usually arrived through schools, communities, or families, often delivered by trained non-specialists in strained settings. Controlled studies showed modest, uneven gains in trauma symptoms, depression, anxiety, and daily functioning. Programs worked best with structure, supervision, cultural adaptation, and continuity, while digital approaches were still young. Caregiver well-being and daily stressors like displacement mattered greatly but were seldom tested as formal mechanisms, a gap the authors highlight.
pmc-13491910:
Katherine LaMonaca leads a fifteen-author team describing in 2026 how a virtual diabetes prevention program was designed with, rather than for, the low-income communities it aims to serve. Lifestyle programs prevent type 2 diabetes in trials, yet uptake stays poor where risk is highest. The Yale-Griffin team interviewed residents and providers, surveyed technology access, and ran a five-week pilot in two contrasting settings.

The resulting design pairs self-paced online lessons with a health coach, then adds care coordination from community health workers and hospital nurses to handle social needs like food and transport. Pilot feedback exposed confusion about who does what, prompting clearer role descriptions and richer orientation materials. The program is now entering a full implementation trial, and the authors share their pathway tool for other teams.
pmc-13493910:
Baharvand and co-authors test how well emotion-reading software copes when large glasses cover a person's eyes. Systems that guess feelings from faces lean heavily on the eye region, yet real users wear chunky frames and glare, conditions lab benchmarks rarely include. In the 2026 study, the team pasted simulated oversized glasses over faces in RAF-DB, a standard emotion dataset. They ran three leading models on the altered images and released the doctored version as a public benchmark.

Accuracy fell under the occlusion for every model, confirming the eye region carries real emotional signal. Transformer-based designs, which weigh the whole face rather than small patches, weathered the damage best, with the Swin Transformer Tiny variant most robust. The convolutional ResNet-50 suffered more by comparison. The authors suggest leaning on lower-face cues when eyes are hidden.
pmc-13494110:
Paul AM Smeets and colleagues report a 2026 crossover study of how sweetened flavored waters affect the brain and body in healthy young adults. Drinks with low- or no-calorie sweeteners give sweetness without energy, yet they may act on reward areas of the brain in ways sugar does not. Thirty volunteers each tried six drinks across visits, from plain water to water sweetened with sugar or one of several sweeteners.

Brain scans tracked blood flow before and after each drink, while blood tests and stomach scans followed sugar, insulin, and stomach emptying. One midbrain reward area showed a smaller flow rise after sugar than after water or some sweetened drinks. A blend of allulose and stevia slowed stomach emptying much like sugar did, though only sugar raised blood sugar and insulin. The authors say most sweetened waters acted much like water, with a few clear differences worth follow-up work.
pmc-13495010:
Anu Anu, Sneh Lata, and Barnali N Chaudhuri report a 2026 study of ParB1, a protein that helps split chromosomes when a cell divides. ParB proteins clamp onto DNA near a site and spread to form an assembly that pulls the copies apart. How the parts fit together to start that assembly was little known, so the team studied ParB1 from Vibrio cholerae, the cholera bacterium.

ParB1 burns CTP, a cell fuel, as its switch, which places it in a rare protein class. A model of ParB1 bound to its DNA site, checked against X-ray scattering data, shows the site priming the clamp to slide and forming a tunnel for DNA. A cut-down front segment of the protein clumps when concentrated, while a flexible linker in the full protein holds that urge in check. The authors name that front segment's clumping drive as a step toward the assembly.
pmc-13495310:
Bolukçu, Yücel, and Yücel investigate cyberchondria, the pattern where anxious online health searching makes worry worse instead of better, during the COVID-19 pandemic. They surveyed 427 adults across eight central districts of Ankara, Turkey. Their 2026 analysis measured coronavirus anxiety, attitudes toward coping with the pandemic, and cyberchondria severity, then modelled the relationships.

Anxiety and coping attitudes together explained a large share, over two fifths, of the variation in cyberchondria between people. Stronger coronavirus anxiety clearly meant more cyberchondria. Surprisingly, stronger coping attitudes also came with more of it, not less, in the model. Yet coping attitudes neither transmitted nor moderated anxiety's effect, since the two predictors barely related to each other at all. The authors suggest coping efforts during a pandemic may partly consist of searching, which blurs the line between healthy vigilance and compulsive checking.
pmc-13495410:
Fredrik Folke leads a large team reporting the design of the HeartRunner trial, a 2026 randomized study in Denmark's capital region on app-summoned help for cardiac arrest outside hospital. Survival after such arrests stays low, yet a shock within minutes can save half of victims. The region had enrolled over fifteen thousand volunteer responders and mapped thousands of public defibrillators before the trial began.

Cases of suspected arrest were assigned by lot to standard care or standard care plus volunteers sent by phone app to start resuscitation or fetch a defibrillator. The main measure was survival at thirty days, with bystander shocks, resuscitation rates, and one-year survival also tracked. The trial also watched for harm or strain among the volunteers themselves. Enrollment closed in early 2026 after a planned run of about seven years, setting up the outcome analysis.
pmc-13495510:
Ibrahim Aliyu and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a button battery that sat in a teenager's airway for five years. The boy, of Hausa background, had breathed in the battery at age nine with no check at the time. A year of quiet followed, then four years of mild cough, and at fourteen a sudden sharp chest pain on the right brought him in.

X-ray showed a disc of metal with the double-ring halo of a button battery in the right airway, with two lung lobes collapsed. A scan confirmed scar tissue around it. A scope attempt to pull it out failed because scarring had sealed the airway, so surgeons opened the chest and the airway to retrieve it. The lung re-expanded and his symptoms cleared. The authors warn that inhaled batteries demand urgent imaging even years later.
pmc-13498910:
Rodolfo I Cabrera-Silva and colleagues investigate in 2026 why the colon lining heals poorly in ulcerative colitis, a long-term inflammatory bowel disease. Signals from the WNT pathway, which guide stem cells that renew the lining, go awry in this disease for reasons that were unclear. The team grew miniature colon tissues, called colonoids, from healthy donors and from patients with quiet or active disease.

Combining gene activity and chromatin maps, meaning records of which DNA regions sit open for use, they found a distinct cell group in active disease with altered WNT signals. A regulator named RUNX2 stood out in that group, tied to weaker stem-cell upkeep and slower maturation. Blocking RUNX2 with a test drug lowered the abnormal signal and restored a key maturation marker, pointing to a possible treatment target.
pmc-13500810:
Md Al Amin leads a five-author team with a 2026 study of the fractional Schrödinger-Hirota equation, a model for light pulses travelling through optical fibres. The equation includes higher-order dispersion and fractional scaling, which change how pulses spread and interact. The team worked with a beta form of the fractional derivative. They applied an extended Riccati scheme, a step-by-step method for building exact answers to nonlinear equations.

The method produced many exact forms, including kink, dark, periodic, and mixed bright-dark soliton profiles, where a soliton is a wave packet that holds its shape as it travels. Planar dynamical system theory and bifurcation analysis sorted the possible equilibrium states. Adding a periodic disturbance pushed the system from regular oscillation into chaos, confirmed with Poincaré sections and a Lyapunov exponent. A linear stability check backed the physical soundness of the results.
pmc-13501810:
Lingxiao Guo leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 spatial analysis of how well elder care supply matches elder care demand across China. Panel data from 31 provinces and municipalities spanning 2014 to 2023 fed the study. The team scored supply and demand with an entropy weight method, combined them in a coupling coordination model, mapped clustering with Moran's index, and ran a spatial Durbin model. That model separates direct effects from spillovers onto neighbouring provinces.

Coordination inched upward over the decade yet stayed low overall. A stark geography emerged: high coordination in the east and low in the west, with the gap widening and clusters of high-high and low-low provinces forming. Supply quality lagged behind upgrading demand, which the authors call the core constraint. Drivers such as population ageing, economic development, and government spending acted differently by region. The paper argues for differentiated provincial policies rather than one national recipe.
pmc-13504210:
Faraz Fotouhi and three colleagues compare blood serums for healing chemical burns on the surface of dogs' eyes, in a 2026 study. Alkali burns cause deep corneal ulcers that can blind. Serum drops carry growth factors that may speed repair, and serum can come from the patient, another dog, or another species.

Ulcers were made on both eyes of fifty healthy female dogs in five groups. Groups got serum from self, same species, or other species, standard drops, or salt water. Checks over three weeks tracked ulcer size and eye thickness by ultrasound and exam. Foreign serum shrank ulcers fastest, with gains clear by day seven. By the third week all real treatments beat salt water on healing signs.
pmc-13504810:
Sabri Gökdere leads a team comparing two ways to leave the tips of flexible nails in children's broken forearms, in a 2026 study. The nails slide inside the bone to hold the break; tips can rest under the skin or poke through it. Exposed tips ease later removal but may invite more trouble.

Records covered 99 children treated at one center over twelve years, split near evenly between the two methods. Infection, re-break, and total complication rates did not differ overall. Removal came months earlier with exposed tips, a matter of ease rather than faster healing. One age split stood out: children past about ten with exposed tips faced clearly higher re-break and complication risk. The authors treat that age line as a caution flag, not a hard rule.
pmc-13506110:
Abhishek Soni and co-authors describe a positioning trick that fixes imaging registration failures during robot-assisted spine surgery in very heavy patients. Standard reference markers can fall outside the scanner's field of view when body mass is high, stalling the operation. Their series covered sixty-three patients with body mass index above forty, treated between October 2023 and November 2024.

Placing the marker on the patient's side, exploiting the scanner's wider sideways coverage, was used in seventeen cases. No patient with lateral placement needed repeated registration attempts, while a few standard-placement patients needed two or more. Registration ultimately succeeded in every case, and screw placement accuracy stayed equally high under both approaches. Repeat attempts, when they happened, added scanning time and radiation dose. The authors note the fix needs no new equipment, only a change in marker position guided by a quick preliminary scan.
pmc-13507110:
Nijad Emer, Lanzhou Chen, Haijun Wang, Youcheng Song, and Quan Wang simulate, in 2026 work, land change to 2030 across three provinces in the middle Yangtze River region of China. They fed land data from 2000 to 2020 into a patch-based model and valued nature services in money terms, with crop returns allowed to shift over time. Four futures were tested, from business as usual to ecology-first growth.

Growth-first growth expanded built land and sharply raised very low-value zones, with a small net loss in service value. Ecology-first growth cut urban land by about a tenth through restoration and halted the decline. Water and forest lands supplied most value. Policy choice clearly steers the balance.
pmc-13507210:
Yuan Ren leads a 2026 team that links a hormone-related switch, ERRα, to drug resistance in ovarian cancer through sugar burning. Resistant tumors often burn sugar fast and stockpile lactate, its waste product. Gene data tied high ERRα and its target enzyme LDHA to poor outcomes, and blood enzyme levels rose in resistant patients.

Lab tests showed ERRα binds the LDHA gene switch directly and turns it on. Extra lactate then muted a fiery cell death program called pyroptosis by lowering its core parts. Blocking ERRα restored drug sensitivity in cells, and paired treatment worked better in mouse tumors. Cutting this metabolic shield may reopen chemotherapy response.
pmc-13508410:
Einar Thokle Hovden and six co-authors screen stroke patients in Norway for sleep apnea, a breathing disorder that raises stroke risk, in 2026 work. The disorder often goes undiagnosed before a stroke strikes. The study enrolled 124 patients admitted with ischemic stroke or a brief mini-stroke at one hospital between 2023 and early 2026. Within days of arrival, patients answered two short tools about their pre-stroke state: a risk questionnaire and a sleepiness scale. Chart data added risk factors and stroke causes.

Two thirds of patients landed in the middle or high risk band for sleep apnea on the questionnaire. Excessive daytime sleepiness, by contrast, showed in only about one in seven patients. Higher risk scores did track with higher sleepiness scores, yet most high-risk patients felt no sleepiness. The authors conclude the two tools catch different things. Relying on sleepiness alone would miss most at-risk stroke patients.
pmc-13509410:
Beggs and colleagues co-designed an exercise program for lung cancer patients to use before radiotherapy, in a 2026 co-design study. They worked with patients and families rather than designing for them. Exercise may make radiotherapy work better by reducing low-oxygen resistance in tumors. Yet recruitment to exercise trials in lung cancer is poor, with under two fifths of invited patients joining.

Beggs ran workshops with seven people, three with lung cancer and four family members, plus a panel, and sorted the discussions by theme. Participants judged training workable for treatment courses at about twenty minutes, with effort set by each person and self-paced rather than fixed. The group listed fifteen barriers and forty helping factors, with how coaches act and study design standing out most: guided sessions and relationships with staff mattered most. The authors present the program as the first built this way.
pmc-13509910:
Qingshan Shen, Yanli Ma, Chunhui Zhang, Yujie Guo, and Xiaojie Qin test a supplement drawn from cartilage in rats that model life after menopause, in 2026 work. The supplement, chondroitin sulfate, is widely sold for joint health. Rats lacking ovaries gain weight in ways that mirror postmenopausal change, so the team fed the supplement to such rats and tracked weight, fat cells, gut microbes, and blood chemistry.

Supplemented rats gained less weight, and their fat cells kept a healthier shape. Gut microbe variety fell, with two bacterial groups dropping and one rising. Blood levels of several sugars, fats, and related compounds rose, and some of those levels tracked body weight. Pathway checks pointed to a few metabolic routes. The authors stress the findings are correlational and in rats only, so use in women needs direct testing.
pmc-13510510:
Ghani and colleagues report a 2026 brain imaging study of chiropractic care in 76 adults with chronic low back pain. Half received chiropractic care plus usual care, and half received usual care alone. The team recorded EEG, a measure of brain electrical activity, at rest and during sensory tests, before care, after care, and four weeks later.

Resting connectivity in the alpha band within the default mode network, a brain system active during rest, was higher in the chiropractic group right after care. That difference was still present four weeks later. Other changes appeared in specific frequency bands across the salience and executive networks, which handle attention and control. The authors call the analysis exploratory and say larger studies should link these brain changes to pain outcomes.
pmc-13510610:
Carlos Alexis Mascote Rodriguez, Yoeli Escandon-Espinoza, and Katia Lopez Garcia summarize two years of gut endoscopy in children at a large referral hospital, in 2026 work. Reports from Latin American centers remain scarce, so the team reviewed records for every scope procedure in patients under eighteen. The set held 88 procedures in 77 children, with an average age near twelve years.

Upper scopes of the food pipe, stomach, and upper bowel made up about four fifths of procedures, with colon scopes a smaller share and bile duct scopes rare. Leading reasons were reflux disease, bleeding from the lower gut, and swallowed foreign objects. Meaningful findings appeared in most procedures, led by stomach lining irritation, food pipe inflammation, and foreign bodies. The authors say the record supports the value of pediatric scope services at referral centers in the region.
pmc-13511210:
Iva Zeneral Žuža and ten co-authors test how a titanium dioxide coating changes bacterial sticking on a plastic widely used in medicine and dentistry, in 2026 work. The plastic is easy to shape and strong enough for many uses, yet germs settle on it and build biofilms. The team laid down ultra-thin coatings atom by atom at low heat, safe for the plastic, on bone cement and dental grades of the material.

Coating sharply raised surface roughness at the nanoscale, and polishing before coating raised it further into tangled micro and nano terrain. Tests against two major germs measured free growth and biofilm building, with light activation and polishing also weighed. Surface shape proved a central factor in how bacteria first grip the material. The authors say tuning that terrain may help design plastic parts that resist colonization in the mouth and body.
pmc-13513110:
Marzieh Kashkouli, Jahangir Khajehali, and Mohammad Mehrabadi probe the microbe partners living inside two major whitefly pests by disrupting them with antibiotics, in 2026 work. Whiteflies rank among the most damaging farm pests, draining plant sap and spreading viruses. The two species studied dominate warm open fields and greenhouses respectively, and both depend on internal bacteria for nutrition.

Disturbing the bacteria badly hurt whitefly growth and survival in both species, proving how essential the partners are. Whiteflies with altered bacteria also lost their knack for quieting plant defenses, so attacked plants mounted stronger resistance. Effects split in detail between the two whitefly species, matching their distinct lifestyles. The authors propose that aiming control at the microbe partners could yield greener pest strategies that weaken the insect and free the plant to defend itself at once.
pmc-13513610:
Hee-Eun Hong and eight co-authors scan the brains of 29 healthy adults as they smell a natural insect scent, in a 2026 controlled imaging study. Smell links tightly to mental health, yet insect-derived scents had never been tested in the brain. Responses under the insect scent were compared with an alcohol-based control scent inside a functional magnetic resonance scanner.

The insect scent raised activity in regions that merge the senses, regulate emotion, and handle memory, beyond what the control scent produced. Responses also shifted with each person's psychological profile, varying by levels of depression, anxiety, and stress. The authors read the pattern as proof that insect scents can reach emotional and cognitive networks. The work lays groundwork for non-contact, insect-based approaches to support mental well-being, with clinical testing still to come.
pmc-13515810:
Ran Duan leads a twelve-author team characterising two toxin proteins of the plague bacterium, Yersinia pestis, in a 2026 study. The proteins, YPO3609 and YPO3615, belong to the Rhs family, whose members often serve as weapons against rival bacteria. Their tail ends were suspected of cutting DNA. The team combined computer analysis with growth tests, DNA damage checks, stress reporters, and gene switching in a harmless host bacterium.

Both tail ends proved toxic when switched on: growth stalled, DNA degraded, stress alarms fired, and cells stretched into filaments. Each toxin had its own antidote protein next door in the genome, and swapping out single key building blocks dulled the toxins. One toxin's tail used a known nuclease motif, the other a scissor-like pair of acids. Relatives of both tails spread widely among related bacteria. Duan's team frames the pair as complete toxin-antidote modules that enrich plague biology.
pmc-13516210:
Vitale and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how variants in the UGT1A1 gene affect the safety of cancer drugs built on SN-38, the active form of irinotecan. The gene controls an enzyme that clears this drug, and weaker versions let the drug build up, raising the risk of low white cell counts and diarrhoea. The team weighed original studies, pooled analyses, and guidelines from several regions on gene-guided dosing.

Vitale found that reduced-function variants clearly raise harm risk, above all at higher drug doses. Yet societies differ on who to test, when to test, and how much to cut the dose. What the variants mean for newer antibody-drug conjugates carrying the same payload is still unclear. Cost, access to testing, and uneven clinic routines also block wider use. The authors urge harmonised rules and stronger prospective studies to make testing routine.
pmc-13516810:
Xu Huang and seven colleagues explore a hidden pocket on a cell-cycle protein in a 2026 simulation study. The protein, CDK4, drives cell division and is a proven breast cancer target, yet tumours learn to resist drugs that plug its active site. Using accelerated molecular dynamics and Markov state models, the team watched the protein flex and catalogued shapes. A loop near the active site swung aside in one state, opening a previously unseen side pocket.

A lab-made compound, referred to as 8i, touched a key residue and steadied exactly those pocket-opening shapes. That suggests a way to hobble the protein: not by filling the active site, but by holding the side pocket's door open, an allosteric grip. Huang's team offers the mechanism as a design route toward next-generation CDK4 drugs that might sidestep current resistance. All of this rests on computation, awaiting wet-lab confirmation.
pmc-13518810:
Xiao Wen and a large team trace in 2026 how fatty liver disease hardens into its inflamed form, called MASH, which carries real risk of liver death. Simple fat buildup, or MASLD, progresses in only some patients, and the spark for lasting inflammation was unclear. The enzyme ACSS2, known for fat making, sits at the center of their account.

Working with partner protein KAT5, ACSS2 adds crotonyl marks to histones, the spools DNA wraps around, switching on the inflammatory gene AIF1. Inflammation then ages liver cells early, and those aged cells release more inflammatory signals, feeding a vicious cycle. Blocking ACSS2 could offer a treatment target, the authors propose.
pmc-13518910:
Jin Zhang proposes PD-IntelliFusionNet in 2026, a single system that both sorts partial discharge types in power transformers and grades their severity. Partial discharges are tiny sparks inside insulation that slowly destroy it, and catching them early prevents costly failures. Most earlier systems tackled one task at a time.

The design fuses acoustic and ultra-high-frequency sensor signals, physics-based models, and signals drawn at several scales, from raw waveforms to wavelet patterns. A multi-task neural network with attention then sorts type and grades severity in one pass, sharing what it learns. Zhang frames the output as feed for a reinforcement learning system that could plan maintenance. Field testing remains a next step the design invites.
pmc-13519010:
Yudong Yan and four colleagues track single sleep-related neurons over time in 2026 and find their allegiances drift. Textbooks sort hypothalamic neurons into stable wake, non-REM, and REM camps, each with signature chemistry. Imaging calcium in freely sleeping male mice told a less tidy story across several neuron types, including orexin and MCH cells.

Individual neurons shifted which state they favored as sessions wore on, yet the overall share of active cells per state stayed steady. Sleep deprivation barely dented the selectivity patterns. The sedative diazepam recruited fresh non-REM cells, some previously inactive or wake-linked. Yan and colleagues conclude populations stay organized while members rotate.
pmc-13519610:
Troy C Lund leads a nine-author comparison in 2026 of two transplant strategies for cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy, a childhood brain disease caused by faulty fat breakdown. Gene therapy using the patient's own corrected blood stem cells and donor cell transplant can both arrest the disease, yet their biochemical footprints may differ. The team tracked two blood biomarkers for 12 months after treatment.

The fatty marker C26:0-lysoPC fell 48.4 percent after donor transplant but only 6.7 percent after gene therapy. The nerve injury marker neurofilament light chain dropped after donor transplant and rose sharply after gene therapy. MRI severity also progressed more in the gene therapy group, and transplant type was the lone significant predictor in adjusted analysis.
pmc-13520210:
Phúc Q Phan, Thomas P Le, and Jason M Nagata model in 2026 how dating app use may feed disordered eating among queer Asian American men through racism experienced on those platforms. No earlier study had linked geosocial networking apps, racial stressors, and eating concerns in this group. A survey recruited through Prolific enrolled 265 men aged 18 to 65.

Serial mediation analysis traced a chain: heavier app use and sex-seeking use predicted more sexual racism encountered, which predicted internalized racism, which in turn associated with greater disordered eating. Both pathways reached statistical significance, though effect sizes were small. The authors suggest apps could run educational messaging and enforce antiracist policies that flag racist language in profiles and chats.
pmc-13520310:
Chen-Xi Jin and colleagues examine in 2026 two simple blood-based ratios as markers of large-vessel complications in type 2 diabetes. One ratio compares urea nitrogen with albumin, while the other combines white-cell counts into an inflammation index.

Records came from 2,911 inpatients at Nanfang Hospital. Higher values for each marker, and for both together, went with higher odds of vessel complications. The combined marker sorted patients slightly better than either marker alone, though all three performed modestly. For clinicians, the appeal is low cost, since both ratios come from tests already ordered during routine diabetes care.
pmc-13520410:
Hamidreza Moosavian and colleagues report in 2026 a 6-year-old Pomeranian dog with a severely inflamed kidney condition that looked like a tumour on scans. The illness, called xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, destroys kidney tissue and is well known in people yet had never been documented in dogs.

The dog had shown mild tiredness for a month. Ultrasound and CT scans found a markedly enlarged right kidney with several pale areas, prompting removal surgery. Tissue study confirmed extensive destruction, abscesses and fat-filled immune cells. The authors urge vets to consider this diagnosis when kidney images suggest a mass or abscess.
pmc-13520510:
Antonella Girgenti and colleagues purify in 2026 two blue-green pigments from Spirulina algae and test whether each can protect nerve-like cells from oxidative stress. A new ultrasound plus membrane method yielded analytical-grade C-phycocyanin and allophycocyanin for separate testing.

Both pigments proved safe for neuron-like and immune-like cells up to the stated dose. One pigment showed stronger iron-reducing antioxidant power, while both lowered internal reactive oxygen and shielded cells from a chemical stressor. Inflammation-driven nitric oxide also fell. Gut-cell layer tests showed slow crossing without damaging the layer, and microscopy confirmed uptake inside neuron-like cells.
pmc-13520710:
Erik Hill reports an education study, published in 2026. It uses a cheap 3D-printed smartphone mount in a biology laboratory course. The course is for first-year undergraduates. The hands-free adapter holds a student's own phone steady. It sits at the microscope eyepiece. It fits different phones and microscopes. It damages neither.

Across a semester, the mounts were used in four lab modules. They captured pond water life. Stained bacteria results were captured too. Live water fleas were imaged. Students measured their heart rates from the images. Before use, nearly three quarters of 330 surveyed students strongly wanted phone recording of lab data. The adapter is a low-cost way to meet that demand, the author presents.
pmc-13522310:
Jie Xue and colleagues review in 2026 the anticancer potential of dipyridamole, a long-used anti-clotting and vessel-widening drug, focusing on how platelets shield travelling cancer cells and help them seed new tumours.

Once cancer cells enter blood, platelet clumps protect them from immune attack and trigger shape changes that favour spread. Dipyridamole blocks platelet clumping and interrupts that shape-change programme through a growth signalling pathway, according to gathered studies. Mechanistic evidence remains incomplete and scattered, which the review organises by pathway. Repurposing a cheap, familiar drug appeals strongly, yet patient-level proof of anticancer benefit is still lacking.
pmc-13522410:
Klein and co-authors examine how anxiety and stigma intertwine when Australians with borderline personality disorder try to use mental health services. The diagnosis itself attracts notorious prejudice inside healthcare, which patients internalise as dread of being dismissed. Their 2026 analysis draws on a 2017 national consumer survey covering 423 adults with the diagnosis, over nine tenths of them women. It models which experiences predict feeling very anxious about specific aspects of care.

Most respondents felt anxious approaching services whether or not they had an anxiety disorder, which the authors read as stigma generating anxiety rather than anxiety generating itself. Having an anxiety disorder multiplied the dread of not being taken seriously several-fold, yet those respondents worried less about cost, oddly. Being previously refused public hospital admission sharply raised anxiety about both cost and waiting lists.
pmc-13522510:
Chen and a large team watch quantum effects speed up a chemical reaction inside frozen helium droplets. Their 2026 paper uses femtosecond pump-probe spectroscopy on pairs of hydrogen or deuterium molecules held in helium nanodroplets chilled to 0.37 kelvin. Nuclear quantum effects, the fuzziness of light atoms, are suspected of reshaping such ultracold chemistry, but their timing had never been resolved directly.

In the droplets, the product H3+ formed in about 59 femtoseconds, against about 152 in the gas phase, a dramatic acceleration. The heavier isotope responded far less, its formation time easing only from about 153 to about 111 femtoseconds. Simulations attribute the effect to quantum delocalisation, stronger for light hydrogen, amplified by cryogenic confinement. The authors present helium droplets as nano-scale cold reactors that harness quantum behaviour to steer reaction speed.
pmc-13523210:
Mehdi Dehghani, Farzam Sariri, and Mehrdad Zeinalian report a possible new link between an inherited enzyme disorder and recurrent anal infection in a 2026 case report. A sixteen-year-old boy had five years of recurring perianal abscess and fistula, an abnormal tunnel near the anus, despite earlier surgery. His mother and brother reportedly had similar problems.

Blood tests showed anemia and inflammation, imaging found a fistula tract between the sphincter muscles, and a scope examination showed focal inflammation of the small bowel without classic Crohn features. Whole-exome sequencing found a disease-causing change in the G6PD gene, which normally protects cells from oxidative damage. The authors propose that impaired immune defense and tissue repair in this deficiency may sustain chronic perianal disease, while calling for further study.
pmc-13523310:
Kelechi Ichie, Azuoma Asomugha, and Izuchukwu Okafor test whether age changes vulnerability to a Parkinson-linked weed killer in rats in a 2026 study. Sixty-three male rats were split into juvenile, young adult, and adult groups, each with control, exposed, and recovery subgroups. Paraquat was given twice weekly for three weeks, and recovery animals were then kept for two months. Behavior, brain tissue structure, and levels of the protein alpha-synuclein were measured.

Adult rats showed the clearest harm, with reduced movement and more prominent damage in the substantia nigra, the brain region lost in Parkinson disease. Tissue partly recovered after exposure stopped, yet residual changes persisted, especially in adults. Alpha-synuclein levels in brain and blood mostly did not track the damage, leading the authors to question blood levels as a stand-alone marker.
pmc-13524610:
Qian and colleagues identified in 2026 a protein axis that restrains luminal breast cancers, the most common breast cancer type. The team studied USP11, an enzyme that removes ubiquitin tags from proteins, stabilising them.

USP11 suppressed growth and migration of luminal cells but not of basal-like cells. In mice it curbed luminal tumour growth and spread, yet promoted basal-like tumour formation, a striking split. Mechanistically, USP11 stabilises GATA3, a master regulator of luminal identity, by removing its ubiquitin tags. GATA3 then switches on genes for p27, a cell-cycle brake, and for the estrogen receptor. Removing GATA3 erased USP11's protective effects, and USP11 made luminal cells more sensitive to the drug tamoxifen. The authors name the USP11-GATA3 axis a guardian of luminal fate.
pmc-13526110:
Neal E. Storm leads a large industry team in a 2026 case study on using real-world evidence to judge whether a needed pediatric trial was feasible. Regulators had needed a randomized trial of denosumab in children with glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis as a condition of the drug's registration. Enrollment stayed very low despite repeated mitigation efforts.

The team turned to three large health databases in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Germany to count how many children in fact meet the diagnosis. Across all sources, very few pediatric patients qualified as having steroid-induced osteoporosis under the trial's clinical definition. The analyses suggested the eligible population was simply too small for the agreed design to recruit. The authors present the exercise as a model for using epidemiology to test trial feasibility before sponsors and regulators lock in pediatric requirements.
pmc-13527910:
Remziye Semerci Şahin leads a seventeen-author team reporting in 2026 on ChemoNurse, a mobile guide built to help oncology nurses handle chemotherapy drugs safely at the bedside. Nearly all rated it easy to use, every participant found the content understandable and relevant, and most said the drug information was sufficient for practice. pmc-13528010:
Alime Aksel, Yasemin Çelik, and Pakize Özyürek survey nursing students in western Türkiye about attitudes toward diabetic foot care in a 2026 study. The sample held 230 third- and fourth-year students with clinical practice experience. A standard form scored attitudes in three parts: thinking, feeling, and doing. So did students who had seen a diabetes-related amputation during training. All three attitude parts rose and fell together. The authors advise more hands-on teaching that builds emotional awareness, not just knowledge.
pmc-13529610:
Mahshid Mandani, Mohammad Javanbakht, and Abolfazl Mirani harden tool steel surfaces with a welding arc in a 2026 study. The steel, H13, serves in hot, wearing jobs. A tungsten arc melted thin surface layers under argon or argon-nitrogen gas. Current strength and gas mix were varied. Some pieces then got standard hardening heat treatment.

The best recipe, nitrogen-bearing gas plus tempering, reached about eight hundred hardness units. That is near four times the base steel. Microscopy and X-ray checks backed the picture. pmc-13530110:
Jianan Yang and colleagues build a 2026 risk model for lung adenocarcinoma based on genes tied to basement membranes. These thin sheets support cells and guide their growth, so changes there may shape how a tumor behaves. Single-cell and bulk gene data together mapped the tumor surroundings.

Trajectory analysis traced five cell groups at different stages of change, each with its own clinical pattern. One signaling route, called MIF, stood out as highly active in the tumor setting. Six membrane-linked genes formed a score that predicted survival on its own and may help guide choices about immune therapy.
pmc-13530710:
Nault and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 23, a motion analysis study of walking after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in children. It asks whether adding a lateral extra-articular tenodesis, a reinforcing procedure on the knee's outer side, distorts gait. It lowers graft failure risk but might overconstrain the joint.

The study compared 29 children who had reconstruction plus the tenodesis against 35 who had reconstruction alone and 15 healthy controls. Both groups walked with more knee flexion during stance than healthy controls, an adaptation of roughly fourteen and a half degrees against under ten in controls in the same measurement. The authors conclude the added procedure did not alter gait biomechanics.
pmc-13534410:
Elisabetta Lambertini and colleagues study in 2026 the P2X7 receptor inside the nucleus of human cartilage cells. The receptor is best known at the cell surface as a sensor of damage signals. Finding it in the nucleus hints at roles in gene control and force sensing.
