pmc-13534710:
Ranjit R Desai and colleagues build in 2026 an AI-driven framework to judge local permitting processes for energy projects across the United States. Varied local rules delay projects and raise soft costs for builders. A language model tuned for energy gathered rules from nearly 300 state, county, and city documents.

Checks put the final database accuracy near 95 percent. A new scoring method rated clarity and efficiency, and average local documents scored low, implying half of builder-facing rules are unclear. A generalised permit path highlights shared steps and fixes towns can make.
pmc-13538510:
Marios Impraimakis, Daniel Vazquez, and Feiyu Zhou add a trust layer to fast object detection in a 2026 study. Detectors label objects quickly yet hide whether each confidence score deserves trust in blurry or blocked scenes. A curve-based network modeled trust from seven shape and meaning features tied to each detection, keeping every feature influence visible. A vision-language model also captioned scenes without disturbing the trust layer.

Tests on a large public photo set and campus images showed the layer correctly flagging low-trust calls under blur, blocking, or weak texture. Smooth feature maps revealed exactly when confidence stood on solid ground and when it wobbled. The authors offer the system as a transparent perception piece for self-driving and mixed-media tools that must justify acceptance or review.
pmc-13538710:
Sunyong Park, Kwang Cheol Oh, and DaeHyun Kim compare heating fuels for Korean greenhouses across climates in a 2026 cost assessment. Diesel, raw biomass, and two grades of heat-treated biomass were weighed for seven horticultural regions and three crops with distinct warmth needs. Fuel use and yearly cost were modeled with price sensitivity, equal efficiency, transport distance, and break-even checks.

Heating demand ran lowest in the warmest region and highest in the coldest for every crop, rising from strawberry to tomato to pepper. The most heavily treated biomass needed least fuel and cost least across all crops and regions under baseline terms. Its edge survived equal efficiency and transport tests, yet price mapping showed rivals winning in many price corners. The authors frame results as screening guidance, not farm bill forecasts.
pmc-13539710:
Daniel W Nebert, Zijuan Liu, and Vasilis Vasiliou argue in a 2026 invited review that self-copying lipid droplets preceded genomes at life's origin. Evidence hints the last universal ancestor already carried a sizable genome surprisingly soon after Earth formed, during an era of molten surfaces and heavy bombardment. The puzzle is how fragile molecules survived such violence long enough to evolve.

Under a lipid-first view, tiny fat droplets that copy themselves could have crowded deep sea vents and turbulent surface waters within Earth's first few hundred million years. Acting as protective capsules, they would shelter early nucleic acids and proteins while evolution proceeded inside. The authors frame today's human genome as the culmination of over four billion years of that process, driven by shifting pressures to eat, escape, and breed.
pmc-13539810:
Tom Osborn and ten co-authors present a 2026 study validating a ten-question survey on harmful childhood experiences for young people in Kenya. Such experiences are tied to later mental illness, yet most measurement work comes from wealthier countries.

Data came from 2,842 students aged 11 to 25 at 42 secondary schools across four Kenyan counties. Statistical checks supported a two-part structure for the questionnaire, and higher scores tracked with more depression, more anxiety, and more bullying. The link with bullying ran stronger among boys. The authors call for care that recognises past trauma, plus more study of what protects young people against these effects.
pmc-13539910:
Cheng and colleagues pilot a combined look at kidneys, toxins, and thinking in chronic kidney disease. Their 2026 study enrols twelve outpatients with stage three to five disease and early cognitive decline, none on dialysis. The team measured two uremic toxins that build up as kidneys fail, indoxyl sulfate and p-cresyl sulfate, alongside computerised cognitive tests and brain MRI scans.

Both toxin levels rose as kidney filtration fell, though with only twelve patients those correlations were not statistically firm. One clear signal appeared: better filtration tracked with stronger strategy use on a spatial working memory task, a correlation of about 0.70 that did reach significance. No clear link emerged between thinking scores and the severity of artery narrowing in the brain scans. The authors present the work as a pilot, mapping which measures deserve a properly powered follow-up study.
pmc-13540510:
Rujuan Dai and four colleagues examine, in a 2026 mouse study, an unusual class of T cells that pile up in lupus yet stay poorly understood. These double negative T cells carry neither of the two usual surface markers, CD4 or CD8.

Deleting a gene called Egr2 in the lymphocytes of lupus-prone mice sharply shrank the main double negative population. The deletion also changed which inflammatory signals the cells produced and normalised several surface markers toward healthy levels. Single-cell sequencing showed distinct cell clusters shifting with the deletion. Production of these cells fell both in the thymus and from mature cells in culture, placing EGR2 at two stages of their making.
pmc-13540810:
Yixuan Ma and five colleagues review, in a 2026 single-centre study, short-term results of blinatumomab for high-risk B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in China. The drug links T cells to leukaemia cells bearing CD19, and trial success needed real-world confirmation in this harder-to-treat group.

Every patient with the Ph-like subtype cleared disease, while results weakened sharply for two genetic patterns: a T315I change in the BCR::ABL1 fusion and an E2A::PBX1 rearrangement. Serious blood toxicity touched nearly half the cohort.
pmc-13540910:
Majd Abdullah Kalloumeh and five colleagues review, in a 2026 systematic review, how orthodontists keep upper front teeth from tipping too far while pulling them backward into space left by extracted premolars. Protruding upper incisors are a frequent problem, and trials disagreed on the best mechanics.

Twenty randomised trials with 568 patients aged twelve to thirty-five were pooled. Every technique tipped the incisor crowns backward significantly, with loop-based mechanics tipping slightly more than sliding mechanics, a gap too small to matter clinically. Pulling all front teeth at once versus in two steps showed no clear difference. Evidence on vertical movement was patchy and weak, the authors report.
pmc-13542110:
Kaitlin Merkowsky and colleagues expose mice in a 2026 study. The mice were female. Exposures were glyphosate weedkiller, bacterial lipopolysaccharide, or both. The goal was to test lung inflammation from farm air. Women in agriculture breathe dust and pesticides daily. Most inhalation research has used male animals.

Twenty mice got nose-delivered treatments for five days. The combined exposure gave the worst picture. Airways grew tighter, and inflammatory signals rose. More cells flooded the air spaces. Airway lining damage showed on special X-ray images. Those images came from a synchrotron facility. Glyphosate alone did far less harm. The authors suggest adaptation may begin within five days.
pmc-13543610:
Aby Charles and colleagues published a 2026 education study using a simulated trauma ultrasound module to teach abdominal anatomy to first-year medical students. The module rehearsed the EFAST scan, the emergency ultrasound survey used after road accidents, under an emergency physician's supervision. Two cohorts, of ninety-one and ninety-seven students, took knowledge tests before and after on ultrasound use, clinical reasoning, and anatomy, and joined focus groups about the experience.

One cohort improved by over forty percent and the other by over twenty-one percent. Students welcomed the hands-on format and reported clear educational value. Learning anatomy through a simulated emergency, the authors argue, ties structure to purpose from the very first year of training.
pmc-13545610:
Duo Sun and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how a nuclear medicine scan of the lymph system performs in kaposiform hemangioendothelioma, a rare vascular tumor seen mostly in infants and young children. The scan, lymphoscintigraphy, traces lymph flow and can reveal blockage and swelling. Records covered 25 patients, nearly all with a tumor on a limb.

Abnormal scans appeared in 22 of the 24 limb cases, and every abnormal case showed lymph stasis inside the tumor, with swelling only on the tumor side. Flow looked restricted in about two thirds of abnormal cases. Among six patients scanned again later, five showed no real improvement in drainage. The authors see the scan as useful for diagnosis and for following lasting swelling.
pmc-13546710:
Maksuda Aktar and co-authors fed a Bangladeshi crossbred duck, the BAU Black and White, four different protein levels in 2026 to find the ration that grows the best birds. Starting with 264 day-old ducklings, the groups received feed containing protein from about 16.5 percent up to 21 percent. Weight, feed use, blood measures, carcass traits, and meat quality were recorded through ten weeks of age.

The middle-high ration, near 19.5 percent protein, gave the heaviest birds, the fastest daily gain, and the most efficient feed conversion, along with the best carcass and breast meat weights. Meat differed mainly in water loss and color, and blood counts were mostly unchanged. The authors recommend that protein level for raising this duck.
pmc-13547210:
Movahed, Toosi, and Nael teach feature selection to adapt while a model learns. Their 2026 paper tackles multi-label learning in high-dimensional data. Items often carry several labels at once here. Redundant and noisy features drag accuracy down badly. Standard selection methods pick features once and freeze them.

Their framework, called PG-GFE, treats selection as a staged decision process. A mixed graph links features, labels, and data instances together. A graph neural network scores each feature's reliability live. Uncertainty estimates feed those scores throughout training. An evolutionary step then removes weak features in stages. Eight benchmark datasets tested the approach thoroughly. Two standard classifiers, MLkNN and BR, ran the comparisons. Hamming loss and ranking loss both fell noticeably. Average precision and F1 scores rose at the same time. Statistical tests confirmed the gains were robust. Very large datasets strain memory, the authors concede.
pmc-13547410:
Natela M. Shanidze and co-authors linked lifetime noise exposure to hearing test results in 2026 using a structured interview that tallies work, leisure, and firearm noise across a whole life. Fifty-four adults aged 23 to 82 gave their noise histories, self-rated their hearing, and completed tone and speech tests. Statistical models separated the effect of accumulated noise from the effect of age itself.

Age raised hearing thresholds at every frequency, as expected. Heavier lifetime noise independently worsened low-frequency hearing in both ears together, specific tones in each ear, and speech reception in the worse ear. The authors present the interview as a practical clinical tool and read the results as evidence that lifetime noise speeds age-related hearing decline.
pmc-13548710:
Mei Feng and colleagues identify a mouth bacterium living inside cervical tumors as an active driver of the cancer's aggression, in a 2026 integrative study. Fusobacterium nucleatum is known for promoting gut cancers, but its role in the cervix was unexplored. Combining computing analysis with gene sequencing of patient tissue, the team located the bacterium inside tumor cells, confirming its presence with imaging and electron microscopy.

In culture, the bacterium invaded cervical cancer cells, spurred their growth and spread, blocked their death, and sped tumor growth in mice. It worked by raising a protein called HMGB1 and switching on an inflammatory relay that released two signaling molecules. The authors cast the bacterium as a prognostic marker and a possible treatment target in cervical cancer.
pmc-13549010:
Daniel Meleschko and colleagues forge a double bond between cobalt and antimony, one of the heaviest stable elements, in a 2026 chemistry paper. The compound reacted with an alkyne and with an azide to form small rings, echoing lighter-element behavior. The authors offer the cleavage route as a general recipe for heavy multiple bonds.
pmc-13550610:
Sara Milijanovic, leading nine colleagues, published a 2026 comparison of extracts from Gentiana dinarica, an endangered Balkan plant, grown wild and in laboratory culture. pmc-13551410:

Since allergy remains common despite rare use, the authors suggest the legal limit may still be too high to protect users.
pmc-13551510:

Family trees suggested gene gains and losses that may track differing scent behavior among species. pmc-13551710:

pmc-13551810:

Affected pathways covered brain development, metabolism, and immune regulation, and the diabetes group showed fewer helper T cells with more killer T cells and neutrophils. pmc-13552510:

pmc-13554110:

The authors link repeat placement to how this deletion formed.
pmc-13554610:

pmc-13554910:

pmc-13555910:

Most canines sat on the palate side and leaned toward the midline. About two thirds of patients had a stuck tooth on one side only. Roots reached into the sinus in a small share, and ties to the nasal floor were slightly more common in men. Linked problems appeared in about a fifth of teeth, led by inner tooth wear and root damage to side incisors.
pmc-13556010:

pmc-13558710:

pmc-13560410:

pmc-13562410:
Puth and colleagues argued in 2026 that Cambodia needs coordinated One Health research to prepare for H5N1 bird flu. One Health means treating human, animal, and environmental health as one system. H5N1 keeps spreading in Cambodia, with most human cases tied to sick or dead poultry contact.

Ongoing spread, they argue, reflects unresolved gaps between veterinary, medical, and environment agencies. Cambodia's case fatality share has been high, and mild infections likely go undetected under current event-based tracking. The authors frame coordination as the missing step between data collection and real readiness for animal-borne disease threats.
pmc-13562710:

pmc-13563710:

pmc-13563810:

pmc-13563910:

Falling levels also showed a modest link with higher event risk in the analysis. pmc-13566410:
Cristina Marrocchio, Michele Ligorio, and Nicola Sverzellati review, in a 2026 article, precision imaging for interstitial lung diseases, a family of more than two hundred disorders that scar lung tissue. pmc-13571710:

Median time fell from 256 weeks to forty-three weeks, a sharp drop Almeida Souto reports. The later group also trended toward lower risk levels at diagnosis, though that gap was not significant. The authors credit team follow-up after embolism for catching the condition beyond specialist centres.
pmc-13572310:

The authors map ongoing trials and open questions, framing addiction care around metabolic circuits rather than willpower alone.
pmc-13572510:

On the MetaWorld test suite, the method learned with fewer trials and won more often than past leaders. Code is posted online for others to check.
pmc-13575210:
Avinash Singh and Mohammad Soyeb Alam model ground sinking above an underground copper mine in India in a 2026 study. Mining out ore can let the surface sag, harming buildings, land, and safety. The mine uses blast-hole stoping, a method that removes ore in large blocks.

Their three-dimensional computer model built in faults, rock joints, and the planned mining sequence. It simulated the untouched state, current workings, and forecasts five and ten years ahead. Rock properties were tuned by matching the model back against observed behaviour, which sharpened the predictions. Output maps show strain and movement in all directions for each phase. The authors present the approach as a practical route to site-specific subsidence forecasts for working mines.
pmc-13576310:
Linlin Wang leads a 2026 study building a prediction score for a common snag in heart stent work: loss of blood flow in a side branch after the main vessel is stented. Forked artery narrowings are frequent and tricky to treat. Records covered 830 patients treated at one Chinese hospital between 2022 and 2023.

Four factors made the final score: age, plaque position on the same side as the branch, flow grade before stenting, and a heart stress blood marker. The chart-style model scored 0.651 on the accuracy curve, easing to 0.641 after internal correction, a modest level of discrimination. Calibration checks showed predictions matched observed rates well. The authors offer the score for sorting risk before the procedure and choosing a strategy, while noting its limits.
pmc-13578710:
Miao Xie and colleagues present a two unit tracked machine that bolts mine tunnel roofs in tight spaces, in a 2026 study. Most coal tunnels in China are too narrow for big automated rigs, so roof supports still go in by hand after cutting, a slow and risky order. Their machine links two tracked units in a line, with four crawler sets in total, so it fits slim tunnels.

The hard part is keeping the front and rear units moving as one. A physics model of track and ground contact feeds a motion simulator, run under matched, squeezed, and pulling modes. A full size prototype matched the simulator within a few percent on average. The authors offer the design as a safer path for the bulk of tunnels that big rigs cannot enter.
pmc-13582710:
Shah and colleagues published a 2026 study on flipped classrooms in medical microbiology teaching. In flipped classes, students study material first and use class time to apply it. The team split exam questions by thinking depth using Bloom's levels. They compared 204 flipped-class students with 200 taught by plain lectures.

Both groups scored alike on basic recall questions in the exams. Flipped students scored clearly higher on application and problem-solving questions. That pattern suggests class time built deeper learning, not more facts. Most students, 88 percent, rated the flipped approach positively overall. The authors tie gains to prework covering basics before class time. Prework used videos and readings prepared by the course directors themselves. The course covered microbiology for second-year medical students specifically.
pmc-13586110:
Lian Wu and colleagues find a gene that sets how widely rice leaves lean out from the stem. Leaf angle shapes how light falls through a rice canopy and thus how much grain a dense field can yield. Their 2026 study started from a mutant rice line with extra-wide leaf angles and traced the cause to a DNA insertion that turned up a gene called OsWRKY11.

Raising that gene in normal plants copied the wide-angle look, while damping it in the mutant restored upright leaves, which pins the trait on that gene. The mutant also reacted more strongly to brassinosteroids, plant hormones that bend leaves, and held more of the active hormone. The gene was shown to switch on a second gene, OsGSR1, which boosts hormone making. The pair forms a control module breeders could tune.
pmc-13587310:
Jiang Yuan and colleagues chart sleep and mood paths in women going through chemotherapy for breast cancer. Poor sleep and anxiety-depression often travel together during treatment and can sap the will to keep going. Their 2026 study followed 150 patients through four rounds of chemotherapy, grouping the paths of both symptom sets at once and then mining seventy candidate factors with machine learning.

Two paths emerged. Three quarters of patients stayed broadly stable, while a quarter slid downhill on sleep and mood together. A set of warning flags marked the downhill group, among them high inflammation and uric acid readings, smoking, a past round of chemotherapy, and a certain tumor pattern. The authors say watching those flags could trigger support early, before symptoms lock in.
pmc-13594010:
Florian Beignon leads a large team reporting a previously unknown human form of TRPV1, the heat-sensing channel, that sits inside mitochondria rather than on the cell surface. Their 2026 study found this variant, named mitoTRPV1, embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, built from a mitochondria-targeting start joined to most of the regular channel.

Mitochondria burn fuel to make energy and heat, and theory suggests they could run near fifty degrees, so something must cap their temperature. Switching the new channel on let a little calcium into the cell's fluid and cooled the mitochondria without slowing energy production. The authors propose mitoTRPV1 as that missing thermostat, shedding heat while sparing output. They flag possible links to diseases of temperature control, to be tested in living models next.
pmc-13595610:
Basma T Abd-Elhalim and Mona A Ashour coaxed bacteria into turning shrimp shell waste into chitinase, an enzyme with uses from farming to cosmetics, using the shells as the microbes' only food. Four heat-loving strains were screened, and one, Priestia megaterium AMD 2024, digested the shells most eagerly.

Tuning the fermentation one factor at a time set the recipe: five percent shell waste, warm and neutral conditions, three days of shaking. Statistical optimization then nearly tripled the enzyme yield compared with the one-factor approach. A simple salt precipitation step recovered most of the activity in a partially purified preparation. Tests on normal human skin cells found the enzyme compatible at the full working strength. The authors present the process as a green route for a waste stream that is otherwise landfilled or dumped at sea.
pmc-13596010:
Mingming Li and co-authors tested a routine blood gas value, standard base excess, as a survival signal in sepsis complicated by acute kidney injury. Drawing on the MIMIC-IV intensive care database, their retrospective study covered 16,842 adults and compared death rates across four bands of the measure, which summarizes the blood's acid-base balance.

Patients in the lowest band, whose blood leaned most acidic in metabolic terms, died at the highest rates over both twenty-eight and one hundred eighty days. The relationship bent rather than running straight, and it survived adjustment for other severity factors, though subgroup interactions differed between the two time horizons. The value is already measured in every critically ill patient. The authors therefore propose it as a cheap addition to risk scoring. The scoring targets this dangerous combination of sepsis and kidney failure.
pmc-13599710:
Isabella Freijah and colleagues review how health promotion for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia could better reckon with trauma. Colonisation brought oppression and violence whose effects pass down through generations and shape present-day health gaps. Programs that urge healthier living already try to be culturally responsive, yet the team asked whether they take trauma into account in any planned way.

Searching scholarly and grey sources across 2025, with an update in mid-2026, the reviewers found little practical guidance. Frameworks for trauma-informed care exist, and so do frameworks for health promotion, but the two rarely meet, and where they do the advice stays broad rather than usable. Ignoring trauma, they warn, can push people away or cause fresh harm. Their conclusion calls for a community-led framework that names how trauma shapes health behavior, so programs can be designed, run, and judged with healing in view.
pmc-13601510:
Katia Andrade and five colleagues report in 2026 that failing to notice one's own mistakes may speed decline toward Alzheimer's disease. Anosognosia, unawareness of one's deficits, predicts faster worsening in Alzheimer's, but the mechanism has been unclear. The team followed unimpaired at-risk adults in the INSIGHT-preAD cohort, testing word recognition yearly for five years and asking participants to judge their own answers.

People who later progressed lost accuracy over time, while stable amyloid-positive participants kept learning and amyloid-negative peers stayed accurate. Weak error monitoring early on predicted later performance decline in the progressing group. Drilling down, the problem was mainly error unawareness: not registering mistakes at all. The authors argue that missed errors break the feedback loop learning depends on, so wrong patterns go uncorrected. Catching this sign early, they suggest, could flag people whose decline is about to accelerate.
pmc-13601910:
Ali and co-authors reviewed a 2026 precision feeding framework for enriching meat, milk, and eggs with antioxidants and omega-3 fatty acids. Shoppers increasingly want animal foods with healthier fat profiles and protective nutrients. Feeding strategies must match each species' digestion, since ruminants and single stomach animals handle fats very differently.

Organic forms of selenium and zinc generally beat inorganic forms across the reviewed studies, Ali summarises, thanks largely to better absorption. Protected fats that survive the rumen intact enriched ruminant products best, though some unprotected sources partly worked too. Pigs and poultry need oils already rich in the long chain omega-3s EPA and DHA because they convert plant forms poorly. Selenium spares vitamin E by destroying fat peroxides, and vitamin C recycles vitamin E, so doses should be tuned together.
pmc-13602610:
Samuel Weber leads an eight-author team building in 2026 a standard scorecard for judging combat trauma care in simulations. Modern battlefields produce complex blast and crush injuries that Swiss teams, civilian or military, rarely meet in daily practice. Ahead of a planned multicenter simulation study, the team needed one fair tool to assess how teams manage such cases against civilian and military standards.

Fourteen experts from emergency medicine, military medicine, trauma surgery, and anesthesiology refined items through a nominal group session and five Delphi rounds. The finished tool holds 35 items spanning prioritization, procedural quality, core trauma principles, and time to critical actions. Early civilian-military disagreements, over neck immobilization, neurological checks, clotting, and fluids, were resolved inside the process. The framework robustly compares performance across care levels, the authors present, with disputes mapped honestly.
pmc-13609610:
Qing Wang leads an eight-author team simulating the electric arc inside a magnesium smelting furnace. Electrofusion furnaces melt magnesite with a direct-current arc between a top electrode and the furnace bottom, and short arcs behave differently from the long arcs most models describe. The team built a two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic model coupling electromagnetic, heat, and flow fields, validated against classic free-arc experiments.

The simulated arc squeezes into a tight column with its hottest, fastest region near the center. Because the short arc reaches the anode before its jet can spread, momentum lands concentrated on the pool surface, producing sharp pressure peaks. Raising current heated the arc, sped the jet, and strengthened pressure and shear on the pool. Lengthening the arc did the opposite, and arc length mattered more than current overall. The authors offer the results as guidance for furnace operation and energy use in magnesium production.
pmc-13612210:
Shuo Zhang leads an eight-author team pinning down a helper protein behind aphid insecticide resistance. The spirea aphid, Aphis spiraecola, damages orchards worldwide and has grown resistant to both neonicotinoid and pyrethroid sprays. Detox enzymes called P450s do the chemical work, but need electrons from one partner protein, NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase. The team cloned the aphid's version of that gene and measured where and when it switches on, across strains.

The gene ran highest in wingless adults, especially in blood and gut tissue, and both insecticides provoked it, raising expression about fivefold. Silencing it cut P450 activity by roughly 17 to 18 percent in resistant strains. Sensitivity snapped back accordingly: the lethal dose fell 57.6 percent for imidacloprid and 49.8 percent for lambda-cyhalothrin. The authors also produced the protein in vitro to confirm activity. This single reductase underwrites resistance to two insecticide families at once, making it an attractive target.
pmc-13612710:
Sang Hee Kim and colleagues present a 2026 South Korean study comparing nerve-related side effects of two groups of cancer immunotherapy drugs in people with lung cancer. One group blocks a protein called PD-1, and the other blocks its partner, PD-L1. Such side effects are uncommon, yet they can be serious, so knowing whether one drug group carries more risk helps doctors choose and monitor treatment.

Using nationwide health data and a design that mimics a clinical trial, the team matched 931 patients in each group. Nerve problems in the limbs were more common with PD-L1 drugs overall, at 19.2 percent against 14.1 percent. Timing differed too: early problems within 30 days were more common with PD-1 drugs, while the pattern shifted after three months.
pmc-13614310:
Lenin Kumar Verdhi and Nicolai Cramer report a cobalt-catalysed reaction that joins carbon and nitrogen onto allene molecules. The reaction keeps tight control over the product's handedness, a long-standing challenge in this corner of chemistry. Starting from a mixed, racemic set of allenyl esters, their chiral cobalt catalyst picks out one form and builds valuable chiral products called enamido esters. Yields reached 88 percent, with near-perfect handedness ratios above 99 to 1.

The reaction works by kinetic resolution, meaning the catalyst reacts faster with one mirror form and leaves the other behind in enriched purity. Tuning pushed that sorting power to a factor of 138. As a showpiece, the team resolved a natural compound that acts as the male bean weevil's pheromone, a scent chemical of farm interest. Chemists gain a selective route to building blocks that are hard to make cleanly by older means.
pmc-13614810:
Alok Kumar Sahoo and colleagues report a 2026 study of anxiety in Indian parents whose children were having planned surgery at a large hospital. Parental worry before a child's operation is common, yet it is rarely treated as part of care, even though it can affect how the whole episode goes. The study followed 216 parents and scored their anxiety at admission, just before surgery, and at discharge using two standard scales.

Clear anxiety before surgery showed in 56 percent of parents, and mothers scored higher than fathers, at 67.3 percent against 56.9 percent on one measure. Schooling, income, past surgery in the family, and the type of operation all played a part. Naming the parents at highest risk gives hospitals a way to offer calm, clear information where it is needed most.
pmc-13616610:
Anthony L. Carbone and colleagues present a case report of a 19-year-old man in high-intensity Air Force special warfare training. His vague back, thigh, and foot pain hid an extreme spread of bone stress injuries. Such overuse injuries are common in athletes and trainees, yet they usually strike one or two bones with pain matching the damage. Scans showed grade 3 and 4a stress injuries, near the top of the severity scale, across numerous bones in both legs.

The mismatch drives the report: widespread, severe bone injury with oddly mild, diffuse symptoms. The authors also weigh whether low physical activity during his teenage years left his bones under-built for the sudden training load. Trainers and military doctors are urged to image early when a trainee's pain is vague but stubborn, since stress injury can be silently extensive.
pmc-13617210:
Liya Hou and four colleagues survey animal models of aortic valve disease, a growing cause of death for which no drug treatment yet works in the clinic. The disease, covering valve calcification, narrowing, and malformation, makes up more than sixty percent of all valve heart disease. Because its mechanisms remain poorly understood, researchers rely on animal models to test ideas before human trials.

The review walks through the major model types, explaining how each is created, what valve damage it produces, and where it fits best in research. Every model is weighed for strengths and weaknesses, since none copies human disease perfectly. Tables and comparisons aim to help basic and preclinical researchers pick the right model for a given question. The authors hope better model choices will speed the search for drug targets.
pmc-13617610:
Ellen Oudkerk-Sodia and eight colleagues introduce nanolipogels, hybrid lipid and polymer nanoparticles designed to deliver messenger RNA into cells more cheaply and gently than current carriers. Existing carriers can need costly multi-step synthesis, vary between batches, or provoke immune reactions. The particles start from a synthetic phospholipid made in a single enzyme-catalyzed step, then polymerize in water in one pot.

Two partner chemicals give either a permanently charged or an acidity-responsive shell for loading the negatively charged RNA. The finished particles measure under two hundred nanometers, capture more than three quarters of their RNA cargo, and release it steadily over seven days in cell-like conditions. In human and mouse cell tests they kept cells alive as well as optimized liposome controls and far better than a common commercial reagent. One version produced about eleven times more reporter protein than the commercial reagent.
pmc-13618910:
Michelle Heck and five colleagues test whether human sign-trackers, people whose eyes lock onto reward-predicting cues rather than the reward's location, also show stronger bias toward alcohol. Animal work links sign-tracking to addiction vulnerability, and this Pavlovian framework is being translated to human eye-movement tasks. One hundred fifty-nine volunteers completed the cue task, an alcohol attention test, and questionnaires on drinking and personality.

Sign-trackers showed a tendency toward greater alcohol bias than intermediate responders, though not compared with goal-trackers. No differences in alcohol consumption appeared across the behavioral profiles, failing to replicate earlier reports. The authors blame a weak setup: fictitious token rewards and a passive task likely muted the effects. They call the support for the theory preliminary and small. They urge better paradigms with more engaging stimuli and real rewards before the framework's boundary conditions can be judged.
pmc-13620210:
Julieta Benítez-Malvido and seven colleagues studied how gut worms affect male and female spur-thighed tortoises differently across southern Spain. The team sampled tortoises in five land types, from Mediterranean shrubland to farm fields and pine plantations, and measured body traits, growth, and the roundworm communities living in each animal's hindgut.

Worm burden and spread looked similar in both sexes, yet the costs split sharply. Heavier infestation tracked with smaller size and slower growth only in males, while females kept growing steadily. Females also carried more diverse and evenly spread worm communities, arranged in networks that suggest easier transmission among them. Infestation fell in both sexes where unproductive land made up more of the landscape. The authors argue tortoise conservation should plan for the sexes separately, since females seem harder for worms to drag down.
pmc-13623010:
Tadahiko Ohtsuru leads a study comparing one injection against three injections of a freeze-dried platelet concentrate for knee osteoarthritis, the wear-and-tear joint disease that limits walking in older adults. The concentrate, made from the patient's own blood platelets, aims to ease pain without surgery. Earlier work tested single shots only, so the benefit of repeat dosing was unknown.

Patients chose their schedule with their doctors: 1,054 took one injection and 317 took three. Both groups reported pain and function on a standard knee survey over twelve months. The three-injection group edged ahead in the first month, and the edge lasted longer for early-stage disease but not for advanced disease. After adjusting for patient differences, the repeat group more often met the bar for a real clinical response at one year. Side effects per injection were similar, which the authors read as acceptable safety.
pmc-13623110:
Lele Chang and co-authors test a drug pairing for recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer that carries a PIK3CA mutation, a common gene change. The pairing combines immune checkpoint inhibitors, which release the immune system to attack tumours, with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which block growth signals. No standard approach targets this mutation group.

Data came from two prospective trials plus hospital records, covering fifty-five patients. Twenty-seven received the pairing and twenty-eight received doctor-chosen conventional treatment. Tumours shrank in most patients on the pairing, more often than on conventional care, and the time before cancer grew again more than doubled. Survival leaned the same way without reaching statistical ground. Side effects such as high blood pressure, rash, and thyroid problems were more common with the pairing but were managed, with no treatment-related deaths. The authors call the results a strong case for larger trials.
pmc-13623810:
Samir J Sheth and colleagues published a 2026 follow-up survey of long-term results after a sixty-day nerve stimulation treatment for chronic low back pain. Thin wires placed through the skin deliver stimulation to nerves in the lower back for two months, then come out. Earlier studies hinted the relief could outlast the treatment, and this survey tests that idea in everyday practice.

The survey reached 602 patients who had responded to the treatment, at times ranging from six months to over five years later. Four in five had needed no follow-up procedure such as nerve burning, a permanent implant, or surgery. Among those who avoided further procedures, most reported pain relief or clear gains in quality of life, movement, mood, or sleep. People hoping to dodge surgery or a permanent implant succeeded. The authors present the short treatment as a possible long-lasting, low-risk option.
pmc-13624310:
Jiaxin Li leads a study of how colorectal tumours recruit neutrophils and turn their web-like DNA traps into a spreading weapon. The white cells cast these traps, called NETs, to catch microbes, yet inside tumours the same webs help cancer cells spread. The team focused on a tumour protein, MIIP, known to restrain cancer growth.

In patient tissue, tumours low in MIIP carried neutrophil loads and traps, and patients showed more distant spread and fared worse. In dish experiments, fluid from low-MIIP cancer cells drew neutrophils and triggered trap release, and the traps made the cancer cells more mobile. Tracing the wiring, MIIP binds a signalling protein and damps a pathway that produces a neutrophil-summoning chemical. In a mouse model of liver spread, a trap-dissolving enzyme slowed metastasis, and restoring MIIP strengthened that effect. The authors propose the traps as a treatment target.
pmc-13625210:
Lucas Berger Munaro, Daniel J Tolhurst, and Jessica E Rutkoski show how a profit-based scorecard can steer wheat breeding in Illinois. Breeders often pick lines by yield alone, yet farmers earn from test weight and maturity too. The team priced each trait from the region's cropping system and grain price rules. They then fed a genomic model data on 2,995 wheat lines, five traits, and twelve test settings from 2022 to 2024.

The combined multi-trait model explained most inherited variation and predicted breeding values with high accuracy. Picking by the profit index returned about 120 dollars per hectare, beating both a single-trait model and yield-only picking, which returned under 100 dollars. Trait links also shifted with setting, a warning that one fixed recipe fits poorly.
pmc-13628910:
Guo Guo and two colleagues reviewed the evidence linking childhood adversity to disturbances of oxytocin, the hormone system tied to bonding and stress control, in people with severe mental illness. Their 2026 systematic review gathered fourteen studies with 5,624 participants, covering schizophrenia, major depression, and bipolar disorder.

Nearly every study found that patients carried heavier childhood adversity scores than healthy controls. In most studies that measured it, oxytocin levels ran lower in the patient groups. Variants of the oxytocin receptor gene also nudged risk in both directions, some raising susceptibility and others appearing protective. The authors read the pattern as support for oxytocin signalling as one biological bridge between early trauma and later severe illness.
pmc-13629810:
Kah Shuen Thong and ten colleagues audited the use of antibacterial drugs among COVID-19 patients in northern Malaysia. The audit covered ten government hospitals. Their study sampled 476 patients from over nineteen thousand hospital stays. The span ran from February 2020 to December 2021.

Just over a third of patients got these drugs. Most were ordered on suspicion, not on proven infection. Drugs against fungi were rare. Resistant germs appeared in under a tenth of cultured patients. Drug use rose and fell with surges in admissions. Severe disease drove the ordering. So did conditions like diabetes and chronic lung or kidney disease. The authors argue that pandemic ordering followed severity more than proof. They recommend stewardship ready for outbreaks, plus steady tracking of use.
pmc-13630810:
Rex Fernando and two colleagues present a protocol that lets a network of computers reach agreement. It works even when up to a third of the members are malicious. Each member sends remarkably little data. Such Byzantine agreement underpins blockchains and secure joint computation. The challenge is scaling it without exotic assumptions.

Earlier efficient designs leaned on strong, non-standard proof systems. The new protocol rests only on the Learning With Errors assumption. That is a standard, well-studied hardness base for post-quantum cryptography. It still needs a public key setup and a shared reference string. Its route runs through a generic use of batched argument systems. The authors frame the result as scalable agreement on conservative foundations.
pmc-13632810:
Anja I. Frei and seven colleagues published this 2026 study of aggression and violence against intensive care nurses in Basel. They reviewed nurses' reports from 2023 and 2024 at a large university hospital unit. Aggression meant hostile behavior or resistance without intent to harm. Violence covered verbal, physical, or sexual acts meant to threaten or harm. The team counted incidents and searched for signs that an incident would repeat.

Across more than two thousand shifts, three hundred eight incidents were reported, touching about one shift in seven. Three quarters involved violence, and patients caused nearly all of them. Repeat incidents happened in about one quarter of cases. Longer stays and a first incident built on aggression or verbal violence predicted repeats. Nurses were rarely hurt themselves, yet patients often suffered complications from sedation or restraints used in response. The study names early warning signs units can act on.
pmc-13642110:
Shuang Xu and three colleagues present a neural network method, IPGRU, for filling in missing values in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Dropout events hide many true gene readings, which biases later analysis and weakens conclusions about cell identity.

The method recasts the filling task as many single-gene predictions handled by parallel gated recurrent units, a network type that learns patterns across genes. Tests showed accurate recovery of missing values and cleaner data for cell clustering and for tracing how cells change type over time. The authors offer the approach as a sturdy preprocessing step for single-cell studies and precision medicine.
pmc-13643810:
Maria-Eleni Parakatselaki and four colleagues present a 2026 study showing that fathers' mitochondrial DNA leaking into offspring is genetically controlled in fruit flies. Mitochondrial DNA is normally inherited only from the mother, and leakage has been treated as random error.

Crossing several Drosophila simulans lines with a sister species, the team measured mixed mitochondrial types in hybrids. Leakage levels ran consistently within families, repeated across experiments, and ran higher in males than females. Estimated heritability was high, and wild-derived lines varied more than inbred stocks. The authors argue leakage is a governed trait with possible long-term effects on mitochondrial genome stability.
pmc-13645610:
Wei Yang and three colleagues build a risk model for thyroid nodules whose needle test results land in an uncertain middle class, Bethesda category III. Their records cover ninety-three patients treated at a Jiangsu hospital between July 2020 and June 2025, all of whom later had surgery. The model combines two antibody blood tests, an ultrasound grading system, and a gene mutation test. A chart called a nomogram turns the model into individual risk estimates.

Most nodules in this surgical group proved cancerous, which reflects the high-risk setting. The gene test alone was the strongest single predictor, yet the combined model scored clearly better than any one part. The authors say the combined approach can help doctors sort patients before surgery and choose who needs an operation most. They also note the model was checked only within the same patient group, so wider testing is still needed.
pmc-13645810:
Yalong Deng and twelve colleagues examine a membrane protein called CYBRD1 in the deadliest form of ovarian cancer, in a 2026 study. Spread of the disease and resistance to the drug cisplatin drive most deaths in high-grade serous ovarian cancer. Earlier work by the group had flagged this protein as a marker of poor outlook. Here they test what the protein actually does in cancer cells and mice.

Resistant cancer cells carried more of the protein than sensitive ones. Blocking it restored drug sensitivity and slowed growth, movement, and invasion. The protein switched on a growth pathway through a partner called JAK2, and one precise chemical tag on the protein proved essential for that link. In mice, pairing the blockade with cisplatin cut spread. The authors propose drug pairs aimed at this protein for patients whose cancers resist standard treatment.
pmc-13646110:
Li Wang and three colleagues report the survival of a woman poisoned by the weed killer paraquat while thirty-two weeks pregnant, a situation that usually ends in death. Paraquat has no specific antidote, and dose decides most outcomes. Her blood carried very high levels of estrogen-related hormone, which the team links with protection of her lungs, the organ paraquat harms worst. An emergency cesarean delivery was performed, and the baby also survived.

Lab testing found a trace of paraquat in the newborn's blood, firm proof that the poison crossed the placenta. That finding explains the baby's short-lived liver and kidney problems. Care also covered mouth ulcers and psychological support for the mother. The authors present the case as a call for paired mother-and-baby poison testing in future cases, and as a hint that pregnancy hormones may blunt this poison's worst effects.
pmc-13647310:
Mikhail V. Polynski and four colleagues shine visible light on a family of ring compounds to see how side groups steer their shape-shifting. These styryl pyrimidinones can flip between two forms under light, and the flipped forms of some members already show antifungal promise. The team watched the flips live with a light-equipped magnetic resonance setup. Computer calculations then explained why members behaved so differently.

Compounds carrying electron-donating side groups flipped most eagerly, reaching up to ninety-five percent conversion within a few hours under modest light. The flipped forms lasted from hours to days before relaxing back. A competing reaction that welds two molecules together also varied with the side groups. One computed measure of light absorption predicted performance best. The authors offer the scaffold as a tunable light switch for chemistry and drug design, with a cheap screening workflow attached.
pmc-13648310:
David Reissig and a large group for the IVDK network analyze in 2026 how often workers become allergic to parts of epoxy resin systems. These are the strong glues and coatings used in construction and manufacturing. They drew on patch test records from German dermatology departments spanning 2008 to 2022.

Allergy to the main resin ingredient fell over the period, from about four percent to under three percent of tested workers with job-related skin disease. Risk ran highest in plastics processors, bricklayers, and painters. Many resin-allergic patients also reacted to thinners and hardeners in the same products. Testing the main resin alone would have missed hundreds of sensitized workers. The authors urge fuller test panels and tighter workplace exposure control.
pmc-13649410:
Yaqian Li and three colleagues introduce a set of 11 studies on helpful microbes and the chemicals they make for plant health. Farms need to keep yields high while using less chemical fertiliser and spray. Helpful microbes can feed plants, fight germs, and ease stress, but their effects hinge on the crop, the local microbes, and the weather.

The studies span new microbe finds, how they attack plant germs, and how products are made and tested in fields. One predatory bacterium harmed a wilt fungus and shielded cotton seedlings. A newfound species stopped a sugarcane smut fungus from mating by making its surroundings acidic. The editors stress that names alone do not predict what a microbe will do.
pmc-13650010:
Guixiang He and six colleagues look for what travels with anxiety in people who have just been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and have not yet started medication. Anxiety is common early in the illness, yet its companions among the non-motor symptoms, the problems beyond movement, are poorly mapped in untreated patients.

The study compared 284 newly diagnosed patients with 147 healthy controls of similar age and sex. Anxiety was far more common in the patient group, and the mental-worry form dominated. After accounting for movement severity and background factors, stronger depressive symptoms went with more anxiety, while better sleep and a sharper sense of smell went with less. Movement problems themselves showed no clear link once other factors were counted. The authors suggest routine checks of mood, sleep, and smell at diagnosis to flag patients who may need support.
pmc-13650710:
Misa Iizawa and two colleagues, publishing in 2026, investigate a curious pattern in plasma medicine, where ionized gas is used on living cells. Treated cells first lose viability, then recover beyond expectations with longer waiting, and the team asked whether undamaged neighbors share in the effect through signals released into their shared liquid.

Liquid that had bathed plasma-treated mouse tumor cells was transferred onto untreated cells of the same types. The borrowed liquid significantly raised viability in the fresh cells, in a pattern resembling hormesis, where a mild stress provokes a strengthening response. Two different plasma sources produced the same behavior, which argues against a quirk of one device. The authors conclude that soluble factors shed by damaged cells drive a bystander effect that helps explain the rise-and-fall shape of plasma responses, a finding that matters for dosing plasma therapies.
pmc-13651610:
Yu-Cheng Liu and eight colleagues review tandem catalysts that turn carbon dioxide into multi-carbon products with renewable electricity. Copper is uniquely able to stitch carbon atoms together into fuels and chemicals, yet it wastes effort on hydrogen and spreads its output across many products. It fades at industrial current levels, largely because carbon monoxide coverage on its surface runs short.

A tandem layout stations a carbon monoxide factory next door: silver-copper interfaces, single-atom alloys, or isolated-atom sites on copper generate the monoxide and hand it to copper coupling sites. The review organizes recent work in flow cells and near-industrial conditions around four design levers. The levers are how much monoxide is made, how it travels, how the interface is structured, and which coupling paths it feeds. Done well, the division of labor sharpens selectivity toward the valuable two-carbon-and-beyond products.
pmc-1852410:
Gupta, Stamatoyannopoulos, Bailey, and co-authors explain Tomtom, a method for comparing DNA motifs. Motifs are short patterns in DNA that proteins recognise when switching genes on or off. New patterns are found often, but judging whether one matches a known pattern needs sound statistics.

Tomtom measures how similar two motifs are and tests whether that likeness could arise by chance. Users can search a database of known motifs with a newly found one as the query. Reliable matching helps researchers name the proteins likely to bind a site and plan follow-up tests.
pmc-2707010:
Liberati, Altman, Tetzlaff, and co-authors explain the PRISMA Statement for reporting systematic reviews. Systematic reviews and pooled analyses judge whether health care treatments work. Readers can only trust such reviews if the methods are reported fully and clearly.

This long companion paper explains each item of the updated PRISMA guidance and gives examples. It shows authors what to report about searching, selecting, and combining studies. Journals worldwide adopted PRISMA, so the explanation shaped how evidence summaries in medicine are written and checked to this day.  Checklists in the paper show authors exactly which details reviewers will seek.
pmc-2816710:
Larsen, Vogensen, van den Berg, and co-authors compare gut microbes in adults with type 2 diabetes and adults without it. Recent evidence had suggested a link between metabolic disease and the bacterial populations living in the gut. Whether diabetic gut communities truly differ was still an open question.

The team assessed the make-up of intestinal microbes in both groups as controls against each other. Finding real differences would support the idea that gut bacteria play a role in diabetes, not merely reflect diet or drugs. The study helped launch wide interest in microbe-based diabetes care.
pmc-2946910:
Huynh-Thu, Irrthum, Wehenkel, and co-authors test tree-based methods for inferring gene regulatory networks from expression data. Rebuilding the wiring diagram of which genes control which others is a pressing open problem in systems biology. Gene expression measurements from microarrays offer clues, but the network itself stays hidden.

The authors assess their approach within a community benchmarking effort for reverse engineering networks. Tree-based methods treat each gene's activity as something to predict from other genes. Knowing which methods recover real networks best guides the search for drug targets and disease mechanisms.
pmc-3965110:
Finn, Bateman, Clements, and their co-authors described Pfam in 2014, a database of protein families. A protein family is a set of proteins that share a common part and often a common job. Pfam is served from sites in the United Kingdom and the United States and is used worldwide.

Release twenty-seven held close to fifteen thousand entries, each checked by hand by an expert. Users can search a new protein sequence and learn which known families it belongs to. That match gives a strong first clue to what the protein does, which guides lab work on genes, disease, and drug targets.
pmc-4402510:
Ritchie, Phipson, Wu, and their co-authors described limma for RNA sequencing in 2015. Limma is an R and Bioconductor package that gives an integrated way to analyze gene expression data. It handles complex study designs and borrows information across genes to cope with small sample sizes.

The paper shows how limma's methods, first built for microarrays, were extended to RNA-seq counts. Borrowing strength across genes steadies results when only a few samples exist. That is the common case in costly patient studies. Limma became a core tool for finding genes that differ between healthy and diseased tissue or before and after treatment.
pmc-4614810:
Eren, Esen, Quince, and their team presented Anvi'o in 2015, a platform for omics data. High-throughput sequencing and related technologies were transforming studies of natural microbial communities. Full study of microbial lifestyles needs ways to organize and view genetic information interactively.

Anvi'o lets users explore genomes and metagenomes together with their own added data layers. Researchers can inspect, compare, and share analyses through a visual interface. That interactivity helps teams form and test ideas while looking at the data, not after. The platform supports work on how microbes live, interact, and drive processes in oceans, soils, and hosts.
pmc-5715110:
Peter Bankhead and colleagues introduced QuPath, open source software for digital pathology, in 2017. Pathologists now scan whole slides into large digital images, but viewing and measuring them by hand is slow. A free, flexible tool was missing for research use.

QuPath lets users view whole slides, mark regions, and train the software to find tumor areas. It can measure large numbers of cells in a batch and export the results for statistics. Because the code is open, labs can adapt it and share methods. The tool helped make digital slide analysis routine in cancer research.
pmc-6004510:
Godfred Boateng, Torsten Neilands, Edward Frongillo, and colleagues wrote best practices for building survey scales in 2018. Health and social research depends on scales that measure attitudes, symptoms, and behaviors. Building a sound scale takes many steps that are easy to do badly.

The primer walks through item writing, expert review, pilot testing, and checks for structure and reliability. It explains common traps, such as too few items or samples that are too narrow. Each stage has clear advice a small team can follow. New researchers can use it to produce measures that others can trust and reuse.
pmc-8012210:
Jeffrey Granja and co-authors introduced ArchR in 2021, a software package for studying how accessible the DNA is inside single cells. Methods that profile chromatin accessibility one cell at a time can map the regulatory landscape of a tissue in fine detail. The data grew faster than the tools, leaving researchers with huge datasets and slow ways to read them.

ArchR was built to handle that scale, pulling biological meaning out of accessibility data quickly and in an integrated workflow. The authors describe how the package aligns cells, finds marker regions, and links them to genes. For labs working with single-cell regulatory data, it turned an unwieldy analysis into a manageable routine.
podcast-joerogan-ZkJjqGLoK10:
Director Neill Blomkamp talks about eternal recurrence in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Blomkamp, who made District 9, is known for gritty science fiction with real-world teeth. Here the subject is an old idea: that time loops, and all things return exactly as they were.

He and Rogan test the notion against his films, his life, and the strange pull of patterns that repeat. Rogan asks whether living as if life recurs would change how a person acts. The segment is the filmmaker's most philosophical hour on the show, a break from craft talk into the deep structure of time itself.
podmore-newer-spiritualism-1910:
Frank Podmore took his keen tools to fresh marvels in The Newer Spiritualism, his book of 1910. New stars of the dark room then drew crowds with forms that took shape and things that moved at no touch. Podmore sat, watched, and checked each claim as he had for years. His finds are grave for the faith's fans.

Trick ropes, hid hands, and stage craft fill his case. He grants the odd scrap, yet finds the new wave weak. The book is the best bust of its age. It ends his long watch with a sigh.
pound-provenca-1910:
Provença, published in Boston in 1910, is Pound's early collection of translations and originals drawn from the troubadours of medieval Provence. Before Pound was a modernist leader, he was a scholar of these twelfth-century love poets, and this book shows why.

He renders Arnaut Daniel, Bertran de Born, and others into English verse that strains to keep their music and difficulty. Original poems in the same manner stand beside the translations. Pound believed modern poetry had to pass through this medieval discipline. The book is the record of that apprenticeship, and of a young poet finding his masters.
price-cost-indexes-from-1875-to-1989-est:
Michael S. Hart, the founder of Project Gutenberg, wrote this essay on price and cost indexes running from 1875 toward 2010. First published as a column called the Rate of Change of the Rate of Change in the Electronic Journal of Virtual Culture and expanded for release in November 1993. His opening paradox sets the argument: computers look like an incredible bargain. They are twice the bargain they seem, because the dollars themselves keep shrinking.

Hart works the arithmetic of his own drives, where each year's gear is cheaper and faster than the last. His tables of indexes turn anecdote into series, an early attempt to measure deflation in information goods. The essay is also a Gutenberg manifesto in disguise: if computing power halves in price while doubling in worth, free digital libraries become inevitable.
prize-money-sailor-s-knots-part-10:
W. W. Jacobs placed a comic tale from his Sailors' Knots of 1909 in the tap-room of the Cauliflower inn at Claybury, where an old man holds court by the fire. Snow lies on the fields, horses steam outside, and talk turns to how Claybury men amuse themselves.

The old man rails against Bob Pretty, whom he calls the biggest rascal and poacher in the village, and hints at a story about a prize hamper. Jacobs builds the tale from pub talk, sly tricks, and village rivalry. Readers get his well-known blend of dry humour and seaside character.
promptuarium-alchemiae-das-ist-vornehmer: A German title page, worn and hard to read in the scan, announces a storehouse of writings on the stone of the wise. The book gathers choice pieces by learned philosophers, with skilled alchemist hand-work and tested ways of making medicines. Its sources come from animals, plants, minerals, and metals, offered as needful to alchemists and doctors alike. The page carries a grant of privilege and names its publisher, the front door of an old German work on hidden arts.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
Charivaria fronts Punch for March 10, 1920, in volume 158, gathering short comic notes on Ireland, Poland, boxing, and dentistry. The London weekly kept its peacetime readers supplied with a joke for nearly every headline.

London is said to hold one hundred thousand more people than New York, though they are only just living. A warning that the Home Rule Bill would cause friction in Ireland is met with sorrow at the very thought. Poland's finance minister asks for a loan of three thousand million francs, Dempsey faces a draft-dodging charge, and gold in the mouth is declared out of date.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: A publisher's header alone introduces the tenth volume of The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte in the pages shown. Title, author, and language are its whole news: the work is Constant's, and the text is English. No preface explains this part, no contents page maps it, and no opening line of narrative is printed. What Constant recounts in volume ten, and at what point of Napoleon's life it begins, are facts that these opening pages do not supply.
ricardo-high-price-bullion-1810:
David Ricardo made his name with The High Price of Bullion, a pamphlet of 1810. Britain's Bank Restriction had freed the Bank of England from paying gold for notes. Bullion prices rose, and Ricardo blamed paper money issued in excess. His tract applies the quantity theory of money to the case.

Too many notes, he argues, cheapen each one against gold and goods. The cure was a return to cash payments under strict rule. The pamphlet's clarity won him a hearing among statesmen and thinkers. It set the terms of the great bullion debate. Economists still cite it as a model pamphlet. Ricardo the theorist enters history here.
rilke-malte-laurids-brigge-1910:
Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge, Rilke's only novel, appeared in German in 1910. The text here is the German original; the first English translation came in 1930 and is not in the public domain. Malte, a young Danish nobleman without money, lives in a cheap Paris room and writes what he sees.

Fear walks with him through hospitals, crowds, and streets full of the poor. Memories of his childhood home in Denmark break into the Paris notes without warning. Rilke breaks the tale into fragments, more diary than plot. The book became the first great German novel of modern city consciousness. Its dread and pity still feel new.
robinson-town-down-the-river-1910:
Edwin Arlington Robinson published The Town Down the River in 1910, returning to the Tilbury Town portraits that had made his reputation. By then Robinson had won powerful admirers, including President Theodore Roosevelt, who found him a government job. This volume is the essential middle collection of his career.

New townsfolk join the gallery: failures, dreamers, and quiet sufferers rendered in exact, ironic verse. Robinson also includes poems on larger themes, among them a notable piece on the painter George Crabbe. His sympathy never turns soft, and his endings often twist the knife gently. Readers who want Robinson beyond the famous anthology pieces should start with this book and its haunted New England streets.
rolland-jean-christophe-cannan-vol1-1910:
Romain Rolland began his long novel Jean-Christophe in 1904, telling the life of a German composer. Gilbert Cannan translated the work into English, and volume one appeared in 1910. It holds the first four books: Dawn, Morning, Youth, and Revolt.

Young Jean-Christophe Krafft grows up in a small town on the Rhine, poor and gifted. Music becomes his refuge from a drunken father and a narrow world. He fights the stale taste of his elders and starts to find his own voice. Rolland wrote the cycle as a hymn to art, freedom, and the kinship of peoples. The full work later helped earn him the Nobel Prize in literature.
russell-philosophical-essays-1910:
Philosophical Essays, published in 1910, collects Russell's early papers from the decade when analytic philosophy was being invented. The subjects are truth, knowledge, and ethics, treated with the new logical tools he was forging with Whitehead.

The volume includes his essay on the elements of ethics and his engagements with pragmatism, whose theory of truth he resisted. Russell's prose here is already the famous instrument: lucid, cool, and quietly devastating. These papers bridge his Leibniz book and the Principia then in press. For readers of Russell, this is the workshop where the mature voice was made.
russell-principia-mathematica-vol-1-1910:
Principia Mathematica, published in three volumes between 1910 and 1913, was Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell's attempt to derive all of mathematics from logic. This first volume lays the foundations: propositional logic, classes, and relations.

Working in a dense forest of symbols, the authors build number and proof from a handful of primitive ideas. One famous proof, that one plus one equals two, arrives hundreds of pages in, with a note that the proposition is occasionally useful. The labor took a decade and changed both fields. Logicism, the program it founded, shaped a century of thought.
sbe-50-index-1910:
M. Winternitz made the General Index that ends the Sacred Books of the East. Book Fifty came out in 1910 and caps the whole vast set. The set ran to fifty books of texts from the faiths of Asia. Muller, its first head, had died ten years past.

The index lists names and themes from all the books in one A to Z run. A reader can trace a god, a rite, or a rule through the whole set at once. Short heads tell which faith and which book each text sits in. The book is the key that makes the great set of use.
scheible-das-kloster-vol10:
Band ten of Das Kloster, cells thirty-seven through forty, appeared in 1848 from Johann Scheible's Stuttgart house. Ten bands of complete reprints had made Scheible the keeper of Germany's folk print past. His rule never changed: print the whole text, however odd, however feared.

So the grimoires come entire, Faust books and Höllenzwänge among them, with nothing struck out. Folk charms hold their place beside works of high ritual, and chapbooks fill the gaps between. For the student of German magic, such fullness is the point. A cut text hides what its makers believed; Scheible's pages hide nothing, and band ten keeps that faith.
seligman-melanesians-of-british-new-guin:
Charles Gabriel Seligman led the Cambridge expedition's work in The Melanesians of British New Guinea, published in 1910. The volume reports on the Papuan coast: sorcery, secret societies, and mortuary ritual among the peoples studied. A chapter by F. R. Barton adds his own years of local knowledge to the team's findings.

Seligman's party worked village by village, recording custom before deep change reached the coast. Masks, feasts of merit, and the handling of the dead pass in careful detail. The book stands as a standard early ethnography of Papua, exact and humane in equal measure.
shahnama-warner-vol-5-1910:
Volume 5 of the Warner brothers' Shahnama of Firdausi appeared in 1910, midway through their nine-volume English version. Firdausi spent decades on the Book of Kings, Persia's national epic. The Warners matched his patience with a translation project that ran from 1905 into the 1920s.

Kings rise and fall in this volume as the epic moves from legend toward firmer history. Battles, embassies, and family feuds fill the verse, along with wise counsel from viziers and elders. The translators added notes to guide readers through names and customs. The middle volume holds the epic's long arc together, linking the heroes of myth to the shahs of record.
shaker-testimony-christs-second-appearin:
The Shakers set out their whole faith in the Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing, first printed in 1808 and reissued in 1810. The United Society of Believers speaks here as one voice. Mother Ann Lee, their foundress, is presented as the vessel of Christ's second appearing, the hinge of their system.

Celibacy, shared goods, and confession of sin flow from that claim, and the book argues each from scripture. It is systematic, dense, and meant to answer critics who saw only dancing and strangeness. As the charter theology of American Shakerism, it remains the movement's fullest statement of itself.
spr-proceedings-vol23-1909-1910:
Volume twenty three binds parts fifty eight and fifty nine, for 1909 and 1910. The Society for Psychical Research carries its record into the years before the Great War. Thought transference trials appear with new statistical checks. The census tradition still governs how spontaneous cases are gathered.

Trance sittings with Piper and her successors in the files fill long sections. Investigators try proxy sitters and other guards against hidden knowledge. Apparition reports continue, each tied to named witnesses. Volume twenty three sustains the primary archive of the evidential debate. Its tone is sober where its subject is strange. That contrast defines the whole Proceedings run.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5010:
George Washington gives eight yearly addresses, from January 8, 1790, to December 7, 1796, parted by three stars. The first opens with glad thanks for the bright state of public affairs. North Carolina has lately joined the Constitution, the country's credit and good name rise, and concord, peace, and plenty bless the land, all happy signs for the nation's future.

Washington tells Congress that the work of the last session pleased their voters as well as the newness and weight of the task let them hope. More will be asked in this grave session, and cool, firm wisdom must do it. Among the objects before them, he singles out the common defense as fit for special care. To be ready for war, he holds, is one of the surest ways to keep peace, and a free folk should be both armed and trained.
striking-hard-deep-waters-part-10:
Striking Hard belongs to Deep Waters, a set of comic tales by W. W. Jacobs about sailors and waterside folk. Mr. Porter comes home and tells his wife, busy at her ironing, that the men have struck at last, after standing more than flesh and blood could bear.

Mrs. Porter is not impressed. She recalls the last strike, when everything they had saved for a rainy day went bit by bit, and asks what they will live on now. Her husband trusts the committee and its speakers; she suggests he practice singing in the street. Jacobs draws the humor from the gap between dockyard pride and kitchen sense.
suso-eternal-wisdom-1910:
A Little Book of Eternal Wisdom, by Blessed Henry Suso, was printed at London by Burns, Oates and Washbourne, publishers to the Holy See, with the church's approvals dated 14 April 1910. Walter Hilton's Parable of the Pilgrim is added at the back.

A foreword opens with the names Jesus and Mary, models of true manhood and true womanhood in the writer's mind. Suso, a fourteenth-century German Dominican mystic, cast the book as a dialogue between Eternal Wisdom and the servant who longs to follow Christ. Its short chapters teach suffering, detachment, and love of God in plain, tender speech, and it stayed a favorite of Catholic devotion for centuries.
suso-life-by-himself-1910:
The Life of Blessed Henry Suso by Himself was translated from the original German. Thomas Francis Knox, a priest of the Oratory, made the version. Burns, Lambert, and Oates printed it at London in 1865. Suso, a German Dominican of the fourteenth century, wrote the life as the record of his own road to holiness.

Knox's preface tells how Suso was born at Ueberlingen, near Constance. He was of noble stock on both sides. He took his mother's maiden name out of devotion to her holiness. He set his father's surname aside. His baptismal name was Henry; the preface adds that God later changed it to Amandus, or Beloved, a secret found among his papers after death. The life mixes outward events with visions and hard penances.
the-alchemy-of-happiness-by-al-ghazzali-: Al Ghazzali wrote The Alchemy of Happiness, here rendered from the Hindustani by Claud Field for the Wisdom of the East set, shaped by L. Cranmer-Byng and S. A. Kapadia and printed in London by John Murray in 1910. A motto from Abu'l Feda heads the title page: knowledge of a part is better than ignorance of the whole.
the-alchemy-of-thought-1910: L. P. Jacks, dean of Manchester College, Oxford, and editor of The Hibbert Journal, wrote The Alchemy of Thought, printed in London by Williams and Norgate of Henrietta Street in 1910. The front pages carry long praise for his Mad Shepherds and other human studies from The Times, Country Life, the Westminster Gazette, and The Daily News.
the-book-of-the-thousand-nights-and-a-ni: The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 9, is set down here under Richard F. Burton's name. Only the Project Gutenberg head pages are shown, with no page of the tales. They give the title, Burton's name, a release date of September 2002, and an edition note. They also say the file was scanned by J. C. Byers and proofread by Doris Ringbloom. The head pages warn readers that rights law shifts from land to land and urge them to check the law at home first.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-10:
Volume 10 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XIII inside the governor's house. The Vekeel treats the house as his own. All he finds there stirs his greed and his interest alike. His first aim is a document that might back his moves against Orion, and the seizure of Orion's estates, in the eyes of the rulers at Medina.

The more gold the Vekeel can soon send the new sovereign, the surer his favor. He goes room to room with a child's greed, testing pillows, smelling scents, and peering into scrolls he can't read. In the dead woman's trunks he finds costly jewels and gold coins. He sticks her finest diamond ring on his own gem-covered finger. His interpreter, who reads Greek, must render each document found, and at the last a basket of discarded tablets by the writing-table catches his eye.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-10:
Part X of The Caxtons turns on the mystery of Francis Vivian, as Pisistratus tells it. The narrator is the family's son, writing his own life as he goes. His scholar father and a shrewd uncle weigh the clues with him.

The uncle's guess about the parentage of Francis Vivian strikes the narrator as a true discovery. On that view, the willful boy made a bold love match no father would approve. Thwarted and stung, he threw himself on the world. The narrator likes this account because it clears Vivian of mean or criminal acts, leaving him rash and at fault, but not base.
the-complete-works-of-brann-the-iconocla: William Cowper Brann's Iconoclast writings reach volume 10 in this Gutenberg text of June 1996, etext 568. A header defect is worth noting: its inner line still calls the book volume 1. The header also says the full set runs to twelve volumes. Beyond that header nothing is present, so Brann's essays in this volume cannot be described.
the-complete-works-of-james-whitcomb-ril: Volume 10 of the complete works of James Whitcomb Riley was issued as a Project Gutenberg text in October 1996, etext number 692, as the second item in that series. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, with its standard notes on copyright, donations, and advance release dates.The book itself never opens here.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book X of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume X of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. The strength that a momentary effort gave Rousseau to quit the Hermitage left him the moment he was out of it.

Scarcely settled in his new habitation, he suffered often from retentions, joined by a new complaint, a rupture he had long felt without knowing what it was. The physician Thieiry, his old friend, came to see him and made him acquainted with his situation. The sight of all the apparatus of the infirmities of years taught him a hard lesson: when the body is no longer young, the heart cannot be young with impunity. The fine season did not restore him, and he passed the whole year 1758 in that state.
the-daisy-chain-or-aspirations-pg3610:
Charlotte Yonge's preface to The Daisy Chain, or Aspirations, dated February 22, 1856, calls the book an overgrown work of a mixed class.
